- Social media users are spreading a TikTok video of a woman in Cook County, Illinois, who claimed that she received a notice that said, "People are not typically voting for this person," when she attempted to choose a Republican judicial candidate.
- While posts suggest that what allegedly happened to the woman must be a widespread issue, there's no evidence that any other voter has shared a similar experience. Furthermore, there are no Republican judicial candidates on the 2026 Cook County ballot.
- Election officials in the area from both parties refuted her claims, and the Cook County Clerk's Office said that they have received no other complaints or reports about this supposed issue, despite people already casting 54,000 early voting ballots in the jurisdiction.
- In a follow-up video, the woman said she would take down the original clip to avoid spreading misinformation and acknowledged that there are no judicial candidates in Cook County. She also said she was not trying to mislead anyone and maintained that she saw a notification that said the candidate she chose was unpopular.
- Based on the information available, it seems likely that the woman simply misread an "undervote" notification that tells voters when they have not made all available selections. Snopes reached out to the woman and awaits a response.
As early voters flocked to the polls ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, a rumor spread online about alleged voter interference in Cook County, Illinois.
Social media users spread a TikTok video of a woman from Cook County, Illinois, who claimed that when she attempted to vote for a Republican judicial candidate, the voter machine shared a pop-up notice that said, "People are not typically choosing this person!"
The claim circulated on Facebook, X and YouTube. The voting machine at the center of the claim came from Dominion Voting Systems, which U.S. President Donald Trump has previously and falsely targeted for allegedly deleting votes from his supporters. (The company was later sold to a former Republican official.)
However, there are no Republican judicial candidates on the ballot in Cook County — a heavily Democratic area — this year. Both Democratic and Republican officials told Snopes that the claims in the TikTok were inaccurate.
Given that there is no evidence of widespread voter interference in Cook County aligning with the woman's claims, we have rated this claim false, with the caveat that it is still unclear what, exactly, the TikTok user experienced at the voting booth. It seems likely that she simply misread a notification about not choosing the full available slate of candidates. We reached out to her for more information using an email attached to her TikTok account and await a response. 
The woman also later uploaded a far less popular video (archived) under her TikTok handle, @bauerbabe21, that said "she wasn't trying to be deceitful," but she was going to take down the clip so she would not continue to "spread misinformation." In that video, she acknowledges that she was wrong about the judicial candidates but maintains that she received the notification while voting for other candidates.
It is worth noting that a former Republican election official, Scott Leiendecker, acquired Dominion Voting Systems in 2025 and rebranded it to "Liberty Vote." A spokesperson for Liberty Vote directed us in an email to the Cook County Clerk's statement about this video, which called it "false and misleading."
Officials from both parties address claims
Cook County's clerk, Monica Gordon — a Democrat — explained in a Facebook post what may have happened in this particular instance (emphasis ours):
The facts: Voting equipment does not tell voters which candidates are more popular, nor does it discourage voters from selecting any particular candidate.
The equipment may display a notification if a voter leaves a contest blank or does not make all available selections (an undervote).
This standard ballot-review feature gives voters an opportunity to review their ballot and confirm that it reflects their intentions before casting it.
The choice is always yours. Voters are free to select the candidates of their choice or leave any individual contest blank.
The Cook County Clerk's Office takes election integrity seriously. Claims that voting equipment attempts to influence voters are false and misleading.
Frank Herrera, a spokesperson for Cook County Clerk's Office, echoed Gordon's statement in an email to Snopes.
"This is the only report of this type that has been brought to the Clerk's Office attention in a jurisdiction with nearly 1.8 million registered voters," Herrera said. "With more than 54,000 Early Voting ballots already cast, the Clerk's Office has received no similar reports. The absence of any similar reports further undermines this false claim."
In the original video, the woman identifies herself as a resident of Streamwood, a township in Cook County. Here's what Aris Garcia, Streamwood village clerk and a Republican, said in an emailed statement to Snopes that was also posted on Facebook (emphasis ours): 
I am aware of the claims circulating regarding an alleged message displayed on a voting machine in Streamwood.
We have attempted to recreate the reported message and were unable to reproduce the experience described. It is also important to clarify that there are no Republican judicial candidates on the ballot in Cook County for the November 3, 2026 election. Therefore, the claim that she selected a Republican judicial candidate is inconsistent with the ballot.
The integrity of our elections is fundamental, and it is important that concerns regarding election procedures are taken seriously.
I encourage anyone who experiences an issue while voting to report it immediately to an election judge or the Cook County Clerk's Election Division.
TikTok user claims she misspoke
The woman's follow-up video includes an email from an unnamed "gentleman who works for Streamwood Township" who theorized that she received a notification while attempting to vote for three Republicans for Metropolitan Water Reclamation District Commissioners — a position which manages wastewater treatment and flood control for Cook County.
The man also noted, as officials above stated, that the system displays "undervote" notifications if a voter leaves a contest blank or does not make all available selections. (We asked both Garcia — who is named in the email — and the woman to clarify the identity of the man who sent the email and await a response.)
The woman said that she now believes she received the notification in question when attempting to vote for the commissioner positions, but disagreed that the notification was about an "undervote" issue.
"I feel guilty that I said the wrong thing," she said in the video (see 3:42). "Even though I know I was wrong, I know for a fact that message still appeared...my kids were moving around, there was an election judge trying to talk to my kids, I was super haywire. I read it though, and it said, 'fewer people' or 'less people' voted for this candidate."
However, in her original video, she says the error message went away after she selected all three Republicans — indicating that it's likely she simply received an undervote notification and misread it in the chaotic environment that she described (see 1:15).
Cook County's election machine testing process
Claims about "rigged" voting machines often fail to consider the detailed standards and processes that officials, from the local to federal level, use to prepare for U.S. elections.
In Illinois, all equipment is "tested and approved by both an independent voting system testing laboratory (VSTL) and by the State Board of Elections' team of election specialists." The state also requires public tests of equipment at least five days ahead of Election Day, which are open to "representatives of the political parties, the press, representatives of the State Board and the public."
In Cook County, those tests are happening on Oct. 27 for the general election.
For more on voting machine conspiracy theories, see our story debunking claims that voting machines are deliberately switching votes from one candidate to another.

Approach African GP with humility, says Hamilton
- Published
Lewis Hamilton has addressed concerns on human rights grounds about holding an African Grand Prix in Rwanda by saying people should "approach it with humility".
Formula 1 has signed a 10-year deal with the central-east African country starting in the early 2030s.
Briton Hamilton, who has campaigned for a race in Africa for many years, said: "I don't get to choose where we go. Naturally, there are problems all over the world today, so I've seen many of the stories. But I think we really have to approach it with humility.
"There's a lot that we don't know. Growing up in England, they never taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism and the West intervening."
Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.

And the DRC's Minister for Foreign Affairs Therese Kayikwamba Wagner said in a statement last week that "giving (Rwanda President) Paul Kagame this platform would help polish the image of an authoritarian leader whose government has helped fuel a devastating war in our country".
She pointed out that the US had sanctioned the Rwandan army and four senior officers for their role in destabilising the region, conducting military operations inside the DRC and supporting, training and fighting alongside the M23 rebel group.
She added that F1 "should require credible, independent guarantees that no money used to host the race comes from conflict-linked minerals or the exploitation of Congolese resources".
Hamilton, who will be 42 in January and has a contract until 2027, has suggested he could prolong his career in order to race in Rwanda.
"I'm now forced to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa, and that's been my dream, to be able to race in Africa," Hamilton said.

"Africa is a place that deserves to have a grand prix. It's about more than just one country. It's about the continent itself, and there are so many beautiful countries within it.
"The people are so lovely. The culture is so rich, and I think it's important that we get to show that to the world. We get to do that with our sport. We get to go to all these different countries, and people see some of these countries they didn't really know too much about.
"All of a sudden, it becomes something that's on the screen, and kids are talking about it. They go to school talking about it. So, I'm really, really hopeful for that grand prix."
However, the Ferrari driver added: "Going there doesn't mean that you neglect the things that are happening there.
"So hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more about what is happening there and what has happened there for hundreds of years. I hope that does spark the conversation.
"And then I guess I'll finish it off with this: I think we need to make sure we're pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there's a lot of peace that I'm hoping we get to at some stage."

Low price for an OLED. Deep and rich blacks. Easy setup and install. Great refresh rate for video games. The skintone test was better than average.
TIRED
Did not perform as well as a Micro RGB for brightness and contrast.
It’s amazing what can happen in just one year. The LG B6 is the cheapest LG OLED model around (priced lower than the LG C6 and LG G6), but it also has some stiff competition. New art televisions like the Amazon Ember Artline (which costs under $1,000) use a matte display that renders masterpiece paintings in convincingly realistic glory. RGB televisions like the LG Micro RGB Evo and those from Samsung and Hisense have also burst onto the market, making a convincing argument for choosing an RGB screen over an OLED one.
Last year around this time, we reviewed the LG B5 and ranked it a solid 8/10, but there was less competition. The LG B6 is still a good budget OLED TV, it’s just beset on all sides by better, brighter options, including from LG’s own LG C6.
Sleek Angles, Less Sleek Remote
Photograph: John Brandon
The first thing that struck me while setting up the LG B6 is that it’s incredibly thin—just 1.8 inches at the base and about a quarter-inch at the top and around most of the bezel. The OLED panel doesn’t need any backlighting like most LED or RGB televisions, so it can be extra thin. The lower portion of the TV is thicker because of the four HDMI ports (all of which support a 120-Hz refresh rate), an optical audio out, two USB 2.0 ports, and one LAN port. The TV only supports Wi-Fi 5, certainly not the latest standard.
The B6 comes with two legs that are easy to install (two screws each), though I generally prefer a single pedestal stand design. The 65-inch model I tested fit comfortably on two 38-inch IKEA SPIKSMED TV benches set side by side that measure 76 inches long.
Like all LG TVs, setup involves LG’s own WebOS interface or ThinQ app, not built-in Google TV or Fire TV. It was easy to complete the setup using the LG ThinQ app on my iPhone—in minutes, I was loading my usual assortment of apps like Prime Video, Disney+ and Apple TV+.
The B6 is packed with features too. A few of my favorites include a gaming mode that helps improve low latency gaming, AI picture enhancements that actually work and make a discernible difference, an artwork mode called LG Gallery+ that costs $5 per month, and an LG music app in case you don’t like Spotify or other music apps. It also has settings for audio dialogue sync, similar to what you can do with powered speakers like the Klipsch The Fives II. A desktop mode means you can mirror your laptop screen and even run a Gmail app.
Photograph: John Brandon
I have mixed feelings about WebOS, though. My main gripe is that you cannot disable the pointer on the LG remote, and it jumps around a lot. When you press the center dial on the remote, it turns off temporarily as though LG user interface designers are admitting it isn’t that great. I also have mixed feelings about the remote—it’s hard to use in the dark by feel. The Home button is offset so it’s hard to find, and shortcuts for Netflix and other apps are situated at the bottom, but not backlit.
OLED Strengths, OLED Weaknesses
Based on the pricing, it’s obvious LG has positioned the B6 as the entry-level OLED in their line-up. That became crystal clear once I started testing movies and TV shows.
In the official specs, LG only lists “wide color gamut” and not a percentage for the specific BT.2020 spec, nor a specific brightness rating. This is where the benchmark testing comes in handy, and what I tested right away.
One win for the B6 is blacks and grays, which have great texture and clarity, a surprise given how many midrange televisions make dark, shadowy scenes look washed out. Scenes from Awake and The Creator, very dark movies, were clear and detailed, after tweaking a few picture quality settings (namely changing to Vivid mode).
Photograph: John Brandon
Photograph: John Brandon
Contrast and brightness are more of a mixed bag. I watched House of the Dragon and Game of Thrones (yes, the infamously dark season eight, episode three) to stress test these specs, and the B6 struggled. On better TVs (and home theater projectors), you can see trees in the background of a scene where a character emerges on a frozen lake. On the B6, they are completely black—e.g., a contrast problem.
Color saturation and luminance could be better too, especially compared to RGB TVs I’ve tested recently. The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, with its various blooming effects, wasn’t exactly terrible looking, but certainly not as crisp as on something like the LG Micro RGB Evo. (The less technicolor The End of Oak Street fared better.) During a demo reel benchmark, green grass by a fence in winter looked a bit too brown for my taste (again, color saturation issue), but skin tone variation was surprisingly good.
LG is not the first brand I think of for playing video games (it’s Sony), but the B6 deserves some extra credit here. The 120-Hz refresh rate screen does its job, and made all my movements playing Crimson Desert on PC crisp and responsive. Resident Evil: Requiem looked almost photo realistic, with gleaming statues and surprisingly good color quality, even zooming in on crumpled leaves.
Watching sports and news didn’t yield any surprises—a Baltimore Orioles baseball game looked rich and textured, but not very bright.
Affordable, But Outclassed
LG B6 may be an entry-level OLED, but, like an entry-level BMW, it has a lot of the bells and whistles of a flagship, with plenty of ports, features, and premium finishes. My main issue with it is brightness and contrast, both could be better. And LG’s WebOS is still not my favorite interface in the world.
The main issue might actually be price. At the time of writing, the LG B6 is on sale for $1,300. The superior midrange LG C6 is also on sale for $1,500. That’s only $200 more for a much better, brighter TV (both 65-inches). That’s not even discussing buying an older (but still brighter) model like the LG C5 (which I found on sale for less than the B6). It all depends on how much you want to spend.

Vikings are last unbeaten team as Chiefs lose - NFL week seven
- Published
Week seven of the NFL left one unbeaten team standing and few - if any - would have picked them out at the start of the season.
The Kansas City Chiefs were beaten at defending champions the Seattle Seahawks while the San Francisco 49ers also suffered their first loss.
But the Minnesota Vikings marched on to maintain their 100% record, and there were also big wins for the Cleveland Browns and Denver Broncos.
Here are the biggest stories from Sunday's games in the NFL.
Seahawks show championship pedigree
Kansas City and Seattle have not only won three of the past four Super Bowls, they came into week seven with this season's best offence and best defence respectively, in terms of total yards.
Sunday's primetime match also marked the return of Kenneth Walker, the Most Valuable Player in last season's Super Bowl, to former team Seattle after joining the Chiefs in the off-season.
The running back has made a stunning start with Kansas City, leading the NFL in rushing yards per game (133) after six weeks, but Seattle's defence was determined to show why they became known as 'the Dark Side' during last season's championship run.
They stifled Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs, restricting Walker to 36 yards from 14 carries as KC tied for their fewest points in a game with Mahomes as their starting quarterback.
Seattle quarterback Sam Darnold also continued to lean on Jaxon Smith-Njigba, with last season's offensive player of the year claiming 150 receiving yards and a touchdown, while new running back Emanuel Wilson finished with 100 rushing yards and a score.
The Seahawks ran out 20-3 winners to improve their record to 4-3, while the Chiefs are now 5-1.
Purdy blots copybook
Brock Purdy went to the top of the all-time list for career passer rating last week but did not hit his normal high standards as the San Francisco quarterback was frustrated by the Atlanta Falcons.
The hosts forced four turnovers, including two Purdy interceptions, as they won 29-20 to inflict a first loss on the new Super Bowl favourites.
The 49ers are 6-1 while NFC West rivals the Los Angeles Rams - the pre-season favourites - got back to winning ways.
The Rams are 3-4 after winning 35-21 at the Las Vegas Raiders, where Matt Stafford became the first player to lead two teams for touchdown passes.
Last season's MVP previously set the franchise record for the Detroit Lions before joining the Rams in 2021.
They next face the Los Angeles Chargers, who are the last remaining winless team after the Miami Dolphins won 28-25 at the New York Jets.
Vikings stretch surprise run
For the first time in the NFL, two divisions will go into week eight with all four teams having a record better than 50%.
One of those is the NFC North, topped by the Minnesota Vikings. Before the season, half the NFL was considered to have a better chance of winning the Super Bowl.
But they are the last undefeated team at 6-0 after coming from behind to win 16-10 at home to the Indianapolis Colts.
Their defence has been one of the league's best, Will Reichard is yet to miss a kick and - although their offence is yet to catch fire - the Vikings keep grinding out victories.
Including the end of last season, Kevin O'Connell's team are on an 11-game win streak, but they face a test at divisional rivals Detroit next week.
After naming new signing Kyler Murray as their starting quarterback, the Vikings traded JJ McCarthy four weeks ago and he impressed on his first start for the New York Giants on Sunday, leading them to a 27-21 win in overtime at the Houston Texans.
Elsewhere in the NFC North, Jessie Bates kicked a field goal as time expired to hand the Detroit Lions a 20-17 win over the Green Bay Packers.
Only three field-goal attempts have been missed from inside 35 yards all season and Green Bay rookie Trey Smack missed two of them on Sunday.
Watson keeps Browns on top
All AFC North teams also have at least four wins, with the Pittsburgh Steelers kicking off Sunday's action by beating the New Orleans Saints 16-10 in the NFL's first game in France.
The Cleveland Browns (5-2) then regained top spot after Andre Szmyt made his third game-winning kick in four weeks to claim a 27-24 win at the Tennessee Titans.
Deshaun Watson was booed by Cleveland fans in pre-season but has now led five game-winning drives this season and is beginning to look like the player he was at Houston, which convinced the Browns to sign him on a fully-guaranteed deal in 2022 worth $230m (£172m).
Their other divisional rivals went head-to-head. The Baltimore Ravens had to manage without quarterback Lamar Jackson for a third straight game and led the Cincinnati Bengals 13-0 at half-time.
But the Bengals stormed back to win 35-13, with Joe Burrow throwing for four touchdowns and 292 yards as the Ravens suffered a second straight loss.
Baltimore have not set a return date for two-time MVP Jackson (ankle) and have a tough trip to the Buffalo Bills next week.

Broncos back near their best
The Denver Broncos earned the top seed in the AFC Conference last season but, although they beat Buffalo in the divisional round, the win was overshadowed by a late injury to Bo Nix.
A broken ankle meant the Broncos had to do without their starting quarterback the following week as the New England Patriots denied them a spot in the Super Bowl.

Very often, a viral news story about animals is a comedy to its audience and an unmitigated tragedy to its subjects. That was the case this past weekend, as footage of bands of juvenile cows dashing through the streets of Kansas City stampeded across the internet.
A truck full of cows crashed in Kansas City. It reveals a bigger everyday horror.
Our relentless appetite for meat puts animals through grueling journeys.
The details are as follows: Last weekend, in the middle of the night, a semitruck carrying close to 120 young cattle plunged off a highway interchange in Kansas City’s downtown, spilling out dozens of animals. The truck driver and one other person sustained minor injuries. Dozens of the cows were killed, many others were seriously injured, and still others went running into the city. Some of them traveled for several miles, the city’s fire chief told the Associated Press. The animals were chased around the streets by first responders and self-described “cowboys” (one of them appearing to carry an electric cord as a lasso); authorities said all were rounded up by the end of the day.
To many people, freak accidents like these understandably look a little funny, even fantastical. “We take free roam BBQ very seriously,” one Reddit comment, with more than 400 upvotes as of this writing, said. “Much as I lament the tragic loss of bovine life, these videos have brought such joy to our fair city,” another commenter wrote.
The clips undoubtedly have a certain charm. If only the animals were as carefree as they appeared in those brief moments — and if only they could truly escape the fate that humans had in store for them. But as my colleague Kenny Torrella has written, the strange animal stories that periodically capture the public’s imagination almost invariably circulate stripped of the darker reality from which they emerge — humanity’s dominion over nonhuman animals. In this case, the cattle crash illuminates one of the most overlooked cruelties of modern animal agriculture: the nightmare of livestock transportation.
When you imagine the lives of animals raised for food, you might think of a factory farm (in a large majority of cases, very cruel) or a slaughterhouse (likewise, and not just for animals raised primarily for meat — dairy cows and egg-laying hens are slaughtered, too). But the animals need to be transported from the farm to the slaughterhouse, and also between numerous different facilities — breeding farms, hatcheries, feedlots, auctions — over the course of their lives as they progress through different stages of the livestock supply chain. Most cattle raised for beef and dairy are transported multiple times in their lifetimes; between four and six journeys is common. A recent US Department of Agriculture report found that half of cattle shipped to feedlots traveled for more than 250 miles, and 22 percent traveled more than 500 miles.
Kansas City, along with Chicago, St. Louis, and Omaha, Nebraska, was once a major national hub of livestock transportation, with cattle arriving by the trainload at its busy stockyards (earning the city its nickname, “cowtown”). But the rail-based livestock trade that made it famous has largely vanished, replaced by a sprawling system of truck transit that carry animals between farms, feedlots, and slaughterhouses across the country. These form the connective tissue that makes it possible for the American livestock industry to raise and slaughter nearly 10 billion land animals every year.
You’ve probably seen livestock trucks on the interstate, with their long, aluminum bodies and oval ventilation holes. They appear unremarkable enough from the outside. But the most important thing to understand about farm animal transportation is that these creatures are not handled like passengers, the way you or I would be treated on a long-distance trip. Rather, they are freight, loaded into metal trailers, often packed tightly together for long, very uncomfortable, sometimes dangerous stretches of highway travel. Picture yourself hurtling down the interstate in a box at 70 miles an hour, struggling to balance for many hours, without a seat, a seat belt, heating or cooling, or any of the other protections designed to keep human passengers safe and comfortable. As the hours pass, urine and manure accumulate beneath the animals’ feet, which can cause them to slip.
The trips “can span many hours and thousands of miles, potentially exposing livestock to overcrowding, extreme temperatures, limited ventilation, and lack of access to water or food, among other things,” according to a damning report on farm animal transportation released over the summer by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO). “If not managed properly, these conditions can lead to injury, illness, or death.”
Even the process by which animals are herded onto the trucks is often highly stressful, with frightened animals pushed, prodded, pulled, and otherwise handled roughly. I have reviewed, over the years, more videos than I can count of stressed farmworkers treating cows and pigs in ways that appear appalling to people not steeped in animal agriculture, simply because they’re desperate to meet the demands of their jobs and get the animals to move.
According to a 2022 investigation by The Guardian, more than 20 million animals every year “are dead on arrival, or soon after,” when they reach a slaughterhouse. Most of those are chickens, the species that makes up the overwhelming majority of land animals raised for food; about 166,000 of them, per The Guardian, were cattle.
Catastrophic crashes like what happened in Kansas City are far rarer than the more routine, mundane cruelties of livestock transportation, but they do happen regularly. On a cursory search, I was able to find 20 others that have occurred in the US so far this year. Aaron Caster, who owns the towing company that handled the recovery operation in the crash, told me that almost all of the animals were female, and estimated they were around 6 months old, not yet fully grown. They’d been shipped from Virginia, he said, and had been on their way to Nebraska.
Caster’s account of the scene of the crash is harrowing. “The cab was ripped off the truck, the trailer was on its side with the entire trailer blown apart,” he told me. “Just cows everywhere. Some alive, some were dead.” Some had “really busted legs, ripped up pretty good,” and were euthanized. Caster, who is also a rancher, said he took more than 50 surviving cows to his property in Bates City, Missouri, to recover. Two of those have since died, he told me earlier this week, including one who had been “cut up pretty bad” in the crash and was euthanized after developing an infection.
In the US, there’s one major law designed to protect the well-being of livestock animals in transit: The Twenty-Eight-Hour Law of 1873, which says that livestock in transit traveling across state lines can’t be confined for more than 28 hours without being unloaded for rest, food, and water.
That rule excludes poultry birds entirely, meaning that the vast majority of animals raised for food aren’t covered — a major oversight. But even for those species that nominally benefit from it, the law is very rarely enforced. Farmed animal advocacy groups have documented and complained about that for years, and the GAO this summer similarly reported that enforcement is extremely limited. The report paints a picture of the federal system for protecting farm animals in transit as woefully inadequate and largely toothless, dating back to the era when livestock traveled primarily by rail.
The report identified six factors that contribute to cruel conditions for animals on the road, including not just the length of the trip but also temperature extremes, unsafe and unsanitary vehicles, rough handling, and being transported when they’re too sick, injured, or vulnerable (like animals who are extremely young or heavily pregnant). Federal law fails to cover most of those dangers while offering almost no meaningful enforcement of the 28-hour duration rule that is in place.
Between 2013 and 2025, the USDA investigated just 23 suspected violations of the law, resulting in no fines and only four warning letters — and in 2022, the GAO report notes, the USDA stopped issuing even those. The GAO contrasts the US system with more modernized protections in Canada, Mexico, Australia, and the European Union, which include requirements around animals’ fitness for travel, adequate space, humane handling, and vehicle safety.
Some of the most heartbreaking livestock transportation conditions that I’ve personally covered have been in the dairy industry, where it’s common to ship fragile newborn calves, just separated from their mothers, across long distances. It’s also routine to ship dairy cows on long journeys to slaughter once they’re no longer profitable. On these trips, they’re often exhausted, pregnant, and in poor physical condition: A 2022 industry audit found that roughly one in three had impaired mobility when they arrived at the slaughterhouse.
A modern and comprehensive system overseeing farm animal transportation might prevent some cases like these, which are among the most wretched miseries found in our food system. It wouldn’t stop every horror that unfolds inside a livestock truck, nor could it eliminate the most visible disasters, like the crash in Kansas City; for that, we’d need to more fundamentally alter our relationship with animals and our prodigious appetite for meat.

Quick Answer
Apple’s HomeView is a $299 smart home hub with a 7-inch touchscreen, A18 chip, AI-powered Siri, and personalized experiences for up to six users. Available in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, it offers smart home controls, FaceTime, and voice and face recognition, but has limitations with apps, games, and video.
It was pretty much THE product in the spotlight at Apple’s recent Welcome Home event. The HomeView marked Apple’s debut in the smart home hub segment. Of course, it does what every smart hub is supposed to do – let you control different smart devices in the house – but hey, this is an Apple product, so some distinct, different (and odd) touches have been added to the regular mix. As we wait for the HomeView to arrive in India at $299/Rs 39,900 on November 13, here are fourteen things worth noting about Apple’s most high-profile entry into the smart home segment:
Table of Contents
Totally buttonless with clean, smooth sides
Yep, Apple has finally delivered a touchscreen device with zero physical buttons. Only it is not an iPhone, as many had been predicting. The HomeView has only a single Type-C port (for power requirements) and no physical buttons or switches at all. Even the Type-C port is on the back of the wall-mounted version and in the spherical base of the regular version, so the sides of the HomeView are totally plain. Minimalism unlocked!
Comes in regular (iMac G4) and wall-mounted versions…and they both cost the same!
The HomeView is fundamentally a 7-inch touchscreen tablet that gives one access to different smart devices in the house, as well as does some very cool things (more on that later). It comes in two models: the regular version, which comes attached to a spherical, dome-like base and flexible “arm”, making it look like a small iMac G4 (the Sunflower Mac, remember?) and is meant to be used on a table, and there is a “Wall Mounted” version, which is just a tablet that can be mounted on a wall. Both need a power outlet as they have no battery of their own. Rather remarkably, both versions come at the same price: USD 299 (Rs 39,900). This is kind of odd because they both have rather different components and requirements, as we shall see.
Want more for your bucks? Get the regular HomeView; the Wall Mounted one has a few things missing (and fewer colors)
They might have the same price tag, but the regular HomeView is much more value for money than the Wall Mounted one. The HomeView comes with two full-range drivers, a down-firing woofer, and also has dual force-canceling radiators for spatial audio and better bass. The Wall Mounted variant, on the other hand, is more of a tablet. It has only the two full-range drivers, and no woofer or radiator. What’s more, the wall mount for it costs extra – USD 59.95 or USD 79.95 depending on the option you choose from Schneider Home (more options are expected to come shortly). The regular variant also comes with a 1.5 meter Type-C cable and a 30W power adapter, which the Wall Mounted variant lacks (the mounts give these options).
As if this were not enough, you even get more color options in the regular HomeView – it comes in Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Grey, while the Wall Mounted variant has just Silver and Space Grey! If money is (relatively) tight, the regular HomeView is a no-brainer. You get additional speakers, more color options, a charging cable, and a Mac-ish design for the same price! Those speakers and that Mac-ish design at the same price as the Wall Mounted option would do it for us. The presence of that base does add to the weight of the regular HomeView – it is 952 grams as compared to the 286 grams of the Wall Mounted one.
As bright as an iPad (with also the lowest nit count on an Apple product)
The HomeView is basically a 7-inch touchscreen tablet. It comes with a Liquid Retina True Tone LCD display which is totally square in shape, with a resolution of 1088 x 1088 and a pixel density of 220 ppi. Interestingly, while its other specs are inferior to those of the iPad and iPad Air range, the HomeView comes with the same level of brightness – 500 nits. This means that the HomeView will have the same exceptional brightness that the iPad and iPad Air offer. 500 nits is also the brightness level of the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air. Interestingly, the HomeView also comes with the lowest brightness of any Apple product ever – a stunning 0.3 nits.
There’s an iPhone 16/ MacBook Neo family chip inside it
The HomeView is powered by the A18 processor, which is similar to that seen on the iPhone 16, 16 Plus and 16e. In purely tablet terms, this makes the HomeView more powerful than the base iPad (11th generation), which runs on the A16 Bionic. Interestingly, even the MacBook Neo launched earlier this year was powered by a similar processor, the A18 Pro.
Runs on…anonymous (as of now) OS
Although it says that “Apple HomeView is powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI,” Apple has not yet released the name of the operating system on which HomeView runs. It is a blend of iOS and iPadOS, and is believed to have been codenamed HomeOS. What it will be finally called is anyone’s guess.
You cannot install apps on it
Rather surprisingly, given Apple’s stress on apps, the HomeView has no app store of its own at the time of writing. It comes with a number of preinstalled apps (on Built-In Apps, as Apple calls them), but there seems to be no provision for installing apps on it. The HomeView can, however, run some apps from the iPhone – Audiobooks, Classical Music, and Apple TV. Rather interestingly, there is no visible support for any maps app yet.
It can identify faces and voices too (but seemingly does not have Face ID)
The HomeView comes with face identification through a single camera, and Apple says that it also recognizes voices, and comes with special “Secure Exclaves” that process camera and microphone feeds in a secure zone where they cannot be accessed by other software on the device or even by Apple. Interestingly, there is no mention of Face ID in the tech specs of the HomeView, so we are assuming that the feature is not available on the HomeView and the face identification system on the device is a different one.
Can handle up to six users…but guests are allowed
A single HomeView can have up to six different users who can use all its features and functions. The device takes information from iPhones or iPads, such as contacts and calendar, from the iPhone or iPad of the user to customize experiences for them. However, every user’s information will be kept private and not shared with others. There can be guest users too, but they will be able to access only a limited number of functions, such as controlling smart home accessories, checking the weather, setting timers, and playing music.
The camera is only for calling, as of now – no photography!
The HomeView comes with a 12-megapixel camera with an f/2,4 aperture, but from what we can see so far, its function is limited to identifying the user and making FaceTime calls. It comes with Center Stage that keeps you in the center of the frame during FaceTime calls, but as of now, it cannot record video or take pictures.
And it can switch seamlessly and speedily between users
Perhaps the most spectacular feature of the HomeView is the fact that it literally transforms itself depending on who is in front of it. It works with the iPhone or iPad of each user and shows them the content when they use the device. Every user has their own customizations and information, which the others cannot see, and the HomeView literally presents each user with their own version every time they appear in front of it and are identified – and judging by what we have seen in the demos, it does so almost instantly, while maintaining the privacy of the previous user. That A18 chip and that 12-megapixel front-facing camera are incredibly fast!
A tab that does not do too many videos…yet
In spite of being relatively large in size, the HomeView does not come with a dedicated app for videos – as per the Apple website, it does not even come with Apple TV preinstalled. While HomeView does not have a dedicated Apple TV app preinstalled, Apple confirms support for Apple TV content and compatible third-party video apps. However, the range of supported services and how they work on HomeView remain worth checking.
No fun and games either…yet
Rather remarkably for a device that is designed to be used by the family, the HomeView does not come with any games at the time of writing. We are so hoping that changes and Apple adds some fun, turn-based, multiplayer games to the tablet. Imagine being able to play Ludo, Scrabble, Chess, or Monopoly on this!

Ballon d'Or 2026: Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal in race for men's award - stats and pundits' opinions
Harry Kane, Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe battling for 2026 men's Ballon d'Or on Monday; Kane odds-on favourite to become first Englishman to win the award in 25 years; Lamine Yamal, 19, aiming to become youngest-ever Ballon d'Or winner; Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher backing Kane to win
Monday 26 October 2026 07:24, UK
Harry Kane is the odds-on favourite to win the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or, which could be one of the tightest results in recent history.
England captain and Bayern Munich striker Kane is the bookmakers' favourite to become the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001.
Victory would see Kane become just the fifth English winner of the Ballon d'Or after Sir Stanley Matthews, Sir Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen, while he would also become the first Bayern player to claim it in 45 years.

When asked after Bayern's Champions League draw against Arsenal last Wednesday about winning the Ballon d'Or, Kane told Sky Sports News: "It'd be incredible if I do. It'd be special for sure. I'd love to win it, but we will have to wait and see. A big night, but I'm not getting carried away."
Kane's caution comes due to stiff competition from LaLiga duo Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.
Spain World Cup winner and Barcelona forward Lamine Yamal, who is 14 years Kane's junior at the age of 19, is aiming to become the youngest-ever Ballon d'Or winner - an award he has been campaigning for.
"Being completely honest, it's not just this year I've been at a Ballon d'Or [winning] level, but longer," he told The Guardian in September, having also appeared to dismiss Kane's credentials earlier that month in a Spanish interview.
Lamine Yamal had been the bookmakers' closest challenger to Kane for the award, but a late surge in the betting means Real Madrid striker and France captain Kylian Mbappe is now second-favourite behind Kane.
A first-time winner looks set to win the award on Monday night, with Kane eyeing a poetic victory in London, where the ceremony is being held to pay tribute to inaugural winner Matthews.
Here, Sky Sports assesses Kane, Lamine Yamal and Mbappe's stats, and hears the pundits' views on who should win the 70th edition of the Ballon d'Or…
The honours…
It is important to note that players are judged for their performances over the entirety of last season from August 3, 2025 until July 19, 2026.
Looking at that period domestically, Kane helped Bayern to lift the Bundesliga and the German Cup, while Lamine Yamal won LaLiga but missed out on the Copa del Rey as both players won their respective Super Cups.
But Mbappe failed to win a trophy with either Real Madrid or France last season.
In Europe, Kane went further than Lamine Yamal and Mbappe as Bayern reached the Champions League semi-finals after a thrilling 6-5 last-four aggregate defeat to eventual winners Paris Saint-Germain.
Lamine Yamal's Barcelona and Mbappe's Real Madrid both exited the tournament in the quarter-finals.
But Lamine Yamal enjoyed the ultimate success with his country as he helped Spain earn World Cup glory in the summer, while Kane and England won the bronze medal after beating Mbappe's France in the third-place play-off.
The stats…
The goal statistics are what make Kane the favourite for the award.
He hit an astonishing 73 goals for club and country last season, while Mbappe fired in 58 and Lamine Yamal scored 25 goals.
Kane's goal-laden campaign led to the ex-Tottenham striker picking up the Golden Shoe, the award for Europe's leading goal scorer, for a second time after he claimed it in 2023/24 in his debut Bayern season.
Kane hit 61 goals for Bayern across all competitions last season, 19 more than any other player in Europe's big-five leagues. In fact, it was the most by a player in a season since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014/15.
Kane also scored 12 goals for England, with his six goals in the Three Lions' 2026 World Cup semi-final run seeing him become England's all-time leading World Cup scorer.
But Mbappe scored more goals than Kane at the World Cup and in last season's Champions League.
The ex-PSG forward won this year's World Cup Golden Boot with 10 goals - the most by a player in a single edition since Gerd Muller scored 10 in 1970 for West Germany.
The 27-year-old is now the all-time scorer in World Cup history with 22 goals.
At club level last season, Mbappe was the top goal scorer in LaLiga (25 goals) and in the Champions League, despite Real's last-eight exit, as he scored 15 goals - one more than Kane.
It was a quiet World Cup for Lamine Yamal, scoring only once in Spain's run to glory as team-mates Rodri and Pau Cubarsi picked up the player of the tournament and young player award, respectively.
Lamine Yamal, however, came into his first World Cup off the back of a hamstring injury which had initially led to doubts whether he would even play in the tournament.
Lamine Yamal picked up the injury in mid-April while playing for Barcelona, and he missed the remainder of the season before making his return as a substitute in Spain's goalless draw in their World Cup opener against Cape Verde on June 15, with his first start coming six days later as he scored Spain's first in their win over Saudi Arabia.
Despite his disrupted preparation for the tournament, he made the most dribbles both at the World Cup (58) and across Europe's top-five leagues (265) during the 2025/26 season.
Where Lamine Yamal is superior to Kane and Mbappe is in the assist column.
The winger provided 20 assists for club and country last season, while Mbappe had 13 and Kane had just eight.
It takes Lamine Yamal's goal involvements to 45, but that figure is not close to Kane's 81 and Mbappe's 71.
The pundits have their say...
Jamie Carragher: "Kane should win the Ballon d'Or and the reason is because he's scored 73 goals in a season and only Lionel Messi has scored more in a season.
"He also won the double with Bayern Munich and was part of an England team that got to the World Cup semi-finals."
Paul Merson: "It's such a hard one because Kane's scored a million goals and has been phenomenal, but Lamine Yamal's been phenomenal too and he's won the World Cup.
"But I'm hoping Kane because Lamine Yamal's going to win it three to five times in years to come, so I'd like Kane to win - and it's in London, which ticks another box.
"So I'd just go with Kane, but I wouldn't be shocked if it wasn't him."
Tim Sherwood: "Kane should win the Ballon d'Or - and I'm not being biased. I think he's had an unbelievable season with the amount of goals he's scored for Bayern Munich.
"There's a lot of pressure playing for big club like Bayern, but he never feels the pressure and he continues to score for England. If he doesn't win it now, then he never will."
Sue Smith: "Kane has got to win the Ballon d'Or. He's been absolutely brilliant. His goals, his movement, the way he drops into the No.10, the ability he's got and he's been outstandingly consistency."
Michael Dawson: "I believe it should be Kane. I'm probably slightly biased as I was lucky to play with him. The goals and everything he's given in the last year, he has to be the winner but Lamine Yamal is the guy he has to beat."
Clinton Morrison: "Kane should win because he's had a fantastic season at Bayern Munich and he leads England by example. Lamine Yamal and Michael Olise could dominate for years to come, but Kane thoroughly deserves it this year."
A third year in a row for a first-time winner?
Should Kane, Mbappe or Lamine Yamal be crowned the Ballon d'Or winner, it will be a third year running a new name has been awarded the gong after years of Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo dominance.

Seven out of 10 people in Japan would prefer to shelter at home after a major disaster if their homes are considered to be safe, according to a recent survey by market research firm Macromill.
The survey also showed that only about 15% of respondents had a detailed understanding of the preparations needed to shelter at home, with regional differences in levels of understanding evident.
The survey, conducted annually since 2024, was carried out online from Sept. 4 to 15, with valid responses obtained from 200,000 people across Japan.
Asked how they would seek shelter if their homes were not at risk of collapse or flooding following a disaster, 72.5% said they would prefer to remain at home. This was far higher than the 11.9% who said they would go to a designated evacuation center even if their homes were safe.
Another 4.8% said they would stay with relatives or acquaintances or at a hotel, while 1.8% said they would shelter in their cars.
Central and local governments recommend sheltering at home if homes are safe to ease overcrowding at evacuation centers and reduce stress among evacuees.
To shelter at home, adequate supplies of food, water and portable toilets, as well as alternative means of securing essential utilities, are indispensable.
Only 14.7% of respondents said they had a detailed understanding of the necessary preparations, while 50.1% said they had heard about the preparations and 35.2% said they knew nothing about them.
Prefectures affected by major disasters in the past had higher proportions of respondents who said they had a detailed understanding of the necessary preparations. Kumamoto Prefecture ranked highest at 26.5%, followed by Miyagi and Fukushima prefectures at 23.3% and 20.0%, respectively.
Wakayama had the lowest share among the country’s 47 prefectures, at 8.9%, followed by Tokushima Prefecture at 9.0%, and Okinawa Prefecture at 9.3%.
“People’s understanding of the specific preparations needed remains insufficient,” a Macromill official said. “Practical public awareness campaigns are needed.”

Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
- Published
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.
Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since the return to civilian rule in 1985 to win an election after losing the first round of voting.
Lula told celebratory crowds this election is a "loss for negativity, lies", later adding "long live democracy".
Flávio Bolsonaro, who is the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled, which experts say is unlikely.
In an unprecedented move, polls were also extended for two hours on Sunday evening after both candidates made requests for different reasons.
Lula's team had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Senator Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as the reason for their request.
The decision - issued by the Supreme Court just as polling stations were due to close - meant that some had already shut and were not able to re-open.
Supreme Court President Kassio Nunes Marques - appointed by the older Bolsonaro - confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voting extension did not cause issues for the count or the electoral process.
Lula secured 51.79% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.21% - a difference of 4.4 million votes between the two candidates.
The result came as a surprise after Bolsonaro - who has the backing of his father - won the first round of voting on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%.
But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one.
Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the first and second rounds of a presidential election since 1989.
As disconsolate Bolsonaro supporters left the house in Brasília where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in São Paulo to celebrate and address his supporters.
"This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country", the former metal worker said. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people."
Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin told him: "You, for the second time, have saved Brazilian democracy."

  - Published2 hours ago
Bolsonaro, who had been poised to give a victory speech, said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable" and "impossible".
But electoral law experts have told BBC Brasil that the chances of the results being annulled are remote.
Fernando Neisser from the Institute of Lawyers of São Paulo (Iasp) said it would be "difficult from a legal standpoint" given that the margin of victory was relatively large, and would depend on the "narrative" his lawyers put forward.
Expert Alberto Rollo said that dates for presidential elections in Brazil are fixed and determined by the constitution, which would add another complication to getting it annulled.
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.
His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.
But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.
Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" - which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".
Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.
Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.
While Trump has yet to react, other world leaders have been congratulating Lula on his win.
Ecuador President Daniel Noboa Azin said the region had "common enemies, shared challenges, and much to gain when we work together."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory", saying "the comeback of global progressivism has just begun". French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world".
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world".

Singer Chris Brown to be sentenced over bottle attack at a London nightclub
Grammy-winning singer Chris Brown is to be sentenced Monday over brawling at a London nightclub in 2003
LONDON -- Grammy-winning singer Chris Brown is to be sentenced Monday over brawling at a London nightclub three years ago.
Brown, 37, pleaded guilty to a count of affray at London’s Southwark Crown Court in July for attacking a music producer with a bottle on the head.
Brown had denied attacking Abraham Diaw with a bottle at the Tape nightclub in the swanky Mayfair neighborhood in February 2023. But prosecutors said the fight was caught on surveillance camera in front of a club full of people.
In return for the guilty plea, prosecutors dropped charges of assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm and having an offensive weapon, a bottle.
Brown's friend and vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu also pleaded guilty to affray. He will be sentenced too.
Brown left the United Kingdom after the brawl but was arrested in May 2025 at a Manchester hotel after flying to the city for a concert.
Brown had been free on bail of 5 million pounds ($6.7 million), which allowed him to tour Europe and North America last summer. He was freed on bail again Friday and will be sentenced Oct. 26 on the affray charge, which carries a maximum sentence of three years in prison.
Brown, who rose to stardom as a teen in 2005, won his first Grammy for best R&B album in 2011 for “F.A.M.E.” He earned his second in the same category for “11:11 (Deluxe)” in 2025.

Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement.
Photos and video of the 22 October meeting show a group of bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.
Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity".
Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the administration's immigration policies. But Trump has typically enjoyed the support of Catholic voters.
In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons".
"In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said.
"I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added.
A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media.
Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump.
Grob said images of the meeting later caused concern among some of his congregants.
"I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he wrote.
"I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family have been harmed by the president's policies," he added.
Grob said none of the participants in the meeting gave permission for the public distribution or posting of video or photos of the event.
When contacted for comment by the BBC, the White House did not directly address questions regarding the meeting or subsequent comments by the two bishops.
"There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it," White House Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
According to Pew Research Center, which analyses religion in the US, opinions of Trump's performance have slipped among all major religious groups. In a survey this month, 30% of all US Catholics said they approved of his job performance, compared to 47% when he returned to the White House in 2025.

The Best Folding Phones Now Includes Apple's iPhone Duo
Featured in this article
You may be scoffing as you read this. The best folding phones? Really? Aren’t those just gimmicks? I'm here to tell you they're pretty darn useful. And yes, there are quite a few now (even Apple is in on the action), so you have options. Folding phones are an evolution of the traditional single-screen slab of glass we've all been using for nearly two decades.
They largely come in two forms: a folding flip phone or a folding book-like phone, enabling you to either relive the glory days of small phones or expand your multitasking options while on the go. A folding phone is a personal decision—arguably even more than a traditional smartphone, since it hinges (heh) on what style you prefer. We have tested almost all of them, and these are our favorites.
Check out our other mobile buying guides, including the Best Android Phones, Best iPhones, Best Cheap Phones, Best Samsung Phones, Best Google Pixel Phones, Best Motorola Phones, Best Phones With a Headphone Jack, and Best Phones You Can't Buy in the US.
Updated October 2026: We've added the Apple iPhone Duo, more on the Z Flip8 after testing, and updated prices.
Other Folding Phones to Consider
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra for $2,100: The Z Fold8 Ultra is a refined release with a 6.5-inch cover display that opens to an expansive 8-inch screen that feels like two 6.5-inch displays side by side. It's fast and smooth, with a 5,000-mAh battery, but it's the camera that earns it the “Ultra” title. It's an impressive combo, including a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and a 10-megapixel telephoto lens that supports 3X optical zoom. Sadly, it lacks Qi2 support for magnetic wireless charging, and the camera module makes it rock when lying flat on a surface. But the main reason it misses out on a place above is that the smaller Fold8 is so much easier to handle.
Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 for $1,200: If you want something compact, the Galaxy Z Flip8 is the lightest and thinnest flip phone in the world with a redesigned chassis, and it comes a close second to Motorola's Razr Ultra. It has a 4.1-inch cover screen, and it flips open to become a 6.9-inch candy bar. It's also more durable than ever and boasts the same excellent chipset and performance as Samsung's larger Fold models. The 4,300-mAh battery is solid, but the camera system is relatively basic, comprising a 50-megapixel main shooter backed by a 12-megapixel ultrawide.
Motorola Razr Fold for $1,900: The first book-style foldable from Motorola is good, but not great. The front screen feels very much like a normal phone, and you can open it to enjoy the vast 8.1-inch display inside. Sadly, the Razr Fold lacks the top-end processor of the year, which is disappointing at this price. The highlight is the massive 6,000-mAh battery, which can stretch to nearly three days of use. Thankfully, it does come with seven years of software updates (unlike Motorola's Flip family). Motorola has also added a telephoto lens to the capable, triple 50-MP camera. But, overall, we prefer Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold.
Motorola Razr+ 2026 for $1,100: The awkward middle child in the Razr lineup lacks the bells and whistles or top-notch specs of the Ultra, but still costs more than $1,000. You can get very close to the same experience from the cheaper Razr and save hundreds. Even battery life is unimpressive, because it has the smallest capacity of the Razr family. The cover glass isn’t the ceramic glass mixture as on the Razr Ultra. I found out the hard way after dropping the phone once, roughly a 4-foot drop onto asphalt, and the front screen shattered. Get a screen protector!
Oppo Find N6 for $1,929: With an 8.12-inch internal display, the Find N6 is a beautifully engineered folding phone that’s impossibly slim and light. Despite its promise of being creaseless, the fold is still discernible. You’ll hardly notice it when the screen is on, though you’ll feel it if you use the optional stylus. Performance is impressively slick, with enough stamina to see you through a busy day, and the camera system is excellent. It’s a big step up from last year’s N5, with a 200-MP main shooter, 50-MP telephoto, and 50-MP ultrawide. The global model can use familiar Google apps, but you’ll have to import it, as this phone won’t officially be released in the West.
Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold for $1,799: The only reason to consider the Pixel 10 Pro Fold right now is if you see it on sale. Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold is superior, but the 10 Pro Fold isn't far behind this year's release. It's still a reasonably slim device with a large front screen that feels like a normal phone, an excellent 8-inch inner screen, and a triple-camera system that delivers great results, though not as great as the Pixel 10 Pro series. Read our Best Pixel Phones guide for more.
Xiaomi Mix Flip for $899: Xiaomi’s first flip phone has a lovely design with excellent displays inside and out, long battery life with fast charging, and flagship-level performance. It also boasts a solid dual-lens camera, opting for telephoto instead of ultrawide alongside the capable main shooter, which is more useful for most folks. The software lets the party down a little; there’s no IP rating, and it is pricey, but I had fun with this flip phone.
Things to Know Before Buying
Folding phones are more fragile than normal phones. Folding phones have more parts than a traditional smartphone, not to mention a hinge. Companies advertise how many folds these devices have been tested for—usually around 200,000 or 500,000 folds—but a single drop can be incredibly damaging. They are not as dust-resistant, and some aren't as water-resistant (only the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and iPhone Duo are IP68-rated in the US), so you'll want to be especially careful. Use a case, and it may be worth investing in the manufacturer's device care policy.
Don't remove the built-in screen protector. Most of these folding phones have a film over the inner screen. You might be tempted to remove it, but don't—it can damage the display. The packaging usually includes instructions not to remove it and how to care for your device.
There's a small learning curve to the software. Flip-style folding phones are fairly straightforward, but book-like folding phones that double as tablets have new multitasking tricks that will take some getting used to if you want to make the most of them. I recommend taking some time to run through these features so you understand how they work.
They're expensive. Do you need one? Nobody needs a folding phone. If you think you'll benefit from one, know they're frequently discounted during big sale events like Black Friday, and you can also knock a few hundred dollars off if you trade in an eligible device.
Which Type of Folding Phone Is for You?
Folding flip phones are for people who want a compact device. Think of a normal phone you can fold in half. That's pretty much what you get, plus a screen on the front to monitor widgets and texts. This does mean you can flip the phone to answer a call and flip it shut to end one—super cool. You can put the phone at a 90-degree angle, and some apps will adapt to show controls on the bottom and important details at the top, like in video calling apps or when watching videos on YouTube, though this depends on the phone. Folding flip phones typically have mediocre battery life, and their cameras aren't as good as their non-folding counterparts.
Folding book-like phones are for people who want the big-screen experience. Are you constantly watching full-length movies on your phone? Or do you always find yourself jumping back and forth between two apps? Then these are for you. They have good battery life and better cameras (though not as good as non-folding phones), but they're far more expensive. These include the short-lived triple-screen folding devices like Samsung's Galaxy Z TriFold. They're thick and heavy, though we're seeing newer models that are surprisingly thin. Still, you may have a hard time fitting them in your pockets.
Is Now a Good Time to Buy?
If you're team Android, this is a good time to buy. Samsung and Google just updated their foldables, and Motorola released its first big foldable in the summer and won't announce the Razr 2027 lineup until the spring. For folks outside the US, we probably won't see new foldables from Honor or Oppo until the spring, too.
If you're considering an iPhone, Apple is likely to unveil a new folding phone soon, so you might want to wait and see what it looks like.
My Favorite Folding Features
Whichever style you go for, my favorite feature of folding phones is the ability to see the viewfinder on the external screen and snap a selfie with the high-quality rear cameras—just set the phone down slightly folded so it stays upright, and there's usually a button you can click in the camera app to send the preview to the external screen. You can usually trigger the shutter hands-free with a palm gesture. (Motorola's Razr Ultra lets you start and stop video recordings with hand gestures, too!) It's excellent when traveling if you want to take a photo of yourself next to a point of interest.
Many of these phones offer similar functionality with translation—Samsung and Google, for example, let you show your words translated on the external screen so the person you are speaking to can see it, and then they can tap a button on the screen to have the phone start translating their words, which you'll see on the internal screen. It's a much nicer system than using Google Translate on a candy bar phone. —Julian Chokkattu

Evidence from photojournalists on the scene confirms Trump was appearing to wave at people working on the construction of the new White House ballroom and saluting officials visible far behind and to the left side of the helicopter.
In mid-to-late October, a video spread purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump waving to and saluting nobody on the White House South Lawn prior to boarding his helicopter, Marine One.
For example, Democratic commentator Harry Sisson said the footage (archived) highlights how Trump is experiencing increasing "mental decline."
The clip shows Trump walking toward Marine One — the call sign officials use when a president flies on a special fleet of helicopters — waving toward his left, continuing to walk and then waving, saluting and waving again in a slightly different direction, also off to his left. At the end of the clip, he salutes a Marine and boards the aircraft.
Numerous social media users and other left-leaning commentators shared the video and iterations of the rumor, including former cable news hosts Don Lemon and Joy Reid, as well as fellow progressive voice Adam Mockler. All three have prominent presences on YouTube.
Similarly, The New Republic initially reported, "Trump, 80, Wanders Off While Waving and Saluting to No One." The publication displayed that headline as an image on social media.
In sum, while the clip is authentic, meaning it displays no signs of artificial-intelligence manipulation, evidence shows Trump was appearing to wave at people working on the construction of his new White House ballroom, which has replaced the demolished White House East Wing. He was also saluting and throwing smaller waves to other darkly-dressed officials positioned far behind and to the left side of the helicopter. Therefore, the above social media posts miscaptioned the video.
Fox News broadcast the same live moment leading up to the moment in question, helping to confirm the date this occurred, Oct. 19, as well as providing a clearer look at two or more darkly-dressed individuals standing next to a white fence whom the president appeared to salute (pictured below, to the left of Trump).
(Fox News)
Snopes contacted Lemon, Reid and Mockler to ask if they wished to address this matter but did not receive responses prior to publication. The New Republic declined to comment, but said it updated its report to include a new headline and other updated information. We also emailed the White House to ask if a spokesperson wished to respond to people sharing the false claim. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Reputable media-licensing website Getty Images hosts several photos with text captions providing more information about the moment in question. For example, a picture of Trump waving (shown at the top of this article) is captioned, "U.S. President Donald Trump waves to people working on building the new ballroom as he departs the White House on October 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C." Other photographs show the ballroom construction happening behind Trump and people working on the project both on the ground and up high.
(Brendan Smialowski via Getty Images)
One of Getty's captions says the picture below shows a construction worker giving Trump a thumbs-up sign as Marine One prepared for takeoff.
(Chip Somodevilla via Getty Images)
The Associated Press' image-licensing website also provides more data, including a photo of the ballroom construction from the White House South Lawn, a glimpse of both the White House and ballroom construction from the Washington Monument, a view of Marine One flying over the work zone on the same day, and Trump giving a similar acknowledgement to workers with a fist sign last week.
