'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
- Published
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.
"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.
Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.
"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.
"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.
The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.
"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.
She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.
"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"
Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.
"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."
"What else would we do?"
Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.
In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.
The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.
"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.
The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.
A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.
The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.
At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.
Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.
Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.
Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."
Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.
For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.
"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.
The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.
Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.
"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.
Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.
The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.
His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.
Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.
"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.
While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.
"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.
The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.
When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.
"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.
His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.
For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.
"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"
Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.
Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.
Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.
This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.
For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.
What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.
Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.
At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.
Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.
Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.
Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.
If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.
The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.
She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.
"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Macklemore dedicated his “Free Palestine” tour date to “love and liberation” as he kicked off the three-show trek in Dublin, Ireland, just over a month after he was dropped as an opener for Ed Sheeran following a political speech on stage.
After bringing out Hozier and Kneecap as surprise guests, Macklemore took a moment to share what the evening meant to him in the wake of the controversy. “Six weeks ago, it was two words. Two words is all that it took. Two words that are rooted in love and liberation,” he said. “Not against anybody, not divisive. Not a call for hatred. But a call to recognize our shared humanity. Free Palestine. I said free Palestine! The same thing that I want for all of us, freedom, dignity, the right to exist without fear. Being able to raise our children in the homes that we grew up in, not having to prove our humanity to the rest of the world.
“And yet,” he continued, “those words, those two words, right, those two words are so threatening to some people. They would rather silence those two words than confront what they actually mean. Because freedom that requires another person’s oppression is not freedom at all. I said freedom that requires another person’s oppression is not freedom at all. And while the world debates those words, we see the videos, we see the footage, we see parents pulling their children out of the rubble. Families erased. Devastation beyond our imagination. And somehow, those words have become more controversial than the suffering that made them necessary. That’s why we are here tonight. That is why we are here, because throughout history, music has given people a place to resist, to come together as a collective, to share our grief, to share our stories, to move from the heart, to mobilize people with the frequency of love. The heartbeat in our drum that makes us feel alive, that makes us feel connected.”
The Dublin concert is the first of a three-show stint that will see the “Thrift Shop” rapper also perform in Paris and London alongside special guests, with all proceeds going to charities supporting Palestine. Macklemore also donated his $1 million salary from Sheeran’s tour to the cause.
On Sept. 14, Macklemore was dropped from the remainder of Sheeran’s U.S. “Loop” tour after he said “free Palestine” on stage and gave political speeches over two concerts at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sept. 4 and 5. “A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: ‘Free Palestine.’ I said, ‘Free Palestine!’” Macklemore said at the Sept. 4 show. “I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them.”
The speech went viral, sparking backlash from pop star Pink and a petition from the Israeli American Council calling for Macklemore to be removed from Sheeran’s tour. “This was an Ed Sheeran concert — not a political rally, not a protest and not an activist event,” they said. “The issue is not whether Macklemore has the right to hold political views. The question is where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda.”
On Sept. 5, he once again said “free Palestine” but also added that his declaration was “in no way a criticism” of Jewish people. A week later, he was dropped from the tour. At the time, Messina Touring Group — the promoter behind Sheeran’s U.S. tour — said they had been “notified by venues” that “they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans. After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.”
In solidarity with Macklemore, Sheeran’s other opening acts — including Finneas, Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe — as well as most of his backing band dropped out of the tour.
Macklemore then claimed that Robert Kraft, owner of the Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts, refused to let him play at the venue and urged other stadium owners to do the same. Kraft responded by announcing that both he and Sheeran would be donating $2 million to “aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis.” Sheeran also posted a lengthy statement saying that the decision to drop Macklemore was the promoter’s, not his, and explaining why he chooses not to speak out on political issues, which generated further backlash against him.
“Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care. Nor does it mean I don’t support causes in my own, personal way,” Sheeran wrote. “There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics — my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds. Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore’s strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes. However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace. I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change.”
But at his first show since Macklemore was dropped, on Sept. 19 in Philadelphia, Sheeran changed his tune and did speak up about the Israel-Gaza war. “What happened in Israel and at the Nova Music Festival on Oct. 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable, and disproportionate,” he said. “Our hearts can be broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’ lives, children’s lives and the systemic injustice we’re seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked.”
Macklemore, who performed a one-off show on October 22 at Colorado’s Red Rocks Amphitheatre, continues his “Free Palestine” tour in Paris on Thursday and in London on Friday.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced the "Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability" initiative on Sept. 30.
Fox News reported the 90-day requirement on Oct. 25 and quotes department spokesperson Sean Parnell throughout the article. Though Parnell shared the report on X that day, he has not confirmed the 90-day requirement.
In October, a claim circulated online that the Pentagon had announced an initiative called FORTRESS that would require military bases in the U.S. to be able to operate for at least 90 days without relying on civilian power, fuel, water or supply lines.
For example, one Facebook user who made and posted a video about the alleged measure wrote (archived):
The Pentagon just Built a 90- Day Survival Plan.
Under FORTRESS (Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability), every major U.S. military base is being ordered to operate for 90 days with no civilian power, fuel, water, or supply chains, using portable nuclear reactors, microgrids, and stockpiles. The military is hardening itself for a grid-down war. Civilians are on their own.
Snopes readers contacted us to ask about the initiative, while similar posts about FORTRESS and what it entails also circulated on Instagram and Reddit (archived, archived).
FORTRESS is a real Department of Defense initiative and social media posts detailing what it involves are broadly accurate. The acronym stands for "Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability." Though the measure itself is new, it also includes some energy and manufacturing-related programs that already exist within the DOD.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced FORTRESS during a speech in Quantico, Virginia, on Sept. 30. His speech and a department memo released that day describe the initiative as an "insurance policy" for the United States.
On Oct. 25, Fox News reported more details about the measure (archived), mainly saying it would require U.S. military bases to "keep operating for at least 90 days without outside support."
Fox News reported Defense Department spokesperson Sean Parnell has led the initiative. Parnell is quoted throughout Fox's report, which he posted to X (archived) that day. His posting of the article, however, does not explicitly confirm the 90-day operating requirement. Therefore, we've rated this claim mostly true.
Snopes contacted the DOD for official confirmation of the 90-day requirement and any additional information it could provide about the FORTRESS initiative. We await a reply to our inquiry.
FORTRESS merges existing DOD programs
The Sept. 30 department memo says FORTRESS would focus on five pillars: "Energy independence; supply-chain and defense-industrial base resilience; a strategic defense reserve; installation hardening and cyber resilience; and resilience in space and spectrum."
Hegseth explained the changes the initiative would bring as follows (at 32:07):
Every major military installation in America is going to generate its own power independent of the civilian grid. If an adversary takes down the grid by cyber attack, by sabotage or by any means, our bases stay lit. Our aircraft keep flying. Our command centers never go dark.
We're bringing our critical supply chains home: the rare earths, the specialty metals, the semiconductors, the propellants mined in America, refined in America, built in America by American workers.
We are building long-overdue strategic reserves deep enough to fight through disruption. Think munitions, fuel, medicine, blood. Deep enough that if the world's supply lines break, and in a real war they're going to break, America keeps fighting anyway.
We're hardening every installation on American soil against cyber intrusion, sabotage and drones.
And we're securing the high ground and the airwaves, our satellites, our spectrum, our ability to see, to navigate and to talk to one another.
Fox News reported that a "central concern" that FORTRESS would address is the military's reliance on the civilian power grid. Under the first pillar of "energy independence," Fox News said the measure would see the U.S. military developing its own sources of power such as "portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage and microgrids."
Around a month before the DOD made FORTRESS public, the department had already announced five vendors to build and operate nuclear microreactors at Fort Benning, Georgia; Fort Bragg, North Carolina; Fort Campbell, Kentucky; and Fort Drum, New York; and Fort Hood, Texas, as part of the Janus Program.
That program aims to supply U.S. military bases with "the energy resilience necessary to project combat power globally, without relying on potentially vulnerable external grids," according to the DOD, and seeks to build at least 20 microreactors.
FORTRESS would reportedly also use another existing DOD program — the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network — to identify domestic factories that could switch to manufacturing for the military in a crisis even if normal supply chains are disrupted.
Hegseth said during his Sept. 30 speech that FORTRESS was not meant to spread concerns about war on American soil. Rather, he said (at 33:56):
We'll make certain that America cannot be starved out, shut down or cut off. A fortress is not a place where you hide from. It's a ground you stand on, the foundation you fight from, the strength that lets you reach anywhere in the world, precisely because you are fully prepared at home.
It is unclear how the initiative would affect civilian disaster preparedness. Writing in The Wall Street Journal on Oct. 9, Tim Echols, who has served on the Georgia Public Services Commission since 2011, suggested the initiative could benefit consumers. Echols wrote that "the learning curve for building nuclear is paid for by the government" through microreactors for U.S. bases, whose technology could also apply to civilian power grids.
Echols also suggested that lessening demand for electricity in cities that provide substantial power to military bases would allow those power companies to retire older units and replace them with more-efficient ones.
Conversely, the user who made and posted the aforementioned Facebook video suggested FORTRESS would leave civilians "on their own" by taking away investment from shared resources.
The U.S. government provides disaster preparedness advice for civilians on Ready.gov.

Former US President Barack Obama has launched a satirical attack on Donald Trump’s White House renovation projects, mocking the planned ballroom, changes to the Rose Garden and extensive gold decorations as he campaigned for Democratic candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Ohio on Saturday (October 24) Obama joked that Trump appeared more interested in home renovations than governing the country.
“I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama said, referring to the television network known for home improvement and real estate programming.
“The guy’s building a ballroom that’s bigger than the White House. Paved over the Rose Garden, put a helicopter pad on the South Lawn, and there’s gold everywhere! What’s up with the gold? Everything—more gold!” he added.
Taking aim at the president’s aesthetic choices, Obama told the crowd: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”
The remark drew laughter and applause from the audience.
Obama’s comments were part of a wider attack on Trump as the former president addressed rallies in Cleveland, Ohio, and Detroit, Michigan, to rally Democratic voters before the midterm elections.
Obama framed the November 3 elections as an opportunity for voters to hold the Trump administration accountable. Republicans currently control both chambers of Congress, and Democrats are seeking to regain control of one or both.
Acknowledging that Trump would remain in office for another two years, Obama argued that voters could still change the balance of power in Washington by electing Democrats.
“Like it or not, we’re stuck with two more years of this, but we’re not stuck with a spineless Congress,” Obama told supporters.
He added that voters had a chance to reject what he described as two years of “chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence”.
“We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government,” Obama said in Michigan, describing the election as an opportunity to rein in the administration.
Obama also urged voters in Ohio and Michigan to cast their ballots early, saying the election presented a chance to bring about political change.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Obama’s criticism of Trump’s renovation projects.
Obama remains a prominent figure among Democratic voters, and the party is seeking to use his campaigning to boost candidates in closely contested races ahead of the midterms. The November 3 vote will determine control of the US House of Representatives and a portion of the Senate, shaping the balance of power during the remainder of Trump’s term.

Mumbai local train services restored after almost 10 hours after Kanjurmarg fire hits ops
A fire in Kanjurmarg station’s signalling relay room around 9:33 am caused signals between Vikhroli and Bhandup to go blank.
Mumbai local train services were restored on all four suburban railway lines at Kanjurmarg on Monday morning after a signalling system failure disrupted operations for nearly 10 hours, a Central Railway official told PTI.
The disruption began around 9:33 am after a fire broke out in the signalling and telecommunications (S&T) relay room at Kanjurmarg station, causing signals between Vikhroli and Bhandup to go blank. According to Central Railway Chief Public Relations Officer Swapnil Nila, restoration work was carried out on a war footing to resume normal train operations.
“A fire incident occurred this morning in the S&T relay room at Kanjurmarg station, due to which all signals between Vikhroli and Bhandup went blank,” Nila told ANI.
"The signals on the up through line, towards Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, have been restored, while restoration work on the remaining lines is ongoing. The overhead wire problem that occurred this morning between Mulund and Thane stations at around 9 AM was restored at approximately 10:40 AM, and operations there are now running normally... We are making every effort to restore all systems as soon as possible and provide passengers with smooth local train services.”
Trains delayed due to signalling failure
Following the technical failure, trains were operated at cautious speeds under special authority, leading to bunching and delays across the suburban network.
Central Railway said trains were initially operated using A-board signals at Kanjurmarg and between Vikhroli and Bhandup. Absolute block working was also introduced on the Vikhroli–Bhandup section, while train movements were regulated under TD 912 authority.
The railway's technical teams were deployed to restore the signalling system and minimise disruption to commuters.
Overhead wire issue between Mulund and Thane resolved
Separately, an overhead wire problem reported between Mulund and Thane stations around 9 am was resolved at approximately 10.40 am, Central Railway said.
Train operations on that section have since returned to normal.
The railway said it was making every effort to restore services and ensure smooth operations for passengers. It also regretted the inconvenience caused by the disruption.

In a major defence acquisition push, India on Monday cleared procurement of a range of military platforms and weapon systems, including light multi-role helicopters, long-range Kamikaze drones and radars, at a cost of ₹2.12 lakh crore to boost the combat prowess of the defence forces.
The procurement proposals were approved by the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), the defence ministry's highest decision-making body on military procurement. It was chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh.
The DAC accorded Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) or in-principle administrative approval to various capital acquisition proposals of an estimated cost of about ₹2,12,000 crore, the defence ministry said.
For the Indian Army, approval was accorded for the procurement of high mobility vehicles (HMVs), self-propelled tracked gun system, gun shot response system (GSRS), light multi-role helicopters (LMRH), very short-range air defence system (VSHORADS) and counter unmanned aerial system (C-UAS), it said.
The DAC also cleared the acquisition of other unmanned aerial system, surveillance aerial vehicles, integrated surveillance and strike system and long-range Kamikaze drone system for the Army.
While the HMVs are expected to enhance operational capabilities, logistical support and mobility in challenging terrains, the self-propelled tracked gun system will provide mobility and firepower to mechanised formations.
The GSRS will serve as a force multiplier, providing real-time situational awareness, the ministry said.
It said the LMRH will be used by both the Indian Army and the Indian Air Force for a range of purposes including reconnaissance and surveillance, combat, search and rescue of troops, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief.
The VSHORADS will engage new-generation small-size aerial threats, while C-UAS will enhance the survivability of tanks in the modern battlefield. The surveillance and drone systems will enhance the surveillance and targeting capabilities of the Indian Army, according to the ministry.
For the Indian Navy, approval was given for the procurement of active offboard decoy system (AODS) and other major naval platforms. The AODS will enhance the credibility of anti-missile defence, especially against modern anti-ship missiles of adversaries, the ministry said.
The indigenously designed and constructed major naval platforms will possess modern-day warfare capabilities and enhance the combat capability of the navy, it said.
The DAC approved procurement of helicopters, air defence systems and weapons and mobile X-band Doppler weather radar system to enhance the air defence and warfighting capabilities of the force.
"The procurement of special utility helicopters will help the Indian Air Force to meet the important air transport requirements. The X-band Doppler weather radar system will provide high-resolution, localised weather surveillance in forward areas," the ministry said in a statement.
Out of the total AoNs accorded, approximately 82 per cent of the procurements will be made from the Indian industry, it noted.

The iPhone Duo is finally here. Apple's first folding smartphone arrives seven years after Samsung pioneered the category with the Galaxy Fold. That gave Apple plenty of time to refine the hardware behind closed doors rather than in public view—and the results show: The Duo is a pretty dang good foldable.
Whether your Duo just landed on your doorstep or you're still weighing that $1,999 price, here's what you need to know before unfolding it.
Apps Aren’t Optimized—Yet
The iPhone Duo is a new shape and size for Apple, so many of your apps likely aren't optimized to show up properly on the unique 5.4-inch outer screen or the 7.6-inch inner display. Apple also changed how navigational elements appear on the Duo, aligning them on the right rail instead of centering them on the bottom like every other iPhone.
Apple apps, redesigned for the Duo, look great. Many third-party apps look like the Google Home app in the picture above: a strip down the middle with thick, black bars on the sides. Several major app developers have already optimized their apps for iOS 27.1—Slack, Instagram, DoorDash, and WhatsApp, for example—but I've noticed that even some optimized apps like Instagram can still have broken user-interface elements. It will take time for every app in your library to work perfectly across these new screens.
It might be a good thing that the Duo is back-ordered for several weeks. By the time you snag yours, app developers will likely have caught up to the new device, and you might enjoy a richer folding experience.
Say Goodbye to Face ID
Nearly a decade ago, Apple introduced Face ID as the future of the iPhone, eventually replacing the fingerprint-based Touch ID. So it might be confusing to hear that Apple's first folding phone doesn't have Face ID at all and instead relies on the older biometric authentication method. (Likely because Face ID tech takes up too much space in the thin iPhone Duo.) Touch ID never disappeared—Apple has used it on the iPhone SE and still features it on iPads and MacBooks—but this is the first time it has returned on a flagship iPhone.
Using your thumb again will take some getting used to, but it's not a deal-breaker. Some folks will miss the convenience and speed of Face ID, where all you needed to do was stare at the screen, instead of now reaching for the Touch ID sensor on the right side. Others who hated facial authentication might actually like the return of the fingerprint sensor.
Apple also introduced the Dynamic Island a few years ago—the pill-shaped island around the Face ID camera sensors that shows live app activities, like the next turn on your navigation or music currently playing, giving a second job to the camera cutout. Without Face ID, Dynamic Island hasn't disappeared from the iPhone Duo. Instead, Apple moved it to the top-right edge around the outer selfie camera; on the inner display, it appears at the top-right edge when a live activity is in progress.
You Need a New MagSafe Wallet
The iPhone Duo supports MagSafe just like the rest of the iPhone lineup, so you can magnetically stick your favorite phone grip on the back, or attach the phone to a magnetic car dock, bike mount, or wireless charger. One thing to note: If you unfold the Duo and attach it to a car dock or tripod, the phone will tip to one side because the magnet can’t keep it held straight given the uneven weight distribution. Third-party accessory makers could address this with anti-rotation magnets, but it might mean upgrading your current accessories.
Wallets, unfortunately, are the one accessory that won't really play well with the Duo. Yes, you can still attach a MagSafe wallet, but because the Duo is shorter than other iPhones, the wallet sticks out awkwardly past the lower edge. Apple doesn't have an official solution, so if you want to use a magnetic wallet with your iPhone, you'll have to look at third-party accessories.
Use the Rear Camera for Selfies
Everyone knows the rear cameras on your smartphone are better than the selfie camera on the front. One of the best features on a folding phone is the ability to take a selfie with those superior rear cameras and still be able to see a preview with the outer screen.
Don't confuse this with “Duo Preview” as I did, though. That's a feature that lets you show the person you're photographing the camera's viewfinder, so they can make sure they look picture-perfect before you tap the shutter. The setting to enable this is on the left edge of the camera app, where you can also turn on “Kids Cue” to have Snoopy animations play on the outer screen to get the attention of a kid for the perfect photo.
But if you're taking a selfie yourself and want the camera controls on the front screen, all you need to do is launch the camera and flip the phone around—you'll see a slider that says, “Slide to show camera.” Slide it, and the full camera app will show up on the outer screen, so you can switch modes and access Photographic Styles right there and enjoy the higher-quality results from the superior cameras. Doing this also crucially disables the inner screen, so your fingers won't accidentally switch modes.
You Can Create App Pairs
Filling the inner 7.6-inch screen with two different apps running side by side is incredibly handy and one of the cornerstone features of any folding phone. Whether you're on a phone call and want to pull up a confirmation email, or want to browse two different Safari webpages, you can drag an app from the bottom and pull it to the left or right side to enter the split-screen state.
One trick that isn't immediately obvious is that you can create app pairs. Just tap the middle bar between the two apps once, and it'll glow white, meaning that those two apps are now locked and can be accessed at any moment from the Recent apps menu. You can't save that as an app icon combo, though. This is still very handy if you know you'll always want to open two apps simultaneously on the big screen.
Be Careful of the Inner Screen
I get it, you're going to want to protect the fragile screens of your $1,999 iPhone. A case is smart—folding phone cases aren't like normal cases, as they usually come in two shells that attach to each side of the phone. You can also totally add a screen protector to the outer 5.4-inch screen.
But for the 7.6-inch matte inner screen, exercise some caution. You might see chatter online that you can “remove” the Duo's nano-texture finish, but it's an “integral” component of the inner display—as Apple says on this support page. “Don't attempt to remove it,” Apple writes. (Apple also has a page on cleaning the nano-texture display properly here.) Attempting to remove the finish is likely a surefire way to void your warranty. Apple doesn't say anything about using third-party screen protectors, but using one could compromise the display performance.
If you scratch or damage the nano-texture finish, Apple says you can take it to any Apple Store or an Apple Authorized Service Provider and have it replaced for $19 (or $49 if the phone is out of warranty). That's not the same as if there's an actual crack in the inner display—that'll run you a cool $999 if you don't have AppleCare+.
You Can Split the Keyboard
The iPhone Duo is a wide phone. If you've complained about the size of modern smartphones and how it's hard to reach the top of the screen, well, you might still have some issues reaching the sides of the Duo. There's some good news, though. Apple lets you split the keyboard to make typing on the inner display a little easier.
Later this year, Apple will also issue a software update bringing Reachability to the Duo. On other iPhones, this brings the top of an app down, making it easier to reach. On the Duo, it will move an app to the left or right so you won't have to stretch those fingers as much.
Apple Pencil Support Is Coming
Have you always wanted to use a stylus on an iPhone? Soon! Steve Jobs is probably rolling in his grave.
Apple will bring support for the USB-C Apple Pencil (and only that Apple Pencil model, not others) in a software update later this year. Paired with the 7.6-inch screen's nano-texture finish, it should make writing and drawing on the iPhone Duo feel paper-like. Sadly, there's no place to store the stylus on the iPhone like you can on an iPad. I'm sure someone will make an accessory for it.

Rama Rao Malla, the son of a farmer from Anakapalli, went on to earn a B.Ed., an M.Sc. and a Ph.D. in biochemistry from Andhra University. During Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Prof. Malla, of the Department of Life Sciences at the Gandhi Institute of Technology and Management (GITAM) (Deemed to be University), is leading research to develop a blood test for one of the most aggressive forms of breast cancer.
The first graduate in his family, Prof. Malla has been a teacher for more than three decades. He joined GITAM early in his career in 2001 and, after completing postdoctoral work at the University of Illinois College of Medicine, returned to set up the university’s cancer research laboratory in 2011. He has guided 14 doctoral scholars and completed several projects on breast cancer, with four more under way, he says.
His current research focuses on triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), which lacks the receptors for oestrogen, progesterone and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), the targets of certain cancer therapies. Patients are treated mainly with chemotherapy, to which many develop resistance. TNBC accounts for 10% to 15% of breast cancers, he says, and is increasingly being diagnosed in women in their mid-30s and 40s. Mammography may miss small tumours, particularly in younger women. “If we can identify this cancer at an early stage, we can successfully eliminate the tumours by surgery,” he says.
The project, titled “Exploring Serum Exosomal microRNAs as Minimally-Invasive Biomarkers for Early Diagnosis of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer”, has been sanctioned under the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)’s “Follow-on Nischayak Anveshan” Extramural Grants programme, with Prof. Malla as the principal investigator. He says the project has an outlay of more than ₹2 crore over three years.
The study will examine exosomes, nanosized vesicles released by cells, including tumour cells. Their microRNA content can reflect that of the cells from which they originate. The researchers will compare serum samples from patients with early-stage TNBC, provided by the Mahatma Gandhi Cancer Hospital & Research Institute (MGCHRI) and the GITAM Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (GIMSR), with samples from healthy women. Sequencing and digital polymerase chain reaction (PCR) will be used to identify candidate microRNAs, and a machine-learning model will be trained to distinguish patients with early-stage TNBC from healthy individuals. The ultimate objective is to develop a kit-based test.
“We hope we can achieve something after three years that will be useful for society,” he says.
The co-investigators are P. Kiranmayi, P. Vasudevaraju, A. Krishna Chaitanya and M. Srivenkatesh of the GITAM School of Science; K. Viswa Kalyan of GIMSR; and V. Muralikrishna of MGCHRI.
The World Health Organization advises that any abnormal breast lump should be examined by a health professional, even if it is painless.

The Senior Women’s T20 Trophy 2026 got underway on Monday, October 26, with the domestic women’s T20 cricket tournament running until November 20. Organised by the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI), the competition will feature 37 teams across the Elite and Plate divisions, with 134 matches scheduled.
The tournament, which began in the 2008-09 season as the Senior Women’s T20 League, will enter its 18th edition this year.
Maharashtra will enter the competition as the defending Elite champion after winning its maiden title last season. It defeated Madhya Pradesh in a rain-affected final in Surat to lift the trophy.
The defending champion has been placed in Elite Group A alongside Assam, Karnataka, Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh, Bengal, Goa and Jammu & Kashmir.
Senior Women’s T20 Trophy 2026: Teams and Groups
Elite Group A: Maharashtra, Assam, Karnataka, Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh, Bengal, Goa, Jammu & Kashmir
Elite Group B: Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Baroda, Saurashtra, Rajasthan, Haryana, Andhra, Odisha
Elite Group C: Railways, Tripura, Vidarbha, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Sikkim, Kerala
Elite Group D: Delhi, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Uttar Pradesh, Pondicherry
Plate Group: Bihar, Nagaland, Mizoram, Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur
Senior Women’s T20 Trophy 2026: Players to Watch
India wicketkeeper-batter Richa Ghosh is set to captain Bengal, subject to her availability, with pacer Titas Sadhu named as her deputy.
Vidarbha will feature Bharti Fulmali, who was part of India’s gold medal-winning team at the Asian Games. Kerala’s squad includes Asha Sobhana, Sajana Sajeevan and Kiran Navgire.
Senior Women’s T20 Trophy 2026: Format Explained
The Elite division comprises four groups, with three groups featuring eight teams each and the fourth containing seven.
The top two teams from each Elite group will qualify for the Super League. The eight qualifiers will be divided into two groups of four, with each team playing three matches.
The two group winners will meet in the Elite final on November 20 to decide the champion.
The six Plate teams will compete in a round-robin league, with the top two advancing to the Plate final on November 4.
Senior Women’s T20 Trophy 2026: Venues
The Elite group-stage matches will be held across Surat, New Chandigarh, Mohali, Lucknow and Pune. The Plate competition will take place in Sovima, Nagaland.
Ahmedabad will host the Super League matches and the Elite final.
Senior Women’s T20 Trophy 2026: Promotion and Relegation
The Plate group winner will earn promotion to the Elite division for the following season. Meanwhile, the lowest-ranked team across the four Elite groups will be relegated to the Plate competition.
Senior Women’s T20 Trophy: Most Successful Teams
Railways is the most successful team in the competition’s history, with 11 titles.
Other teams to have won the trophy include Delhi, Punjab, Mumbai and Maharashtra. Mumbai claimed its maiden title in 2023 and successfully defended it in 2024, before Maharashtra won its first championship in the 2025 season.

MADRID — A type of targeted chemotherapy developed by Merck and China’s Kelun-Biotech cut by one-third the risk of death in patients with advanced endometrial cancer, a common gynecological cancer, according to randomized Phase 3 study results presented Monday.
The drug, called sacituzumab tirumotecan, or sac-TMT, has already shown survival-extending benefits for patients across multiple cancer types in studies conducted by Kelun in China, where it’s approved.
Merck is conducting 18 global Phase 3 studies of sac-TMT, including 10 studies in women’s cancers, to support approvals in the U.S., Europe, and elsewhere outside China. The drug plays a crucial role in Merck’s efforts to replace revenue that will be lost when Keytruda, its blockbuster immunotherapy, loses patent protection in 2028.

Heavenly Creatures killer Pauline Parker dies in Orkney, aged 88
- Published
To her neighbours and friends, Hilary Nathan was a quiet, religious woman who ran a riding stable in the small Orcadian island of Burray.
But her death in an island care home last week at the age of 88 closes a chapter on an extraordinary life that began 70 years ago on the other side of the world with a sensational murder trial.
As a 16-year-old and under her birth name of Pauline Parker, she was convicted alongside her schoolfriend Juliet Hulme of the murder of her mother Honora Parker.
The case shocked New Zealand – and the rest of the world.
The court heard the girls had become inseparable at Christchurch Girls' High School. Fearing that they'd be separated following the divorce of Juliet's parents and a planned move to South Africa, they plotted to kill Mrs Parker, who they believed stood in their way.
They lured her to a park and bludgeoned her to death with a brick inside a stocking.
By the time filmmaker Sir Peter Jackson was born in 1961, both girls had served five years in prison, been released, given new identities, and left New Zealand for good.
"It was known for its tabloid sensational aspect. I know a lot of English tabloids flew to Christchurch, New Zealand, to cover the case of the 'evil schoolgirl killers'," he told the BBC's Late Show in 1995.
"Repeating that stuff would have been easy, but that's not what we wanted to do. We wanted to understand more about Pauline Parker and Juliet Hulme, and what made them become friends."
His film Heavenly Creatures starred Kate Winslet as Hulme and Melanie Lynskey as Parker. It showed how their intense friendship spilled over into a strange shared fantasy life which culminated in the brutal murder.
The defence argued insanity, but both girls were found guilty of murder and only avoided the death penalty because of their age.
In 1960, having served five years in separate prisons, they were given new identities and moved away from New Zealand.
The court ordered that they should never meet again, and yet they lived part of their lives about 80 miles (129km) apart.
When the film came out in 1995, Juliet was living in Portmahomack in Rosshire, where she'd become a crime writer living under her new name, Anne Perry.
She told the Late Show that she didn't plan to see the film.
"It would be too harrowing," she said. "What was close to the truth would be distressing and what was far from the truth would be even more distressing."
"It's a bit like being stripped naked in the High Street for everyone to come and look and pick and poke. I'd rather put my clothes on and go back home, thank you."
During filming, Kate Winslet said she had no idea where the two women were, and after Anne Perry's identity was revealed, the actress expressed the hope that Pauline Parker would be able to retain her anonymity.
"These are two women who, for the last 40 years, have had to overcome so much in order to get on with their lives and just survive," she said.
"I hope she is never found."
But in 2011, Parker was found by lawyer and true-crime author Peter Graham, who had written a book about the case called So Brilliantly Clever, its title taken from her diary, which was used as evidence in court.
She, like Juliet, had come to the UK, where she had settled in a small village in rural Kent and opened a riding school. By 2011, and now known as Hilary Nathan, she had moved to Orkney, running another stable.
For both women, religion and small tight-knit communities provided a haven. According to an interview her sister gave to the New Zealand Women's Weekly, Nathan was a devout Catholic who led a reclusive life.
Perry was a Mormon, enjoying the support of her own community when reporters began to arrive after Heavenly Creatures was released.
She said: "The media descended on Portmahomack. I was horrified, especially since my mother lived in the village. It's not just the people the film is about, it's all the people around them. I felt it might ruin my family."
Although her books were hugely successful in America, she never really found the fame she merited here in the UK, partly because of her reticence to do any promotion.
Prime Suspect creator Lynda La Plante expressed interest in a TV version of Perry's books, but the author vetoed the plan for the same reason.
In 2001, I visited Perry in Portmahomack for a rare interview for Newsnight Scotland. At that stage, she was a glamorous author, with a back catalogue which had sold 15 million copies around the world.
"I think after 51 years, you can let it go," she told me. "It's not who I am now. It's not who I have been for decades."
We didn't talk about the murder directly, but you don't have to look far in her books for insight into what happened and how her life had turned out. Her detective, the Victorian policeman William Monk, suffers from amnesia, and sometimes wonders exactly who he is.
"Monk sees himself as just himself but because of his memory loss, he has to deal with the fact that he may be someone else. That comes from my own sense that other people view me as a monster," she admitted.
"Of course it affects what I write. I have far more compassion and understanding for people who do wrong things than I'd ever have if I hadn't been in that position.
"The questions of right and wrong and compassion and forgiveness concern me in a way they wouldn't have, had I not had the life I had."
Anne Perry died in Los Angeles in 2023 at the age of 84.
Hilary Nathan's death last week brings their strange story to a close.
How they reinvented themselves out of the world's harshest headlines, and found redemption in the smallest of Scottish communities.
"I would say if you had something which harrowed you, or caused you to feel shame, you should never give up," Anne told me.
"There's more forgiveness, understanding and help out there than you might think."

A video (here & here) purportedly showing US Senator Richard Blumenthal calling India a failed state with a collapsing economy is being shared on social media as a genuine video. Let’s verify the authenticity of this clip.
Claim: The video depicts genuine footage of US Senator Richard Blumenthal calling India a failed state with a collapsing economy.
Fact: The video is an AI-generated deepfake. The original footage is from a September 2026 press conference where the Senator merely urged India and China to stop buying Russian oil, and he did not make any derogatory statements about India. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the original, full-length footage (here & here) from 17 September 2026. The video shows a bipartisan press conference following a House vote on a Russia and Iran sanctions bill.
In this video, Senator Blumenthal urged India and China to stop buying Russian oil and to seek alternative sources. However, he did not make any of the comments heard in the viral video. We then analysed the viral clip using AI video detection tools (here & here), which confirmed that the footage had been digitally altered.
Furthermore, a PIB Fact Check also confirmed that the video is a deepfake and that the Senator made no such statement.
To sum it up, the viral video is an AI-generated deepfake, and Senator Blumenthal never made the derogatory remarks about India being a failed state.

Directed by Anubhav Sinha and produced by Gauri Khan under Red Chillies Entertainment, Ra.One was released worldwide on October 26, 2011, during Diwali. Starring Shah Rukh Khan, Kareena Kapoor Khan and Arjun Rampal, the sci-fi film combined superhero storytelling with visual effects and action sequences that were ambitious for Indian cinema at the time.
15 Years Of Ra.One: Anubhav Sinha looks back at the film that pushed the boundaries of Indian VFX: “2011 wasn’t ready for it”
The film set box office opening records upon its release and went on to earn over Rs 200 crores worldwide. It also received recognition for its technical work, winning honours at major award ceremonies, including the National Film Awards and the Filmfare Awards.
Fifteen years later, Ra.One continues to be discussed for its scale and technological ambition. While the film attempted to bring a high-tech superhero universe to Indian screens at a time when the genre was still developing, its approach to visual effects and computer-generated imagery has remained an important part of conversations around Indian sci-fi cinema.
To mark the film's 15th anniversary, director Anubhav Sinha and Benaras Mediaworks took to social media to look back at the journey of creating the Shah Rukh Khan-starrer. Reflecting on the challenges and ambition behind the project, Sinha wrote, “2011 wasn't ready for it. Somewhere between magic and madness, we made the future.”
Released at a time when large-scale visual effects-driven superhero films were still relatively uncommon in India, Ra.One sought to explore a different kind of cinematic storytelling. From its futuristic costumes and CGI-heavy sequences to its action set-pieces, the film represented an attempt to expand the technical possibilities of mainstream Hindi cinema.
The project required the team to work on a scale that was still emerging within the Indian film industry. Its ambitions extended beyond a conventional superhero narrative, with an emphasis on creating a distinct visual world for audiences.
Over the years, Ra.One has continued to attract attention for its technical experimentation and its attempt to bring a science-fiction spectacle to Indian audiences. As the film completes 15 years, Sinha's reflection revisits the ambition behind a project that sought to push the boundaries of visual effects and superhero storytelling in Indian cinema.

They also serve science, who are not scientists. One of science’s most egregious instances of epistemic dominance, where a powerful institution overrode and exploited a marginalised individual - was Henrietta Lacks – donor of the famous, immortal HeLa cell line. Cells extracted from her, without permission, transformed medical research, but her story was ignored, erased and obscured for decades. The scientific world that generously used this unique cell line for successful research into virology, vaccines, genetics and even cancer care, but the erasure of the donor of those cells was historic in its completeness.
Lacks, an African American tobacco farmer from southern United States, sought treatment at the ‘coloured ward’ in Johns Hopkins Centre for cervical cancer, way back in 1951. While it was common for medical professionals, in those days, to take samples and cells without the express permission of the patient, particularly if it was an African American woman, these cells were different. Johns Hopkins used the cells from her tumour to culture a line of cells that was extraordinarily durable outside the body. Usually human cells die outside of the body. Anonymised by a laboratory acronymn, Lacks’ cells (HeLa) turned out to be the first human cells to successfully grow, divide, and survive indefinitely outside the human body.
HeLa was a miracle that scientists had chanced upon. With HeLa, they could mass produce human cells in a standard format that could be used for biomedical research, and would underpin several breakthrough discoveries, that would revolutionise medical care. No one knew, however, of the immense exploitation behind this miracle cell line, and the profound lack of consent in procuring the samples.
Lacks, who died at merely 31 years, and was buried in an unmarked grave, remained invisible, not even a footnote, completely uncredited and her family entirely in the dark about her contribution to the world of science. Henrietta Lacks’ family first learned about her cells in nearly quarter of a century later, when scientists reached out to them, requesting blood samples once they suspected that the HeLa cell line had contaminated other research samples. This came as a bolt on the family, who could not fathom how cells from their mother had survived this long outside of her, and how this strange situation had come to be. While the academic world and several sections of the corporate world benefited richly from the HeLa cell line, Lacks’ own family had remained entrenched in poverty and struggling to make ends meet. The struggle of the family to come to terms with this exploitation, and the battles they had to fight with the system and science itself is well curated by Rebecca Sloot in her best selling book The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks.
In the 1950s, bioethical norms, particularly around informed consent were either non existent, or, at best, weak. But, in this particular case, Lacks was a black farmer from a rural unit, being treated in a segregated section in a large hospital. Consequently, an entrenched rascism, still alive in the southern United States in the 50s, and class bias contributed in good measure to the shabby treatment of this very valuable patient. Unhesitatingly and boldly, Sloot dragged this out into the open, through the book, knocking on the consciousness of the world and science, biomedical research, urging a discussion, a debate and at the end of it, a nod to what happened. It took years before these units would shamefully acknowledge the great injustice meted out to Lacks’ and her family.
The book, published in 2010, drew attention to the larger debate of patient rights and bodily autonomy. Sloot also underlined the fact that donors need to be acknowledged, heralding a new woke world of bio ethics, laboratory practices and the responsibilities of researchers. No longer could a moral failure be allowed to take patients for a ride, rules and regulations should replace the conscience and a situation like this would hopefully never happen again.
But this story does not end this way. After nearly 75 years of fighting this battle, the Lacks’ family finally found some closure. Reparation was finally achieved with the family settling with Johns Hopkins and other associated institutions in a landmark agreement that firstly acknowledged harm had been done, and also included measures to compensate the family and honour Lacks’ role in science. This included significant financial recompense, and involving the family into research using HeLa cells.
This agreement did reinforce the supremacy of informed consent practices, thus refining research ethics policy, but it also expanded the involvement of the patient and the community in research work. The Lacks’ family success is a milestone of sorts in biomedical research, with calls now being made to improve how institutions and labs credit how their biological materials, and also look at reparative action for families historically exploited by science.
Lacks’ story is a cautionary tale for science. It’s a reckoning with what has historically gone wrong, to set some wrongs right , and make sure the violations of the past are not repeated, but do inform the future, so that scientific progress can proceed without losing respect for human dignity. For this stupendous achievement, we have Henrietta Lacks to thank. From being denied even the footnote in history, she has created a brave new world in science.

Swiggy’s results for the second quarter (Q2) of the financial year 2026-27 (FY27) show that the tug of war between growth and profitability is intensifying, as Instamart’s mounting losses threaten to overshadow the improving performance of its food-delivery business. On October 23, 2026, the company’s shares fell around 15% to ₹179.90 on the BSE, wiping out roughly ₹9,000 Cr in market capitalisation in a single session. The sell-off came after Swiggy reported its results, with widening losses at Instamart overshadowing improving profitability in its food delivery business. The stock has also lost more than half its value since its market debut in November 2024. The company’s revenue from operations increased 36.1% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr in the September quarter. Its consolidated net loss narrowed to ₹922 Cr from ₹1,092 Cr a year earlier, but widened from ₹791 Cr in the preceding quarter. The contrast within the business is becoming more pronounced. Food delivery reported record adjusted EBITDA, supported by advertising revenue and delivery efficiencies. Instamart, meanwhile, saw its adjusted EBITDA loss widen to ₹895 Cr from ₹849 Cr a year earlier, even as its net order value (NOV) grew 13.4% sequentially. This has put investors in a spot, questioning whether Swiggy’s rising investments today can deliver sustainable returns tomorrow. Or will the coming quarters reveal whether Instamart’s renewed growth can translate into better margins? But before that... Instamart’s Growth Comes At A Cost Instamart’s Q2 numbers show a recovery in growth momentum, but not yet a corresponding improvement in profitability. The business’s net order value (NOV) rose 13.4% QoQ to ₹6,594 Cr in Q2 FY27 against 2.5% growth in the preceding quarter. Orders rose 29.3% YoY to 130 Mn. Instamart added 1.3 Mn monthly transacting users during the quarter, taking its user base to 14.8 Mn, up 23% YoY. These are meaningful signs of demand. Management has also pointed to higher order frequency and stronger retention in the earnings call as evidence that Instamart is building shopping habits rather than relying solely on one-off purchases. Its strategy is to deepen engagement through everyday categories such as fresh produce and staples, while using differentiated assortment to give customers reasons to return. However, customer and order growth are only one side of the story. Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr in Q2 FY27, while its contribution margin deteriorated. According to the foodtech’s shareholders’ letter, Instamart reported a contribution margin of -1.0% of gross order value (GOV). The number suggests that the business is still spending heavily to attract and retain customers, fulfil orders and build out its network. “This creates a difficult trade-off. Promotions and pricing investments can help drive orders, while more stores can improve proximity and delivery speed. But both require capital and operating expenditure. Unless higher order volumes, better monetisation and denser delivery networks improve the economics of each order, growth can continue to increase the absolute loss,” an industry source said. The Swiggy management believes Instamart’s customer cohorts are becoming more productive and that differentiated assortment can improve retention over time. The company is also working to increase revenue per order through product mix, private labels and advertising, while reducing costs through network densification, automation and operating leverage. The break-even ambition, however, remains elusive. Management has said Instamart needs to reach roughly 2.3X its current scale, with annualised NOV of around ₹60,000 Cr against approximately ₹26,400 Cr at present, alongside a contribution of about ₹30 per order. Swiggy estimates that roughly two-thirds of the improvement needed would come from higher revenue per order and the remainder from lower costs per order. This is a roadmap rather than a near-term result. The company has not been able to give a detailed timeline for reaching break-even or quantify how much each lever would contribute. Investors will, therefore, need to look beyond headline growth and track whether contribution margin, order economics and adjusted EBITDA improve together. Management expects double-digit sequential NOV growth in Q3 and an improvement of around 100 basis points in adjusted EBITDA margin QoQ. This makes the next quarter an important juncture. Blinkit Raises The Bar For Instamart Instamart’s challenge is not simply to grow. It has to build a network capable of competing with Blinkit while improving the economics of that expansion. The difference in store footprint is also considerable. Instamart added 69 net dark stores in Q2 FY27, taking its total to 1,240 across 133 cities. Blinkit added 308 stores during the same quarter, taking its network to 2,751. Blinkit’s network is now more than twice the size of Instamart’s. Scale matters in quick commerce because it affects how close a platform can be to customers, how efficiently it can fulfil orders and how much volume it can route through its network. A larger footprint can also provide more opportunities to improve availability and spread certain operating costs. But store count alone does not establish which business has better economics: store maturity, order density, basket size, local competition and the cost of operating each location all matter. The financial contrast in Q2 is also stark. Blinkit reported positive adjusted EBITDA of ₹184 Cr, compared with Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹895 Cr. Blinkit’s NOV grew 22.2% sequentially, ahead of Instamart’s 13.4% growth. Eternal’s management has cited store paybacks and lower competitive intensity in Tier II markets, while maintaining its FY29 EBITDA ambition for Blinkit. In contrast, Swiggy has emphasised building customer habits, improving retention and developing its existing Tier I and II network. Instamart’s management did not commit to a new accelerated expansion plan in the earnings call, suggesting the near-term focus is on making the existing network more productive rather than simply matching Blinkit store for store. “There is a reasonable case for this approach. Adding stores without sufficient local demand can dilute returns, and a smaller network can still be productive if it generates enough orders per location. But restraint also carries a risk: a weaker physical footprint can limit reach and availability in a market where speed and convenience are central to the proposition,” the executive quoted above said. Therefore, the key question is whether Instamart can close the gap through better throughput, assortment and monetisation, rather than relying primarily on expansion. Swiggy’s shareholder letter also points to a planned transition to an inventory-led model, under which Instamart would own the inventory it sells. Management expects this to improve contribution margin by around 80 basis points and shorten the working-capital cycle. The transition is expected to begin mid-Q3 FY27 and take two to three quarters to complete. What Can Support Swiggy’s Valuation? Swiggy’s market fall also reflects the tension between a relatively stronger food delivery business and a quick commerce operation that continues to consume substantial resources. Food delivery GOV grew 17.7% YoY to ₹10,054 Cr in Q2 FY27. Adjusted EBITDA increased 42% to ₹341 Cr, with the adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 3.4% from 2.8% a year ago. Higher advertising revenue and delivery efficiencies supported the performance. This business provides an important counterweight to Instamart’s losses. Its profitability shows that Swiggy can generate operating earnings from an established marketplace, even as it continues to invest in newer businesses. It also gives the company a base from which to fund growth. The difficulty is that stronger food-delivery performance has not yet offset the pressure from Instamart. Swiggy’s consolidated net loss widened sequentially, and analysts have questioned whether its quick commerce growth is keeping pace with expectations. Citi, for instance, noted that Instamart’s sequential NOV growth was below its estimate, while its adjusted EBITDA loss was higher than expected. CLSA also flagged slower-than-expected growth and wider losses, while other brokerages have lowered price targets amid concerns about execution and the time required to reach profitability. This, however, does not mean that Instamart’s growth strategy cannot work. Quick commerce requires upfront investment in stores, inventory, customer acquisition and logistics, and some of those costs may become more efficient as order density improves. The issue is how long investors should be expected to wait for those benefits. Therefore, Swiggy’s immediate task is to show that Q2 was a turning point in loss trajectory, as management expects, rather than another quarter in which growth came at a higher cost. The next set of results will need to show sustained sequential NOV growth alongside improving contribution and adjusted EBITDA margins. Customer additions will matter, but so will repeat ordering, store productivity and the extent to which revenue per order rises. The inventory-led transition will be another milestone to watch. For now, as Swiggy continues to get stuck in a tug-of-war between profitability and growth, its market fall is a reminder that revenue growth alone is unlikely to reassure investors.
