Vice City returns in GTA 6 at the heart of Leonida and the game’s main urban setting. The modern neon-filled city combines beaches, nightlife, high-rises, residential neighborhoods, ports, and busy streets, giving Jason and Lucia plenty of places to explore. Here is a detailed GTA 6 Vice City guide so you know every key area and point of interest in this iconic area.
GTA 6 Vice City Overview
Vice City is the county seat of Vice-Dale County and is Rockstar’s modern take on Miami in GTA 6. The city is well-known for its beaches, hotels, nightlife, diverse neighborhoods, and busy waterfront areas.
Rockstar describes Vice City as the “sun and fun capital of America,” with everything from the white sands of Ocean Beach to the panaderías of Little Cuba and the Tisha-Wocka flea market. This GTA 6 location also extends toward the VC Port, described as the cruise ship capital of the world.
Vice City is also central to the story of Jason and Lucia in GTA 6. Both characters have been shown throughout the city, while several supporting characters and businesses are directly tied to its lively nightlife and music scenes.
Where to Find Vice City in GTA 6?
Vice City is located in Vice-Dale County in southeastern Leonida in the GTA 6 map. It is the main metropolitan area of the game and contains several recognizable districts, beaches, landmarks, and major transport locations.
In both trailers, the extended look of GTA 6, and regular screenshot drops, we can see Vice City from different perspectives. While bright neon life is the key ingredient for the city, beaches and the waterfront border it perfectly for some extra activities in GTA 6.
Key Areas and Locations in GTA 6 Vice City
Now that you know more about Vice City, you must understand that the GTA game locations are always iconic thanks to the explorable places within them.
Here is the complete list of all key areas in Vice City in GTA 6:
| Key Locations | Description | 
|---|---|
| Ocean Beach | Bustling beachfront packed with tourists | 
| South Beach | Coastal district filled with nightlife | 
| Little Cuba | Bustling neighborhood with Latin characters | 
| Little Haiti | Residential area with a street-focused atmosphere | 
| Downtown | High-rise heart of Vice City | 
| Washington Beach | Coastal neighborhood along Vice City’s shoreline | 
| Vice Point | Named neighborhood within Vice City’s urban landscape | 
| Rockridge | Urban area with residential and commercial spaces | 
| Vice City Port | Major waterfront transportation hub | 
| Vice City International Airport | Major airport serving Vice City | 
| Jack of Hearts | Major strip club owned by Boobie | 
| NINE1NINE | Nightclub | 
| Belville | A neighborhood near Ekanfinaka | 
| Ekanfinaka | Located near State Route 10 | 
| Peacock Bay | Banana Grove from GTA Vice City | 
| Stockyard | Multiple stores and car meets | 
| Tequesta | Tall buildings and hangouts | 
| Tisha-Wocka | Includes the flea market of GTA 6 | 
Ocean Beach
Ocean Beach is one of Vice City’s most recognizable coastal areas. Its wide sandy beach is packed with tourists, swimmers, joggers, and people relaxing in the sun, while hotels line the surrounding streets (with the iconic Ocean View making a return from the original GTA Vice City).
The first GTA 6 trailer prominently features Ocean Beach, including the Atlantis Hotel and the area’s busy beachfront. It is one of the clearest examples of Vice City’s modern Miami influence.
South Beach (Southside)
South Beach is another major beachfront area shown in Vice City. The district adds more coastal streets, hotels, pedestrians, and nightlife to the city’s southern waterfront.
Later, we can see Jason and Lucia in swimwear at South Beach in the GTA 6 Extended Look. We also get to see larger NPC density on the busy beach.
Little Cuba
Little Cuba brings a distinct Latin American character to Vice City. Rockstar’s official description highlights its bustling panaderias, giving the neighborhood a different atmosphere from the city’s wealthy beachfront districts.
Little Haiti (La Perle)
Little Haiti is another key location in the Vice City neighborhood. It sits among the city’s more residential and street-focused areas and adds further variety to the urban environment.
The GTA 6 trailers feature references to the San4San (S4S) street gang, whose name comes from the Haitian Creole phrase for “blood for blood”. They could be one of the key players in this part of the city.
Downtown
Downtown is the high-rise core district of Vice City, with a dense skyline. The area provides the strongest contrast to the city’s beaches, with tall buildings and busy urban streets dominating the view.
The district includes the Megamundo Building, NINE1NINE, Sahara Arena, Shorefront Building, The Sumerian, and the Vice City Arts Center.
Washington Beach
Washington Beach is one of Vice City’s coastal neighborhoods, farther away from the main city. It sits among the city’s collection of beachfront areas and provides another stretch of the urban coastline to explore in your GTA 6 cars.
Vice Point
One of the key areas of the Vice City broader collection of neighborhoods is the Vice Point landmark in GTA 6. It covers the northern island and beach districts of Vice City (modeled after North Beach, Miami Beach).
Like its original appearance in Grand Theft Auto: Vice City and Vice City Stories, Vice Point features coastal high-rise hotels, apartment complexes, commercial strips, and shopping centers like the iconic North Point Mall.
Rockridge
Rockridge is another identified Vice City location. It appears as part of the city’s urban landscape alongside its residential neighborhoods and larger commercial areas.
It is a civic building modeled after the Miami Police Department South Station in Little Havana.
Vice City Port
While we don’t see Vice City Port in full view, in one of the driving sections from the GTA 6 Extended Look, we see it on the right. The port is one of the major transportation areas shown in GTA 6.
Rockstar’s official description calls Vice City the cruise ship capital of the world, making the port an important part of the city’s coastal identity. The classic 3D Universe equivalent is known as Viceport from Grand Theft Auto: Vice City and Vice City Stories.
However, the new version is part of the sprawling, open-world state of Leonida in GTA 6 rather than being boxed in by invisible boundaries.
Vice City International Airport
Vice City International Airport is one of the city’s major landmarks. Some of the road signage in GTA 6 also confirms the location of Vice City International Airport.
The airport plays an active role in GTA 6 missions. This includes an extended story sequence where protagonists Jason and Lucia enter the private terminal to handle a security assignment for Andres de Leon.
If you are coming from the original Vice City, don’t expect empty scenery. GTA 6’s version of the Vice City International Airport features a larger variety of commercial and private liveries. This includes new regional and airline brands. The VCIA also consists of active passenger waiting areas and extensive runway and highway connections.
Jack of Hearts
Missing Malibu Club from the original Vice City? While we don’t know if it exists in the game, a solid upgrade is there in Jack of Hearts. Jack of Hearts is the major strip club in Vice City owned by Boobie Ike in GTA 6.
It is closely connected to Boobie’s wider business empire and Dre’Quan Priest’s music operation with the record label Only Raw Records. Well, unlike the previous strip clubs in GTA games, Jack of Hearts is linked to the criminal economy. It serves as a money-laundering front and a hub for story missions, meetings, and music industry connections.
NINE1NINE
NINE1NINE is a nightclub in Vice City where Jason and Lucia have been shown dancing together. It represents the city’s nightlife scene and gives the protagonists another place to spend time away from their criminal activities.
Belville
Belville is a neighborhood in Vice City located near Ekanfinaka. It forms part of the city’s wider urban landscape alongside several other mainland districts.
Ekanfinaka
Ekanfinaka is a Vice City neighborhood located near State Route 10. Its position connects it to the city’s broader network of roads and surrounding residential areas.
Peacock Bay
Peacock Bay is one of the most beautiful waterfront neighborhoods in GTA 6 Vice City. Its name and setting draw from Miami’s Coconut Grove area, giving it a distinct coastal atmosphere within the city.
Peacock Bay has no direct named counterpart in the original GTA: Vice City, although its waterfront setting fits the same coastal identity seen throughout the older game. Especially if you draw a comparison to the Banana Grove location from the first Grand Theft Auto game.
Stockyard
Stockyard is a Vice City district associated with stores, street culture, and car meets. The area gives Vice City another commercial and automotive-focused neighborhood away from its beaches and high-rises.
Tequesta
Tequesta is a named Vice City neighborhood surrounded by modern urban development. Its identity is associated with tall buildings and busy city hangouts, adding another dense area to Vice City’s landscape.
Tisha-Wocka
Tisha-Wocka is home to a flea market known for its bootleg brands. Rockstar highlights the market as one of Vice City’s distinctive local attractions.
GTA 6 Vice City Key Characters
Several of the most important characters in GTA 6 are directly tied to Vice City, with Jason and Lucia at the center of its criminal world. Boobie Ike, Dre’Quan Priest, and Real Dimez are also closely connected to the city’s business and music scenes.
| Character | Role in Vice City | 
|---|---|
| Boobie Ike | Vice City businessman and local legend | 
| Dre’Quan Priest | Rising music mogul in Vice City | 
| Real Dimez | Popular rap duo chasing Vice City fame | 
| Jason Duval | Main protagonist | 
| Lucia Caminos | Main protagonist | 
Boobie Ike
The kingpin, Boobie Ike is one of Vice City’s most established figures and has turned his history in the streets into a legitimate business empire. His interests include real estate and the Jack of Hearts strip club.
He is also a major figure in Vice City’s music scene through his partnership with Dre’Quan Priest. Only Raw Records gives Boobie another way to expand his influence across the city.
Dre’Quan Priest
Dre’Quan Priest is an aspiring artist who has spent years trying to break into Vice City’s music scene. From the streets and acts at Boobie’s strip club, he turns to music – his bigger ambition.
Dre’Quan now works with Boobie on Only Raw Records and has signed Real Dimez to the label. His story gives Vice City another side beyond crime, providing more of a solid connection to the GTA 6 songs.
Real Dimez
Vice City’s rapper duo Real Dimez consists of Bae-Luxe and Roxy, two longtime friends who have built a following through music and social media. Their early success came from an older hit with local rapper DWNPLY, which helped push the duo into the spotlight.
Their connection to Vice City gets stronger with the association of Dre’Quan. Real Dimez are part of Ike’s Only Raw Records.
Jason Duval
Jason Duval is one of GTA 6’s two protagonists and is closely connected to Vice City’s criminal world. Jason’s story brings him directly into Vice City’s streets, businesses, nightlife, and criminal activity. His meeting with Lucia becomes a major turning point as the pair attempt to build a better life together.
Lucia Caminos
After leaving prison, Lucia determines to change her circumstances and sees a life with Jason as a possible way forward. Her plans quickly pull her into Vice City’s criminal underworld. Lucia and Jason visit several Vice City scenes, including security ops and criminal activities.
So, which GTA 6 weapons will you use to clear the criminal missions of the city? Do tell us in the comments.
Who are the main characters from GTA 6 Vice City?
Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos are the two protagonists at the center of Vice City’s story. Boobie Ike, Dre’Quan Priest, and Real Dimez are also closely connected to the city’s business and music scenes.
What businesses are important in GTA 6 Vice City?
The Jack of Hearts, owned by Boobie Ike, is one of Vice City’s major businesses and is connected to his wider empire and Only Raw Records.
Which old Vice City locations return in GTA 6?
Several familiar locations from the original GTA: Vice City return in GTA 6, including Ocean Beach, Vice Point, Little Haiti, Downtown, and Washington Beach.

The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP) has supported the Kerala Health Department’s decision to provide a low-cost generic version of the drug Risdiplam to patients afflicted with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a rare and threatening genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness.
In a statement, KSSP president C. Ramakrishnan and general secretary V. Manoj Kumar said that access to this medication is crucial for improving the quality of life and life expectancy of patients.
The statement from the pro-Left people’s science movement comes close on the heels of public health experts such as B. Ekbal, K.P. Aravindan, and V. Ramankutty endorsing the government’s stand.
The KSSP functionaries pointed out that Natco Pharma is an Indian pharmaceutical company that plays a key role in making affordable cancer treatments more accessible to the general public, both in India and in international markets. They claimed that the department’s decision is not merely aimed at saving public funds. It is a humanitarian responsibility to ensure that life-saving treatment is accessible to more SMA patients, they added.

6+ ways you can use your PlayStation 5's USB ports
Those USB ports are for more than topping off your controller battery.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
It's not as immediately apparent what to do with your PS5's USB ports compared to the many uses for your phone's USB port or everything they can do on your PC. And while you might have used them for some basic purposes, there are others you may not have considered yet.
All PS5 variations have two 10 Gbps USB-A ports on their rear, but the front USB ports are slightly different depending on which model you have. On the original PS5, there's one USB-A 2.0 port and a 10 Gbps USB-C port. On the PS5 Slim and PS5 Pro, the front USB 2.0 port is USB-C instead. Avoid the slow USB 2.0 port for speed-sensitive purposes like external storage.
Add more storage
It's easy to run out of space on your PS5 given how much storage modern games take. The best long-term solution is adding an M.2 SSD to your console, but that can be prohibitively expensive given the current cost of storage. Another option is connecting an external SSD or HDD to expand your system's available room.
Unfortunately, you can't play PS5 games from an external drive, as they're designed to run only from speedy internal storage or M.2 SSDs that meet Sony's requirements. Instead, you're able to move PS5 games from your console storage to an external drive for archival purposes, then shift a title back over to your system when you're ready to play it again. It's an especially helpful option if your home internet is slow or has a data cap. You can play PS4 games from external storage.
To use a drive for game storage, it must be at least USB 5 Gbps (USB 3.0) and between 250GB and 8TB in size. You can't use more than one at a time, and it won't work if connected to a USB hub. Go to Settings > Storage > USB Extended Storage > Format as USB Extended Storage with a drive connected to format it, which will erase any existing data.
The other major use for external drives is storing screenshots and video clips from your console. You can't use a single drive for both, though. You must format a drive as USB Extended Storage for your PS5 to store games on it, compared to a standard exFAT or FAT32 drive for screenshots. Consider two drives if you need long-term storage for both games and media, or use a flash drive for quick transfers to your computer.
Charge and pair controllers
The most immediately obvious way to use the USB ports on your PS5 is for charging your controllers, either at the end of a play session or connecting permanently if you don't want any latency. It's also easy to forget that connecting a DualSense controller to your PS5 is the fastest way to pair the two.
This hopefully isn't something you'll need to do often, but it's relevant if you take the controller to a friend's house, use it with your PC or have a second console in another room. It's thus worth having a cable plugged into the slow USB 2.0 port on the front so you don't have to hunt for one when you need it.
If this is how you charge your PS5 controller most of the time, make sure you have the right power option selected under Settings > System > Power Saving > Features Available in Rest Mode. Choose 3 Hours to shut off the ports after this time in Rest mode. Choosing Always will waste energy beyond that point. On the PS5 Slim and Pro, you can instead choose Adaptive to automatically stop supplying power when the controller is charged.
Connect other peripherals
Beyond standard controllers, the PS5 has a lot of input options to change how you interact with games. The biggest one is PlayStation VR2, which uses a much simpler connection than the original model. You must plug its single USB-C cable into the speedy port on the front of the console (the bottom one on Slim and Pro consoles). The original PS VR works on PS5, but only with the PS4 camera, which you'll need an adapter for since the PS5 lacks its proprietary connection. Sony stopped giving away these adapters in 2024.
The PS5 HD Camera is another USB accessory, though one with limited usefulness. It isn't needed for PS VR2 and doesn't work with the original PS VR. Its main purpose is showing your face while streaming to Twitch or YouTube, so if you don't do that, there's not much use to it. Third-party cameras don't work on PS5 natively.
The USB ports are also vital for connecting gaming headsets, whether they're fully wired or use a dongle for wireless transmission. For example, my SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Wireless headset uses a transmitter that initially connects to PS5 (and other consoles) via USB-C, then my headphones connect wirelessly to it.
Additionally, some types of games can get a more authentic experience by using different controller formats. Racing wheels and fight sticks are two solid options if you enjoy those types of games.
While you don't typically associate a keyboard and mouse with console gaming, many PS5 games support them. Connect your USB dongle for a wireless keyboard to send messages to friends or via in-game chat much more quickly, or even try using a full keyboard/mouse combo for supported games. This varies by title; for example, Overwatch has a toggle for KB/M mode, which disables aim assist and puts you into PC lobbies.
Other ways to put those USB ports to use
If you don't have a PlayStation Plus subscription or want an extra copy of your PS5 data, you can back it up to a USB drive. After connecting a FAT32- or exFAT-formatted drive (it can't be one set up for storing games), go to Settings > System > System Software > Back Up and Restore > Back Up Your PS5. Choose what you want to back up, then proceed through the process to do so.
Note that this doesn't back up some data (trophies and M.2 storage are excluded). Importantly, it's all-or-nothing; you can't choose individual games to back up, and the Restore Your PS5 option requires you to reset your system. You're able to back up individual PS4 game save data to a USB drive under Settings > Saved Data and Game/App Settings > Saved Data (PS4).
If you're so inclined, the PS5 also supports video playback from a USB drive, though you'll need to follow Sony's instructions for correct formatting and folder naming. In case you need to connect more USB devices to your PS5, a USB hub is a possibility, though not all devices will work with a hub. And if you need to capture more footage (without streaming) than the built-in tools offer, hooking up a capture card to your PS5 is also an option.
If you have any other random USB devices, plug them into your PS5 and see if they work. At worst, you'll see a "not compatible" message, or nothing will happen. Don't forget about other great PS5 accessories, too.

The sale of books has emerged as the latest political flashpoint in West Bengal, with under-construction book stalls run by Left parties allegedly vandalised in Kolkata’s Dhakuria and elsewhere, amid chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s call to deny the CPI(M) space at Durga Puja venues.
The alleged attack in Dhakuria on Wednesday left senior activists of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation and local Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), workers injured. The structure of a book stall being set up by the Communist Party of India (CPI) was also vandalised.
The incidents come weeks after Adhikari, on September 10, urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for book stalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated the position two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Left-wing parties have been setting up book stalls during Durga Puja and other festivals in Bengal for decades. The practice dates back to 1954, when the undivided CPI set up the first festive book stall in Park Circus under the leadership of communist leader Muzaffar Ahmed.
Despite repeated electoral setbacks since 2011, the CPI(M) continues to have a network of festive book stalls across the state. The CPI, CPI(ML) Liberation and the Socialist Unity Centre of India (Communist), or SUCI(C), also set up stalls according to their organisational strength. Such stalls are set up during Kali Puja, Christmas and Eid as well.
In recent years, the Trinamool Congress, the BJP, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and its affiliated organisations have also begun setting up book stalls. However, the public call by a sitting chief minister to deny Left parties space at festive venues marks an unprecedented escalation in the dispute.
Attack on Book Stall in Dhakuria
According to eyewitness accounts, the CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI have been setting up book stalls near the Dhakuria bus stand during Durga Puja for decades. On Wednesday, around 5.30 pm, a group of 10 to 12 men arrived while CPI(ML) Liberation workers were supervising the construction of their stall. The men allegedly ordered them to stop work, identified themselves as BJP-RSS workers and demanded that the site be vacated, claiming they intended to set up their own stall at the same location.
Manas Chatterjee, also known as Babun, a member of the CPI(ML) Liberation’s Kolkata district committee, said the party had been operating its book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since at least 1985.
“From the very beginning, the body language of the group was extremely hostile. They said that beef is consumed at our book stall and that they would not allow us to set up our stall this time,” Chatterjee said.
According to him, the group claimed to have permission from the police to set up a stall at the same location and demanded that the Left workers produce their own permission. “When I confronted them, asking who they were to demand such permission, they said that their ‘Raj’ had started and that now everything had to be done according to their whims,” he said.
Chatterjee alleged that the group repeatedly claimed to have permission from the joint commissioner of Kolkata Police and said this entitled them to set up a stall wherever they wanted.
When Chatterjee tried to prevent the group from tearing down a hammer-and-sickle flag, he was allegedly assaulted. Between 10 and 15 youths pinned him to the road and kicked and punched him on his waist and chest, he said. The under-construction stall was subsequently ransacked and uprooted.
Chatterjee alleged that police personnel were present near the site, but left when the assault began.
Amalendu Bhushan Chowdhury, an 89-year-old CPI(ML) Liberation activist, was also allegedly assaulted when he tried to protect Chatterjee.
As the confrontation escalated, local CPI(M) leader Achyut Chakraborty intervened. He alleged that members of the group splashed hot tea on him and assaulted him.
Chakraborty said the CPI(M) had been setting up a book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since 1977, with the CPI and CPI(ML) Liberation subsequently joining the practice.
“What happened this year is unprecedented,” he said. According to Chakraborty, the group aggressively demanded to see police permission for the stalls and began assaulting Left workers when questioned about its authority to do so.
He alleged that the BJP workers initially outnumbered the Left activists after mobilising around 40 to 50 people over the phone. Party workers and local residents then gathered at the spot, but the Left workers tried to prevent the confrontation from escalating further.
“Book stalls during the puja have always been a defining feature of the festive season in West Bengal. The BJP’s fascist brigade is vandalising such stalls. At a book stall near Dhakuria bridge in Kolkata, our local committee secretary and State Committee member Comrade Babun Chatterjee has been seriously injured by the fascist goons. Veteran octogenarian Comrade AB Chowdhury has also been beaten up. Condemn this fascist assault on comrades and on the progressive cultural tradition of West Bengal,” CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya said in a Facebook post.
Police Permission Becomes a Point of Contention
Following the incident, CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI workers approached Lake police station to lodge a complaint. According to the Left parties, police said the stalls did not have the required permission and that, since the parties had only informed the police about their plans to set them up, and not sought formal permission, the police could not intervene.
Chakraborty said the police repeatedly asked whether the parties had obtained permission from the joint commissioner of police. “It intrigued us that the tone of the BJP workers and the police sounded similar on this issue,” he said.
The Left parties maintain that the land belongs to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), to which they have paid the required fees to set up their stalls. They said the established practice has been to inform the local police station rather than obtain police permission, and that this arrangement has been followed for close to 50 years.
Chakraborty said police were unable to produce a notification establishing that the rules had changed and that prior police permission was now mandatory.
According to CPI(M) and CPI(ML) Liberation leaders, the issue of police permission has not arisen in other parts of Kolkata, where stalls have been set up after informing the police.
On Thursday, Left party workers marched from the Dhakuria bus stand to Lake Police Station. The rally was attended by CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh, former CPI councillor from KMC Ward 92 Madhuchanda Deb and CPI leader Prabir Deb, among others.
Police, however, maintained that the stalls lacked the required permission and that they could not assist the parties because the joint commissioner had not approved them.
“It won’t be an overstatement to say that the Lake Police Station tried using the BJP workers, who are mostly outsiders, to heckle us so that the stalls would not come up,” he said.
Alt News contacted Lake police station, but officials declined to comment. The Left parties said their stalls would be inaugurated on Friday despite the dispute.
Voice of Opposition Should not be Suppressed: HC
The Dhakuria incident is not the only controversy involving Left party book stalls. The CPI(M) has also reportedly faced opposition to setting up stalls in other places in the state. According to a report in Anandabazar Patrika, similar incidents have been reported from Behala and Kasba in Kolkata, Shibpur in Howrah, Naihati in North 24 parganas and elsewhere.
The CPI(M) approached the Calcutta high court on Wednesday in this regard. In their petition, the party mentioned an incident of October 6 in Bongaon. As the party started work for building a book stall there, people allegedly from Hindu Jagran Mancha stopped them. Left workers were allegedly assaulted and threatened against putting up the stall.
Justice Sougata Bhattacharya, hearing the petition, sought the police’s response and observed that the state could not “pick and choose” while granting permission. The opposition could not be denied permission in a manner that effectively stifled its activities, the court said.
“It is not right to allow one party and deny permission to others. The voice of an Opposition political party should not be suppressed in this manner. They are not setting up a lottery shop; they want to sell books. What is the problem?” Justice Bhattacharyya observed.
The state subsequently approached a division bench, arguing that the proposed stall was to be set up on Public Works Department land without permission and that a report should be sought from the department rather than the police. On Thursday, the division bench sent the matter back to Justice Bhattacharya.
Later that day, Justice Bhattacharya directed that the CPI(M) be allowed to set up its book stall within 100 metres of the intended location. The court held that the police would be responsible for dealing with any untoward incident and assigned responsibility for maintaining law and order around the stall to the superintendent of police of Bongaon Police District and the inspector-in-charge of Bongaon.
In its order, the court observed that if other people were allowed to set up stalls selling different items during the festive season, the CPI(M) should not be prevented from selling books.
It added that the dissemination of different political thoughts and ideologies was welcome in a democracy because it made democracy “fruitful, deep-rooted and matured”. The court also said it expected the ruling dispensation to create an atmosphere in which people aligned with different political ideologies would not hesitate to express their views.

Student protests over the condition of schools in France recently escalated to broader demonstrations against a rising cost of living, ultimately splintering into what The New York Times described as "chaos" and sparking an outpouring of false or misleading claims about the severity of the demonstrations.
While shocking truths can come to light thanks to acts of protest, the flip side for fact-checkers is a growing number of requests to verify claims that involve visual media like images and videos. The unregulated use of artificial intelligence tools and the fast-spreading nature of social media have made it easy for such false or misleading claims about protests to spread.
We dug into the Snopes archives to collect a variety of claims that involved fake or misleading images or videos related to protests.

You’re reading our ESMO in 30 Seconds newsletter. Sign up here to get updates from the major European cancer conference in your inbox.
Hello again from Madrid, where we can tell you it’s Day 2 of the European Society for Medical Oncology’s annual meeting, but definitely not what day of the week it is. Perhaps some of the other nearly 40,000 people here can relate?
Enjoy today’s newsletter; we’ll be back with one more edition wrapping up the conference Monday afternoon. And on Thursday, join us for The STAT Recap, where we’ll catch you up on all the ESMO news you need to know, and answer your questions live.
In the meantime, we’re at [email protected] and [email protected].
Inside Moderna and Merck’s ‘presidential’ presentation
Adam Feuerstein/STAT
No surprise, the arena-sized room was packed with ESMO attendees eager to see Georgina Long of the Melanoma Institute Australia present the intismeran INTerpath-001 study results. The unfortunate data leak on Thursday made her talk less dramatic, but at the end, she received extended applause and a limited standing ovation.
Long summarized the intismeran results — a 42% reduction in the risk of disease recurrence and a 38% reduction in the risk of distant metastasis-free survival — as a “new benchmark for adjuvant treatment of melanoma.”
“More critically,” she added, “it establishes intismeran as a landmark advance in personalized cancer medicine.”
The full trial data will be published next month in the New England Journal of Medicine, Long also noted.
Inge Marie Svane of the University of Copenhagen, the discussant following the data presentation, was positive if not overly enthusiastic about the trial, describing the results as “compelling” and adding that they “mark a crucial moment for personalized cancer vaccines.”
But Svane also pointed to a number of outstanding questions, including whether there would be a survival benefit with intismeran, and what exactly was driving the vaccine’s benefit — was it the specific targeting of the neoantigens, or was it the general immune boost that studies have suggested mRNA vaccines provide?
She also took no position on the best way to treat the approximately 40% of higher risk melanoma patients enrolled in the study — a key debate with commercial implications. If intismeran is approved, it will compete against neoadjuvant immunotherapy, or treating patients before surgery. Svane laid out pros and cons of each approach, leaving the question of which will benefit patients more unanswered.
On mistrust and mRNA
The vast majority of the discussion about Merck and Moderna’s cancer vaccine centered on the quality of the data and the further application of individualized cancer therapies. But Toni Choueiri, of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, raised an important point during an address in a special session all about mRNA vaccines.
Mistrust and misinformation, Choueiri said, “is a key challenge to adopting anything that is mRNA.”
It seems that many people who hold unfounded doubts about mRNA vaccines for infectious diseases separate the technology’s potential in cancer — no more so than the people running the U.S. health department. While the federal government is throwing its weight behind cancer vaccines, it’s also drastically cut funding for mRNA vaccine research for pathogens.
But Choueiri said the pandemic highlighted how widely and quickly myths can spread, citing 2022 survey data that indicated 15% of people falsely believed that the mRNA Covid-19 shots could alter human DNA.
The concern is that such misguided fears could have ripple effects to anything called a vaccine, particularly if it’s made with mRNA. Choueiri noted that some people have moved away from using “vaccine” when describing products like the Merck-Moderna treatment, instead calling it a personalized neoantigen therapy.
Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel, speaking to STAT a couple of hours before the intismeran presentation, believes showing the benefits of an mRNA-based therapy in cancer — a disease that has affected a broad swath of Americans — will go a long way towards shifting perceptions of people who might have viewed mRNA in a negative way.
“I think the cancer treatment is going to help a lot,” Bancel said. “People will realize what we already know, that mRNA is a molecule that’s already in your body.”
An expanded use for Amgen’s Imdelltra in small cell lung cancer
The combination of Amgen’s Imdelltra plus Astrazeneca’s Imfinzi used as a maintenance regimen improved overall survival in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer — a successful outcome that is expected to expand the commercial opportunity for Imdelltra in small cell lung cancer.
The presentation also drew a standing ovation from some in the room.
In the DeLLphi-305 study, the median overall survival for patients treated with Imdelltra and Imfinzi was just over 21 months compared to just under 13 months for patients receiving Imfinzi alone. Statistically, the doublet regimen reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to Imfinzi.
Cytokine release syndrome, a type of immune side effect, was reported by nearly half of the participants in the doublet arm, but the cases were mostly mild to moderate.
The 563 patients enrolled in the study had extensive-stage small cell lung cancer that had not yet progressed following first-line immunotherapy. The study was published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.
The results appear to set a new survival benchmark for maintenance therapy in small cell lung cancer. A previous study that combined Jazz Pharma’s Zepzelca with Roche’s Tecentriq reduced the risk of death by 27% compared to Tecentriq alone.
“The separation of the curves that we’re seeing here is not the kind of thing that we typically see in small cell lung cancer,” Jacob Sands of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, who presented the data, told reporters. “These are extraordinary hazard ratios.”
Stephen Liu, a Georgetown University oncologist who was the study’s discussant, echoed that point.
If patients are eligible for the treatment approach, Liu said, “I can’t think of a subset where I would not want to offer this regimen.”
Astrazeneca’s bladder cancer push falls short
The neoadjuvant, or presurgical, use of Astrazeneca’s drug Imfinzi in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer reduced the risk of death by 42% compared to surgery alone. The risk of disease progression or death was reduced by 49% compared to surgery alone.
The positive results, however, don’t quite match the current standard of care.
Astrazeneca’s Phase 3 VOLGA study treated advanced bladder cancer patients with Imfinzi plus Pfizer’s Padcev before surgery, followed by Imfinzi after surgery, and compared their outcomes to patients who only underwent bladder surgery.
The study was published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.
At two years of follow up, 63% and 45% of the patients in the Imfinzi-Padcev and surgery only arms, respectively, were alive without tumor progression. Overall survival at the same time point favored the Imfinzi-Padcev group over surgery alone, with 78% and 69% of patients alive, respectively.
The VOLGA outcomes fell short of the current standard of care for the neoadjuvant treatment of muscle-invasive bladder cancer. Merck’s Keytruda plus Padcev reduced the risk of death by 50% and the risk of tumor progression by 60% compared to surgery alone.

Using Google’s products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world’s largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won’t use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company’s privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall.
On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy, spotted by Android Authority. The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos,” the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language.
This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it’s shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026, allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it’s also proving to be a privacy minefield.
Personal Intelligence connects your data to the Gemini app but also to features like AI Mode search. While the Gemini app does not currently have ads, you may see sponsored content in AI search tools. Google’s changes to the privacy policy appear to acknowledge that data shared with AI search via Personal Intelligence could, therefore, contribute to ad personalization.
According to Google, this clarification still doesn’t mean ads are “based directly” on your personal data. Here’s the company’s full statement:
“Connecting your apps is entirely opt-in. Ads will continue to be relevant to things like your query, the context of the response and your interests. Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library, and as always, sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads.”
Google’s statement is essentially a roundabout way of confirming that Workspace and Photos data may inform ads. If you interact with AI Mode while Personal Intelligence is enabled, there’s a chance that summaries and insights from your data will inform the answers you get. Because that same data is used for ad targeting, it’s accurate to say that your personal data is an element of ad targeting in AI search. The privacy policy now makes that clear.

The story so far:
France reported the first known human infection with Shamonda virus on October 22, 2026. The patient, who was severely immunocompromised and receiving treatment for a serious illness at the Hospices Civils de Lyon, died in early October. Investigations are underway to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the death, and how the patient acquired the infection.
French authorities suspect that the patient was infected by the bite of a Culicoides midge in eastern France, where the virus had been circulating among animals during spring and summer. The specific insect responsible has not been identified. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the virus has been detected in farm animals in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Jersey.
French authorities say that no public health risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge of the virus. The World Health Organization (WHO) has also said that wider spread is unlikely based on the information currently available. However, investigations into the human case are continuing.
What is Shamonda virus?
Shamonda virus is a vector-borne virus belonging to the genus Orthobunyavirus in the family Peribunyaviridae. It is part of the Simbu group of viruses, which also includes Schmallenberg virus and Akabane virus.
The virus was first isolated from cattle in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in parts of Africa and Japan. Before the recent case in France, it was considered an animal pathogen that did not infect humans.
Cattle are considered its main animal hosts, although infections have also been detected in sheep, goats, horses and alpacas. In livestock, infection can cause fever, diarrhoea, lethargy, loss of appetite and reduced milk production. In pregnant animals, it has been associated with abortions and congenital abnormalities in offspring.
Neurological signs have also been reported in horses infected with the virus in Europe. The extent to which the variants circulating in Europe differ in their effects on animal health remains under investigation.
How does it spread?
The virus is understood to spread primarily through the bites of infected Culicoides midges, tiny blood-feeding insects. The precise midge species responsible for transmitting the European variants has not yet been established.
According to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), there is currently no evidence of horizontal transmission, or spread between animals through direct contact or other routes. Vertical transmission, from a pregnant animal to its offspring, has been reported.
Two genetically distinct variants, designated Shamonda virus Europe 1 (SHAV-EU1) and Shamonda virus Europe 2 (SHAV-EU2), have been identified in Europe in 2026. Research indicates that they may have been introduced separately. Their geographical distribution, effects on livestock and long-term significance remain under investigation.
Why is it in the news?
The detection in a human has raised questions about whether Shamonda virus can cause disease beyond its known animal hosts. French authorities have reported that the brain complications observed in the patient before death were considered very likely to be linked to the infection. However, investigations are continuing to establish whether the virus caused or contributed to the death.
The patient was severely immunocompromised and had an underlying serious illness. It is not yet known whether similar complications would occur in people with different health conditions or whether people without immune suppression could develop symptomatic infection.
The case highlights the importance of the One Health approach, which recognises the links between human, animal and environmental health. Monitoring infections in livestock, investigating unusual human infections and sharing laboratory findings can help identify emerging health risks.
The virus is also affecting livestock production. A study of nine French dairy herds found a 15%–75% decline in bulk milk production during clinical episodes associated with infection. Affected cattle also showed symptoms such as diarrhoea, reduced activity and, less consistently, fever. The findings are from a small number of farms and do not establish the typical impact across all affected herds.
How prevalent is it?
The prevalence of Shamonda virus in humans is unknown. The French case is the first documented human infection, but it does not establish when the virus first began infecting people or whether other infections have gone undetected. There is insufficient data to estimate the number of human infections worldwide.
In animals, the virus has been identified in parts of Africa and Japan. Its detection in European livestock in 2026 has expanded its known geographical distribution. By October 22, the ECDC had reported detections in farm animals across 12 European countries and Jersey.
These reports indicate the geographical spread of detections, not the proportion of animals infected. Differences in veterinary surveillance, laboratory testing and reporting make it difficult to compare the burden between countries.
There are no verified figures establishing the prevalence of Shamonda virus in India so far. However, the absence of reported detections does not establish that the virus is absent from the country.
The virus is not subject to routine official surveillance or control measures under the European Union’s Animal Health Law. This may limit the completeness of information on its distribution and prevalence in livestock.
How is it diagnosed and treated?
In animals, the symptoms of Shamonda virus infection can resemble those of other livestock diseases. Laboratory testing is therefore needed to confirm infection. Molecular tests, including polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays, can detect the virus’s genetic material, while genetic sequencing can help distinguish between variants.
Evidence on the clinical presentation and management of human infection remains limited. There is currently no established, Shamonda-specific treatment protocol for human infection. Further investigation is needed to determine how the virus affects humans and what clinical management may be appropriate.
According to WOAH, there are no commercially available vaccines against Shamonda virus. No established vaccine is available for preventing human infection.
What is the public health risk?
French authorities have said that no public health risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge. The WHO has assessed wider spread as unlikely on the available evidence. These assessments reflect what is currently known and may change as further information becomes available.
Key questions include how the patient acquired the infection, whether the virus contributed to the death, whether other human infections have occurred and whether the virus can spread between people. There is currently no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission.
Surveillance of livestock, laboratory investigations and coordination between animal and human health authorities will be important in answering these questions.
For now, the available evidence supports continued monitoring and investigation. The first human case is significant because the virus was previously considered unable to infect humans, but it does not establish that Shamonda virus is spreading widely among people or that a human outbreak is under way.

The Hindu Group, in association with the Cancer Institute (WIA), Adyar, launched Cancer 360: Overview of Detection, Treatment, Palliation, a book examining cancer care from prevention and early detection to treatment, rehabilitation and palliative care. The book was launched at The Hindu office in Chennai.
N. Ram, director of The Hindu Group, launched the book alongside Suresh Nambath, editor of The Hindu. Mr. Ram handed over the first copy to E. Hemanth Raj, executive vice-chairman of Cancer Institute.
Speaking at the launch, Mr. Ram emphasised the importance of making advanced cancer care accessible and affordable. He highlighted the institute’s work in providing treatment to those who need it most and stressed the need to ensure that advances in cancer care reach patients facing barriers to treatment.
Dr. Hemanth Raj spoke about the need to translate advances in cancer research, much of which takes place in the West, into practical interventions in local settings. He also highlighted the institute’s charitable programmes, supported by donations, to help patients access treatment and facilities, and its plans to expand cancer care to reach more patients.
Arvind Krishnamurthy, professor of surgical oncology at Cancer Institute, stressed the need for continued research to improve cancer care and develop better treatments.
The book also addresses care beyond treatment. Mahalakshmi Rangabashyam Shetty, ENT surgeon and lecturer in the Department of Surgical Oncology at the institute, spoke about individualised treatment plans developed through multidisciplinary consultations. She also highlighted the need to tailor exercise and nutrition regimens to individual patients, alongside supportive services such as hospice care.
Surendran Veeraiah, professor and head of the Department of Regional Cancer Centre (RCTC), Cancer Institute, emphasised the importance of psychological support and allied services. He said the book could help make technical information on comprehensive cancer care accessible to more people.
The book features contributions from experts across oncology and allied disciplines. Its chapters cover multidisciplinary tumour boards, psychological care, onco-physiotherapy, palliative care, cancer research, speech and swallowing rehabilitation, early detection, precision treatment, pathology, nutrition and healthcare quality.
The book is available free of cost to The Hindu subscribers at https://www.thehindu.com/premium/ebook/

SS Rajamouli has opened up about his decision to keep details of his upcoming film Varanasi under wraps. Speaking to Brazilian YouTube channel ALMANAQUE21 on the sidelines of the 50th São Paulo International Film Festival, where he received the Leon Cakoff Career Award, the filmmaker said describing the scale of the Mahesh Babu-starrer in words can be difficult.
SS Rajamouli says Varanasi travels across different worlds, time zones and mythology; explains “adventure scheme” of Mahesh Babu-Priyanka Chopra Jonas starrer
Rajamouli said, “Sometimes I don’t, because the words don’t do justice to the scope of the film. That’s the reason why I released a glimpse of what Varanasi is to be. Instead of putting any words to it, we made a video which we released last year. It takes the audience through the worlds of Varanasi, what they’re going to experience, without telling them anything.”
SS Rajamouli reveals Varanasi travels across different worlds
While Varanasi has been described as an adventure involving time travel, Rajamouli added, “It is an adventure which travels through different worlds. It travels through Antarctica, through Africa, through the city of Varanasi, in different time zones. It travels into the time of mythology, where you see giants, Gods, and all that stuff.”
However, according to Rajamouli, the emotional core of the film remains grounded in human relationships. He added, “But everything is driven by the emotion of a father and son, and the emotion of a man and a woman…the love between them. That drives this entire adventure scheme.”
Directed by SS Rajamouli, Varanasi is co-written by his father V Vijayendra Prasad and cousin SS Kanchi. The film is produced by Sri Durga Arts and Showing Business. Mahesh Babu stars as Rudhra, while Priyanka Chopra Jonas plays Mandakini and Prithviraj Sukumaran essays the antagonist Kumbha. The film marks Rajamouli's first feature after RRR, his 2022 blockbuster starring Ram Charan and Jr NTR.

Uganda imposes 21-day quarantine on citizens returning from DR Congo
- Published
Ugandans returning from neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, the health ministry has said, as the country tightens restrictions to contain the spread of Ebola virus.
More than 4,500 people have died in DR Congo since May - the country's deadliest outbreak of the disease - and has since spread to several other countries.
Uganda's restrictions follow questions after two people who had travelled through the country tested positive for Ebola, in Kenya and Nigeria.
The health ministry on Sunday said the 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan Ebola patient had all been discharged.
Announcing the new measures on Sunday, the health ministry said travellers who had been to DR Congo would not be allowed to transit through Uganda.
It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost".
Uganda has also "intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings, supported by screening at designated road checkpoints", it added.
Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme that only essential travellers from DR Congo would be allowed in but would be subjected to "intense public health measures".
"All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola," he said.
Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August.
Concerns have however persisted after the two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day.
The patient in Nigeria is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya, while the Kenyan had travelled from the DR Congo where he had business interests.
Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients.
The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi, and the country has since confirmed eight other cases of Ebola. A second woman, related to the businessman died over the weekend.
Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure.
The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to "remain vigilant".
"We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties," Baryomunsi said.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment - though trials are under way.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

The Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments has raised concerns over including Dr. Naresh Trehan, chairman and managing director of Medanta, in a committee constituted on the Supreme Court’s directions to examine the regulatory framework governing pharmaceutical marketing practices.
In a representation to the Department of Pharmaceuticals, the advocacy group urged the government to replace Dr. Trehan with a member free of potential conflicts of interest, arguing that the panel’s independence and impartiality must be safeguarded.
The committee has been tasked with examining the regulatory framework governing pharmaceutical marketing practices and making recommendations on the voluntary Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP), 2024.
The group said Dr. Trehan’s financial interests and association with the Medanta Group could give rise to a potential conflict of interest. It stressed that the committee’s deliberations and recommendations should be guided solely by public health considerations and the need to promote ethical practices and access to affordable healthcare.
Citing a 2018 report, the group referred to the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s (NPPA) examination of hospital bills across four hospitals, including Medicity-Medanta, which identified instances of overcharging. It also cited subsequent Supreme Court proceedings and assessments by State drug regulatory authorities in Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, and Karnataka concerning high markups in hospital tariffs.
The group said these concerns warranted scrutiny of the committee’s composition to ensure that its recommendations were transparent, impartial and guided by public interest.
While clarifying its support for consultations with a broad range of stakeholders, the group said its objection is specifically regarding the inclusion of a member whose financial interests raise questions about impartiality. Allowing such concerns to undermine the committee’s independence would defeat the purpose of the apex court’s directions, it added.
The representation called on the Department of Pharmaceuticals to reconstitute the panel by appointing a member without such conflicts of interest.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.
