Fintech startup axiTrust is in talks to raise around $5 Mn in fresh capital in its Series A funding round, people aware of the matter told Inc42 on the condition of anonymity. The fresh round is likely to be led by Singapore based Argor.vc, and will see participation from axiTrust's existing investor General Catalyst. Questions sent to axiTrust didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story. The fresh round has come almost a year after the startup raised $2.6 Mn in its seed funding round led by General Catalyst. Other investors including Atrium Angels, YAN Network and Supermorpheous are also on the fintech startup’s cap table. The fresh capital will help the startup build digital infrastructure to accelerate adoption of its surety bonds offering. For context, surety bonds are insurance-backed guarantees that assure a buyer or project owner that a business will fulfil its contractual obligations. Instead of blocking the capital as collateral, they allow the buyers to pay a premium to secure the guarantee, helping free up working capital and reduce financial strain. Founded in 2024 by Aditya Tulsian (CEO), Rajeev Chari (COO), and Mukund Daga (CRO), axiTrust issues, underwrites and manages digital surety bonds, providing an alternative to traditional, collateral-heavy bank guarantees. As per the startup, more than ₹15 Lakh Cr of MSME working capital is locked up as collateral for bank guarantees, and replacing these traditional guarantees with insurance-backed digital surety bonds can free that capital, expand credit access, and improve trust in business transactions. From digital underwriting and AI-based risk assessment to cashflow-based lending and embedded finance, they are filling long-standing gaps that traditional banks could not address efficiently. These solutions are helping businesses and consumers access credit with fewer delays, lighter paperwork, and better transparency. Investors are actively backing such startups because the lending market in India is massive, still underserved, and primed for digital disruption offering both strong growth potential and meaningful financial inclusion. As per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, the fintech sector saw funding of $243 Mn across 13 deals. Of these, the heavy lifting was done by lendingtech startup Centricity ₹280 Cr round and Navi’s $100 Mn pre-IPO funding.

Twenty-one-year-old Saouhum Sharma, a 4th-year History honours student at Hans Raj College, joined the October 12 rally led by Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi to the Supreme Court. By the end of the day, a knife had been slashed across his throat.
The Assault
Sharma and three friends met at Barakhamba Road at 2 pm. They subsequently met more friends and made their way to Mandi House.
“It wasn’t too chaotic at first,” he told Alt News. “We got the call from some Indian Youth Congress (IYC) people who were leading the protest around the area that Rahul Gandhi and everyone was reaching the Supreme Court; we should also reach the Supreme Court. The route from Mandi House to the Supreme Court is a straight road. So we decided to just start walking there. It was two groups of IYC workers and us.”
By 5.40 pm, the group had made some headway towards the Supreme Court when they encountered police barricades. “Some of the IYC people tried to topple the barricades but could not. So we went through a cut onto Sikandra Road.”
As they walked along Sikandra Road, they came across around 15 men standing beside a jeep. Sharma said some appeared to be Hindutva workers, based on what they were wearing.
“They were donning some markers of Hindutva workers. A couple of ‘gamchas’, one in a saffron-coloured T-shirt. Nothing overt, but definitely visible,” he said.
Initially, the men were provocative rather than violent, Sharma recalled. “They were whistling at the female IYC workers — whistling and calling after them. They called a few of them ‘chikni’. They were calling them while standing 20 metres ahead on the side of the road; arms around each other’s shoulders. From afar, they did not look like they would interfere because we outnumbered them. So we didn’t really think of turning back.”
However, as the group approached, the men began taking saffron flags with long poles out of the jeep. “They still weren’t exactly being violent, just provocative.”
Asked whether the men identified themselves as members of any organisation, Sharma said they did not. The flags, too, did not name any organisation, he said. They were generic saffron flags bearing images of an angry Hanuman or the Ram Mandir.
“The men decided to swing the poles, and the IYC workers got a bit agitated, and a bit of a brawl ensued between them; the IYC workers got into an argument with the goons,” Sharma said.
Amid the confrontation, a young man, whom Sharma estimated to be 18 or 19, entered their group. He was not wearing any of the visible markers that Sharma had associated with the men beside the jeep.
“Then this one guy, he was probably 18-19 years old, made his way inside our group. He wasn’t wearing any of those identifiable markers. So we couldn’t tell that he was from the other group. He stood beside me for about five seconds and then… it happened quite quickly.”
“He pulled out a barber’s knife. My friend saw it and dragged me towards herself at which point he swung the blade. He missed my face, and it grazed my neck. He walked away after that.”
Sharma said it took him some time to realise what had happened. “I felt a sting in my neck and realised I was bleeding. At that point, we walked away from the group and decided to head home.”
Encounter with Police
After walking around 500 metres from the spot of the assault, Sharma and his friends encountered a police official on Sikandra Marg, who spotted the blood on Sharma and called out to them.
“He was drinking chai by a police vehicle, wearing a light green vest. There wasn’t a lot of police presence at that point, as we were a little far from the protest site. He offered to give us a ride after he saw the blood,” Sharma said.
As the group considered the offer, the officer turned to the driver seated in the vehicle and asked him to detain them, Sharma alleged. “We got scared, turned him down and left. He insisted at first but didn’t follow us when we left. We immediately left the vicinity of the protest site, went to the Jama Masjid metro station and left.”
According to Sharma, the police official was not wearing a name tag.
“Thankfully, the cut wasn’t that deep as he missed my face and the knife only grazed my neck. After returning, I cleaned the wound a bit and then got a tetanus shot,” he said.

Nepal is set to receive $20 million from the United Nations’ climate loss and damage fund following devastating August floods that killed around 1,500 people and left more than 5,000 missing. But the allocation covers less than 1% of the country’s estimated reconstruction costs, raising questions about whether global climate finance is reaching vulnerable nations at the scale they need. The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) agreed to set aside the money through an emergency procedure at a meeting on Thursday, October 22, the Nepalese government said. The assistance is intended to “help address the severe damage caused by climate-related disaster”, the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment said in a statement, as per Reuters. The allocation marks a significant step for the fund, established to help developing countries cope with climate-related destruction. However, the money has not yet been disbursed. Nepal must submit a detailed proposal for approval by the fund’s board before payment can be made. The disaster began on August 26, when an avalanche of ice and rock near Nepal’s border with China’s Tibet region triggered destructive flooding downstream. According to official data cited by Reuters, the floods affected around 60,000 people across 15,000 families and damaged critical infrastructure, including roads, bridges, schools and 13 hydropower plants. Nepal estimates infrastructure losses at approximately $2.7 billion, while the overall cost of recovery and reconstruction could exceed $4.7 billion. Nepal sought assistance from the FRLD in a letter sent in August, less than a week after the floods. Prime Minister Balendra Shah, in his maiden address to the United Nations in September, described the disaster as a warning to the world and linked it to climate change, despite Nepal’s negligible contribution to global emissions. Nepal had also called for international recognition of the damage caused by climate change. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal clarified later in September that the government had not formally sought compensation from India, China or the United States. The FRLD emerged after years of demands from developing countries, which argue that they face disproportionate climate risks despite contributing relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions. The fund is intended to help countries address climate-related losses that cannot be avoided through mitigation or adaptation alone. With reconstruction needs estimated at more than $4.7 billion, the proposed $20 million contribution is unlikely to make a substantial difference to the overall recovery bill on its own. The decision comes ahead of COP31, the UN climate conference scheduled to take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. The U.S. military has restricted vehicles made by the Chinese car manufacturer BYD from its sprawling Kadena Air Base in Okinawa Prefecture over security concerns about the vehicles.
The ban, which took effect Monday, currently only affects Kadena — one of the largest U.S. Air Force installations in the region.
The U.S. Forces in Japan did not specifically explain what prompted the move, and officials with the Kadena base did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“Installation commanders are responsible for protecting their people, facilities, and assigned missions and may implement lawful, risk-informed security measures necessary to mitigate credible threats,” USFJ spokesperson Col. John Severns said.
The ban comes as the U.S. and other Western countries have been tightening their security messaging following concerns about the smart technology used by Chinese-owned car brands such as BYD, MG and Jaecoo.
In safety advice issued in late September, the Dutch government warned that vehicles’ modern technology — including GPS, microphones, cameras, entertainment systems and Bluetooth connections — could be used for spying by state actors.
Last year, the U.S. also issued a ban on the sale of some Chinese vehicles and related hardware and software if it was deemed they could be a national security risk.
Smart vehicles have raised particular security questions for governments, given the amount of information that app developers, manufacturers and companies can access. This data is valuable to external parties or state actors who could receive the data from companies or obtain it via illegal means like hacking.
In June, the Pentagon added BYD to a blacklist of 188 “Chinese military companies” banning direct procurement or contracting with the firms.
It was not clear whether the BYD ban will be extended to other U.S. bases in Japan.
The Kadena Air Base is a crucial hub for U.S. military operations in the region. The U.S. military’s Typhon midrange missile system — believed capable of firing Tomahawk cruise missiles as far as 1,600 kilometers — is currently being stored at the base after it was deployed for joint military exercises earlier this year.
The decision to “temporarily” store the weapon there, effectively putting parts of China within striking distance, has prompted outrage in Beijing.

Emergency services say 83 injured, 7 seriously, in a bus crash near Barcelona
Local emergency services report that more than 80 people have been injured in a bus crash near Barcelona in Spain
MADRID -- A bus crash in the Barcelona area of Spain injured more than 80 people, local emergency services said Sunday.
The Catalan medical emergency services said 83 peoplewere injured, including seven people seriously, 18 less seriously and 58 with minor injuries, in the crash in Fogars de Monclús near Barcelona.
Spanish news agency EFE said the bus had veered off a narrow, winding road and fallen down a 20-meter (65-foot) embankment on Sunday afternoon.
The exact circumstances of the crash were not immediately clear and were under investigation, EFE said. Emergency services said they deployed 23 ambulances and two medical helicopters to the scene, as well as three joint teams of firefighters and medical personnel and three psychological support teams.
Olga Pane, health minister of the Generalitat of Catalonia, said rescue crews were searching the area to determine whether there might be any more victims.
EFE reported that the fire service also dispatched specialist mountain rescue teams.

Judge says DOJ illegally fired the daughter of former FBI director Comey
A New York federal judge ruled Monday that the Justice Department unlawfully fired former prosecutor Maurene Comey, who is the daughter of ex-FBI Director James Comey.
Maurene Comey served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan for around a decade, working on high-profile cases against defendants like Sean "Diddy" Combs, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. The Trump Justice Department fired her in July 2025 despite her consistently receiving accolades from the department for her work.
In response, she sued the Justice Department and others, arguing that her dismissal was unlawful and unconstitutional. Her lawsuit said she was fired because her father is the former FBI director, a prominent critic of President Trump.
The Justice Department has twice indicted the elder Comey. The first case was dismissed. The second prosecution, which is still pending, accuses him of threatening the president in a photo of seashells posted on social media.
In his ruling Monday, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman, a nominee of former President Barack Obama, wrote that the Department of Justice "invented a new and expansive theory of executive power" in dismissing Maurene Comey, and violated her constitutional right to due process.
"To accept Defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system," the judge wrote.
The opinion adds to concerns of politically motivated dismissals at the DOJ. Several federal prosecutors and former FBI agents have sued the DOJ under the Trump administration over their dismissals, alleging that they were fired for political reasons tied to their work.
Comey's lawyers praised Monday's ruling, and said it reaffirms that the president must comply with the law as part of the Constitution's checks and balances.
"This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law," her attorneys said in a statement.
The judge's ruling calls for Comey to receive back pay dating to when she was fired last year, and for her to return as a prosecutor to the Southern District of New York, if she so chooses.
The Justice Department said it disagreed with the decision, and would appeal in due course.
The court's order is not final. Judge Furman did yet not rule on Maurene Comey's First Amendment argument that she was fired for politically protected speech, and plans to hear further briefings on that claim.

Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
- Published
From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.
There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".
Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.
"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.
The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.
String of incidents
Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.
Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds".
Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.
The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000.
Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".
This was just the start of the problems.
Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team. During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.
In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.
Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations.
"Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said.
"During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."
'Overwhelmingly cheaper'
As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.
GL Events had won the 63bn yen (£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.
A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.
Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.
But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games".
"We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.
Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given.
"Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.
GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.
Hopes for the future
Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.
It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.
Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.
But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit.
"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."
While the Games may be over, the problems aren't.
Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three events. Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also deputy head of the Games organising committee, called it "unacceptable" and offered his apologies.
Prof Tomiyama hopes organisers will take lessons from the past few weeks to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future.

Most people worldwide could be categorised as having a high genetic risk for three of 28 common conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and schizophrenia, even if they might not develop them, a new study has found.
Researchers, led by the UK's University of Exeter, described the 'average' human genome, finding that everyone, regardless of their current health status, could be considered at risk for numerous conditions based on their genetics alone.
Every person's genome, or the average human genome, contains around five million variants, or DNA locations that differ between individuals, the findings published in the journal Genome Medicine reveal.
The locations include around 10,000 variants that alter gene sequences, which can have positive or negative effect, ranging from lactose intolerance to drug response, though are often biologically neutral, they show.
Each person also carries between one and three rare variants previously shown to cause serious genetic diseases, and another 50 rare variants that are currently of uncertain clinical relevance, the researchers found.
The team analysed data from two major population biobanks -- the UK Biobank and the US' All of Us -- that include whole genome sequencing, covering nearly one million individuals.
Senior author Caroline Wright, from the University of Exeter, said, "Whole genome sequencing has become such an important tool in diagnosing genetic disease, and we're increasingly moving towards genetic screening for predicting disease."
"Yet most people are unaware of just how much genetic variation is present in every genome. Actually, variation is the norm. For the first time, our study outlines what to expect in the average human genome, which can benefit clinicians and patients across the word in understanding, interpreting and contextualising genomics," Wright said.
The researchers also analysed numerous polygenic risk scores, which consider all known genetic factors to calculate a person's future risk of developing a disease.
"... applying polygenic scores (PGS) for 28 common diseases within UKB (UK Biobank), we estimate that the average person is in the top 10 per cent for (nearly) three conditions, and around one in five people are in the top one per cent for at least one PGS," the authors wrote.
"Importantly, we found that everyone carries a small number of genetic variants linked to disease, although many of these will not actually cause disease in that individual," Wright said.
The senior author added, "It is therefore crucial to consider context when interpreting findings from genetic testing, including symptoms or family history of disease as well as other clinical and environmental risk factors. Our findings also provide important context for professionals who are interpreting genetic testing results or commissioning genetic screening programmes."
Although the studies are large, participation is skewed towards people of Western European origin, and the researchers acknowledged the need for data from more diverse populations to further improve understanding and impact.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Five days after the spectacle, made possible by compressed-gas thrusters developed by Musk’s SpaceX, he revealed the companies were exploring a merger that could accelerate his push into autonomous driving.
At stake is more than a technological race. Car groups, already grappling with growing Chinese competition, are seeking to move beyond a business model centered on vehicle sales towards one that also generates recurring revenues from software and AI-powered services.
“Automakers are starting to look in the mirror and the software piece is what they are all looking at as the golden goose, because the margins are so high,” said Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner at merchant bank Yorkville Ives.
Even with Tesla’s strategic shift in recent years, its car business remains a crucial cash cow for the group, where it generates 75 percent of total revenues and will be pivotal for the heavy spending Tesla will need to make in AI to compete with its Big Tech rivals.
But Musk faces a vastly different competitive environment from 2008, when Tesla launched its first battery-powered Roadster. Chinese rivals are now winning the electric vehicle race while also investing heavily in software and AI to mount a tech challenge in autonomous driving.
Against that backdrop, Musk’s earlier goal to sell 20 million vehicles a year by 2030 has been watered down to 5 million, but even that is ambitious considering it only delivered 1.6 million last year.
Analysts said the near-term key to driving Tesla’s growth to 5 million sales would be its “Full Self-Driving” software, which, despite its name, still requires humans to sit in the driver’s seat and pay full attention.
Although Tesla ceded its position as the world’s largest electric vehicle manufacturer to BYD last year, Musk has claimed his company remains ahead of Chinese competitors in autonomous technology.
“The biggest driver for demand is Full Self-Driving. And today, there’s really no competitor for FSD in any car that you can buy,” he said at an earnings briefing on Wednesday where the company revealed it had its largest car order backlog in four years.
The proportion of new Teslas sold in North America with the company’s supervised version of FSD reached more than 75 percent, while it now has 1.7 million active FSD subscriptions globally, up 67 percent from a year ago.
The company has not disclosed how much recurring revenue is generated by FSD, which is priced differently depending on market but costs $99 a month in the US.
However, Ives noted that the technology was already the highest-margin segment of Tesla’s business, with the potential to “transform the whole financial model” if it were to be expanded to about 50 percent of its global customer base from roughly 10-15 percent at present.
He argued that such an expansion would contribute more to the business than selling an extra 50,000-100,000 cars a year: “For every dollar of FSD revenue, the market rewards it 50-70 percent more than that dollar they would generate from selling an actual car.”
But realizing that potential will depend on overcoming regulatory hurdles in multiple markets.
Tesla has yet to win any approval for its fully autonomous version of FSD.
Musk’s company and Volkswagen-backed Xpeng are in heated competition to win European approval for their advanced driver assistance and autonomous driving systems.
Tesla’s supervised version of FSD has been approved in the Netherlands and several other European countries, but it is seeking wider EU backing to roll it out across the bloc through a vote of member states that has been delayed until December.
Xpeng is working with German authorities and is targeting EU approval for its FSD rival XNGP after the bloc adopts regulations on advanced driver assistance and autonomous driving, expected early next year. “We aim to be one of the first,” said Xpeng’s general counsel Zheng Yeqing.
A visualization of Tesla’s “full Self-Driving” software in August.
Credit:
Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images
A visualization of Tesla’s “full Self-Driving” software in August.
Credit:
Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images
As competition intensifies, a SpaceX merger could offer Tesla the firepower to take on Chinese rivals as well as big tech groups with far bigger AI budgets.
Combining the businesses would create an integrated company that could accelerate research into materials, AI, and manufacturing while cutting costs and improving access to critical parts such as chips.
“You’re going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company,” Musk said at the flying Roadster event.
Lei Xing, founder of Chinese consultancy AutoXing, said “the future of mobility and vehicles will be autonomous, and autonomy will likely benefit from SpaceX tech.”
Evan Horetsky, a former Tesla executive and founder of industrial project developer Atlas Partners, said Chinese EV growth was “phenomenal and predicated on quick and full value chains of manufacturing—but don’t ever underestimate the Tesla team, always pushing technical boundaries in at least autonomy and robotics.”
One top 15 Tesla shareholder said he supported the merger, arguing that Tesla stood to benefit from “all the AI-related innovations now happening at SpaceX.”
The deal could also significantly increase Musk’s control over the businesses. According to William Blair analyst Jed Dorsheimer, the tie-up, if approved by shareholders and regulators, could allow Musk to control 50 percent or more of the merged entity.
But bringing the two businesses together could multiply existing risks.
“I think Elon Musk is playing a dangerous game,” said Max Willson, an industry observer and Tesla enthusiast. “SpaceX and Tesla have achieved extraordinary things, but combining his businesses risks tying their futures to his most speculative bets.”
“My concern is that trouble in AI could spread across the group, putting otherwise strong businesses at risk,” he added. “SpaceX’s success should be protected, not used to bankroll an ever wider set of ambitions.”
Whether or not the companies merge, Tesla’s technological ambition is already commanding the attention of traditional rivals.
The flying Roadster “certainly shows that even in the car world there’s a lot to do,” Ferrari’s chief executive Benedetto Vigna said at a recent automotive conference in Milan.
Tesla is already driving wider change in the industry. Like Musk’s company, China’s Xpeng, South Korea’s Hyundai, and Japan’s Toyota are expanding their robotics businesses while General Motors and Ford in the US are pursuing new revenue from their energy storage businesses.
Autonomous driving in particular has become a major battleground for the global car industry as EVs with similar ranges and pricing proliferate.
Tom Narayan, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets, said Tesla was “a classic case of an innovator that disrupts and the other follows because they don’t want to be left behind.”
Among traditional carmakers, General Motors last year hired former Tesla executive Sterling Anderson to oversee the Detroit carmaker’s product development, with a mandate to develop a new generation of fully autonomous personal cars.
Other European carmakers such as BMW and Mercedes-Benz have also partnered with technology groups such as Qualcomm and Nvidia to bring a “Level 2 plus” driver assistance system, which requires active monitoring by a human driver behind the wheel.
“The leading carmakers today… are trying to reconsider their strategy completely,” said Igal Raichelgauz, chief executive of Israeli autonomous driving technology start-up Autobrains. He added that manufacturers wanted to move to a subscription model with a more advanced eyes-off technology to generate new revenue.
Volvo Cars chief executive Håkan Samuelsson acknowledged Tesla’s position as the frontrunner in autonomous technology.
“Tesla is probably leading the development in the West,” he told the FT, while claiming that Volvo was still firmly leading in software. “We will, together with Nvidia, develop our cars to be door-to-door automated and that will come in a new Volvo car pretty soon here.”

Australian minister says he is being followed after bullet etched with ‘RAT’ left on car
The former firefighter and Labor member for Frankston in Victoria found the bullet on the bonnet of his car

A bullet etched with the word "RAT" was left on the car of an Australian minister, just days after an attack on MP Helen Haines.
Paul Edbrooke, a former firefighter and the Labor member for Frankston in the Australian state of Victoria, found the bullet on the bonnet of his car on Saturday, after being away from it for about an hour at a community event in his electorate.
It was also etched with his old five-digit firefighter identification number.
Victoria Police said detectives from its security investigation unit are investigating a threat against a member of the state parliament, which was reported to them on Sunday.
"I was pretty shocked to find that it was a bullet, not just a bullet, but a bullet with the word 'RAT' inscribed on it and my firefighter ID on it," Mr Edbrooke told reporters.
"The very fact of the matter that this has been put on my car means someone has been following me. It means someone knows what my car is, and that's really quite scary. But I'm not going to be intimidated by this, and I refuse to be bullied."
The car is also driven by his children, who are young adults, he said.
"It's a car they drive. They've been in this car. It could have been them that found the bullet, and that terrifies me. It's totally unacceptable," he said.
Mr Edbrooke said the identification number was a personal detail "only firefighters would be aware of".
He said he was getting aggressive threats and abuse on social media from a "small minority" of people in the United Firefighters Union (UFU) but that was not representative of firefighters. He said he did not know who left the bullet.
"This is just a small group of people in a union who believe everything they are told by a leadership and think that by somehow intimidating me or bullying me I will support them and give them a taxpayer funded slush fund for their union," he said.
The union is in a long-running dispute with Fire Rescue Victoria, an agency he oversees, over its pay agreement, which the parties have been unable to resolve since 2021, and is taking the agency to the Fair Work Commission, Australia's workplace tribunal.
It has also vowed to run an advertising campaign against the state Labor government, staff polling booths with firefighters and distribute authorised material urging voters to put Labor last in next month's election.
The union's Victorian secretary, Peter Marshall, condemned the threat.
"Threatening anyone, including a minister we strongly disagree with, is the opposite of everything this union stands for," he said in a statement. "I condemn it without qualification."
He said whoever left the bullet "does not speak for or act for firefighters or this union".
Mr Marshall also defended a video the union posted on Friday, in which he said Mr Edbrooke and the state premier, Ben Carroll, were "in the gun". He said he meant at the ballot box.
The incident comes days after the attack on Ms Haines, who lost both legs, and there is no suggestion the two are linked.
"Off the back of the horrific alleged attack with Helen Haines last week, it's incumbent on all of us to make sure we're trying to take the temperature down," Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson, told ABC Radio Melbourne.
The Greens said in a joint statement from their MPs that there was "absolutely no place for threats and intimidation towards MPs, public figures or anyone else in our society".
Mr Carroll said he was "disgusted" by the incident and that Mr Edbrooke "won't be intimidated by this".
Mr Edbrooke urged other parties to reconsider their relationships with the union. Members of the Liberal party, One Nation and the Greens have met the union in recent months, and the Greens appear to have the closest relationship, the Guardian reported.
The Greens candidate for the seat of Pascoe Vale, Angelica Panopoulos, is due to host a joint event with the union on Saturday, which was described on social media as a "free day of family fun with the Greens and United Firefighters Union".

Loggers say Roadless Rule repeal won't solve their biggest challenges
EUGENE, Ore. - President Trump is widely expected to soon open up some 44 million acres of the country's last pristine national forests in a move he says will bring timber jobs back to struggling small towns and help prevent wildfires in overgrown lands.
Trump signaled the move with executive actions last year aimed at dramatically boosting timber sales on U.S. Forest Service land and reversing the agency's 25-year-old Roadless Rule, which blocked most new logging on undeveloped national forestlands.
Today with the formal repeal of the Roadless Rule rule expected early next year, the picture on the ground in timber country looks messier. Those who make a living in the forests say the problems are much bigger than access to more trees.
"I'm not saying these EOs [Executive Orders] are useless, they set the tone," says Sean Smith, CEO of the family owned Starfire Lumber in Cottage Grove, Ore.
Smith, standing in a bustling lumber yard with the sawmill cranking behind four story high stacks of freshly cut timber, says the industry has more pressing challenges now, starting with the record high price of diesel fuel. Economists largely blame that on Trump's war with Iran. And then there's inflation, which is driving up the costs of just about everything.
"Steel, you know, we have to buy sawblades, we have to buy ball bearings," Smith says. "We have to buy a million different parts to keep this mouse trap going."
So repealing the Roadless Rule - which has largely banned new road building and logging projects on some 44 million acres of pristine national forests since 2001 - is lower on the priority list.
Smith, a burly man with a dry sense of humor and a neatly trimmed salt and pepper beard, does support the reversal saying it will eventually give industry a more reliable local timber supply. He says a lot of the nearby Willamette National Forest, roaded or not, is dangerously overgrown. That built-up fuel makes these forests more prone to catastrophic wildfires.
"This is not a 'gee I sure want more cheap timber volume,' you know, this is not me promoting an agenda," Smith says. "This is a guy who lives here and is tired of seeing these beautiful places burn up."
Trump says a boom is coming but the industry is a fraction of what it was
The administration alongside the timber industry and some local officials are pushing for the repeal, saying it will give the Forest Service more flexibility to carry out wildfire prevention, including tree thinning, on land that's largely functioned as wilderness since 2001.
But under recent Republican and Democratic administrations, the Forest Service has struggled to get those projects going on forests that already have roads. Lawsuits and red tape are an ongoing challenge, as is finding enough workers.
"Right now, there's not a ton of people that want to wake up at 2 a.m. and drive a log truck for the same price that you could go work at McDonald's for," says Jeff Brink, a second generation logger near Eugene, Ore.
Brink says the industry is a fraction of what it was when his dad and uncles started Brink Land Development in 1981. The company is getting by ok, for now he says, due to a steady stream of forest restoration projects on private land as well as some recent salvage logging timber sales from nearby wildfire burn scars.
But for many smaller, less established loggers already struggling, Brink says, labor shortages and high diesel prices could be the tipping point.
"For an industry already operating on low margins, this is a tough one," Brink says.
Due to tightening environmental laws and other market forces including cheaper Canadian lumber imports, timber sales on U.S. federal land dropped by close to 90% since the 1990s. Brink says today the infrastructure just isn't there for the forest work that needs to be done, let alone a promised timber boom.
"Rural Oregon is struggling and all the mills that aren't along the I-5 corridor or near urban centers that can source wood are closing," he says.
Since the 1990s, an estimated 400 mills across the broader Northwest have closed, amounting to the loss of about 35,000 jobs. Seven mills have closed in Oregon since 2024 alone.
Industry experts project that overturning the Roadless Rule could lead to a five to ten percent boost in federal timber sales. That's hardly enough to boost much enthusiasm on the ground.
"We're in an industry that for decades has been in a state of contraction," Brink says.
Several national environmental groups have also already signaled they plan to sue once the administration formally repeals the rule, which is expected to happen by early next year.
Some fear a revival of the bitter Timber Wars
Timothy Ingalsbee turns his hybrid station wagon onto Forest Service Road 2408, near the scene of an infamous year-long tree sit and blockade that he helped lead against a Forest Service old growth timber sale in the nineties.
"The industry [back then] was headed for a crash, they had exhausted the supply," Ingalsbee says, as he stops the car and gets out at a vista.
Today, his hair cropped shorter and greying, Ingalbee notes that many of those towering, old growth trees, their bark cloaked in moss, have burned in recent wildfires. Ingalsbee, a retired Forest Service firefighter, today runs a national firefighter safety and advocacy group.
"The claim that they're going to do all this new road building and logging in roadless areas on behalf of wildland firefighters, and make it more efficient for them, is just a big lie," Ingalsbee says. "Not in our name you don't."
Ingalsbee fears that punching even more roads into these forests will lead to more human-caused wildfires, which have been rising steadily for decades. But he doesn't think any of this is really about wildfire prevention or creating more logging jobs.
"What's driving a lot of Trump's executive orders for public lands management is not real economic drivers. I don't hear industry clambering for this," he says. "It's more ideology."
For Ingalsbee, the U.S. government is just racing to open up as much of the West as possible so industry can squeeze out maximum profits on timber, oil and coal.
Everyone is tired of policies 'whipsawing' from one president to the next
One thing that almost everyone on the ground in the Northwest agrees on is that Congress has largely failed to act on either protecting or opening up federal forest lands to more development.
When President Clinton signed the Roadless Rule by executive order at the end of his second term, Republicans controlled both the Senate and the U.S. House where appetite for passing more wilderness legislation was slim. The rule was the culmination of a sweeping inventory of land conducted by the Forest Service in which the agency had marked certain forests as prime acreage for wilderness protection.
Congress never codified it, and since then, the administrative rule has become an environmental flashpoint in a polarized country.
Back at Starfire Lumber, CEO Sean Smith is tired of federal forest and timber policy whipsawing from one presidential administration to the next.
"Sometimes the cynical side of me says, 'hey, what could be better than a do-nothing Congress at least they're not screwing anything up," Smith says, with a sardonic chuckle. "But that's no way to run a country long term."
Not to mention, he adds, it makes for a hard environment to keep a business going in.

BJP’s Manipur poll plans stalled amid continued violence
With the security situation in Manipur still precarious and the BJP state unit battling rifts, the party is yet to finalise its election strategy
NEW DELHI: Continuing violence and internal divisions have cast a shadow over the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) preparations for the upcoming Manipur elections and its bid to retain power in the state for a third term, party leaders aware of the matter said.
Manipur is slated to go to polls early next year, alongside Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Goa and Uttarakhand. State BJP leaders said they were banking on the Union government to restore peace in the strife-torn state and bridge the divide between warring communities before the polling cycle kicked in.
“Both the union and the state government have been making efforts to end the violence that has left many dead and displaced. But there is a need to take more steps both politically and administratively to end this cycle of violence that has gone on since 2023…” said a party leader on condition of anonymity.
Manipur has been reeling under violence since May 2023, when ethnic clashes first broke out between the dominant Meitei and tribal Kuki communities. Since then, almost every community has been engulfed by the spiralling violence that has led to a complete breakdown of law and order, the creation of ethnic enclaves, nearly 360 deaths, displacement of 66,000 people, and a virtual bifurcation of the state.
With the security situation still precarious, the BJP is yet to finalise its election strategy and campaign plans, leaving the cadre uncertain, people aware of the matter sad. “We are still waiting for the high command to work out the election plan. Last month, the party appointed [Assam legislator] Rajdeep Roy as the state in-charge, but we are still not in a position to hit the ground running,” the leader said.
The BJP, which won just 21 of the 60 seats in the 2017 polls, formed the government with the support of four National People’s Party (NPP) MLAs, four Naga People’s Front (NPF) MLAs, one Lok Janshakti Party MLA and an independent legislator, even as the Congress emerged as the single largest party with 28 seats. In 2022, the BJP returned to power with 32 legislators, while the Congress’s tally shrank to five.
N Biren Singh had become chief minister after both election victories. However, he resigned on February 9, 2025 amid mounting internal discord and the threat of a no-confidence motion as violence continued unabated in the state. A week later, President’s Rule was imposed in Manipur.
On February 4, 2026, former Manipur assembly speaker and BJP leader Yumnam Khemchand Singh, a Meitei, took oath as the chief minister. Along with Singh, two deputy chief ministers representing the Kuki-Zo and Naga communities — Losii Dikho and Nemcha Kipgen — also took oath in a low-key ceremony at the Lok Bhavan in Imphal.
However, the new government setup has also come under strain. Ties between Dikho and Kipgen have deteriorated amid clashes between members of the Naga and Kuki communities. On September 1, Dikho and eight other Naga lawmakers wrote to Union home minister Amit Shah seeking action against Kipgen and her husband, alleging that they were colluding with Kuki militants. Kipgen has rejected the charges.
“The state unit has been divided. On several occasions, the high command has to step in… even now, when there is a new chief minister [Yumnam Khemchand Singh] at the helm, there are camps and groups that sometimes seem to work at cross purposes,” the leader quoted earlier in the story said.
According to the leader, the Centre will need to announce specific rehabilitation and relief measures as a first step towards addressing the grievances of affected communities. “Ethnic violence and suspicion between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo and Naga groups has made the situation very challenging. These fractures will need to be handled carefully as the Opposition will use these to their advantage,” he said.
The prolonged unrest has also given Opposition parties, particularly the Congress, an opportunity to challenge the BJP’s claims of efficient “double-engine” governance.
The Congress has been seeking the dissolution of the assembly and fresh elections. Last week, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge posed three questions to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Shah, asking how many more innocent lives must be lost before they act.
“...Since May 2023, over 300 precious lives have been lost, while 24,530 are forced to be in relief camps in pathetic conditions. Women, children and vulnerable families continue to bear the brunt of this prolonged tragedy. The BJP’s political machinations, from imposing President’s Rule to replacing the Chief Minister and reinstalling its own government, have yielded no peace. PM Modi, who did not even set foot in Manipur for nearly 29 months after violence erupted, has abysmally failed on his so-called assurance in Parliament,” Kharge said in a post on X.

Barnes Ice Cap sits on the central plateau of Baffin Island, in the Canadian Arctic. It is the last surviving fragment of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, which at its peak buried most of Canada under two miles of ice and locked away around 80 meters of sea level. That remnant has now yielded direct physical evidence that ice sheets might have reversed their retreat and started to grow again thousands of years ago.
In a recent Science study, researchers show that the Laurentide reached its smallest size about 3,600 years ago, then started re-expanding roughly 2,000 years ago, which the team interprets as the opening move of the next glaciation. Apparently, this brand-new ice age was on its way until about 1960, when human-caused climate warming reversed it.
Frozen to the bed
“Barnes is the last remaining piece of one of the domes of the Laurentide Ice Sheet,” says Nicolás Young, a geologist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and lead author of the study. As that enormous dome thinned through the Holocene, its margin withdrew up onto Baffin Island, and what’s left today is the deflated core of something that was once two miles thick. The reason Barnes can testify about its own history, Young explains, comes down to the temperature at its base.
Most glaciers are warm-based, meaning meltwater at the bed lets them slide, and sliding ice grinds up everything beneath it, erasing the record. Barnes is cold-based, and thus frozen directly onto the bedrock beneath it, which prevents it from sliding.
“If there is an ice event where you live and you have to go and scrape off your windshield, that ice that’s plastered to the windshield of your car, that’s a good example of how cold-based ice operates. It’s sort of just stuck to what it’s on,” Young says.
This stuck ice preserves what’s beneath instead of eroding it. As the Laurentide retreated across the plateau, tundra plants colonized the newly bare ground. When the ice came back later, it simply smothered them in place and held them there, intact, for two millennia. To pinpoint the exact moment of this turnaround, Young’s team used two independent dating methods.

The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday (October 23, 2026), the head of the World Health Organisation said.
Also Read: Congo’s Ebola outbreak records more than 4,000 deaths
The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
The trial began with the first shot of Ervebo being administered in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the outbreak.
"Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means 'hope' in Swahili," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X.
"This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work," he said, adding that in the meantime, the existing Ervebo vaccine would be tested.
"WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives."
Two vaccines in the pipeline
The so-called Tumaini trial is a single trial framework that can test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines.
The trial will use a ring vaccination approach: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
It is gearing up to incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are currently advancing through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the U.S.-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Both have received funding from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, and are expected to enter the trial "shortly", CEPI said in a statement.
"Tumaini will work closely with affected communities, health authorities and outbreak response partners to generate robust evidence on vaccine performance that could contribute to curtailing the epidemic, saving lives, and strengthening preparedness for future Bundibugyo outbreaks," said CEPI.
The trial will include pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials.
'Important step'
WHO emergencies director Chikwe Ihekweazu said the trial was set up to generate the rigorous evidence needed to determine whether the participating vaccines could protect people at risk.
"If successful, this would be the first time we have clear evidence of vaccine efficacy against Bundibugyo virus — a major advance that could transform how we respond to this outbreak and prepare for future outbreaks and help save lives," he said.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
"Bringing this trial into the Ebola response is an important step towards addressing the urgent needs of affected communities," said Steve Ahuka-Mundeke, the DRC Ebola response incident manager.
The DRC declared its 17th outbreak of Ebola on May 15, and the WHO, two days later, triggered a public health emergency of international concern, its second-highest alert level.

Women’s hearts are different from men’s. Research from clinical trials that have required female participants only since 1993 have repeatedly drummed home that message, from varying chromosomes in heart muscle cells to different heart attack symptoms and causes. Yet wide gaps remain in heart health care for girls and women across specialties.
Recognizing that clinical fragmentation and the resulting harm to women’s health, four medical societies — the American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine, and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — have issued a framework intended to unite clinicians and patients over a lifetime of care, all aimed at dethroning cardiovascular disease as the leading cause of death in women. In that spirit, three articles offering guidance across the course of a woman’s life were published Monday in Circulation.
Their message: Because female-specific biology affects girls’ and women’s hearts throughout their lives, it requires connected, holistic care starting in adolescence to reflect transitions not found in the male models that have dominated health care: periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.
“What happens in adolescence and young adulthood impacts your life for years and decades to come, so having action at that point can really change the course of someone’s cardiovascular health story,” Sadiya Khan, chair of the writing group and professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, said. “So that these are all connected and not siloed, even though that’s typically how we have approached care, will require an integrative approach.”
Perimenopause in particular is a cardiovascular inflection point, the guidance says. It’s defined as the transition to variable period cycle length, skipped cycles, and hormone changes, occurring from about age 45 to 51. That’s when changes in cholesterol and metabolic health can be early signs of cardiovascular risk. “Identifying risk early and acting on it may reduce risk of cardiovascular disease,” she said.
Khan talked with STAT about the new guidance, where it came from and where its framers hope it will go. This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
What problem were you trying to solve?
Women uniquely see many different clinicians, yet there wasn’t a shared playbook. We were all working on our specific problem area or focus, but that misses the connections between them.
What’s an example?
We’ve really seen that with pregnancy. There’s been so much great work that has helped to highlight the connection between blood pressure and diabetes in pregnancy. That matters not just during that pregnancy, but across the life course. 
How does that play out?
The importance of transitioning from postpartum care to primary care to preventive care for the life course has gained a lot of attention. And we’re seeing a similar bubbling to the surface around perimenopause now, and how we’re addressing symptoms of menopause, but also the cardiovascular risk that’s changing during that time.
These things aren’t happening in isolation. They inform where their health is now, and what they do now matters for their health in the future.
Tell me how adolescence fits into this framework.
It is really critical that we recognize that hormonally mediated transitions are biologically unique to women. Those first few years, or perimenarche, at the time around the first period, is the departure from sex-agnostic medicine that should then continue. It doesn’t end with reproductive or hormonal health. It’s connected to cardiovascular health, and so is its impact on psychosocial health. Those things are really connected and need to be assessed together.
What is the psychosocial piece?
We know that hormone biology influences the heart as well as the mind and brain. So when we think about mental health and well-being, we know that depression and anxiety in teen girls starts to increase, and that continues for the rest of life. And particularly in key periods like in pregnancy and postpartum, those things can really increase, and that’s related to the hormonal changes that are happening. It’s all connected.
How can this play out?
Eating disorders and disordered eating bring in this additional layer of societal and structural differences in gender and the gendered norms that can also influence health. Women are more likely to live in poverty, are less likely to be compensated fairly, are more likely to be single parents. So when you start to incorporate some of those structural issues related to societal gender norms, they’re also a part of cardiovascular health.
What else is important to watch for in adolescence?
Changes in periods related to cycle duration and the amount of bleeding are important for two reasons. Heavy menstrual bleeding can lead to iron deficiency, and that can actually impair a girl’s ability to participate in activity or exercise, and also can impair cardiovascular health. It can serve as a flag for polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, as it’s now called [formerly PCOS, or polycystic ovary syndrome]. It’s really important to have that on our radar because it takes years, usually, before it gets diagnosed for most teens and young adults.
Is there a through-line you recommend to coordinate care?
For adults or adolescents, we’ll talk about what they should expect with their periods, what’s normal, and what is not. Similarly, around perimenopause and menopause, we’re clearly hearing, “I didn’t know what to expect. What is normal? What should I be looking out for?”
We should have a shared language for clinicians and patients so that we understand where someone is in their health journey and what to expect or anticipate for what comes next, so we can prepare people. And I think in adolescence, that’s the forward-looking part of it, so that they have this roadmap. It reminds me a lot of what we do in pediatrics already.
Such as?
The Ages and Stages Questionnaire is a fundamental part of the first two years of life. I still remember from my kids, right? When are they going to crawl, when are they going to walk? Everything is framed from positive developments and positive health changes.
We are now extending that across the life course for female-specific biology that is unique and accounts for transitions that men don’t experience around periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and importantly, also recognizing that postmenopause has a lot of cardiovascular implications that we want to make sure that we’re monitoring.
What about midlife and later?
I think one of the key things in this framework is calling out perimenopause as its own stage. I think there’s confusion on what is menopause, what is postmenopause, what is perimenopause. And what should that tell you about evaluating your cardiovascular health and making sure that symptoms are getting assessed and treated if needed.
Looking ahead, what do you see?
We’re focusing on women’s health, but everything we learn here means that we also need to understand what the differences are for men and how we can approach this for every single patient. How do we use all of this to really advance personalized medicine at the end of the day? Sex is a part of that, and it’s really about saying, how are we taking care of the patient in front of us.

Five years after being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, actor Christina Applegate revealed this week that she had been misdiagnosed. Her experience puts a public face on one of the most consequential challenges in neurology: how to diagnose a complex disease early enough to prevent irreversible damage without sacrificing accuracy.
How MS is diagnosed has changed dramatically during my nearly four decades in the field. When I began my career, physicians often had to wait for symptoms to recur before they could confirm MS. Today, advances in imaging, biomarkers, and diagnostic criteria are helping us recognize the disease earlier, when treatment may have the greatest opportunity to prevent irreversible neurological damage.
But progress brings a critical responsibility. Too many people still spend years searching for an accurate diagnosis, while others are told they have MS when another condition is responsible for their symptoms. Applegate’s experience is a powerful reminder that the future of MS diagnosis cannot be about speed alone. Our goal must be both: diagnosing MS earlier and getting the diagnosis right.
The challenge is that MS does not look the same in everyone, and other neurological disorders can produce similar symptoms. Signs such as numbness, vision changes, fatigue, and difficulty walking can occur in many other neurological disorders. Even abnormalities detected on an MRI are not necessarily unique to MS.
The consequences of both misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis can be substantial.
Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may receive treatments they do not need, potentially exposing them to unnecessary risks while delaying appropriate care for the condition actually causing their symptoms.
For people whose MS goes undiagnosed, time matters enormously. While there is not yet a cure for MS, there are more than 20 therapies that can help reduce disease activity and slow worsening for many people living with MS. Research has demonstrated the importance of initiating appropriate treatment early in the course of disease, before neurological damage accumulates. Every unnecessary delay can mean a missed opportunity to protect long-term neurological health.
Fortunately, decades of research have fundamentally changed what is possible.
Today, we have better diagnostic tools, more sophisticated imaging technologies, and a deeper understanding of MS than at any point in history. Yet significant challenges remain in ensuring that these advances reach the people who need them.
One of the most significant developments has been the evolution of the McDonald Diagnostic Criteria, the internationally recognized guidelines physicians use to diagnose MS. Working in partnership with the European Committee for Treatment and Research in Multiple Sclerosis, the National Multiple Sclerosis Society helped advance these criteria, contributing to progress that has shortened the diagnostic process from years to months in many cases. The latest revisions incorporate new imaging techniques and biomarkers designed to improve both the speed and accuracy of diagnosis.
One particularly promising example is an MRI technique that identifies the central vein sign, a feature that can help physicians distinguish lesions associated with MS from abnormalities caused by other conditions. Alongside progress in spinal fluid biomarker research, this technology offers the potential for earlier, more accurate diagnoses.
Artificial intelligence and sophisticated data analytics may eventually help clinicians recognize patterns in imaging and other clinical information, identify people who warrant further evaluation, and improve diagnostic precision.
These tools are still evolving, and they will require rigorous research and validation before they can be widely incorporated into clinical practice. But even the most sophisticated diagnostic tools cannot improve outcomes if patients cannot access the specialists and health care systems equipped to use them.
Access to neurological care across the country is uneven. Some communities face significant shortages of neurologists, particularly those with specialized expertise in MS. Patients may wait months for appointments, travel long distances to see specialists, or encounter lengthy referral processes before receiving the evaluation they need.
Clinician education is equally important. Primary care providers are often the first professionals to evaluate someone experiencing unexplained neurological symptoms. Helping them recognize potential early signs of MS and understand when to refer patients for neurological evaluation can make a meaningful difference.
Applegate’s willingness to share her experience has brought attention to an issue that extends far beyond any one person’s diagnosis. We have transformed our ability to recognize and treat MS over the past several decades, but scientific progress alone is not enough. The next challenge is ensuring that these advances translate into earlier answers, more accurate diagnoses, and better outcomes for everyone affected by the disease.
That will require continued investment in research to develop and validate better diagnostic tools, better education for the clinicians who first evaluate patients with unexplained neurological symptoms, and improved access to neurologists and MS specialists. Together, these efforts can help smooth the often difficult path from the first unexplained symptoms to an accurate diagnosis, while reducing the risk of both misdiagnosis and unnecessary delays.
The goal is not simply to diagnose MS faster. It is to get the diagnosis right, as early as possible, so that no one loses precious time, or the opportunity for appropriate treatment, while searching for answers.
Bruce Bebo, Ph.D., is chief research and medical affairs officer at the National Multiple Sclerosis Society. A cellular immunologist, he has dedicated nearly four decades to advancing research into multiple sclerosis, a commitment inspired by his mother’s experience living with the disease.

Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.
Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.
The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.
Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6.
“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”
Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability.
The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.”
Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.”
Cotton’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the US Justice Department did not answer questions WIRED sent Friday about the delay.
Clayton, who is legally responsible as director of national intelligence for declassifying the ruling, has made no such promise. Asked before his July confirmation whether he would ensure the opinion was public before Congress voted on reauthorization, he wrote only that the government was “working arduously to expeditiously declassify” it and had made the full opinion available to lawmakers.
Some of what the court found is already known. A FISA court opinion declassified last year described a similar FBI tool, a “participants filter” that let agents select people in contact with surveillance targets and read their messages. In February 2025, the Justice Department’s National Security Division told the court the tool had been running searches no one counted. The FBI shut it off the next month and switched it back on later that year, after the department approved a rebuilt version.
This year’s ruling went beyond that. The court found that tools agencies use to narrow intercepted data to an American’s messages amount to searches of Americans, subject to the same limits, and ordered them rebuilt, The New York Times reported in April, citing unclassified administration talking points sent to lawmakers. Senator Alex Padilla said in a written question to Blanche that the Justice Department “is appealing portions” of the ruling “limiting the government’s use of certain filtering tools.”
While the ruling stayed secret, seven intelligence agency fact sheets from March 2026, one dated the day of the ruling, cited a 98.9 percent compliance rate for FBI searches of Americans and credited Section 702 with stopping a planned terrorist attack on a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna. None mentions the court’s findings. The figure appears nowhere in the Justice Department inspector general’s October 2025 review of those searches, which put the compliance rate at 98.6 percent and could not conclude that “the FBI’s querying compliance issues are entirely in the past.”
According to the fact sheets, FBI auditors review every such search. FBI director Kash Patel closed the bureau’s Office of Internal Auditing last May and moved its auditors into another division. The bureau’s search counts before 2025 also omit queries run through the participants filter, searches the government’s own privacy watchdog says are “not possible to track.”
Lawmakers who have read the ruling hint that it says more. Senator Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, urged colleagues on the Senate floor in June to read it in a secure room. “I have seen it,” he said. Once they did, he told them, “your opinion of the role of FISA and the rights of Americans will be impacted for sure.”
Wyden has also warned about a classified interpretation of Section 702 that he says multiple administrations have relied on and refused to declassify. “When it is eventually declassified,” he said in March, “the American people are going to be stunned that it took so long and that Congress had been debating this authority with insufficient information.”
The Trump administration has until November 6 to answer the senators. The court’s current approval of the program expires in March.
Surveillance reform advocates say the administration may try to avoid that fight by attaching a renewal to the annual defense authorization bill, which Congress usually finalizes in December. In 2023, lawmakers extended Section 702 for four months through that year’s defense bill after a Senate effort to strip the provision failed. This year’s House and Senate versions of the bill do not yet include it.
