Woodside Energy’s plan to drill for gas off Western Australia’s north-west coast could significantly damage “exceptional” coral reefs and it may be impossible to reduce the risk of an oil spill to an acceptable level, according to advice from the state’s independent environmental watchdog.
A draft letter from WA’s Environmental Protection Authority written in 2023, seen by the Guardian, sharply criticised Woodside’s proposal to develop the Browse gasfield, saying its plans to protect endangered turtles and blue whales near Scott Reef would be ineffective.
Woodside, Australia’s largest fossil fuel company, is hoping to win approval next year to develop the Browse basin, about 300km off the Kimberley coast. Scientists have warned it could damage the Scott Reef ecosystem, which is home to more than 1,500 species, many unique to the area.
EPA staff presented the draft letter to the authority’s board for approval in December 2023. In February 2024, two months after it was discussed, the EPA sent a letter to Woodside saying its preliminary view was to reject development of the vast gas reserve.
It was a significant setback to Woodside’s plan to drill more than 50 wells and pipe the gas 1,000km to its ageing North West Shelf gas export plant adjacent to the world heritage-listed Murujuga rock art.
The company won approval last year to run the North West Shelf until 2070. But it needs the gas from the Browse basin – Australia’s largest undeveloped source of gas – to feed it. If the processing plant was to operate until 2070 it could lead to about 88m tonnes of carbon dioxide being released into the atmosphere each year after the gas was burned.
The concerns presented in the letter to the EPA board show the pressure on authorities to recommend against the gasfield development being approved. The development is being assessed by both the state and commonwealth EPAs. Ultimate decision-making power lies with environment ministers.
The letter shows the EPA board was advised by its staff that there was a threat of serious or irreversible harm to turtles and whales and more generally due to oil spills. The threats were considered serious enough that the staff said the precautionary principle should be invoked. It meant the EPA should assume the worst possible outcomes could occur.
In response to this near rejection of its proposal, Woodside added explosive-driven shear rams to its drilling plans, a step that could allow it to seal a leaking well in seconds. The company said this would reduce the “longest credible duration” of a “highly unlikely” well blowout, and potential oil spill, to about 12 hours.
Not all companies have faith in shear ram technology. In 2024, fellow WA gas exporter Chevron rejected “pyrotechnic shearing” technology for its own wells, describing it as unproven and impossible to test in the field.
A Woodside spokesperson said if the shear rams failed it would deploy a capping stack to stop the oil flow within 16 days.
But the EPA was advised in 2023 that if a well leaked for 13 days it was possible there could be “irreversible consequences” to Scott Reef.
The draft letter said Sandy Islet, a part of Scott Reef considered critical to the survival of endangered green turtles, would be threatened if the seabed subsided after Woodside extracted gas from beneath it. It said a proposal to top up the sand on the islet, where about 1,000 turtles breed each year, was a “high-risk” measure and its success was “likely to be limited”.
Woodside said it would address this by changing its plans so that no wells would be drilled within 20km of Sandy Islet. It also said the flaring of gas, which produces bright light that can confuse turtle’s navigation, would be restricted.
The EPA board was also told noise, traffic and vessel strikes would have a significant impact on pygmy blue whales migrating between Timor and southern Australia. Scott Reef is the only known whale feeding ground on the migration route, according to the draft letter.
Woodside’s spokesperson said the company understood whales did feed at Scott Reef, but that this was opportunistic and the area was not as important as the ocean off Perth and other areas further south. Woodside agreed that Scott Reef and Sandy Islet had exceptional environmental value and it was important to protect them for future generations.
Glenn Walker, Greenpeace head of nature, said Woodside’s plans to address the concerns raised by the EPA did not go far enough and relied on “fanciful and unproven technology” to prevent a catastrophic oil spill.
“It would be a major backflip for both the WA EPA and the national EPA to now recommend approving this project,” he said. “It is now critical that these regulators maintain their independence from corporate and political influence and reject this destructive project.”
Greenpeace last week nominated Scott Reef for national heritage listing based on its ecological and scientific values.
Just two of the current nine-strong WA EPA board were in place when the watchdog told Woodside it was set to reject Browse.
One of those – the current chair, Darren Walsh – said in a statement the assessment had been lengthy because it was a complex project in a sensitive area. He said a final state report and recommendations on the proposal would be provided to the WA environment minister, Matthew Swinbourn, when it was complete. There would then be a three-week public appeal period before a decision was made.
A spokesperson for the national EPA said the development was being assessed under the national Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, and the “decision clock” had been paused while the agency waited on “further technical advice”.
Issues that have to be considered under national law include the potential impact on pygmy blue whales, green turtles, the marine environment in commonwealth waters and Murujuga rock art near the gas processing facility.

The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”
Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”
Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.
The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.
Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.
“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.
When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.
Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”
US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.
Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.
US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.
Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.
Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.
His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.
Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.
The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.
Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.
“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.
Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.
Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.
Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.
Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”
Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.
“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”
Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.
Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.
Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.
Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.
David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”
The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”
Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.
Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.
Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.
Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”
In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.
Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.
El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.
Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.
Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.
For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.
“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.
Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

Forty Iranian sailors rescued off Sri Lanka coast after medical emergencies
- Published
Sri Lanka's foreign ministry says it has coordinated efforts to treat and repatriate 40 Iranian sailors suffering from unspecified medical emergencies in international waters off the island's southeastern coast.
Ministry spokesperson Thushara Rodrigo told BBC Sinhala they received a distress call on Saturday from Iranian ships "regarding an urgent medical need".
The rescue operation was planned by the Iranian Embassy in Colombo, he said.
Iranian ships have been stranded at sea due to a US naval blockade. Sri Lanka stresses it is neutral in the conflict, but has at times offered help to Iranian sailors in what it says is an obligation to international law.
A BBC Sinhala report last month found that there were 21 Iranian vessels located in international waters near Sri Lanka.
The 40 rescued sailors served on different ships - though Sri Lankan authorities do not have information on how many ships they belonged to, Rodrigo said.
The sailors were brought ashore and taken to Colombo for medical treatment before being sent back to Iran by plane on Saturday night, he added.
He said that several agencies were involved in the operation, including local shipping companies.
According to Rodrigo, Sri Lanka was obliged under international law and humanitarian grounds to provide the necessary facilities for medical emergencies.
"This does not mean that we will provide assistance to those ships," he said. "It is generally an internationally accepted tradition to respond to a distress call after receiving it."
"We have dealt with such cases before. This is a normal process that continues to be implemented."
The ongoing conflict in Iran started when the US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on the country in February. Iran responded by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international trade route.
Attacks by both sides have persisted as negotiations stalled.
Sri Lanka has sought to remain neutral in the conflict, having rejected military access requests from both the US and Iran and urged both parties to prioritise dialogue.
It has also offered assistance to Iranian ships caught in the conflict on what it argues are humanitarian grounds.
In March, Sri Lankan authorities said they responded to a distress call from the Iranian ship the Iris Dena, which had sunk off its coast after a US torpedo attack.
More than 80 crew members were killed in the attack, and injured survivors were taken to a hospital in the Galle Harbour.
The following day, Sri Lankan authorities allowed another Iranian naval vessel to dock at one of its ports, with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake saying that they would "never hesitate to protect humanity".
Sri Lankan authorities said earlier this month they had no immediate plans to send aid to 19 Iranian ships near its coasts which had reported shortages of food, water and fuel. The authorities said they had to prioritise national interests, the Associated Press reported.

Step 3: Wait for Phubloxity to create a portfolio website. Once done, it will show you the portfolio.html file. Click on it to preview.
Step 4: After you check the preview, click the download option, download it as an HTML file, and save it locally on your device.
How to Publish Your Portfolio Website for Free
To publish your portfolio site, there are plenty of options, but in this guide, I will show you two free, reliable options: Netlify Drop and GitHub Pages.
Method 1: Publish Your Portfolio Website Using Netlify Drop
Step 1: Create a free Netlify account. First, go to netlify.com and sign up with your email. You can also sign up using Google or GitHub.
Step 2: Go to app.netlify.com/drop and drop the index.html you created using Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google AI Studio from your downloads folder, or click the file and select it.
Step 3: Next, it automatically creates a free address. After a few minutes, your project shows as published with a random address such as sunny-tulip-tf52.netlify.app in my case. You can also click on that link to see the live site.
Step 4: However, if you think it can have a better name, open the project settings and change the project name to something short, such as meera-ai. Your address becomes meera-iyer.netlify.app. Make sure your site name is unique, since there will be hundreds of free Netlify sites out there.
Step 5: Once you have hosted the site successfully, you can share your link. Your portfolio is now live for anyone on any device to access it.
Method 2: Publish Your Portfolio Website Using GitHub Pages
Now let’s look at how to publish it for free using GitHub Pages.
GitHub also lets you host a simple website for free, and you can do everything on the GitHub website without installing anything. However, it takes a few more clicks than the Netlify Drop process.
Step 1: First, create a GitHub account. To do that, sign in to your free account at github.com, then go to github.com/new and create a new repository. For example, you can create ramesh.portfolio and set it to public. Remember that free accounts need a public repository for Pages to work. Turn on “Add a README” and finally tap on Create repository options.
Step 2: Once done, you can upload a file to the repository. Click Choose your files or drag and drop the index.html file, and at the bottom type a short message such as “Add portfolio website” and click on the Commit changes button.
Step 3: Once done, open the repository and go to Settings. Then click Pages in the left sidebar. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch, pick main and / (root), and click Save.
Step 4: Now wait until GitHub says the changes can take up to 10 minutes. Wait for your site to go public, refresh the page, and wait for it to update. Once it’s done, click Visit site.
That’s it. GitHub will create your page under your name using a GitHub subdomain.
Final Thoughts
This is how you can use free AI tools to create free portfolio websites. Whether you are a beginner and have never written code before, you can follow this simple step-by-step process to create your first portfolio website.
If you have never built one and don’t even have an idea of creating profile sites, you can simply upload your resume into the AI tool and ask it to convert it into a portfolio website and generate an index.html page. Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Sparking speculation of a new strategic alignment between the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Nationalist Citizen Party of India (NCPI) ahead of municipal polls, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday (October 25, 2026) visited the residence of NCPI leader and Kolkata North MP Sudip Bandyopadhyay.
The meeting was described as a courtesy call by the Chief Minister, but the meeting has led to a change in the stance of party bigwigs towards NCPI. While the leaders of NCPI have been making statements that they want to ally with the BJP in the upcoming civic polls, senior leaders of the BJP had ruled out any such possibility.
Union Minister and BJP MP Sukanata Majumdar, who has been appointed the chairperson of the committee overseeing the party’s preparation for civil polls, had earlier said that the party will field candidates on all 209 seats of Kolkata Municipal Corporation. On Monday (October 26, 2026), Mr. Majumdar said that there is always some “permutation and combination in politics”. State’s Minister for Industries and Commerce Tapas Roy who is considered an arch rival of Sudip Banerjee on Monday (October 26, 2026) said that BJP was an all-India described himself as someone who will also abide by the party discipline.
After the defeat of the Trinamool Congress in the West Bengal Assembly polls in 2026, 20 MPs of the party joined the little-known NCPI. NCPI, which has veteran MPs like Sudip Banerjee and Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar, claims itself as the second biggest constituent of the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) after the BJP.
The new bonhomie between the BJP and NCPI has caused heartburn among many in the BJP, including old-timers like Samik Bhattacharya, the West Bengal BJP president. Responding to questions by journalists on Monday (October 26, 2026), Mr. Bhattacharya said that “it would take us some thinking before holding hands of those believing in Congress ideology as blood of Syama Prasad Mookerjee is on Congress hands”.
Mr. Bhattacharya has often described Trinamool Congress leaders as a product of the Congress ideology. “BJP has always contested alone. I have been associated with the party when the vote percentage of the party was one percent. I never joined another party,” he said.
The State BJP president made the remarks a day after the State Chief Minister gave a certificate to six-time MP, Sudip Banerjee, by saying, “ I do not think that Sudip Babu has tormented any BJP worker,” Mr. Adhikari had said.
It is not only the bonhomie between the BJP and NCPI that has upset the old-timers in the BJP, but also the warmth between the Democratic Trinamool Congress and the saffron party. DTP, led by Ritabrata Banerjee and Arup Roy, has the support of 65 MLAs in the West Bengal Assembly out of the 80 who were elected on the ticket of Trinamool Congress.
Upset with the rapprochement between former Kolkata Mayor and DTP MLA Firhad Hakim and the ruling party, BJP leader Rakesh Singh, who contested and lost to him from the Kolkata Port seat. made a sarcastic comment. “If everyone in Trinamool is good, what is the problem with Mamata Banerjee? She can be inducted in the BJP too,” the BJP leader said.

Every morning during the Martian spring and summer, a thin and extremely long cloud emerges, only to disappear again. The wispy formation appears near the volcano Arsia Mons and gradually elongates until it reaches over 1,000 miles—about the distance from New York to Kansas City as the crow flies—before dissipating. This cycle then repeats for several months.
Since it was first recorded by a probe in 2018, scientists have been unable to find a plausible explanation for the existence of this cloud, often referred to as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). Until now. Recently, researchers successfully modeled the cloud’s formation for the first time, their results suggesting that it may be driven by a physical process that has never been directly observed in any planet’s atmosphere.
“We found that we needed to include some exotic physics… physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before,” Jorge Hernández-Bernal, a planetary scientist at Paris’ Sorbonne Université and lead author of the study, said in a press release. “Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.”

Questions over an IPO and ESOPs, huge investments in quick commerce and food delivery and the pressure to deliver profits: Flipkart is juggling one too many hot potatoes for the past year. In that time, the ecommerce giant has seen 14 senior level exits, including three more VPs who are set to leave the company next. The latest executives to leave are Kanchan Mishra, VP of smartphones; Amit Sachan, VP of product and tech; and Kamal Chopra, VP of corporate, as Moneycontrol reported. While Mishra spent more than a decade at Flipkart, Sachan and Chopra have been with the company for four and five years, respectively. As their tenure shows these are not employees who had just joined the company one or two years ago in the wake of all the IPO talk. These were executives who had seen much of the restructuring at Flipkart in the post-pandemic years. Plus, these departures come at a time when the company’s employees have raised concerns over ESOP liquidity and the company’s long-awaited IPO remains without a firm timeline. It has coloured these exits with a darker tint as a result. Walmart has reportedly asked the company to prioritise profitability before going public, while the expansion of its quick commerce business, Flipkart Minutes, requires significant ongoing investments. Employees holding stock options, meanwhile, are waiting for an opportunity to cash out. Sources told Inc42 that some of these executives left as they were unable to see a clear opportunity to liquidate their ESOPs, while others moved to new jobs or wanted to start their own ventures. It must be noted that at this middle management level, Flipkart has around 30 executives in VP roles and more than a dozen senior vice presidents, so these departures will not necessarily destabilise the company, but it is a sign of bubbling discontent. ESOP Liquidity Dispute Widens In fact, sources told us that the frustration over stock options has moved beyond internal discussions, with former senior executives approaching Walmart’s board to seek a fair opportunity to realise the value of their vested ESOPs. Earlier this month, former Flipkart executives, including ex-Myntra CEO Mukesh Bansal, former chief business officer Ankit Nagori and former CFO Sanjay Baweja, wrote to Walmart’s board seeking fair treatment and a full cash-out opportunity for their vested options simply because they left the company. The issue has gained importance because an IPO has long been seen as a potential exit route for employees holding Flipkart shares or options. With the listing pushed back, those employees have little clarity on when they can realise that value. For senior executives who have spent a year at Flipkart, the delay also affects decisions about whether to stay or pursue opportunities elsewhere. While ESOP liquidity is one reason behind some departures, the company’s leadership churn is also a result of executives moving into new roles or setting up their own ventures. The founder of a unicorn startup with over 30,000 employees told us that while Flipkart has the responsibility of providing liquidity to employees, listing in a hurry to meet these demands would be a mistake. “At the end of the day, Flipkart’s management and Walmart have to do the right thing by the company. If they have already done a $50 Mn ESOP buy back last year, then they already provided some liquidity opportunity. If an employee has already made ₹10 Cr - ₹15 Cr through that, then they need to give the company some more time for the next event. But if an employee who has made a few lakhs of rupees via the buyback is upset, then the management needs to address that. What’s the point of listing in a rush, without getting a good market value?” the founder said on the condition of anonymity. Walmart Wants Profit Before IPO The fact is that Flipkart’s listing plans have been discussed for years, but the immediate priority appears to be improving its financial performance. In May 2026, Moneycontrol reported that parent Walmart wanted Flipkart to achieve EBITDA breakeven by the end of FY27 before considering an IPO or another external fundraise. The report said the decision followed Walmart CEO John Furner’s visit to Bengaluru. The reported directive adds another hurdle for a company that completed its reverse flip from Singapore to India in March 2026, ahead of a potential domestic listing. There is the looming valuation question. Flipkart currently commands a valuation of $35 Bn - $36 Bn and earlier was eyeing a valuation of $50 Bn. This valuation expectation complicates finding the right window for the listing. Walmart can afford to wait for improved financial performance which would justify the valuation, but that’s not the case with employees seeking liquidity. “In a current situation, getting a $50 Bn valuation will be extremely difficult. It is indeed a tricky position for the company,” the founder quoted above added. Others believe that Flipkart cannot go into an IPO with the narrative of a growth-at-all-costs tech startup. The company is far too mature for this. “Flipkart will likely face pushback and could be forced into a valuation haircut to land in the $25B–$30 Bn range. This will match global tech-retail multiples,” Rahul Sharma, Head of Research at Equity99 said. On the other hand, the company can position itself as a disciplined, maturing omnichannel ecosystem. “A concrete roadmap to profitability can successfully defend the $35 Bn mark that Flipkart is said to be seeking,” he added. The delay is particularly striking because other Indian ecommerce companies have already reached the public markets. Meesho listed on the NSE and BSE on December 10, 2025, following a ₹5,421 Cr IPO. Snapdeal’s parent, AceVector, listed on October 5, 2026, after a ₹420 Cr public issue. Their listing gives investors a way to set benchmarks for ecommerce, while Flipkart continues to work towards its own debut. However, the comparison also shows that going public does guarantee a strong market reception. AceVector shares listed at an issue price of ₹32 and subsequently traded below that level. For Flipkart, the question is whether stronger financial performance can support its valuation expectations without forcing the company to slow its growth plans. Flipkart Minutes Complicates Profitability Push The push to improve profitability comes amid Flipkart’s aggressive investments in quick commerce. Flipkart Minutes has expanded its dark store network to compete with Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto. The business gives Flipkart a way to serve customers looking for rapid delivery of groceries, electronics and other everyday products. However, the expansion requires spending on dark stores, inventory, fulfillment and delivery operations. New stores need time to build order volumes and improve their economics. Until a store reaches sufficient throughput, its operating costs can weigh on the business. Flipkart Minutes has scaled to 1,000 micro fulfillment centers across 130+ cities and 8,000+ pincodes in under two years. The current scale of Minutes’ spending is not publicly disclosed. However, its expansion presents a challenge for Flipkart as Walmart reportedly seeks EBITDA breakeven before an IPO. Now, Flipkart is preparing to enter another competitive market with its food delivery service branded eat-in by Minutes. Currently available for its 8,000 employees, will soon be available to the public by the end of this month. The food delivery business could add to Flipkart’s spending requirements. The company reportedly will use a dedicated delivery fleet through its logistics arm Ekart. Moreover, it will also require onboard restaurants and attract customers in a market where established players spend on discounts, promotions and customer acquisition. These costs could build before the service reaches sufficient order volumes to support its operations. The launch puts Flipkart in the position of investing in two businesses that require scale to improve their economics, even as Walmart reportedly wants the group to reach EBITDA breakeven before an IPO. While food delivery could bring more frequent customer visits to Flipkart’s app, it will also require spending to compete with established platforms. Losses Grow, Pressure Builds Flipkart’s financial performance will also remain under scrutiny as it works towards a potential IPO. The Flipkart Group reported an 18.2% YoY increase in consolidated revenue from operation to ₹1.45 Lakh Cr in FY26, compared with ₹1.23 Lakh Cr in FY25. Its consolidated net loss narrowed marginally by 2.1% to ₹8,468 Cr from ₹8,646 Cr in the previous year. The financial results cover the wider Flipkart Group, including Myntra, Cleartrip, logistics, and other business, rather than the ecommerce marketplace alone. The group said its gross margins rose 23% during FY26, while adjusted EBITDA improved by around ₹1,500 Cr. Adjusted operating margin improved by 230 basis points, from -7.7% to -5.4%, while adjusted operating business losses narrowed by 17%, or around ₹1,600 Cr. However, the improvement in operating performance translated into only a modest reduction in net loss. Higher finance cost, the recognition of deferred tax assets and certain exceptional items weighed on the bottom line. The ecommerce vertical, Flipkart Internet, reported a 19.3% YoY decline in revenue from operations to ₹16,295 Cr in FY26. Its net loss rose to ₹5,498 Cr from ₹1,694 Cr in FY25. A significant portion of that is likely due to the redomiciling to India which was completed in March 2026. As Flipkart works on its public market plans, the combination of profitability targets, valuation expectations and employee concerns over stock liquidity is likely to remain in focus. For senior executives weighing their next move, the absence of a firm IPO timeline leaves questions unanswered: when will the equity they have accumulated at Flipkart become liquid wealth? Angry players urge ATP rethink over doubles cuts
- Published
More than 150 men's doubles players - including British world number one Henry Patten and the legendary Bryan brothers - have urged the ATP Tour to rethink "drastic" changes which they believe could kill the format.
In a show of collective action, the players have written an open letter to the men's governing body as they fight proposals which would cut draw sizes and reduce prize money from 2028.
"We're at risk of losing a discipline of tennis which is historic - but has a big future," Dutch player Sem Verbeek, one of the architects of the letter, told BBC Sport.
"These proposals would destroy careers, livelihoods and dreams."
The ATP proposed halving the doubles draws at its flagship Masters 1000 events to 16 teams, with smaller tournaments reduced to eight teams.
The percentage of prize money devoted to doubles could fall from 20% to 10% - with the difference redistributed to singles players.
On Monday, a group of 137 current players, 28 legends and 20 national federations signed a letter which they hope will pressure the ATP into rethinking the proposals.
The tour's board - comprised of chairman Andrea Gaudenzi, four tournament representatives and four player representatives - will vote on the plans at next month's ATP Finals in Turin.
The doubles reform is part of a wider review by the ATP, which it says is designed to "strengthen" the tour from 2028.
The ATP aims to create "a more sustainable long-term model", insisting it wants to "maintain the important role" of doubles.
"Commercial success matters. Fairness, player welfare and the long-term health of tennis matter just as much," the players' letter says.
"Let us grow tennis together, without leaving doubles players behind."
Why is doubles under threat?
The proposals provoked an angry response from the men's doubles cohort when they were revealed in July.
British pair Lloyd Glasspool and Julian Cash, who won Wimbledon in 2025 and became world number ones, accused the ATP of trying to "kill part of the sport".
Others within tennis believe reform is needed. They suggest a 20% share of the prize money for doubles is disproportionate to the interest shown by fans.
The doubles players argue the ATP should do more to promote their discipline and attract greater audiences, pointing out it is the format played by most club members and therefore more relatable.
The ATP says the proposals are based on data-led analysis centred on costs, revenue and viewership.
With fewer singles players now competing in doubles, it believes the current size of the standalone doubles events puts severe strain on tournaments.
"We support progress. We also understand the need to grow the sport, strengthen tournaments and increase commercial value," the players' letter says.
"Still, the proposed reforms go much too far."
Might the dispute lead to legal action?
Reigning Wimbledon champion Patten recently told BBC Sport the players were facing "an uphill battle", but remained "optimistic" the tour would consider counter-proposals. Since Wimbledon there have been several meetings between both sides, including recently at the Shanghai Masters.
Many players still believe there is little appetite for negotiation from the ATP. But ATP sources insist a compromise is likely to be found.
Mike and Bob Bryan - the identical twins considered the greatest doubles pair of all-time - said they would support the group considering legal action to protect their discipline.
In 2005, the American brothers led players in a lawsuit against the ATP, when it planned radical changes to doubles.
"The tour's in the healthiest financial state it's ever been - in our opinion it should be creating more opportunities," Bob Bryan told BBC Sport in an interview at Wimbledon in July.
Mike Bryan added: "These proposed changes are anti-competitive. That's the stance we had to take in 2005. We still believe in doubles and we believe in the players fighting for this."

In 2018, anatomists at the Toho University Graduate School of Medicine, Tokyo, Japan, performed a sleep deprivation experiment on lab mice. Mice usually sleep for 12 hours a day. In this experiment, researchers induced sleep deprivation using the ‘gentle handling method’ during sleep hours so that the mice could sleep only for six hours daily.
They discovered that liver fat content in sleep-deprived mice increased without total weight gain compared to another group who were allowed to sleep normally. The liver cells were stressed, and the activity of certain genes that escalate insulin resistance and fat content within liver cells also increased with sleep deprivation.
Experiment on rats
Three years later, a group of Chinese researchers at the Xinjiang Medical University went one step ahead. In this experiment, rats were severely sleep-deprived, turning into insomniacs. Liver enzymes, blood, and liver fat increased substantially. None of these changes were notable among rats who were allowed to sleep without distractions.
They also found the reason for increased liver fat in insomniac mice — the sympathetic nerves that supplied the liver, best known for their role in responding to stress and danger, were hyperactive. When insomnia was treated with a sleeping pill in these stressed rats, the liver fat was reduced with adequate sleep.
There are lessons here, of mice and men. Sleep is an underrated activity among humans. Sometimes, the intentional and forced lack of sleep ‘to increase productivity’ is advertised by men in power to showcase their self-proclaimed metahuman nature. During an interview in 2011, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he had become a workaholic and hardly slept for 3.5 hours in a day, and that yoga and pranayama routine kept him energised and awake.
But medical science has a different story to tell. A study of nearly 55,500 people from Europe showed that those who slept 7-8.5 hours daily had higher life expectancy than those who slept less than seven hours. In those between ages 50 and 75 without sleep disturbances, the expectation of living longer without chronic disease development was significantly higher.
And yoga interventions improved overall sleep quality, efficiency, latency, and duration, contrary to all claims.
Healthy sleep
Sleep is a vital function of human life and accounts for up to one-third of the lifespan. Contrary to normal belief, during sleep, the brain is not ‘resting’ but is engaged in various activities necessary to improve well-being, increase life, and especially impact the liver. The minimum required duration for ‘healthy’ sleep is seven hours.
When 10,000 persons with sleep disorders were followed up for one year, incident fatty liver disease was noted in 14, while in those without sleep disorders, it was only six. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease association was significantly higher among persons with shorter sleep duration (less than six hours per night) and excessive daytime sleepiness. A high-quality study showed that inadequate sleep duration was strongly associated with an elevated risk of developing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and adequate sleep helped prevent it. With every one-hour decrease in sleep time from the recommended seven-eight hours, the risk of fat deposition in the liver increased by 24% compared with those who slept adequately.
However, when people who lost sleep during the weekdays caught up on the debt during weekends (known as weekend catch-up sleep), the development of fatty liver disease reduced significantly. Compared with non-nappers, long daytime nappers (more than 60 minutes) had a higher risk of developing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
Identification
Correlation may not be causation, but with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which is associated with other conditions such as obesity, high blood pressure, increased waist-hip ratio, low functioning thyroid, and high blood cholesterol, studying and identifying independent associations make realistic sense.
In people who sleep less than six hours at night, have a persistently poor sleep quality, or nap more than one hour during the day, independent of other disease conditions, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease development was a strong association. The next time someone brags that sacrificing time and quality of sleep is an achievement associated with success, know that success comes with fatty liver disease. And it is not worth it.
(Cyriac Abby Philips is a senior consultant and physician-scientist at the Liver Institute, Rajagiri Hospital, Kochi)

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

Caribbean seeks reparations and questions role of monarchy before King Charles visits
The royals are coming, and the Caribbean wants to be heard
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- The royals are coming, and the Caribbean wants to be heard.
Islanders are seeking slavery reparations from Britain, a formal apology for its role in the slave trade and greater independence from the former colonial power.
The Bahamas National Reparations Committee said it already knows what awaits the Caribbean as King Charles III and Queen Camilla prepare for this week's trip: “Schools emptied of children who will stand in the sun and wave for the Crown that has taken everything from their ancestors and comes back smiling.”
Charles is expected to visit the Bahamas on Tuesday to begin the nine-day trip to the Caribbean. His last official visit to the archipelago was in July 1973 as a prince who granted the Bahamas independence, ending 300 years of British rule. But the Bahamas remains a Commonwealth realm, along with six other Caribbean nations that recognize Charles as their king and head of state.
While in the Bahamas, Charles is scheduled to visit Clifford Park, where the archipelago’s black, turquoise and yellow flag was raised for the first time more than half a century ago.
His visit will raise important questions, said Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.
“Why do we still have a king? What does this person really represent to us? Why is he coming and how will that benefit us?” she said.
A psychology professor at the University of the Bahamas, Campbell-Dean said she recently mentioned Charles’ upcoming visit to her students, and they were not excited. She responded: “I know y’all might not care about this man who is coming, but here’s why this is of importance.”
Leaders across the Caribbean have long been pushing for an apology and reparations from Britain.
In early September, Jamaica took its case for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island. It was an unprecedented legal maneuver, even though the British government has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.
After three days in the Bahamas, Charles is scheduled to fly to the South American country of Guyana. The former British colony was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the region during the colonial era, with thousands of slaves uprising during the 1823 Demerara rebellion on the plantation owned by the father of former British Prime Minister William Gladstone.
More than 200 slaves were killed as a result; several were decapitated and their heads placed on poles.
In a recent interview with ITV News, Guyanese President Irfaan Ali said Charles has “rightfully recognized slavery as the darkest days in human history.”
“Moving to the apology is the next step,” he added. “You exploited the region. You destroyed lives. You created underdevelopment.”
While in Guyana, Charles is expected to meet with Ali and elected leaders of Amerindian villages known as “toshaos.”
Nikita Miller, toshao of Chinese Landing, a rural Amerindian community in northern Guyana, said she was not invited.
She noted that her community has been mired in a decades-long land fight with miners seeking to extract gold from the area, and she would have liked the opportunity to talk about an issue that affects other toshaos as well.
“We have been suffering,” she said. “We want the government to respect Indigenous rights. … We have long-standing issues with our land.”
Miller said she believes the king’s visit might help improve things for Guyana overall, but not for Amerindian villages.
After two days in Guyana, Charles is scheduled to fly to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and meet with leaders of 56 member states. Talks are expected to focus on climate, trade and development, but some Caribbean leaders have said slavery reparations should dominate conversations.
The British royals have long visited Jamaica, but it’s not on Charles' itinerary this time.
It’s just as well, said 51-year-old Rastafarian Steven Bennett.
“We don’t need any royal wave or photo-taking while the wounds of our ancestors are still being ignored. He still refuses to formally apologize for chattel slavery,” Bennett said. “Until the British monarchy is ready to stand on Jamaican soil, look us in the eye, apologize, and talk about actual repair and restitution, he has no business here. We want justice, not a parade.”
Jamaica in recent years has been pushing to oust Charles as head of state and become a republic like Barbados did in 2021.
Antonio Williams, a 25-year-old university student, said young Jamaicans have zero connection to the Crown.
“I think Buckingham Palace has read the room after the absolute PR disaster of William and Kate’s Caribbean tour a few years back,” he said, referring to the 2022 visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales to the region, where they faced protests and calls for reparations.
“We are actively moving toward becoming a republic and breaking these colonial ties,” Williams said. “Having the king visit now would just be incredibly awkward. Skipping us is a sign that they know their influence here is expiring.”
But 68-year-old retired civil servant Hermine Reid recalled with fondness how Charles’ mother, Queen Elizabeth II, used to visit Jamaica.
“It was always such a grand, respectful occasion, and people would line the streets in their Sunday best,” she said. “Things are very different now. It’s a little sad for my generation to see how much the relationship has fractured, but I suppose this is simply the modern era. Jamaica is growing up and charting its own course, and the king clearly recognizes that.”
___
Myers Jr. reported from Kingston, Jamaica.

Internal rift: Dipke's selfie with Ranka, Das mocks CJP split rumours
Abhijeet Dipke mocked speculation of an internal rift in CJP with an Insta post with Saurav Dass and Ashutosh Ranka, days after the two were released on bail and the group paused its protests until Diwali.
Amid speculation of an internal rift within the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), its founder Abhijeet Dipke took a humorous swipe at the rumours by sharing a photograph with fellow leaders Saurav Dass and Ashutosh Ranka, captioned "internal rift".
Dipke shared the photograph on Instagram, appearing to poke fun at claims of divisions within the group, days after Dass and Ranka were released on bail from Tihar Jail and the CJP paused its protests.
The picture showed Ranka and Dass playfully holding their fists above Dipke's head as he stood between them.
Dipke also shared a humorous video featuring CJP members, in which he was heard saying, "After this, no one will walk alone in the garden!" The CJP leaders responded, "Okay Shaktiman".
The posts came amid questions about the group’s internal dynamics, particularly after the CJP announced a break from protests until Diwali, citing the need for members to spend time with their families.
Ranka and Das were released from Tihar Jail on October 22 after a special executive magistrate court ordered their release, subject to personal bonds and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each, along with written undertakings to maintain peace.
The two leaders had been in judicial custody since October 13 in connection with a CJP protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi. They were accused of entering the denotified protest site and violating peace bonds.
In their undertakings, Ranka and Das promised not to breach the peace and said they would not call for protests at Jantar Mantar until the site was denotified in accordance with the law. They also undertook to ensure that any protests organised by them remained within the constitutional framework.
In an earlier video, Dipke had publicly credited Ranka and Das with being the principal decision-makers behind the CJP movement, describing himself as someone who followed their instructions.
Dipke said the two co-convenors had played a major role in taking the movement forward and were responsible for several of its decisions.
"I always feel that if anyone has really taken this movement forward, it is Ashu (Ashutosh Ranka) and Saurav. Both of them have had a very, very big role. I was just following their orders, I'm telling you honestly," he said.
Dipke added that although he might appear to be the leader from the outside, Ranka and Das were the ones who told him where to go and what to do.
The comments subsequently drew criticism from some social media users, who accused Dipke of shifting responsibility onto Ranka and Das to distance himself from the movement's activities.
In a follow-up video, Dipke rejected the allegations, insisting that he was not throwing the two leaders under the bus. He described Ranka and Das as his brothers and family and said he had no insecurity about acknowledging their stronger decision-making abilities.
"If someone is better than me, then I don't have even a little insecurity in accepting it, not even a little shame," he said.
Dipke also said the three shared a close personal bond and that the group operated like a family rather than being controlled by one individual.
He also defended Ranka and Das against comparisons between the CJP's protests and violent unrest in France, arguing that the two had chosen peaceful resistance despite their imprisonment.

Lula da Silva has been declared the winner of the Brazilian election, in a result that will send shockwaves throughout South America.
The left-wing candidate defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The senator had finished first in the election's first round and hoped to revive his father's far-right movement.
At times, Lula's reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers' Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping societal changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.
Lula's victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.
"He is a statesman, a giant," leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters

Young adults in China looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having children or pets have found an answer: raising bricks.
Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media.
Raising “brick babies” is easier than caring for house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day then waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article described the bricks as being “practically immortal”. “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.”
A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on the Chinese social media platform Weibo.
Chinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick “parent” told Chinese media the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.
One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”.
Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick.
“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.”
Young people in China are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society, such as having children and working long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- to 24-year-olds, excluding students, are unemployed, according to official statistics. Some estimates put the unemployment rate much higher.
China’s birthrate is in decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of intensely competitive studying, many young people are choosing to shun the rat race and opt instead for “lying flat” – pursuing a low-effort, low-stress lifestyle; one well-suited to raising bricks.
The trend has become so popular that Chinese media have started to warn about the health risks.
Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of itchy eyes and runny noses. Xuedong Li, a retired professor of moss from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged people to keep their bricks in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.

Serbia's Vučić concedes election defeat to student-led protest movement
- Published
Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has conceded defeat to the student-led protest movement in the country's snap parliamentary election.
"We still do not have final results... it is clear that we have lost these elections," the right-wing populist leader said late on Sunday.
Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission indicated a record high turnout, which commentators had suggested would favour the student movement.
Vučić had called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia.
Vučić made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.
There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off.

The former Madhya Pradesh Minister and member of Congress Working Committee Kamaleshwar Patel has accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of undermining democracy and the Constitution through vote chori (vote theft).
Addressing a press conference along with Congress leaders in Hubballi on Monday, Mr. Patel said that the BJP has formed governments in several States through electoral malpractice and accused Mr. Kumar of acting as an agent of the BJP and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).
He cited the deletion of 68 lakh names from the electoral rolls in Bihar and raised a concern over largescale deletions of voters in West Bengal and the irregularities in Maharashtra, including multiple voters being registered under a same address.
Referring to a report in The Hindu on over 60,000 Form 7 applications seeking the deletion of names from Karnataka’s electoral rolls filed by election officials themselves, Mr. Patel said that as per the Registration of Electors Rules 1960, mentioning the reason for deletion is mandatory.
However, no specific reason has been given in the forms submitted by the election officials, indicating the kind of malpractice being done under the guise of SIR.
Mr. Patel also questioned the amendment to Form 6, saying that it has been made without parliamentary approval.
He said that the Congress and the INDI Alliance partners have launched a Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao campaign to protect democracy and the Constitution and oppose electoral irregularities. The campaign will continue until Mr. Kumar, Mr. Modi and Mr. Shah resign, he said.
As part of the month-long campaign, a rally will be held in Delhi on November 1. The campaign will be conducted at various levels, with the first phase focusing on raising awareness and the second marking Democracy Day, he said.
Mr. Patel also said that people are being divided in the name of religion and nationalism while corporate interests are being favoured.
He called for safeguards to protect voter rights, raised concerns over electronic voting machines (EVMs) and demanded that the elections should be held using ballot papers.
KPCC district unit presidents Sadanand Danganavar and Chandrashekhar Juttal, MLC F.H. Jakkappanavar, the former MLC Mohan Limbikai, the former MLA M.S. Akki and others were present.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.
