End approaching for Carrick but Man Utd owners' problems far bigger
- Published
There was an air of inevitability about Michael Carrick's walk around Old Trafford after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth.
It is not unusual for Carrick to applaud the United fans. If anything, his acknowledgements were not as pronounced as they were in Como after the equally devastating loss.
But after eight games without a win, the worst run since 2015-16 and two horrific defeats in a week, the end is approaching for Carrick, with his bosses in serious talks over his future.
However, if anyone in a senior position at the club thinks the issues at Old Trafford will be solved simply by changing the head coach and, more importantly, the fans will be appeased by a new face in the dugout, the reaction from the stands on an awful day on and off the pitch would have very clearly told them otherwise.
On Friday, as he looked back on that 4-1 loss to Como and looked ahead to Bournemouth, Carrick said: "We'll be a different team on Sunday. We have to be a different team on Sunday."
Sadly, they weren't.
Carrick could not answer if he will still be in charge for next Saturday's trip to Chelsea. He does not know.
"The responsibility is mine," he said. "What else can I say really right now? I totally understand the situation. I'm not expecting anything either way. I love this place and I'll always do what I feel is going to be the best for the football club."
- Fernandes left on bench for Man Utd defeat - a failed gamble? 
  - Published8 hours ago
- 'It wasn't a farewell from me' - but horror start leaves Carrick on brink 
  - Published5 hours ago
'Third dismissal in three seasons won't reflect well on anyone'
United's fans delivered their own verdict on the performance as Carrick disappeared down the tunnel to the dressing room.
After repeatedly singing the former midfielder's name, as soon as he was out of view they turned on the players. The booing lasted until the last of them, Diogo Dalot, left the pitch. They simply feel they are either not good enough or don't care enough, or both.
But there was more, much more.
The game was less than a minute old when the first anti-Glazer and anti-Sir Jim Ratcliffe songs were heard.
The Glazer family have been public enemy number one among the United faithful ever since their leveraged takeover in 2005.
The debt they initially landed on the club has now grown to over £1.15bn, according to their latest accounts. The amount it has cost in interest is £852m, according to respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble. In the last financial year, the interest payment was £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year.
The argument is, that money could have been used far more productively to sign better players.
There had been hope Ratcliffe, a boyhood United fan, would change that when he struck a deal with the Glazers to become a minority shareholder on Christmas Eve 2023.
Instead, a succession of decisions have led to major questions over his handling of the club.
On the management side, United's hierarchy eventually backed Erik ten Hag after talking with alternatives in the wake of the shock 2024 FA Cup final triumph over Manchester City, spending over £200m on the likes of Leny Yoro, Matthijs de Ligt and Manuel Ugarte.
Last week, Ten Hag told the Athletic, external the club went back on a promise not to sell homegrown Scotland international Scott McTominay to fund Ugarte's £50m move from Paris St-Germain. They sacked the Dutchman in October 2024.
After that they persuaded Ruben Amorim to leave Sporting mid-season, when he wanted to wait until the summer.
They stuck with him after an unprecedented 15th-place finish, and again after United lost to League Two Grimsby in the EFL Cup, then sacked him in January when he clashed with director of football Jason Wilcox over playing style.
That led to Carrick's arrival to the end of the season, which turned into a permanent appointment after he guided the club back into the Champions League after a two-year absence.
A third dismissal in three seasons would not reflect well on anyone.
The 'Standards' banner that was held up on the Stretford End showing the images of legendary skippers Bryan Robson, Eric Cantona and Roy Keane was there to remind the executives running the club of the history they should be aspiring to.
Recruitment, tickets, new stadium - more reasons why some fans are annoyed
Wilcox has largely operated behind the scenes but he could not fail to hear the obscenities being sung against him during today's game, nor the boos as he climbed into the vehicle taking him away from the stadium nearly two hours after the final whistle.
Recruited from a similar role at Southampton following the Ratcliffe takeover and elevated in status following the dismissal of Dan Ashworth, amid the decision to recruit Amorim, the 55-year-old is blamed by many fans for the club's recent recruitment, even though the budget was set at a much higher level.
Sat next to him at Old Trafford to watch the Bournemouth debacle unfold was chief executive Omar Berrada, who worked with Wilcox at Manchester City.
Having senior figures steeped in City's recent history was always a potential problem if results didn't go well. Berrada played no part in the recent Premier League proceedings that found City guilty of multiple breaches of financial rules, but the link is clear, and United's fans sang about that at Old Trafford as well.
If that wasn't enough, a ticket touting investigation launched in the summer led to condemnation from all United's major fan groups. The club argued they were trying to catch touts, while fans felt it was an attempt to drive regular match-goers out in favour of more corporate sales. The club are adamant that is not the case, but the argument is falling on deaf ears.
The same is also true of plans for a new 100,000-capacity stadium. The club conducted a survey which they said showed the majority of respondents were in favour of a new ground. The stadium is likely to cost in excess of £2bn and United spent £63.5m on land for it earlier this year.

Trump administration illegally fired James Comey's daughter, judge rules
- Published
The US justice department illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director James Comey, a federal judge has ruled.
Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father, a critic of US President Donald Trump, and because of her perceived political affiliations.
Judge Jesse Furman ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.
A spokesperson for the justice department said in a statement that it disagreed with the decision and "will appeal in due course".
In his ruling, Judge Furman said Comey's dismissal violated the US Constitution as well as her right to a fair legal process.
He said the US attorney general can fire federal prosecutors but only "in a particular manner and only for certain reasons".
Furman noted that in Comey's role, "she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases and consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike".
Comey has worked on cases against the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and hip-hop mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs, who was convicted on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends last year.
Furman ordered that Comey be given back pay from July until December 2025, when she accepted a new job.
In a statement, Comey's lawyers said: "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."
Comey had previously said the only reason she was told about her firing was that it "came from Washington".
A complaint filed by her lawyers in September 2025 stated that they believed Comey had been fired "solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both".
The justice department said in court filings that the decision was made by former Attorney General Pam Bondi.
The Trump administration has twice brought charges against James Comey, including for allegedly lying to Congress, but that case was dismissed by a judge who said the prosecutor who brought the case was unlawfully appointed.
Earlier this year, the justice department charged Comey with knowingly and wilfully making a threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm, on the president. He has denied any wrongdoing.
The case stems from a 2025 Instagram post shared by Comey that contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".
"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump.

Israelis have changed. Will they change their leadership?
TEL AVIV, Israel — Israelis are convinced that elections scheduled for Tuesday are the most pivotal in their nation's history.
Will they vote out Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — and his coalition of far-right, ultranationalist and religious political parties — because he failed to prevent the Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust?
Or will they reelect him to continue his campaign of retaliation, waging wars that aim to reshape the Middle East? His main challenger, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, leads a center-right opposition promising more diplomacy and less extremism.
It is Israel's first vote after these years of battle and bloodshed. Israelis are so concerned about their country's future that tens of thousands of expats are expected to fly back to cast ballots, since Israel does not allow absentee voting.
"We almost could have been destroyed on Oct. 7," said Israeli lawyer Shoula Romano-Horing, who flew in from Kansas City, Mo., to vote. "This is why I'm voting for Netanyahu, to make Israel so secure and so safe."
In the opposite corner are those Israelis distressed by the global backlash to the wars Netanyahu's government has waged.
"The actions of this government cause Israelis in general and Jews in general to be tagged as, you know, mass killers," said Yochai Ben-Haim, who works in renewable energy in California and is flying home to Israel for 36 hours just to vote. "This government is led by extremists that do not represent who we are, and we need to change it."
In conversations with dozens of Israelis over the last few weeks, a portrait has emerged of who Israelis are today.
They are a people defiant, but also weary after three years of incessant war. They are enraged at their enemies, but also at their leaders.
Many are impervious to the pain of their Palestinian neighbors, but traumatized from the war they have wrought. They are resistant to Palestinian independence, but also revolted by the Israeli settlers pushing Palestinians off their land.
They are fed up with the world's rebuke over the Gaza war, but also fearful of their growing global isolation. They are a people in a tug-of-war with themselves.
"Israelis want to be feared and to be loved," said Israeli author Micah Goodman. "The problem is that you have two reputations you need to protect, but you can't."
What Netanyahu knew
As elections near, Israelis are learning more about what led up to Oct. 7, 2023.
Throughout that year, as Israelis poured into the streets to protest Netanyahu's far-right government and its plan to weaken the judiciary, Netanyahu's security chiefs warned that regional enemies could take advantage of the turmoil to attack.
Behind the scenes, Israel received direct warnings that Hamas was planning something big. Israel and Hamas had been holding secret talks for more than a year, Palestinian mediator Sufian Abu Zaida said. When the talks stalled, Hamas' leader in Gaza had Abu Zaida relay a message threatening an "earthquake."
What kind of earthquake was unclear, said Abu Zaida, but he insists he relayed the warning to Israeli intelligence. The leader of the United Arab Emirates and Egypt's intelligence chief relayed similar warnings, according to reporting by NPR and other media outlets. "All what happened in 7 of October is needless," Abu Zaida said.
Nearly 1,200 people were killed when Hamas attacked army bases, residential communities and an outdoor music rave — and 251 people were taken hostage back to Gaza. Netanyahu denies he was warned and has never admitted any kind of responsibility for the security failure.
"Within days, his PR people were trying to shape the public narrative about events," said Amos Harel, a defense analyst for the Israeli newspaper Haaretz and author of 06:29 – Anatomy of a Failure, which details the Israeli failures to prevent the Oct. 7 attack. (The attack began that day at 6:29 a.m.) Netanyahu's strategy, he said, was "to shift the blame" to the security services and the military.
For much of the Gaza war, Israeli protesters flooded the streets demanding that Netanyahu strike a deal with Hamas to release Israeli hostages and end the fighting. It would take two years, Israel's longest ever war, before a hostage deal was reached. Netanyahu said he was seeking the total defeat of Hamas, though former officials who worked with Netanyahu allege he prolonged the war for political reasons — a charge that Netanyahu has denied.
"I'm absolutely convinced that this is what happened," Harel said. "He felt that if this would move on too fast, then there will be more of a significant public demand for a national commission of inquiry."
There is a great demand among Israelis for an investigation into the attack, like the 9/11 Commission in the United States. Netanyahu has blocked one in Israel.
So Israelis grappling with Oct. 7 go to the spot of the day's deadliest attack, where hundreds of people were killed when Hamas attacked the Nova music festival. The memorial there is a dusty field of plaques and thin poles bearing the pictures of smiling young people who were partying when they came under attack.
Kati and Meir Zohar, whose 23-year-old daughter Bar was killed there, helped build the memorial with other families. The Zohars say they received no government funding for the effort and no phone call from Netanyahu expressing his condolences.
"We are angry," Kati Zohar said.
She believes Netanyahu bears the responsibility for what happened to her daughter on Oct. 7 and, like other Israelis, hopes Netanyahu faces a reckoning for it on election day.
"It's a hope that something will change," Zohar said. "I hope that someone will come and take his place and be the one who [is] trying to keep this country together."
Who has fought the wars?
The Oct. 7 attack left Israelis in a state of shock.
"I think the general line of thinking — not only among decision-makers, not only among ministers of the government, but also among commanders in the field — was that something biblical has happened to us and that something biblical needed to happen in return," Harel said.
What happened in return was an Israeli military onslaught that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and left most of Gaza destroyed. Today, Israel is fighting back against charges of genocide. Netanyahu faces an international arrest warrant for alleged war crimes. Israeli soldiers who fought in the war risk arrest in some countries.
"I'm proud of what I did and I know what I did," said Lior, 34, who was one of those soldiers. "I don't mind to be in front of a judge."
Lior spoke on the condition that his last name be withheld to protect his family overseas from harassment because of the nature of his role: he commanded an Israeli sniper unit in Gaza and Lebanon, serving over 500 days in uniform.
" When you're inside Gaza, your life is under danger 24/7. There is shooting, there is booming… sometimes you hear about Hezbollah, Hamas, what they are doing. So your body, your mind is under survival tension 24/7," Lior said.
He is among the nearly 19,000 Israeli soldiers who have been newly diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder or related illnesses. It touches every part of his life: He imagines snipers on the streets. He sometimes breaks into tears riding the train. He struggles in his sex life. He and his fiancé broke up.
Lior said he often returns to one memory from Gaza: his order to shoot and kill a man he described as a Hamas terrorist, standing next to his child in a place where he shouldn't have been.
"Unfortunately, yeah, the kid saw his father dying in front of him," Lior said.
He does not regret any of his decisions to open fire.
"To be honest, in my opinion, I don't have any mercy of people in Gaza. I know what's going on there. I know of the poverty, I know about the lack of water, electricity. I don't have any mercy on them," Lior said. "When you see things with your own eyes and you remember what happened on the 7th of October, I'm not forgiving for that."
Is there anybody innocent in Gaza?
"You know, my Jewish identity (is) saying that I'm sure there is, but…I don't see it that way. That's what I told you about the kid," Lior said. "If he have the chance, he will kill me."
He is among the nearly 300,000 young Israeli military veterans ordered to leave their civilian lives and serve as reservist soldiers after Oct. 7.
No mercy
More than 67 percent of Israelis in a July 2025 poll said they were not very troubled about the suffering of people in Gaza. More than 60 percent of Israelis in an August 2025 poll said they believed there were no innocent people in Gaza. That view has been reinforced by mainstream Israeli media.
"There are no uninvolved civilians in Gaza," said Israeli reporter Almog Boker early last year on leading news network Channel 12.
This was not always the way Israeli media covered Palestinians in Gaza. Anat Saragusti, a veteran journalist, used to report from Gaza in the 1990s and early 2000s for Channel 12.
"I tried to cover Gaza as if I was living in a foreign country, to show the complexity of life, to show different stories," Saragusti said from her Tel Aviv apartment. "To show the Israeli audience that Gaza is not what they thought and think now, you know, a black hole of terrorists."
Twenty years ago, after Hamas took an Israeli soldier captive in Gaza, Israel practically sealed Gaza shut to Israeli journalists and to all Israelis. Then, Hamas took control of Gaza, Israel imposed a blockade, there were years of Hamas rocket fire into Israel and Israeli retaliation.
Since Oct. 7, most Israeli media chose not to show what Palestinian journalists were reporting day after day from Gaza: the tens of thousands of men, women and children killed; the forced displacement; the starvation; the misery of trying to survive.
"The majority of the Israeli journalists didn't do one story, you know, not even one story was done on Gaza… to see whether what these Palestinian journalists are claiming is true," said Saragusti. "They were afraid of the pushback by the audience if they dare say something about Gaza."
Harel, who writes a regular column for the Haaretz newspaper, says the nation's continuous war trauma also afflicted Israeli media.
" We were so busy with our pain and our suffering and worrying about the fate of the hostages — hundreds of hostages were held at that time by Hamas — that we didn't focus on what we did to the other side," he said.
What is happening in the West Bank
There is one place where even veterans of Israel's military and security establishment say what Palestinians are enduring has gone too far: the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
Since Oct. 7, Israeli settler violence toward Palestinians has skyrocketed. Settlers have seized more and more land there, with the support of the military and Netanyahu's pro-settler government, which has approved more than 100 new Jewish settlements in the West Bank, a record number.
"We are making a historic revolution," cabinet minister Bezalel Smotrich said this July as he announced the 104th new settlement approved by Netanyahu's current government. He said it "would prevent the establishment of a terror state in the heart of Israel."
A retired Israeli military general, Yaakov "Mendy" Or, leads groups of former Israeli military and security officials to Palestinian communities in the West Bank to show them the radical changes that have taken place over the last three years.
On a recent tour, he brought them to Umm al-Kheir, a Palestinian village surrounded by an expanse of desert hills, where Israeli settlers have set up trailer homes right outside a Palestinian family's property.
Palestinian activist Eid Hatlin said barbed wire in the yard was placed by settlers. The settlers have blocked the family's outdoor bathroom and the Israeli army has blocked the path to their sheep, he said.
"This is nasty. This is evil," said Ari Shuali, a former senior Israeli intelligence official who was part of the visiting group. "I don't believe that we as a people became such kind of unhuman behavior. I'm an Israeli. I'm a proud Israeli and I'm ashamed to be an Israeli [at] the same time."
It's one reason why some Israelis — like him — want to vote Netanyahu out.
Netanyahu's battle cry
Netanyahu has downplayed Israeli settler violence in the West Bank and his allies are campaigning on a pledge to expel Palestinians — what they call encouraging emigration.
Netanyahu is campaigning on what he's done to fight back against external threats — with the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran as examples of how he's making Israel safer since Oct. 7.
"On that darkest of days, our enemies expected us to collapse. Well, we didn't collapse. Instead, we rose and fought like lions!" Netanyahu said at the United Nations last month.
Over the last three years, Israel has killed the leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. It has sent soldiers to capture new territory in the West Bank, Gaza, Lebanon and Syria. It has fought Houthis in Yemen and militias in Iraq. Netanyahu vows to destroy Iran's nuclear capabilities if he is reelected.
"We're entangled in endless wars and this was done on purpose," Harel said. "It's not a bug, it's a feature. The whole idea is for Israel to keep fighting, because endless wars serve Netanyahu to maintain… a constant state of emergency."
Netanyahu has called them wars of "no choice," alongside a "war for truth" waged in international media and social media.
Netanyahu's main challenger
At a recent stump speech, Gadi Eisenkot took the stage. He is short with cropped white hair and he was wearing all black. He was speaking to a crowd in Kiryat Gat, a city near the Gaza border — historically a conservative Netanyahu stronghold.
Eisenkot is the former military chief of staff, appointed by Netanyahu a decade ago, who came back into the public spotlight in the days after Oct. 7 when he joined Netanyahu's war cabinet. Soon after, Eisenkot's son was killed as a soldier in the Gaza war. The very next day, his nephew, too, was killed there.
Eisenkot told the crowd that he began to disagree with Netanyahu's prosecution of the war three months in. "I saw a deep dysfunction in the decision-making process," Eisenkot said. "I saw that political and personal considerations were put above everything else."
He has pledged, if he wins, to launch an official national investigation into the security failure of Oct. 7 — something Netanyahu has refused to do.
"He's straight," said Yair Amar, a longtime Netanyahu voter, who said he has switched allegiances to Eisenkot.
"Many Israelis wish for a saner future," said Harel, the Haaretz columnist. "For somebody who perhaps is not as charismatic and doesn't look the part of an American senator, but is one of us and is seen as somebody who sacrificed a lot."
What happens if neither candidate wins
The race is tight. Most polls show Eisenkot's camp ahead of Netanyahu's, but those same polls show neither has a clear path to victory. To win, parties must form a coalition to control a majority in Israel's parliament. The election could tip on a small amount of votes or it could end in stalemate, forcing a repeat election next year. If that were to happen, Netanyahu would stay in power with full authority to make fateful decisions, like going to war. He strongly suggests he wants to strike Iran again.
If Netanyahu loses, Eisenkot vows a different approach. He has spoken of cracking down on settler expansion and violence against Palestinians in the West Bank and of reaching diplomatic agreements in the wars Netanyahu has kept open, but cautioned he would not withdraw troops from Lebanon and Gaza anytime soon.
"Truth be told," Eisenkot told the crowd, "it will take a lot of time."
On the biggest question of all — how to solve Israel's conflict with the Palestinians — Eisenkot boasted that he "never said the solution was two states for two peoples." Meaning the creation of a Palestinian state alongside Israel — the vision that the U.S. and the majority of the world have advocated for decades. Eisenkot thinks Israel should preserve possibilities for a solution in the future. After Oct. 7, Israelis do not want to discuss a Palestinian state.
"It's not something that the Israeli public can swallow at this time," Harel said. "More and more people suspect that the Arabs, the Palestinians, are out to kill us and that the world is out to get us. And there's less support for any kind of concessions because people keep bringing up Oct. 7."
This is not a race of conservatives versus liberals, right versus left. Eisenkot is leading a group of politicians who are largely right-wing, focused on matters of security and campaigning to enlist religious ultra-Orthodox Jews to the military, which Netanyahu has resisted in order to placate his ultra-Orthodox political allies.
"I'm trusting him on the military level, but is it enough?" said Israeli high school theater teacher Anat Ben-Ari, who came to hear Eisenkot speak. She was almost nervous voicing an unpopular opinion out loud: she wants him to forge peace agreements.
"The only way to end war — all the history says that — is by agreements, is by people talking to people, even enemies. Mostly enemies," Ben-Ari said. "I think we should also pay the price for peace in order for less people to die here and not always live on our swords."
Lior, the soldier, is resigned to a future of war.
"There will always be an enemy, so I think we will always be in a war. We [will] always live on our sword," Lior said. "It will always be."
The zero-sum game of love and fear
Israeli voters now consider two different visions for their country. Should Israel fight to regain the world's acceptance or to increase their neighbors' deterrence?
Israelis yearn for both says author Micah Goodman, who has written about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and previously served as an unofficial advisor to Israeli prime ministers.
"In the Middle East, you wanna have a certain kind of reputation. You want to be seen as unpredictable and a little crazy. Like, don't mess with us… and in the West, we want to be seen as a Norwegian, nice, sweet country playing by the rules, predictable."
Goodman said Israelis made their choice.
"After Oct. 7, the Middle East didn't fear us and you have to restore fear. But everything we did to restore fear eroded the love."

Ambedkar Konaseema, Eluru, West Godavari, Alluri Sitharama Raju, and Anakapalli, while heavy to very heavy rainfall of around 70 mm to 200 mm is likely in the districts of Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, NTR, Krishna, Guntur, Bapatla, Srikakulam, and Parvathipuram Manyam on Tuesday (October 26).

Special Relief Commissioner Rajesh Pravakar Patil said the State has 135 permanent cyclone shelters in the vulnerable districts and 1,600 temporary shelters have been made available.
Eight NDRF teams, 40 Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force teams, and fire services personnel have been deployed across districts.
“We are in constant touch with the Chhattisgarh government. When the cyclone curves away to Chhattisgarh, it will trigger heavy rain. This will send the Mahanadi River in spate. Since we are around the full moon day, discharge of water to the sea would not be that easy. We need to keep the plan ready for water discharge,” said Suresh Pujari, State Revenue and Disaster Management Minister.
‘Very severe cyclonic storm’
On Monday, the cyclonic storm lay centered over west-central and adjoining east-central Bay of Bengal, about 520 km southeast of Gopalpur in Odisha, 540 km east-southeast of Visakhapatnam, 620 km east-southeast of Kakinada, 720 km east-southeast of Machilipatnam, 790 km east-southeast of Bapatla, and 680 km northwest of Sri Vijaya Puram in the Andaman islands.
The IMD said it will move west-northwestwards, intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over west-central Bay of Bengal by Monday evening, and further strengthen to form a “very severe cyclonic storm” by Tuesday. Thereafter, the system, moving northwestwards, will cross the coast close to Yanam as a “very severe cyclonic storm”.

CHENNAI: The Central Crime Branch (CCB) of the Chennai police on Monday arrested former 
Tamil Nadu
 school education minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi in connection with an alleged Rs 100crore scam involving the issuance of recognition and other statutory clearances to private schools.
A CCB team reached his apartment in Aminjikarai and arrested him after 
Madras high court
 dismissed his anticipatory bail application.
The case was registered based on a complaint lodged by D C Elangovan, secretary of the Federation of Associations of Private Schools in Tamil Nadu. In his complaint, Elangovan alleged that B T Arasakumar and Muthukumar, who claimed to be the founder-president and treasurer, respectively, of the Tamil Nadu Private Schools Association, an unregistered organisation, had collected more than Rs 100 crore from private school managements.
The accused allegedly promised to secure permanent recognition from govt, approvals for upgrading schools, Directorate of Town and Country Planning (DTCP) clearances and other statutory permissions. The money was collected under the guise of contributions towards "party funds" for DMK, which was in power at the time.
Arasakumar claimed to have contacts within the govt and assured private school administrators that he could arrange the required permissions. 
However, he neither fulfilled his promises nor returned the money.
The CCB initially registered a case against Arasakumar under Section 7 (acceptance or demand of a bribe) and Section 12 (abetment of offences) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Arasakumar was arrested by the CCB on June 27. Based on subsequent inquiries, investigators began probing the involvement of Anbil Mahesh, who was the school education minister at the time.
On Sept 16, CCB teams conducted searches at nine locations in Chennai and Trichy, including four premises linked to Mahesh, and seized several documents. Similar searches were carried out on Sept 29.
Meanwhile, the Enforcement Directorate registered a case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) on Oct 1 in connection with the alleged racket.

Snapdeal parent AceVector's net loss for the September quarter (Q2) of FY27 zoomed 116% to ₹16.2 Cr from ₹7.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, the company trimmed its loss by 37% from ₹25.5 Cr. Operating revenue increased 17% YoY and 13% QoQ to ₹151.2 Cr. Including other income of ₹2.6 Cr, total income for the quarter stood at ₹153.8 Cr. Meanwhile, total expenses for the quarter also increased 22% YoY to ₹168.7 Cr. Logistics expense was the biggest chunk of expense during the quarter and increased 20% YoY to ₹71.4 Cr. AceVector listed on the bourses earlier this month post completing its ₹420 Cr IPO. The company had disclosed its financial performance for the fiscal year FY26 in its IPO papers. For the first half of the ongoing fiscal year, the company's consolidated revenue grew by 17% YoY to ₹285.5 Cr, supported by growth across Snapdeal and Unicommerce. In this, both Snapdeal and Unicommerce, AceVector's primary business engines, registered 15% YoY jump in revenue to ₹164.4 Cr and ₹110.4 Cr, respectively. Meanwhile, the company's consolidated Adjusted EBITDA loss for the half stood at ₹26.9 Cr. This is about triple the ₹9.3 Cr adjusted EBITDA loss incurred in H1 FY26. AceVector said that the increased loss was due to higher marketing investments in preparation of the festive season and temporary logistics cost pressures at Snapdeal due to macroeconomic factors, alongside investments in Unicommerce to support long-term growth. Snapdeal’s Operational Performance Snapdeal’s net merchandise value (NMV) from fashion grew 31% to ₹407.6 Cr in H1 FY27, accounting for 68.4% of the marketplace’s overall NMV. The value fashion platform’s overall NMV rose 10% to ₹595.7 Cr, while delivered units increased 16% to 150.5 lakh. The growth was driven by rising demand for value fashion and higher app adoption. App-delivered units grew 23% YoY to 133.6 lakh during the half-year, while annual transacting customers increased 12% to 1.31 Cr. Placed order frequency also rose 11% to 4.1 times a year. However, Snapdeal said the shift in festive shopping to Q3 FY27 moderated its Q2 and H1 growth. Early festive momentum has been encouraging, with units growing 60% YoY in the first half of October. The company also stepped up marketing investments in Q2 to acquire new users ahead of the festive season. These investments are expected to have an impact in Q3 FY27 as well. On profitability, Snapdeal’s contribution margin improved to 10.2% of NMV in Q2 FY27 from 8.8% in Q1, as temporary logistics cost pressures eased and monetisation improved. Its Adjusted EBITDA margin also narrowed to -5.2% of NMV in Q2 from -8.5% in Q1, aided by the recovery in contribution margin and lower marketing and fixed expenses as a proportion of NMV. Snapdeal is positioning itself as a value fashion destination for younger shoppers, with products largely priced between ₹300 and ₹800. Its zero-commission model is intended to attract a wider seller base, including small manufacturers and regional businesses, while allowing sellers greater flexibility in pricing. Snapdeal said nearly 65% of its new customers are Gen Z shoppers and more than 80% of its sales come from non-metro towns. Unicommerce Revenue Grows 15% AceVector’s other key business, ecommerce software provider Unicommerce, reported a 15% YoY increase in H1 FY27 revenue to ₹110.4 Cr from ₹96.3 Cr. Its Adjusted EBITDA, however, declined to ₹16.7 Cr from ₹19.7 Cr as it invested in AI-led product innovation, talent and capacity, particularly across sales and marketing. Unicommerce added 121 enterprise clients in Q2 FY27, compared with 103 in the year-ago quarter. Its enterprise client additions increased 24% YoY to 236 in H1 FY27 from 191 in H1 FY26. The company expects profitability to improve in the second half as incremental investments moderate and revenue growth creates operating leverage. It also expects Shipway, its shipping and logistics platform, to return to Adjusted EBITDA profitability in Q3 FY27. Important to mention that Unicommerce announced its quarterly performance earlier last week. The ecommerce SaaS company eported a consolidated net profit of ₹6.4 Cr in the September quarter while operating revenue grew 15% YoY and QoQ to ₹59.1 Cr during the quarter. Shares of AceVector ended today's trading session 0.96% higher at ₹20.93 apiece on the BSE .

Himesh Reshammiya has spoken about his journey in the music industry, his father Vipin Reshammiya’s influence on his career, and his decision to work on his own terms. The composer and singer shared these insights during his appearance on Komal Nahta’s podcast Game Changers: The Music Series.
Himesh Reshammiya recalls his journey in the music industry; says, “I wanted to work on my own terms”
The latest season of the podcast features singers, composers and music personalities discussing their creative journeys, inspirations and experiences in the industry. Hosted by trade analyst Komal Nahta, the series explores the stories behind the music and the people who have contributed to Indian cinema.
During the conversation, Himesh reflected on his early exposure to the film industry through his father, Vipin Reshammiya, who introduced him to the workings of the music business. He spoke about how his father's professional relationships and experience helped him gain access to opportunities that are not always available to musicians.
He said, “I wanted to work on my own terms. That was clear! My father was the first person to introduce electronic instruments in India. He did well and went on to become a producer. Whatever I am today is because of him. He gave me access that most musicians don’t have, but producers do. During my childhood, all the top people from the industry used to come to my house. He signed a film with Salman, was in talks with Aamir, and did a film with Mithun. I wanted to use the access I got through him to get the 300–400 songs I had made to be a part of films. I had 300–400 songs before joining the industry, and now I have 10,000. I have my own music label, so I don’t have to go out searching for music.”
Himesh also spoke about the volume of music he has composed over the years. From having 300–400 compositions before entering the industry to building a catalogue of around 10,000 songs, he highlighted how his approach to music has evolved throughout his career. He also pointed to owning a music label as a way to release his work without depending entirely on external opportunities.
With Game Changers: The Music Series, Komal Nahta continues to bring conversations with music industry figures to audiences. The latest episode featuring Himesh Reshammiya is available on the podcast’s YouTube channel.

US president Donald Trump claimed Brazil’s presidential election looked “rigged” and “so corrupt” after incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated his right-wing ally Flávio Bolsonaro, raising questions over how Washington will respond to the result.
Trump, speaking to reporters as he left Washington for a campaign rally ahead of next week’s US midterm elections, criticised the counting process and a last-minute decision to extend voting hours across Brazil.
“It looked like another rigged election, frankly,” Trump said. “It was a terrible look for the world.”
Asked whether he would take any action over the result, Trump declined to commit to a response, saying he was focused on domestic politics.
“I’m not running for Brazil, I’m running for the USA,” he said. “I like Lula, I get along with him very well. I just thought it was a very bad look, the way it was tabulated — with the extension.”
Trump did not provide evidence to support his claims of irregularities. His remarks came after Flávio Bolsonaro, the 45-year-old senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, called for the runoff result to be annulled. The challenge is considered unlikely to overturn Lula’s victory.
Voting extension becomes focus of criticism
Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered voting to be extended nationwide by two hours on Sunday after both candidates sought additional time in some areas. Lula’s request followed problems involving buses transporting voters in nine states, while Bolsonaro cited heavy rain in southern Brazil.
The extension caused confusion at some polling stations, with reports that voting machines had already been switched off before officials received the order to keep voting open.
Trump described the extension as “very strange” and cited it as a reason the election had a “very bad look”. However, he did not present evidence that the decision or the vote count had altered the outcome.
Flávio Bolsonaro’s demand to annul the result echoes efforts by his father to challenge his defeat in Brazil’s previous presidential election. Jair Bolsonaro was later convicted of plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in an attempt to overturn the result.
Trump’s Latin America ambitions face a setback
Trump’s comments come as he has repeatedly claimed credit for a rightward shift in Latin American politics, pointing to victories by conservative allies across the region. Brazil’s result leaves the country under Lula, a veteran left-wing leader whose government has clashed with Washington over trade and security policy.
“In South America, it was all leaning big left — it’s all right now,” Trump told reporters last week, claiming that every candidate he had endorsed in the region had won.
He described the shift towards conservative leadership as “extremely conservative in a very positive way”.
An ally of the Bolsonaro family, Trump had backed a political direction for Brazil that would bring it closer to his administration. Flávio Bolsonaro had promised to improve ties with Washington and pursue better deals with the US, including in the strategic minerals sector.
Despite the political divide, Trump has also spoken warmly of Lula. The two leaders have previously described their personal exchanges positively despite tensions over tariffs and other policy disputes.
Lula’s victory therefore leaves Washington facing a Brazilian government that has resisted some of Trump’s economic and diplomatic pressure, even as the US president says he maintains good personal relations with the Brazilian leader.

Four friends charred to death in Madhya Pradesh after car hits divider, catches fire
The incident took place around 11.30pm on Sunday on a four-lane highway in Badnawar, near a dhaba between Sadalpur and Kherod.
Four youngsters in Madhya Pradesh’s Dhar district were charred to death and another was critically injured after the vehicle they were travelling in hit a divider before catching fire, police said on Monday.
The incident took place around 11.30pm on Sunday on a four-lane highway in Badnawar, near a dhaba between Sadalpur and Kherod. The sole survivor is in a critical condition, the police said.
“The five friends were returning after visiting the Sanwariya Seth temple. On their way back, their vehicle hit the divider of a culvert. The impact was so severe that the vehicle fell off the culvert and caught fire,” a police officer said.
One of the occupants was thrown out of the vehicle, the officer said. The fire spread rapidly, leaving no chance for the remaining to escape, the officer added.
On learning about the incident, a police team and a fire engine rushed to the spot to douse the flames. The bodies were subsequently sent for an autopsy.
A case has been registered and a probe is underway, the officer added.
The deceased were identified as Ankush Chaudhary (20), Chetan Chaudhary (20), and Aditya Tiwari (19), all of whom were residents of Badi Sagaur, and Abhishek Solanki (21), a resident of Suhagpur, Sagaur.
The injured – Tushar Mandloi (20), resident of Madhopur, Sagaur – was referred to Indore after primary treatment and is believed to be in a critical condition, the officer quoted above said.

Luis de la Fuente won the Ballon d'Or for men's coach of the year on Monday (October 26, 2026) after leading Spain to World Cup glory.
"Teamwork makes us invincible. This is a great honour," de la Fuente said after collecting the award at a ceremony in London.
"The secret is to work with very generous players that put the team first. We've got such an amazing pool of talent, the best in the world, so as a coach I have such a great amount of talent to work with. So this is their success," he added.
In an age of coaches who were previously star players, 65-year-old de la Fuente stands out as a technician who worked his way up through the national coaching ranks in Spain.
After a solid career as a player led to an undistinguished stint in club coaching, he was flicking through the sports pages in 2013 when he saw an advert placed by the Spanish Football Federation for a youth team coach.
He applied, got the job with Spain's Under-19s, and 13 years later, some of the players from that squad were part of the teams he has led to victory in the Nations League, Euro 2024 and then the World Cup.
De la Fuente insisted from the start in the United States this summer that he had the strongest squad in the tournament, even when they stumbled to a goalless draw against World Cup debutants Cape Verde in their opening match.
They built momentum with each match and dispatched one of the pre-tournament favourites, France, in a clinical 2-0 win in the semi-final.
In a tight final against Lionel Messi's Argentina in New Jersey, de la Fuente's men kept their cool in the face of muscular tactics from the opposition and Ferran Torres smashed in the winning goal for a 1-0 victory.
The women's coaching award was awarded to Barcelona's Pere Romeu for masterminding a season in which they won the Spanish league, Spanish cup, Super Cup and Champions League.

Your monthly kitchen and business budgets are set for a fresh assessment starting November 1, as a series of crucial LPG cylinder rules and price updates take effect.
Millions of consumers relying on Indane, HP Gas, and Bharatgas will need to navigate not just the standard monthly price revisions by oil marketing companies (OMCs) but also stricter Aadhaar-based authentication norms to ensure their subsidies remain uninterrupted, as well as the broader shift toward piped natural gas (PNG).
According to media reports, not all guidelines taking effect in November are entirely new; several are existing mandates slated for stricter enforcement over the coming month.
OMCs traditionally review and revise commercial LPG prices on the first day of each month.
According to Goodreturns, commercial cylinder rates rose in October, with a 19-kg cylinder priced at ₹2,810 in Delhi. The November 1 pricing for these cylinders—which are highly sensitive to global energy supply conditions and heavily utilised by hotels and restaurants—will depend entirely on the upcoming OMC announcement.
Conversely, domestic LPG prices have remained stable in recent months. The standard 14.2-kg household cylinder has not seen a price revision since June 7, 2026, continuing to retail at ₹942 in Delhi.
Consumers are advised to verify city-specific rates before booking their November refills, as final prices vary by location.
A critical requirement for households seeking refills at the regulated retail selling price is biometric Aadhaar authentication.
As mandated by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, this e-KYC requirement was officially implemented on 1 October 2026. Consumers who have already completed their authentication process do not need to repeat it.
Eligible users who fail to complete the e-KYC process may be blocked from booking subsidised refills until the verification is finished, Jagran reported.
Those choosing not to authenticate, the report said, can formally register this preference through their respective OMC’s channels and will subsequently only be permitted to purchase 5-kg or 10-kg cylinders at standard market rates.
Download your LPG gas cylinder provider's (eg, IndianOil One for Indane, Hello BPCL for Bharat Gas, or HP Pay for HP Gas) app
OR
Alternatively, verification can be finalised through local distributors or during the delivery of the physical cylinder.
For households transitioning from LPG to PNG, it is important to note that rising crude oil prices do not directly dictate domestic piped gas rates in India.
Instead, the final consumer price depends heavily on the specific city-gas distributor's sourcing mix—namely, the ratio of domestically produced gas to imported liquefied natural gas (LNG).
Government pricing frameworks, distribution logistics, and applicable taxes further determine the final cost to the consumer.

TL;DR: India received 759.4 mm of rainfall during the June–September 2026 monsoon, 12.6% below its long-period average. East and Northeast India recorded their lowest seasonal rainfall since 1901, while the South Peninsula received 24% less rain than normal. Although extremely heavy rainfall events rebounded to 388, southern reservoirs held 24.76 BCM against a ten-year average of 43.33 BCM. Historical records show repeated drought declarations in districts such as Ananthapuramu in Andhra Pradesh, while post-monsoon soil moisture remains below average in several states. Together, these indicators reveal an uneven monsoon impact and highlight areas requiring closer monitoring.
Context
India’s monsoon tells two stories this year. The country received 12.6% less rainfall than normal between June and September 2026, but the shortfall was far from uniform. Eastern and northeastern India received 26% less rain than average, while the southern peninsula recorded a 24% deficit.
The season began on a difficult note, with June rainfall nearly 40% below normal. July brought a brief recovery, with rainfall slightly above average, but the deficit returned in August and September. The rebound, in other words, did not erase the shortfall.
What does this mean for the land and the people who depend on the rain? The IMD had warned of a below-normal monsoon in May, when El Niño conditions were expected to develop. But the national rainfall deficit is only the starting point. To understand where drought risks are emerging, it is necessary to look beyond how much rain fell to where it fell, how long the dry spells lasted, and how much moisture remained in the soil.
Who compiles this data?
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) publishes rainfall data and monsoon forecasts, while the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (NCFC) monitors agricultural conditions using rainfall, soil moisture and satellite indicators. The India Drought Monitor, developed by IIT Gandhinagar’s Water and Climate Lab, tracks drought conditions using meteorological and satellite data.
Where can I download clean & structured data related to this?
Clean, structured datasets related to Indian rainfall, drought conditions, agriculture and water resources are available on Dataful.
Key Insights
India’s 2026 monsoon ranks among the weakest in decades, with sharp regional deficits
India received 759.4 mm of rainfall during the June–September 2026 southwest monsoon, just 87% of its long-period average (LPA). According to the IMD, this was the country’s fourth-lowest monsoon rainfall since 2001 and 13th-lowest since 1901. The national shortfall, however, conceals sharper regional deficits.
East and Northeast India received 1,016.3 mm, or 74% of its regional LPA, making it the lowest seasonal rainfall for the region since 1901. The South Peninsula received 542 mm, or 76% of its LPA, ranking fourth-lowest since 1901 and second-lowest since 2001. Northwest India received 94.1% of its LPA, while Central India recorded 97%, within the normal range.
The shortfall also affected the monsoon core zone, which includes much of India’s rain-fed agricultural area. It received 779.9 mm, which is below the lower limit of the normal category (782.8 to 881.2). Across India’s 36 meteorological subdivisions, 17 (42% of the area) recorded deficient rainfall, 18 (53%) received normal rainfall, and one, in Odisha (5%), recorded excess rainfall. At the district level, 282 of 741 meteorological districts (38% of total area) recorded below-normal rainfall, while 34 (5% of total area) received significantly below-normal rainfall. Another 312 districts (42% of total area) recorded normal rainfall, 90 (12% of total area) received excess rainfall, and 16 (2% of total area) recorded substantially above-normal rainfall.
Extremely heavy rainfall events rebound in 2026, driven by a July spike
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) classifies rainfall of 115.6–204.4 mm in 24 hours as very heavy and rainfall exceeding 204.4 mm as extremely heavy. During the June–September 2026 monsoon, India recorded 1,765 very heavy rainfall events and 388 extremely heavy events. Extremely heavy events rose from 296 in 2022 to 426 in 2023 and peaked at 473 in 2024, before declining to 303 in 2025 and increasing again in 2026. Very heavy rainfall events followed a different trend, rising from 1,875 in 2022 to a peak of 2,632 in 2024, before falling to 2,109 in 2025 and 1,765 in 2026. July 2026 alone recorded 269 extremely heavy events, the highest July count in since 2022, compared with 84 in 2025. These figures show that although the overall frequency of very heavy rainfall has declined since 2024, extremely heavy events rebounded in 2026.
Historical El Niño years show a recurring concern, but widely varying rainfall outcomes
Historical data in the IMD’s El Niño table show why the phenomenon matters when assessing India’s 2026 monsoon, but also why it cannot explain the season’s outcome on its own. Of the 17 El Niño years listed between 1951 and 2023, 12 recorded below-normal June–September rainfall, including seven with deficits exceeding 10%. Yet outcomes varied considerably: rainfall was 22.3% below normal in 1972 and 20.9% below normal in 2002, while 1994 recorded a 13.9% surplus and 1997 ended almost exactly at normal, despite being the only Strong El Niño among all.
Monthly figures reveal another important distinction. In 2002, July rainfall was 50.6% below normal, contributing to a seasonal deficit of 20.9%. In 2023, above-normal rainfall in July and September partly offset August’s 36.1% shortfall, leaving the season 5.3% below normal. A seasonal total can therefore conceal sharp monthly swings, just as a national average can mask regional rainfall deficits.
That distinction is relevant to the 2026 monsoon. India received 759.4 mm of rainfall, or 87% of its long-period average, with particularly large deficits in East and Northeast India and the South Peninsula. IMD reported that El Niño strengthened during the season, but the historical comparisons do not establish how much it contributed to this year’s shortfall. Nor does deficient seasonal rainfall alone establish the severity of agricultural drought.
Southern reservoirs fall to less than half their year-ago levels
The clearest concentration of pressure appears in the reservoir data. On 15 October, CWC’s 178 monitored reservoirs nationally held 68.58% of their live-storage capacity. Their storage was 16.44% below the corresponding ten-year average. Of the 178 reservoirs monitored by the Central Water Commission, on 15 October 2026, 105 held more than 80% of their ten-year average storage, while 73 were at or below that level. Of the latter, 31 had storage at or below 50% of normal.
The shortfall was concentrated in the South. Its 50 monitored reservoirs held 24.76 BCM, against a ten-year normal of 43.33 BCM, a deficit of 18.57 BCM. This accounts for approximately 74.5% of the net national storage shortfall of 24.93 BCM, including the effect of a small surplus in Central India.
State-level departures varied considerably. Storage was 61.50% below normal in Tamil Nadu, 59.33% in Andhra Pradesh and 51.63% in Telangana. Karnataka was 32.28% below normal, while Kerala was 17.67% below. These figures indicate a weaker reservoir position, but do not translate directly into equivalent reductions in water available to every user. Actual supply depends on the reservoirs serving an area, existing commitments, alternative sources and distribution systems.
The timing is also important. Tamil Nadu receives a substantial share of its rainfall during the October–December northeast monsoon, making subsequent rainfall and reservoir inflows important to watch. The 15 October 2026 figures are therefore a snapshot, not a final assessment of water availability for the coming months. Even so, the regional imbalance is clear: the national storage figure masks the depth of the shortfall in southern India.
District data show where rainfall deficiency meets underlying drought vulnerability
It is also important to look at districts apart from broad regions. IMD’s seasonal rainfall distribution records 282 districts with deficient rainfall and 34 with large-deficient rainfall. Together, that is 316 districts, or approximately 42.6% of the 741 districts listed. Further, 312 districts are recorded in the normal category, 90 with excess rainfall and 16 with large-excess rainfall. The distribution confirms that the deficient season was far from uniform. It also needs to be interpreted precisely: a rainfall-deficient district is not automatically a district officially declared drought-hit.
The agriculture ministry’s Crisis Management Plan (CMP) for drought provides a list of districts where state governments declared drought from 2011-12 to 2025-26. It has 472 districts declared drought over the years, and such declarations peaked in 2015-16 with 294 districts declared drought-affected, and in recent years, it declined: 71 in 2023-24 (Karnataka 31, Maharashtra 15, Rajasthan 12, Andhra Pradesh 13), and only 5 in 2024-25 and 4 in 2025-26, all in Andhra Pradesh. Ananthapuramu was declared drought-affected in 11 years, followed by Barmer, Jaisalmer, Bellari and 14 other districts with declarations in 10 years each.
A separate 2024 district risk assessment by the Department of Science and Technology identifies underlying vulnerability. It places 91 districts in the very high drought-risk category and 188 in the high category, 279 districts in total. More than 90% of districts in the Very High category (83 out of 91) are located in Bihar, Assam, Jharkhand, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, and Maharashtra. These classifications combine hazard, exposure and vulnerability. They identify relative structural risk, rather than establishing that all these districts experience drought. The left image provides the Drought exposure Map, while the right image shows the current drought conditions as on 21st October, 2026, according to the India Drought Monitor.
Root-Zone Soil Moisture overlaps with low reservoir storage levels in Southern India
The NCFC’s report dated 19 October 2026 provides a more recent indicator of agricultural conditions. It compares root-zone soil moisture for 8–14 October with the average for the previous ten years.
The report finds that root-zone soil moisture was similar to or better than the ten-year average in parts of Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh, eastern and northern Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. In contrast, soil moisture was below the ten-year average in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and the Northeast region.
The comparison suggests that the effects of the monsoon deficit were not uniform across the country and that some areas entered the post-monsoon period with less soil moisture than their historical average. For agriculture, root-zone moisture is particularly relevant because it reflects water availability in the soil where plant roots draw moisture.
The overlap between below-average soil moisture and low reservoir storage in parts of southern India warrants particular attention. At the same time, soil moisture at or above the historical average in parts of eastern and central India shows why a national rainfall deficit cannot be used as a proxy for conditions in every district.
The coming weeks will bring further evidence about how these conditions develop. In Tamil Nadu, the northeast monsoon and associated reservoir inflows will be especially relevant. Elsewhere, changes in soil moisture and water storage will help clarify whether the seasonal rainfall deficit translates into continuing agricultural or water-supply pressure.
Why does it matter?
A national rainfall deficit reveals little about whether a farmer’s soil holds enough moisture or a household can count on its water supply. In 2026, 316 of 741 meteorological districts recorded deficient or large-deficient rainfall, while southern reservoirs held substantially less water than their ten-year average. The NCFC also reported below-average root-zone soil moisture across several states in October 2026. Together, these indicators point to pressure on water availability, although local supplies depend on reservoir storage, existing commitments, alternative sources and distribution systems. Subsequent rainfall and reservoir replenishment will be particularly important for Tamil Nadu during its northeast monsoon season. Historical drought declarations and district-level risk assessments add another layer, helping distinguish the current rainfall shortfall from recurring drought exposure.
Key Numbers
- 13% below average: India received 759.4 mm of southwest monsoon rainfall in 2026, against a long-period average of 868.6 mm.
- 388 extremely heavy rainfall events: Up from 303 in 2025, an increase of approximately 28%, despite the deficient season.
- 316 of 741 districts: Recorded deficient or large-deficient seasonal rainfall, accounting for approximately 42.6% of the districts listed.
- 42.85% below average: Southern India’s monitored reservoirs held 24.760 BCM on 15 October, against a corresponding ten-year average of 43.327 BCM.

Election Day is almost here — but even after the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, the election won’t really be over. The vote count will take days or even weeks in some states. President Donald Trump seems certain to raise objections to results he doesn’t like — he’s already getting started in Alaska — and he has threatened to marshal the forces of the federal government in his efforts.
The one thing everyone can do to fight for free and fair elections
Trump wants to undermine faith in US democracy. Don’t let him.
It’s an anxious moment for American voters: Will we have a free and fair election — or not? Luckily, says Eliza Sweren-Becker, deputy director in the Brennan Center’s Voting Rights and Elections Program, there is still one thing that every American 18 and older can do to make sure their voice is heard: vote.
“I think that is the intent. It’s to create a lack of confidence. It’s to discourage voters from participating,” Sweren-Becker told Vox’s Astead Herndon on America, Actually. “But the only way that that campaign to undermine our confidence and to sow distrust actually works is if voters stay home. The way to defeat that attempt to shake voters’ trust in democracy is just to participate.”
Sweren-Becker spoke with Astead about what states could do to speed up their vote counts and ensure everyone has a chance to cast their ballot, the need to restore the Voting Rights Act, and the long-term impact of Trump’s election denialism.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
Let’s start with Election Day. More than a dozen states count late-arriving ballots. President Donald Trump has used the shifting vote counts as pretense to further his own election interference claims.
How prepared should folks be for a long wait in November for results? And how that could impact confidence in the results?
You’re absolutely right that we may get results out of states or in certain races in the days following Election Day. Voters should not expect to have the final result on Election Day.
And when you hear reporting on the news that somebody’s ahead or somebody’s behind, remember: They haven’t counted all the votes yet.
The critical thing is we need to count every vote, and every person’s vote needs to be counted.
So while it is true that some states allow ballots to arrive after Election Day, they all have to be cast by Election Day. The Supreme Court just this year said that it’s totally appropriate for states to set their own ballot receipt deadlines. We have to be patient, as an American electorate, to get the proper results to count every ballot and make sure all the voices are heard.
But isn’t it kinda wild that we can’t get results on election night? I saw Donald Trump cite the Brazilian presidential election, and while I know he’s doing that from a self-interested place, I did think for a second: Why does it take so long for us to put these results together?
I could totally understand why people would prefer the results faster. And candidly, could states do better at preparing and counting faster? Sure. But they have limited resources. They are working their butts off to prepare for the election with the staff that they have, and then they work tremendously hard to count properly, accurately, as fast as they can.
Could states change their policies to allow them, in some places, to pre-process ballots, to allow them to get to results faster? Sure. I’m not saying states shouldn’t change their policies to create more efficiency here. But given the rules of the road that we have, we need to make sure that every properly cast ballot is counted.
If I’m someone who is concerned about election security and free and fair elections, what should I be looking out for?
So, for example, I have heard that there is some anxiety about mail voting.
If you want to cast a mail ballot, just know that you probably have a bunch of options in your state as to how you can cast it. You can certainly rely on the mail and have USPS deliver that ballot, but of course, we know occasionally mail gets delayed. Your state may have ballot drop boxes. You may have ballot drop-off at election officials’ offices, or even at polling places.
Find out your options.
Yes, definitely find out your options. Voters should also check their voter registration status. Make sure it’s up to date with their current address. Of course, if you’re not registered to vote and you still have time in your state to register, please do register.
Everyone should participate. Our democracy works best the more of us that can participate. If your registration date has not passed, don’t forget to register to vote. Vote with your friends, vote with your community, vote with your family. Voting should be joyful. It’s a civic experience that I think is really fun.
I try to take my kids with me to vote because it’s exciting. They get stickers. Everyone loves stickers.
It’s half the reason I go.
It’s also a reminder. You get your sticker, other people see you, they know it’s Election Day, maybe they go out to vote.
It’s a way to be part of your community and invest in your community and to choose who you want to be a leader of your community.
What about after Election Day?
Earlier this year, Democrats and Republicans in Congress circulated a letter asking members to commit to recognizing state-certified winners and “oppose any attempt to refuse or delay a seating of a member-elect.” We saw House Speaker Mike Johnson delay the swearing-in of an Arizona representative last year,
That seems to me like maybe a preview of what might be to come. How fearful should we be of these post-election attempts to block members from being seated?
I think those scenarios are highly unlikely. I understand why folks are worried about them, but the reality is, states have their own certification processes, which are laid out in state law and that are mandatory for them to follow. It is not discretionary whether states certify their elections. So once there is a new Congress, we have confidence that they will be seated according to how the voters actually cast their ballots.
I want to end by thinking about Trump’s consistent questioning of the integrity of our election system. If he ultimately doesn’t try to actually steal the election, what is the long-term impact of his relentless focus on it and support for policies like the Save America Act?
Just because we have won in many courts against this administration doesn’t delude me into thinking that this administration is just going to stop in this years-long campaign to sow doubt in our election systems.
I think that is the intent. It’s to create a lack of confidence. It’s to discourage voters from participating. And to some degree, I think the administration has succeeded in creating some confusion about the rules or a lack of confidence. But the only way that that campaign to undermine our confidence and to sow distrust actually works is if voters stay home.
The way to defeat that attempt to shake voters’ trust in democracy is to participate in our democracy and to turn out and to make their voices heard regardless of party, regardless of candidate. To say that we will not be made to fear participation in our democracy, but we are going to continue to seize it and take joy in it and show that we deserve a stronger representative democracy that serves all Americans.
What are things that could happen to inspire trust in our electoral system? Are there reforms that you think might make the public feel a reinvigorated sense of confidence?
There are certainly things that Congress could do to create a national floor of voter access and ensure that someone’s right to vote doesn’t depend on what state they live in. That includes basic reforms like same-day registration, online voter registration, universal access to mail voting that doesn’t require strict satisfaction of certain excuse requirements, which still exists in many states.
I think it’s time for Congress to ban partisan gerrymandering. I also think it’s time to restore the Voting Rights Act, and Congress can enact a statutory right to vote that is meaningfully enforceable so that voters can go to court if their voting rights have been burdened, and they can get a real remedy.
That has been really undermined by the Supreme Court, but Congress can and should respond. They have it within their power. The Constitution gives Congress the power to set rules for elections. They should.

AI-powered healthtech platform BioStack has raised $9.5 Mn (₹90.4 Cr) in its seed funding round led by Peak XV Partners, Afore Capital, DCVC, Emerson Collective, SV Angel, Verdict Capital, Streamlined Ventures, and Y Combinator. The startup plans to utilise the fresh capital to continue expanding its presence in the US and other international markets, including India, Brazil, and Argentina. A chunk of the capital will also be used to scale its tech stack and ramp up hiring across engineering and research teams. Founded in 2025 by Sanat Mishra and Parth Patwa, BioStack claims to be building the data infrastructure for the next generation of medical AI. It combines fragmented clinical information across systems such as electronic health records, medical imaging, clinical notes and medications. The startup then uses this data to create proprietary datasets for research, biotechnology, and the development and training of medical AI models. “We’re building the infrastructure that connects all of the clinical information and makes it useful, both for clinicians making decisions today and for the researchers and AI developers building the future of medicine,” said BioStack cofounder and CEO Mishra. BioStack currently works with multiple hospitals across the US, Brazil and Argentina. In India, it is also connecting cancer patients with an investigational cancer vaccine program. The startup also claims that it offers use cases such as AI model evaluation, disease modeling, biomarker discovery, patient stratification and treatment-response analysis. Besides offering custom workflows to protect patient privacy, the startup claims to have so far processed 10 Cr de-identified patient records, more than “several hundred thousand” fragmented X-Rays, MRIs and CT scans, and “several million” telehealth audio transcripts. For context, de-identified patient records are medical datasets that have had all personal and direct identifiers removed so that the individual cannot reasonably be linked to the data. The fundraise comes as India becomes a training ground to collect datasets for powering AI models and physical AI products. Startups are tapping India’s huge population to collect recordings of workers performing physical tasks, processing the footage, and selling the resulting datasets to frontier AI labs and robotics companies. For instance, the likes of Awign, Objectways and Human Archive are building pipelines to supply first-person footage of human activity to AI developers. Just a day ago, instant home services startup Pronto’s founder Anjali Sardana launched Provision Labs, a US-based venture to collect data for physical AI systems. At the heart of all this is the Indian AI training dataset, which is projected to become a $1.3 Bn opportunity by 2033.

India-Mexico trade deal: Talks to begin this week amid fresh 50% tariffs on Indian exports
India’s merchandise exports to Mexico stood at $5.73 billion in 2025-26, with automobiles accounting for the largest share at $1.92 billion.
India and Mexico will sign the terms of reference (ToR) this week to formally launch negotiations for a preferential trade agreement (PTA), aiming to protect Indian exports from recently imposed high tariffs in the Mexican market, officials said.
The proposed agreement is expected to cover key Indian exports, including automobiles, textiles, footwear, plastics, steel, chemicals and toys, which face tariffs of up to 50% under Mexico’s new tariff regime.
Both countries have finalised the terms of reference and are expected to sign the document in the next couple of days, the officials said, requesting anonymity. Commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal is visiting Mexico from Monday as part of a week-long trade mission that also includes Brussels, the headquarters of the European Union.
The proposed India-Mexico PTA is expected to help Indian exporters mitigate the impact of higher tariffs imposed by the Mexican government on 1,463 items imported from countries that do not have a bilateral trade arrangement with Mexico, such as a PTA or a free trade agreement (FTA).
Experts said signing the terms of reference would mark the first step towards protecting Indian exporters from the higher duties, particularly in the automobile sector.
According to government trade data, India’s merchandise exports to Mexico stood at $5.73 billion in 2025-26, with automobiles accounting for the largest share at $1.92 billion.
The list of products affected by Mexico’s tariff measures includes automobiles, textiles and clothing, plastics, steel, household appliances, aluminium, toys, furniture, footwear, leather goods, paper and cardboard, motorcycles, trailers and glass products.
The tariff measures took effect on January 1 under a decree linked to Mexico’s Plan, which aims to increase domestic content in production chains by 15% by 2030. Launched in January 2025, the initiative seeks to make Mexico one of the world’s 10 largest economies by 2030, revive local industries and create 1.5 million jobs.
PTA seen as faster route to protect exports
Experts said negotiating a bilateral PTA could help India address the tariff challenge more quickly than pursuing a comprehensive FTA, which would take relatively more time to conclude.
One official said the proposed agreement is expected to focus exclusively on preferential trade in goods.
A PTA generally has a limited scope and provides a positive list of products on which tariffs are reduced, though they are rarely eliminated entirely. An FTA, by contrast, seeks to eliminate tariffs on a much wider range of goods, subject to a negative list of excluded items.
India-Mexico trade stood at $7.83 billion in FY26
Bilateral merchandise trade between India and Mexico stood at around $7.83 billion in 2025-26, according to government data.
India exported goods worth approximately $5.73 billion to Mexico during the financial year, while imports from the Latin American country stood at $2.1 billion.
India’s major exports to Mexico include automobiles and auto parts, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods and chemical products.
Mexico’s exports to India are dominated by crude oil, which accounts for almost three-fourths of its total shipments to the country. Other products supplied by Mexico include gold and related jewellery, as well as chemical compounds.
The proposed PTA is expected to provide a framework for preferential market access for selected goods, with negotiations set to begin following the formal signing of the terms of reference.
