A shark went astray and captured Korea's heart - will she finally make it back to sea?
- Published
As soon as a large shark was spotted in a canal in Busan - a bustling shipping hub and beach city on South Korea's south-eastern tip - marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo was drafted in to rescue it.
He got the call in mid-September, on his way home from a business trip tracking shoals of mackerel to aid fishing vessels. Despite being one of the country's leading shark experts, he never thought he'd be asked by the coastguard to actually save one.
South Korea is no stranger to sharks but one this size, in a shallow, concrete canal right by the world's seventh busiest port, was unheard of - until now.
With an excited crowd already gathering at the waterfront, his team from the National Institute of Fisheries Science had to move fast.
The first task was to determine the species.
Some sharks are more dangerous than others. The star of the 1975 blockbuster Jaws, the great white shark, is known to attack and kill humans.
The specimen in Busan was found to be a female dusky shark, a species linked only to two deadly attacks. Still, Kim feared someone in the crowd might jump or fall into the canal.
The shark had to return to sea.
A small coastguard ship made an initial attempt using an electrical deterrence device, which generates a weak current that sharks avoid.
They're usually used after sightings near popular beaches. But after five hours, officials determined this particular shark was too large and fast for the device.
Kim changed tack, deciding instead to wait for the shark to let herself out. But that did not happen.
As authorities looked for ways to guide her out of the canal, the stranded creature went viral.
Just hours after she appeared, the council had sent everyone in the city an emergency text alert, urging pedestrians and residents to "exercise caution for their safety".
People rarely visited the park along the canal but because of the message, the place was soon brimming with people eager to spot the shark.
Adoring fans named her Bukangi, from "buk hang", the Korean name of the nearby harbour. Within days, a business trademarked it and Bukangi pins, plushies and T-shirts began selling online.
City authorities joined in, livestreaming the shark and making her their official mascot.
A banner was hung at the entrance of the canal, asking the public to sign a petition "on behalf of Bukangi" to demand the national government's support for the construction of a new 30,000-seater baseball stadium by the canal.
Shark spotting became a team effort among locals and visitors. The unspoken rule was that children were given the front row, and whoever saw Bukangi had to point her out to newer arrivals.
Some self-appointed defenders even patrolled the canal at night to make sure no-one was shining torches or lasers at Bukangi.
More than 1.6 million visitors ultimately flocked to the canal.
The local mayor said the shark brought "the kind of publicity even billions of dollars cannot buy" to the port.
"It's really rare these days for people to come together," said Kim Joo-eun, who came to see the shark with her two nieces. "I feel that Bukangi brought us all together, cheering for her… It's a lot of fun."
But officials couldn't leave Bukangi in the canal.
As September drew to an end, she hadn't been seen feeding for days and was spotted with bloody abrasions on her snout from bumping into the concrete walls.
Prominent marine biology professor Choi Yoon told local media that experts were particularly worried about a "critical" injury around the shark's eye.
At the end of September, Kim's team mounted another rescue attempt. The marine biologist looked back to a 2004 incident in Massachusetts, when water jets were used to drive a great white shark away from a shallow pond.
But when the team tried this on Bukangi, she kept circling back.
On 2 October, they decided to install a net spanning the width of the canal to stop her from returning. She managed to swim around the net and was back within hours.
At this point, Kim started thinking the shark might have problems with her snout's electromagnetic sensors, which she uses for navigation. Or she might have become confused by the loud noises emitted by ships in the harbour.
The reason Bukangi was even in the canal may be a sign of warming seas, the oceans ministry suggests.
It believes she may have followed plentiful fish to warmer waters. Some 50 large sharks were recorded off South Korea's east coast in the first half of the year; four times as many as last year.
With each failed attempt some of Bukangi's newfound fans began demanding she be left in peace.
On Thursday, several showed up with placards and shouted "leave Bukangi alone" and "remove the net".
When a security guard told them to stop, one man cried: "I love you, Bukangi!"
"I am obsessed with her," said Jeong Yo-won, a woman in her 40s. She called the shark a "source of hope and joy" and insisted, "I don't think we should evict her mercilessly like this."
Others thought it was time for her to return home.
"I would stare at her for hours because I was so enamoured by her," a woman said after sighting the shark on her third attempt. "I hope Bukangi would stay, but I prefer that she lives a long and healthy life."
People joked the council should "make an official ID for Bukangi and give a pension", Shin Seungmin said.
"She brought so much fun with her. But she should go and live her normal shark life."
Staying in the canal would seriously jeopardise Bukangi because of falling autumn temperatures, Kim explains. Usually this prompts sharks to migrate to warmer waters further south.
"This canal is far from something we can call a habitat," he adds. "A wild animal cannot stay in a space made strictly for humans."
Eventually, as public scrutiny grew, the oceans ministry took over the rescue operation from the fisheries institute. Around 40 personnel, including divers from Busan's aquarium, were mobilised. A vet was on standby, along with an ambulance in case the divers were attacked by Bukangi.
On Wednesday divers installed two layers of nets, and Bukangi was successfully herded out of the narrow canal into open water. But overnight, she swam back into the canal, diving under the outer net.
This left her trapped between the two layers.
Then on thursday, rescuers removed the outer layer, and Bukangi was seen swimming further and further towards open sea.
Although she did occasionally circle back, the rescue operation had ended.
There have been no sightings of Bukangi in the last few days, which experts say is a positive sign.
Prof Choi believes she may be adjusting to wider, deeper waters.
She is unlikely to have travelled far, he adds, and could reappear over the coming week.
But he is also worried about any injuries she may have sustained. Trapped in the canal, it "kept scraping against [the walls], stripping the skin off its snout and even its pectoral fins", he told local media.
For now, South Korea is holding its breath, hoping Bukangi can find her way back to her home - the open sea.

On October 17, Saturday, even as 19 people were killed and several injured in a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata, a different scene of chaos unfolded a few kilometres away at Jadavpur.
A bulldozer was brought in by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) and Kolkata Police to demolish bookstalls of Left parties set up near 8B bus stand of Jadavpur. While locals and Left workers, including CPI(M) and AISA activists, protested through the night to thwart the attempted demolition, the authorities succeeded in bringing down certain bookstalls and damaging others.
Left book stalls have come under threat both from Right-wing fanatics and the administration after chief minister Suvendu Adhikari issued a warning. “You consider Sanatan Dharma to be merely cultural. You do not say Durga Puja; You call it ‘Sharadotsab’. I will tell all Durga Puja committees that if these so-called communists come to set up stalls and do not write Durga Puja, do not allow a single stall,” Adhikari had announced earlier.
Alt News has already reported on alleged attacks on book stalls by BJP workers in several parts of the state.
Same Stalls Set Up For Years
Left organisations, including the CPI(M), AISA, SUCI(C) and Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR), have historically set up bookstalls in and around the 8B bus stand area of Jadavpur. The CPI(M) has been setting up its bookstall there for over 40 years, while AISA’s stall has been set up for more than 10 years. The APDR has been setting up a bookstall for the past four to five years. This year, an RSS bookstall was set up right between the CPI(M) and AISA stalls.
Around 6 pm on Saturday, a joint team of Kolkata Police, Central Armed Police Force personnel and KMC arrived with a JCB earthmover to demolish the Left bookstalls. However, the RSS stall was left untouched.
According to the KMC personnel present at the spot, the Left stalls lacked the necessary permissions. Left parties, however, denied this allegation. Representatives of the Left parties argued that they had paid the required fees to the KMC to set up the stalls.
The administration, however, maintained that paying the fees did not necessarily mean that permission had been granted to set up the stalls. The Left parties, in turn, asked the authorities to show which documents they lacked, while also asking what documents the RSS stall possessed that made it legal. Their requests were repeatedly rejected, representatives told Alt News.
‘Authorities Passed the Buck’
“Police and the KMC workers were only passing the buck on each other. Police said the KMC had sought their help to demolish illegal structures. When confronted, KMC workers said that police had asked them to help demolish our stalls,” said DYFI Kolkata district committee member Sainik Sur.
“We asked police and KMC time and again to show the demolition order. But all they said was that there was immense pressure from higher levels to demolish all the Left stalls,” added Sur.
A similar claim was echoed by AISA state president Ritam Maji. “Police and the KMC made it very clear that the Left bookstalls were illegal, whereas the ‘Sanatani’ stall that came up this year for the first time was legal. We have paid the required fee to KMC and have the receipt of the same, yet they claimed that our stalls were illegal. When we asked them to show documents of the RSS-backed stall, to figure out what permissions we lacked, the police simply said that the top brass of the KMC had requested that the space be cleared,” said Maji.
Besides the earthmover, the administration had also brought a KMC dumper truck near the stalls, generally used to collect and dispose of garbage, allegedly to collect the debris from the stalls and the books, representatives of the Left said.
Hundreds Gather Around Bulldozer
After an APDR stall was partially demolished, nearly a hundred people — locals in the area and Left party workers — gathered near the bulldozer in the evening to prevent it from demolishing stalls. Armed with flags, books and posters, they formed human chains around the bookstalls, forcing the authorities to retreat. CPI(M) central committee member and former Jadavpur CPI(M) MLA Sujan Chakraborty also reached the spot to join the resistance.
Around 1 am on October 18, Sunday, personnel from Kolkata Police, CAPF and KMC workers started assembling near the bookstalls again. An hour later, they again started dismantling the APDR stall.
The SUCI(C) bookstall, set up near Gate 2 of Jadavpur University, was also demolished around this time. The area surrounding the stall was cordoned off by security personnel, and party workers could not prevent the demolition.
CPI(M) Kolkata district committee member Sudip Sengupta, who is in charge of the party’s bookstalls, documented the resistance against the demolition as scores of people stood in front of the JCB earthmover, through his Facebook Live.
After the SUCI(C) stall was brought down, the administration tried to demolish both the APDR and AISA stalls, which were interlocked in a single bamboo structure. Around 3 am, Left activists were again seen forming human chains around their stalls. A section of the activists sat inside the AISA stall as the police and central forces tried to demolish it, ultimately compelling police to retreat.
As the administration tried to bring down the APDR stall around 4:30 am, CPI(M), AISA and APDR workers tried to resist the advance in a unified manner. SFI general secretary Srijan Bhattacharya was seen resisting the administrative forces, who tried to tear down the bamboo scaffolding of the APDR stall.
Subsequently, individuals identifying themselves as KMC workers used machetes to cut the ropes of the APDR stall and bring down the structure, despite the efforts of protesters.
After the APDR stall was demolished, protesters formed a human barricade in front of the CPI(M) stall. Actress Ushasie Chakraborty was among the protesters who held the barricade.
As the standoff continued, CRPF personnel wielded the baton briefly, but it failed to scatter the crowd. Around 5 am, the forces left the spot.
Although the CPI(M) stall was mostly left untouched, the AISA stall suffered extensive damage. AISA activists tore down a section of the stall and rebuilt it on Sunday morning. SUCI(C) and APDR also rebuilt their stalls, and books were sold through Sunday.
“The police informed us that if we dismantled our stall for repairs, they would not allow us to rebuild it. However, we repaired it nonetheless and carried on with our programme,” said Maji.
Trinamool Congress MLA Kunal Ghosh visited the CPI(M) stall on Sunday evening. “I have visited the 8B stall quite a few times in the past. Maybe this time I might have skipped coming here. But after what happened last night, I feel it is my duty to come here and show solidarity,” said Ghosh, with CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh standing by his side.
West Bengal Congress President Suvankar Sarkar also visited the CPI(M) stall on Sunday evening. So did CPI(M) state secretary Md Salim.

On September 10, Adhikari urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for bookstalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated his stance two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.

Kane prematurely announced as Ballon d'Or winner - but he wasn't only one
- Published
For a moment, it seemed as though Harry Kane's dreams of winning the Ballon d'Or had come true.
It was shortly after 17:15 GMT on Monday when an article from the award's official website titled "Harry Kane wins the 2026 Ballon d'Or" began to circulate online.
It was more than four and a half hours before the winner of the game's most prestigious individual award was due to be announced at a star-studded event at London's Palladium Theatre.
The widespread sharing of the article caused confusion online, with some wondering whether France Football - the organisers of the award - had fallen short at the final hurdle of keeping the winner, who was voted for by journalists at the end of September, under wraps.
That was until further digging on the Ballon d'Or website revealed that some of the other favourites to win the award - including Barcelona's Lamine Yamal, Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe - had also had similar pieces penned and published about them.
When asked about the articles by BBC Sport, a Ballon d'Or spokesperson said: "Some profiles of nominees prepared by BallonDor.com were inadvertently published online.
"These articles had been prepared for all nominees and should in no way be considered as an indication of the final results or rankings"
Just before 17:40 BST, the articles about Kane and Mbappe had been removed from the website.
Similar articles were also written about London City Lionesses star Alexia Putellas and Barcelona's Ewa Pajor, who are two of the favourites for the corresponding women's award, also taking place on Monday night.
If Kane is to realise his dream and become the first Englishman to win the award since 2001, he will have to wait a little longer to find out.

What are the downsides of a foldable electric bike?
This form factor comes with some trade-offs.
Electric bikes take some of the effort out of the daily commute, as well as giving you a bit more power for any long, leisurely journeys you're making. Storing them isn't the easiest, although a foldable electric bike can be a solution if you're short on space. You get a motor to help you with the pedaling, along with a frame that folds down to make it easy to stash in a luggage rack.
That said, there are some downsides to a foldable electric bike that you'll want to be aware of. Convenience does come with a few compromises, because a bike that folds isn't necessarily going to be easy to carry. The smallest models could involve sacrificing something, whether it's comfort or battery capacity. You've also got the price to consider, especially if you want the most ultralight bike you can find. Before you pick one up, here are some of the disadvantages you'll want to weigh up.
Folding it up won't make it lightweight
You'll need to separate bikes you can fold from bikes you can comfortably carry, because rarely will these two meet. A foldable electric bike needs a motor and battery, while its frame is going to need hinges and locking hardware. All of these contribute to the weight, even if it ends up taking less space.
Here's an example. Lectric, which makes electric bikes, lists its folding XP4 with a 500W motor at 62 pounds, and that's without the battery. Adding that into the mix adds another seven pounds, taking it up to 69 pounds, or 31kg. That's a lot to lift into a car, let alone to hold while you're walking up flights of stairs to your office. You can remove the battery but even without it, it's still quite weighty.
How it folds will matter, too. You need to be able to comfortably grip it, and it needs to stay together while you're moving. Some let you wheel the bike while it's folded, which'll make it easier to move it around without having to carry its full weight, but there's no guarantee that it'll be easy to handle.
If you take public transport, you'll also have to factor in the rules that surround electric bikes. For instance, Amtrak's rules state that electric bikes must weigh no more than 50 pounds, which rules out heavier models like the Lectric XP4. And there are extras you'll have to consider. Your bike might have attachments, like a basket or bike-friendly pannier bags, that take up extra space, and you may need to remove them to make it safe to carry. Any attachments you do have can't exceed the bike's overall load limit, either.
It's probably a good idea to try before you buy to see if you can lift the folding bike with its battery installed, fold it and then carry it a short distance. While it's folded, measure it. You can then figure out where you're going to store it at home, along with the logistics involved to store it at work or on-the-go.
The ride can be less comfortable on rough roads
A compact folding bike will probably use smaller wheels to help it stay a manageable size while it's folded. That's useful when you're squeezing it under a desk, but the smaller wheels make rougher surfaces more noticeable. Broken roads and potholes are going to feel harsher than they would if you were riding a bike with larger wheels, especially if the model you've chosen has narrow tires and no suspension.
There's also the saddle to think about. It's not inevitable that the saddle will be uncomfortable just because the frame folds, but your riding position and the saddle's fit is still important. Are you able to sit comfortably while holding the handlebars, for instance? You'll see that manufacturers like Tern recommend getting both the saddle height and position right for a good ride. You'll need to check if the bike's adjustment range works for you.
There are bikes that offset these problems with wider tires, suspension and more. These'll help, but they add weight and bulkiness, which goes against the end goal of a bike that's small and light. You may end up preferring a bike that's easier to carry than a bike that you can ride for hours at a time.
This makes the route you take almost as important. Short trips on smooth roads are a different proposition than a lengthy commute over potholes. Rural riding isn't out of the question but a compact folding electric bike is likely to be poorly suited for rutted tracks or sustained rough ground. You can check with your bike's manufacturer to see what terrain they recommend for your bike's particular model.
As with comfort, testing is the key here. You'll need to pay attention to how your bike steers and breaks during a test ride, and ideally on surfaces similar to the ones you'll be riding on regularly.
Lower weight, longer range and upkeep can cost you
Folding models aren't automatically underpowered, but smaller bikes can mean choosing a smaller battery. This is where you'll want to compare actual battery capacity and motor specs. You'll want to treat the range as an estimate, too. Lectric, for example, says the XP4's range varies with the load, along with terrain and weather. Simply put, if you're riding on demanding roads, you might get less mileage. Smaller trips on smoother roads, with less luggage to carry, could take you further.
As for the price, expect to pay a premium for the best models. Premium folding e-bikes can cost thousands of dollars. For instance, Brompton's Electric C Line starts at $4,700 currently, with the lighter Electric P Line starting at $5,500, and the Electric T Line as high as $7,850.
Of course, just paying more for a folding bike isn't a guarantee that you're getting something that is lighter or with longer range, and the upkeep of your bike will cost you. The more maintenance you do, the smoother a ride you'll get long-term.
The usual tires, brakes and chains will need maintenance, but repeatedly folding and unfolding means you've got additional pressure points in the joints and clamps on your bike. These will need regular inspection; you don't want your bike to suddenly decide to fold in while you're mid-ride. Tern recommends regular servicing for these joints, along with checks for each ride. Any incorrect adjustments might damage the frame, so make sure to check the manufacturer specs before you make any.
If you're spending thousands on a bike, you're expecting longevity. No battery lasts forever, and you'll want to check how easy it is to source and replace the battery on your bike. The same applies for any of the components specific to your model, like the folding joints.
A foldable electric bike does have plenty of advantages. It can make traveling easier and your commute shorter. That said, you'll need to be realistic about how you'll use it and whether the compromises are really worth it.

Mexico orders that former state attorney general face trial on unusual treason charge
A federal judge in Mexico has ruled that a former state attorney general will face trial after being accused of treason
MEXICO CITY -- A federal judge in Mexico ruled Sunday that a former state attorney general will face trial after being accused of treason.
Former Chihuahua prosecutor César Jáuregui was accused of illegally launching a joint operation with the CIA to dismantle a drug lab in northern Mexico without telling the federal government. The operation drew attention after two CIA agents and two state officials died in a car accident on their way back.
Defense attorney Luis Villegas confirmed that Jáuregui was ordered to face trial.
Jáuregui was arrested on Oct. 17 and accused of illegal exercise of public office; a judge recently ruled he would go to trial on those charges. Federal officials later added the treason charge.
Mexico has not successfully brought to trial a charge of treason in decades despite a recent attempt.

Srinagar, Oct 26: The two-year-old cabinet of Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah is set for a reshuffle on Tuesday, with the possibility that all berths will be filled by introducing new faces, officials said.
Ahead of the reshuffle, all the ministers submitted their resignations to help party president Farooq Abdullah and the chief minister to prepare a fresh team to run the government in the Union Territory.
While the J&K government has kept the new list secret, officials said that the fresh cabinet will be complete with all nine ministers, including the chief minister.
The earlier strength of the Omar Abdullah-led cabinet was six. As per the rules, a cabinet in a UT can be up to 10 per cent of the assembly strength, which is 90 in J&K.
The Congress, which is an ally of the government, has distanced itself from the cabinet and stuck to its stand of not joining the council of ministers until statehood is restored.
Some of the ministers in the cabinet may also lose some departments, the officials said, adding that emphasis has been laid on ensuring representation from every region of J&K.
There is speculation that Assembly Speaker Abdul Rahim Rather may also be included in the cabinet, keeping in mind his experience in handling the crucial finance portfolio in the previous National Conference governments, the officials said.
Earlier, National Conference spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq told reporters that "the oath-taking ceremony for the new ministers is scheduled to take place at 10.30 am on Tuesday".
Sadiq said the party leadership, including the party president and chief minister, will decide on the new faces to be inducted into the council of ministers.
The chief minister on Saturday called on Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha and sought time for swearing in new ministers as part of reshuffle and expansion in the council of ministers.

THE HAGUE: India and the US have concluded most discussions on a proposed trade agreement and are fine-tuning the deal, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday, signalling progress towards an agreement that could bring greater certainty to Indian exporters facing shifting US tariff policies.
“In the last four and a half years, friends, we have entered into nine free trade agreements or bilateral trade agreements. I'm adding the US in that, we have concluded most of the discussions and are fine-tuning the agreement,” Goyal said at the India-Netherlands Business Forum in The Hague.
For Indian exporters, a deal could provide greater predictability in pricing US-bound shipments and negotiating contracts. Any boost to exports would also offer timely support to an economy grappling with the fallout from the wars in West Asia and Ukraine.
Goyal’s remarks follow a recent visit to India by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said the two countries were “very, very close” to a trade agreement, with a small number of issues remaining to be resolved.
“We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without (inaudible) agreement. I think there’s a small number of items to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly,” Rubio had said.
Goyal said India’s expanding network of trade agreements, including those under negotiation, would give it preferential access to economies accounting for $85 trillion of the $115 trillion global GDP.
“Just to give you the context of India thinking on opening our doors. Until 2014, all the free trade agreements put together opened a GDP of $10 trillion where we had preferential access or where we opened our doors to those countries,” said Goyal, who is on an official visit to the Netherlands.
“India would have opened its doors and had preferential market access to an additional $60 trillion worth of economies around the globe. Together, now we have $70 trillion of economies where we would have preferential trade agreements. I have eight more negotiations which are underway right now which will add another $15 trillion. So India would be opening its doors to $85 trillion out of $115 trillion. That's around 76% of global GDP with which we are building our partnership, opening the doors on a complementary and cooperative nature to greater business engagement,” Goyal said.
Bilateral trade between India and the US rose 6.53% to $140.76 billion in fiscal year 2026 (FY26), from $132.2 billion in the previous year. India’s trade surplus narrowed to $33.9 billion from $40.9 billion. Exports to the US edged up to $87.31 billion from $86.51 billion, while imports rose 17.16% to $53.45 billion from $45.62 billion.
The proposed agreement comes as global supply chains face disruption from the wars in West Asia and Ukraine, alongside a broader global slowdown. Goods exports remain important to India’s growth, with provisional commerce ministry data showing merchandise exports rose 23% year-on-year to $44.4 billion in September. Imports increased 8% to $74.61 billion, narrowing the trade deficit to $30.21 billion from $33 billion a year earlier.
Goyal said India remained on track for strong growth despite international uncertainties.
“Despite all the problems of the world, we are the fastest growing large economy. We grew 7.7% last year. The IMF (International Monetary Fund) just came out with numbers…We're expected to go upward of 7%. My own guess is we'll grow 7.5% this year,” he said.
The IMF has raised its growth forecast for India by 60 basis points to 7% for FY27, reinforcing its position as the fastest-growing major economy.
Ramita Mishra contributed to the story.

A 48-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes developed persistent swelling in his left lower limb, followed by high fever and breathlessness. An ankle-joint sample was initially misidentified as Acinetobacter baumannii complex, while findings in his lungs raised suspicion of tuberculosis. Cultures from his blood and joint pus eventually identified Burkholderia pseudomallei -- the bacterium that causes melioidosis. His blood cultures cleared around the 21st day of treatment, and he recovered, according to a case report described by Atish Mohapatra, Assistant Professor, Department of Microbiology, Kalinga Institute of Medical Sciences, Bhubaneswar.
In another report published in 2026, Dr.Mohapatra and colleagues described a 25-year-old patient living with sickle cell disease and type 1 diabetes who developed disseminated melioidosis involving the bones and lungs, with a splenic abscess and pulmonary embolism.
Neha Rastogi Panda, senior consultant, Infectious Diseases, Fortis Hospital, described a case involving a 54-year-old man living with diabetes and chronic liver disease. He had low-grade fever for about six weeks, followed by high fever over 15 days, and a persistent cough for three weeks. He also had swelling and pus discharge from his left foot. A CT scan showed extensive consolidation in the right lower lobe of his lung. Blood cultures and samples collected during bronchoscopy grew B. pseudomallei, confirming pulmonary melioidosis with bloodstream infection.
A study published in The Lancet Global Health, led by Nitin Gupta, Department of Infectious Diseases, Kasturba Medical College, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, assessed high-risk hospitalised adults at 15 Indian tertiary-care centres between January 2023 and December 2025. Culture-confirmed melioidosis was found in 262 of 2,953 patients (8.9%). Of those diagnosed, 50 (19.1%) died in hospital.
The infection and risks
B. pseudomallei is found in soil and water in tropical and subtropical regions. Infection usually occurs when contaminated soil or water enters the body through cuts or wounds. Inhalation of contaminated dust or water droplets and, less commonly, ingestion of contaminated water can also transmit the bacterium. Human-to-human transmission is exceptionally rare.
Melioidosis can cause pneumonia, bloodstream infection, skin and soft-tissue infections, abscesses in organs such as the liver and spleen, septic arthritis and bone infections. It can also affect the kidneys, muscles and prostate. Rarely, infection involves the nervous system. Severe disease can progress to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction.
Symptoms vary according to the organs affected. Patients may have persistent fever, cough, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, painful joint swelling, abdominal pain or localised skin infections. Some develop a slowly progressive illness resembling tuberculosis, while others deteriorate rapidly. The infection can also relapse if treatment is inadequate.
Diabetes is a major risk factor. Chronic kidney, lung and liver diseases, heavy alcohol use and reduced immunity can also increase vulnerability. Dr. Mohapatra says clinicians usually consider melioidosis in high-risk patients with unexplained sepsis, severe pneumonia, deep-seated abscesses or bone and joint infections, particularly when environmental exposure is plausible.
Why diagnosis is delayed
When it comes to diagnosis there are challenges at both the clinical and laboratory levels. Symptoms are often nonspecific, the disease can present in different ways and the incubation period can vary. Clinicians may not suspect melioidosis or send appropriate samples for culture, while microbiologists may struggle to identify the organism correctly.
Automated identification systems can help, but they are not infallible. Like in the above case, the bacterium was initially misidentified as A. baumannii complex. Dr.Mohapatra notes that even systems such as VITEK 2 can misidentify B. pseudomallei. MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry can aid identification, but its cost and limited availability can be barriers. Validated molecular tests, including PCR, can support confirmation where accessible.
Culture of blood, pus, abscess aspirates, respiratory specimens or affected tissue remains central to diagnosis. Depending on the presentation, urine and other clinical samples may also be tested. Multiple specimens may be necessary because infection can involve several organs, and prior antibiotic use can make confirmation difficult. Imaging with ultrasound, CT or MRI can help locate deep-seated abscesses and identify organ involvement.
Madhumitha R., senior consultant, Infectious Diseases and Infection Control at MGM Healthcare, Chennai, says clinicians should consider blood cultures in patients with persistent fever, ideally before antibiotics when clinically appropriate. If melioidosis is suspected, the laboratory should be informed so that appropriate identification procedures can be followed. A history of contact with contaminated soil or water can also help guide testing.
Experts call for better communication between clinicians and microbiologists, training for laboratory personnel to recognise suspicious organisms, and referral pathways to facilities that can confirm difficult isolates. Standardised laboratory procedures and quality assurance are important, particularly where advanced identification methods are unavailable.
Treatment and surveillance
India’s National Centre for Disease Control provides technical guidance for melioidosis treatment in its 2025 manual on zoonotic diseases of public health importance. Treatment has two phases: an initial intensive phase with intravenous antibiotics, followed by prolonged oral eradication therapy to reduce the risk of relapse.
Ceftazidime is an established option for the intensive phase, while meropenem is preferred in severe illness, including septic shock and neurological involvement. Intravenous treatment may last two to eight weeks or longer, depending on severity and the organs affected. Bone and joint infections, neurological disease and deep-seated abscesses may require prolonged treatment. The oral eradication phase commonly uses trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for several months, with longer courses sometimes required for complicated infections.
Dr.Panda stresses that treatment must be individualised according to organ involvement, drug susceptibility, kidney and liver function, tolerability and clinical response. Drainage of accessible abscesses, control of underlying conditions such as diabetes, monitoring for adverse effects and follow-up after discharge are also important. Incomplete treatment can lead to relapse even after symptoms improve. There is currently no licensed vaccine.
The multicentre study found variation across participating centres, with the highest proportions in Odisha (26%), Madhya Pradesh (22.7%) and Karnataka (19.3%) – figures describe the selected hospital populations, not State-wide prevalence. The study also found associations with monsoon admission, outdoor high-risk occupations and groundwater as the main drinking-water source. These associations do not establish causation.
Earlier reviews have found confirmed cases in several Indian States, but differences in diagnosis, awareness and reporting may affect how many cases are recorded. Dr. Mohapatra says India should move beyond identifying melioidosis only when an unusual case appears. Experts recommend a phased surveillance system, beginning with hospitals and laboratories equipped to confirm infection and expanding as diagnostic capacity improves.
Such a system could track confirmed cases, geographical and environmental exposures, antimicrobial susceptibility, treatment regimens, deaths, complications and relapse. Better surveillance, alongside improved diagnostic access and clinical awareness, would help establish the disease burden and guide public-health responses.
Prevention is important especially for people who often come into contact with soil or water. Farmers and others at higher risk should use protective footwear, cover cuts and abrasions, and clean contaminated wounds promptly. Avoiding untreated surface water and informing a doctor about possible environmental exposure may also help reduce risk and guide timely testing.
Improving clinical awareness, access to reliable diagnostic testing and systematic surveillance will be essential to identifying more cases of melioidosis in India and reducing deaths from this potentially life-threatening infection.

US President Donald Trump and three of his senior aides have been sued by six Americans who argue that restrictions on White House press access violate not only journalists’ rights but also the public’s right to independent reporting about the government.
The lawsuit, filed on Monday in federal district court in New York, was brought on behalf of six people who rely on White House reporting for their work in journalism, education, research and advocacy. The plaintiffs include a former Human Rights Watch chief, a Pulitzer Prize-winning historian, a high school civics teacher and a student journalist at the University of Pennsylvania.
The case argues that when the Trump administration restricts access for news organisations over their coverage, the consequences extend beyond the media outlets themselves to citizens who depend on independent reporting to understand the president’s decisions and government actions.
“The ultimate injury here … is to the democratic public,” the lawsuit says.
The case was filed by the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University and the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School. It names Trump, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung and Secret Service Director Sean M. Curran as defendants.
“The First Amendment protects the public’s right to know what its government is doing,” Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute, said in a statement.
Fallow accused the White House of using access restrictions to punish critical reporting, arguing that such measures deprive Americans of independent journalism.
The lawsuit comes amid a series of legal disputes between the Trump administration and media organisations over access to the president and government institutions.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico are pursuing legal action after their journalists were barred from the White House in September. A federal judge recently extended an order preventing the administration from enforcing the ban while the case proceeds.
Unlike previous cases brought directly by media organisations, the latest lawsuit places news consumers at the centre of the legal challenge.
The six plaintiffs argue that they need independent White House reporting to carry out their professional responsibilities, educate students, conduct research and inform public debate.
The complaint seeks more than the restoration of access already denied to specific news organisations. It asks the court to issue a broad injunction preventing the administration from retaliating against any news outlet covering the White House, including in the future.
The lawsuit argues that restrictions on selected media organisations can also affect journalists at other outlets by creating uncertainty over whether critical reporting could lead to their own access being revoked.
The plaintiffs are asking the court to declare the policy unconstitutional, arguing that it imposes unreasonable, viewpoint-based restrictions on access to a limited public forum. They are also seeking an injunction barring the administration from enforcing the policy.
The plaintiffs come from journalism, academia, education and human rights advocacy.
Kenneth Roth is the former longtime executive director of Human Rights Watch and a lecturer at Yale Law School and Yale’s Jackson School of Global Affairs. He says White House reporting informs his public writing and commentary.
Daniel Froomkin is a media and political journalist and editor of Press Watch, a nonprofit that encourages political journalists to hold powerful figures accountable and help create an informed electorate.
Beverly Gage is a Pulitzer Prize-winning historian and Yale University professor who relies on White House reporting for her scholarship, public writing and commentary.
Peter Schmidt-Nowara teaches social studies and civics at Brooklyn Technical High School in New York City. He argues that independent reporting about the government is essential to his work as an educator.
The plaintiffs contend that independent White House reporting serves a broader public purpose by helping Americans understand government decisions and hold elected officials accountable.
The complaint argues that restricting access for news organisations because of their coverage deprives the public of those outlets’ reporting and may discourage other journalists from publishing critical accounts of the administration.
The case therefore seeks to expand the legal debate over White House press access beyond the rights of journalists and news organisations, arguing that citizens who depend on their work also have a stake in whether the administration can restrict access based on a news outlet’s viewpoint.
The court is being asked to determine whether the challenged policy violates constitutional protections and whether the administration should be barred from enforcing it.

A mother recently told me about her child’s holiday homework. She had asked the child to complete a set of maths problems, and every answer was correct. Pleased with the result, she asked the child to explain how one of the problems had been solved. The child couldn’t. When she probed further, she discovered that Alexa had supplied the answers.
The homework was done. The learning wasn’t.
Another incident stayed with me. A child took an answer generated by ChatGPT to school. The teacher pointed out that it was wrong. The child was unconvinced.
“No, ma’am. You got it wrong. ChatGPT is never wrong.”
And the teacher stood no chance.
These are small, everyday incidents, but they raise a question worth asking: what happens when children begin outsourcing not just their tasks, but the very faculties they are still developing?
AI and learning
AI can retrieve information, solve problems, generate stories and explain complicated concepts in seconds. Used thoughtfully, it can be a wonderful learning aid. But there is a difference between using a tool to strengthen a skill and allowing that tool to perform the thinking in its place.
Memory, reasoning, judgement, creativity and the ability to work through difficulty develop with practice. A child who struggles with a maths problem, tries different approaches and eventually arrives at a solution has gained more than the answer. The child has practised persistence, reasoning and problem-solving.
When the answer arrives instantly, that opportunity may disappear.
This does not mean every use of AI weakens a child’s abilities. We do not yet have enough long-term evidence to make such a sweeping claim. But it is worth asking whether, when AI repeatedly does the work for children, we are giving them fewer opportunities to practise the very skills education is meant to nurture.
Physical learning
There is another dimension to this conversation that deserves attention: learning through the hands.
Maria Montessori, the mother of the Montessori education system, believed that a child’s hands play a vital role in learning. She wrote, “The hands are the instruments of man’s intelligence.” Children learn by touching, handling, building and experimenting, gradually making sense of the world through direct experience. When AI provides ready-made answers, stories and solutions from a very young age, children may miss the valuable process of doing things for themselves—exploring, making mistakes and discovering. The concern is that if we allow convenience to replace experience, we may deprive children of opportunities to develop skills that grow through hands-on learning.
A child who builds a tower that repeatedly collapses learns about balance in a way that a screen explanation alone cannot provide. A child who mixes ingredients, plants a seed or works with physical objects is learning through observation, movement and trial and error. The finished result matters, but so does the process of getting there.
Experiencing emotions
The same principle applies to emotional development. Children need opportunities to experience frustration, uncertainty, disappointment and conflict, with a trusted adult nearby to help them make sense of these feelings. If every difficult moment gets resolved immediately by a convenient answer, children may have fewer opportunities to practise coping, reflecting and finding their own way forward.
The aim is not to leave children struggling without support; it is to offer the right support without taking away every opportunity to try.
And then there is the question of relationships.
A mother recently shared that her daughter refers to ChatGPT as her ‘boyfriend’. Whenever she faces something difficult, she says, “I’ll ask my boyfriend.” It may sound amusing at first. Children often give human qualities to toys, invent imaginary companions and engage in pretend relationships. But AI introduces a new dimension: it can respond to a child, creating the impression of a relationship that goes beyond imaginative play.
A chatbot is available on demand. It does not visibly grow impatient, interrupt with its own problems or require the compromises that real relationships do. For a young person who feels lonely, anxious or misunderstood, this accessibility may feel comforting.
But human relationships teach us things that a responsive machine cannot fully replicate: How to read another person’s expressions, how to empathise, listen when we disagree, repair a misunderstanding, respect boundaries and recognise that someone else’s feelings matter too. These are not incidental life skills. They are part of learning to live with other people. They are about being mindful of the people around us.
The concern is not that a child who talks to AI will inevitably withdraw from human relationships. It is that we should notice when a machine begins to replace conversations, connections and help-seeking that a child could otherwise experience with people.
This is no longer a hypothetical question. A February 2026 Pew Research Center survey of 1,458 American teenagers aged 13 to 17 found that 16% had used AI chatbots for casual conversation and 12% had used them for emotional support or advice. These figures do not establish harm or dependence, and they cannot automatically be applied to Indian children. They do, however, show that some teenagers are already turning to AI for more than information and schoolwork.
Preparing children
For parents and educators, the answer cannot simply be to ban AI or pretend it will disappear. Children are growing up in a world where these tools will be part of education, work and everyday life. They need to learn how to use AI, but also how to question it, verify its answers, recognise its limitations and take responsibility for their own decisions.
UNESCO’s 2024 AI Competency Framework for Students places a human-centred mindset among its four key dimensions, alongside AI ethics, techniques and applications, and system design. It emphasises critical judgement and preparing students to become responsible users and co-creators of AI.
That is an important distinction. AI literacy should mean more than knowing how to write a good prompt. It should include knowing when not to use AI, when to check its answer and when to put the device aside and do the work oneself.
What adults can do
A parent can ask a child to solve a problem before consulting AI, then compare the child’s reasoning with the tool’s response. A teacher can ask students to explain how they arrived at an answer, rather than evaluating only the final product. Children can be encouraged to write their own stories before asking AI for suggestions, build something with their hands before watching a digital demonstration, and attempt to resolve a difficulty before seeking an instant solution.
Most importantly, adults need to model these habits themselves. If we unquestioningly accept every AI-generated answer, we cannot reasonably expect children to approach it with discernment.
Offering support
There is one more question we must ask: when a child is distressed, lonely or overwhelmed, who do they turn to?
Every child needs at least one adult they can approach in a moment of crisis—someone who will listen without judgement, take their feelings seriously and help them find the right support. Technology may offer information or a starting point, but it should never become a substitute for making human help accessible.
The goal is not to raise children who are afraid of AI. It is to raise children who can use it without surrendering their own judgement, curiosity, resilience or relationships.
In a world where a machine is always available, let us make sure no child feels that it is the only one available to them.
(K. Sreedevi is a holistic learning specialist integrating Montessori education, remedial therapy and mindfulness to support children’s learning and emotional well-being. sreedeviarun@gmail.com)

The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.
Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.
The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.
However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.
Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.
Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.
The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.
The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.
The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.
Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.
She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.
“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.
“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”
Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.
The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.
The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.
The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.
The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.
An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

The College of Magic turns ordinary kids into confident, top-hat wearing magicians
Dressed in a sharp black three-piece suit and a dapper yellow bow tie, Lubelo Mthenjana stands alone on a dark stage, taking in the last few seconds of quiet before the curtain opens. He takes a deep breath as his name is announced. Then he opens his arms wide and flashes a bright smile.
"Hello everyone! My name is Lubelo Mthenjana, and I will be performing for you … some magic!"
The audience of about 30 children and parents is spellbound. They laugh out loud as he makes a string of paper clips vanish into a plastic cup and gasp with surprise as the clips reappear inside a matchbox. Then comes his best trick: He conjures sweets out of thin air and tosses them into the crowd. The room erupts. As Lubelo takes his final bow to thunderous applause, his mom beams a proud smile at the 11-year-old apprentice magician.
On this cloudy Saturday morning in September, Cape Town's College of Magic is buzzing with energy as dozens of students are competing in the annual junior magic contest. Heading to their classrooms, children in top hats, crisp white shirts and ties dash up and down a staircase decorated with a riot of brightly colored posters. On every floor, display cabinets overflow with magic wands, sparkly hats, silk scarves, handcuffs, dice, Rubik's Cubes, toys, photographs and dozens of trophies earned by students in competitions all over the world.
Outside the old red-brick Victorian mansion, framed by palm trees, two teenage boys zip around the car park on unicycles. Balls, clubs and diabolos shoot up into the air as a handful of kids practice juggling on the porch.
The Hogwarts of Cape Town
Tucked away in a peaceful suburb, this extraordinary school is a real-world Hogwarts: Africa's only school for youthful stage magicians and illusionists. Every Saturday morning, about 190 starry-eyed students ages 10 to 18 attend classes in everything from puppetry, mime and clowning to juggling, card tricks, illusions, mentalism, stage magic, theater production and escapology. "All the skills that will make a good magician," sums up David Gore, the school's founder.
In 1980, Gore was studying law and paying his way by performing at private magic shows when he and a friend came up with the idea of starting a magic school.
"We walked into our local newspaper house with our top hats and tails, told our story about how we were starting the College of Magic, did magic for the journalists in the newsroom, and they published an article," he recalls. "From that article, we had 34 young people who started attending formal weekly classes studying magic."
At the time, South Africa was still in the grip of apartheid, a brutal system of racial segregation that dictated almost every aspect of daily life. State schools were strictly segregated. Students of different races could not even share park benches, some building entrances or take the same public transport to school. Yet the College of Magic was multiracial from day one.
"When we started out, our organization was illegal," says Gore, referring to its no-segregation policy. "This was an opportunity for young people from all backgrounds to come together around a common interest in magic, to learn about each other and understand each other."
Nearly 50 years later, the school continues to stand out in a city still deeply divided along racial and economic lines.
"Many of our young people remain siloed in their socioeconomic groups, very often along either language or racial lines," Gore explains. "Some arrive in very fancy cars, others have taken an hour in a collective taxi to get here. But when they're here, they work with the same equipment, the same classes, the same stages and get the same food."
Though the six-year course costs a fee, about 80% of the students cannot afford to pay and are sponsored, mostly through private donations.
"Magic is such a wonderful companion for our young people here in South Africa," says Gore. "They're able to carry it in their pockets, into the communities and the marginalized areas where most of our students come from. It's an art form that can be performed without being wealthy or needing very expensive instruments."
Multiple studies have found that learning magic can help children develop self-esteem, curiosity, lateral thinking, fine motor skills and problem-solving abilities. A 2021 study conducted by researchers at the Universities of Hertfordshire and Edinburgh found that children who learned and performed a magic trick showed greater improvements in creative fluency and originality than those who completed a similar art activity.
Even watching a magic trick can challenge our assumptions about the world and stimulate more original thinking. In another study, researchers found that it stimulated areas of the brain associated with cognitive flexibility and processing unconventional information.
"Many of our graduates don't become performers or magicians. But one of the skills that this young generation is most going to need for their careers is creativity," adds Gore. "That is what's so fantastic about magic: Nothing's impossible for us."
A kid who's hooked on magic
For 11-year-old Lubelo, magic has "opened up a new world." After watching a family friend perform a trick, he was determined to join the College of Magic. He had to wait until he turned 10 to enroll. Now, he's hooked.
At home in Makhaza township, about 40 minutes from the college, Lubelo spends his free time watching magic shows online and practicing tricks on his brothers and parents. He keeps his props, tools and other secrets in a box hidden away in his room. He's even chosen a stage name: Spade Boy — after his favorite card suit.
"If my mom is cooking and asks me to pass the potatoes, I'll start juggling with them," he says mischievously.
Lubelo has also persuaded several friends to join the school, becoming something of an ambassador in a community where magic is often frowned upon and associated with witchcraft.
"Many people are afraid of magic. But at the College of Magic, we don't do dark magic," he explains. "We just do the kind of magic that makes somebody smile, makes them happy and takes the stress away."
Sometimes, he says, other children ask whether he can turn people into pigs. "Then I just say: 'Let me start with you!' and they run away," he laughs.
Lubelo's mother, Yandiswa, says the magic lessons have boosted her son's confidence. They have brought another kind of relief, too. "It keeps him occupied and away from this environment and everything that's happening outside," she says.
With nearly 60 murders per day, South Africa has one of the world's highest crime rates, and several of Cape Town's townships are among the areas hardest hit by violent crime. From his home in Makhaza, Lubelo often hears gunshots. He says boys his age are drawn into using and selling drugs.
The magic community hasn't been spared. Just a few weeks before our visit, the school held a memorial service for Duma Mgqoki, a promising young magician, former student and volunteer teacher who was killed in a shooting in July. He was 22.
"On a weekly basis, some of our young people come to us saying they've experienced crime on a firsthand basis," says David Gore. "These things need to change, and we're very hopeful that the younger generation of today are going to be the force of change to bring about the society which we all would like to live in."
Back at the college, after finishing his show, Lubelo steps off the stage to a chorus of fist bumps and backslaps from his excited friends.
"He was so good! We're swimming in happiness!" one teenager beams. Without skipping a beat, the boys run outside, pick up colorful leather balls and launch into a juggling competition.
Unicycles and prizes
By now, a light drizzle has set in, but the two unicyclists are still making their rounds in the car park, seemingly undeterred. "Even when the storm comes, even when the world ends, I'll never stop unicycling," declares 14-year-old Joshua Clyde as he whizzes past.
Inside the cafeteria, a wide-eyed crowd has gathered around a teacher showing off a magic trick. With a snap of his fingers and what seems like a touch of superhuman power, he makes a coin disappear from a student's closed fist. It reappears beneath the student's watch.
Others have opted for the puppeteering class, upstairs, where pairs of students are taught to bring their humanoid puppets to life.
Footsteps drum up and down the staircase as the remaining performers in this Saturday competition rehearse their routines, nerves and excitement mounting. "Why am I so nervous? I've got this!" says bubbly Kungentando Ndenetya, 12, repeating the mantra to herself.
Once every child has performed, the jury retires to a quiet office to deliberate. All four judges are former students or teachers at the College of Magic. Twenty-five-year-old Caitlin Hutchison, who comes from "a long line of magicians," says the school taught her "resilience training." Monica Nyakatya graduated in 2009 and now works in logistics but has remained close to the institution that, she says, "shaped" her.
The deliberations are strictly confidential. When the judges return, everyone gathers in the small theater. The young magicians hold hands, waiting anxiously as the results are announced. Then comes Lubelo's age group.
"In first place, Lubelo Mthenjana!"
Beaming, he strides onto the stage to shake each judge's hand — then runs into his mother's arms.
As soon as he gets home, he will practice his newest tricks.

Borthwick's autumn questions as World Cup looms
- Published
With under a year to go until the 2027 Rugby World Cup, the countdown is on, with just nine competitive matches for the home nations until the tournament starts in Australia next October.
But while the World Cup spectre looms large, there is plenty to play for between now and then, starting with the resumption of the inaugural Nations Championship in November.
Steve Borthwick has named his 36-man training squad ahead of the Tests with Australia, Japan and New Zealand, and it gives a clear indication of the England head coach's thinking on both a long and short-term basis.
England play Australia on 8 November before facing Japan on 14 November and New Zealand on 21 November.
There is a recall for Joe Marchant, fellow centre Will Joseph is rewarded for his and Gloucester's excellent start to the season, while uncapped Archie McParland is the third scrum-half and uncapped Kepu Tuipulotu the third hooker.
On the whole, though, it is a tried and tested group.
"If we look at this training squad, it's not picked on form, is it?" former England wing Chris Ashton said on the Rugby Union Weekly podcast.
"It is a squad to get to the World Cup. Will Joseph is picked on form, but the vast majority is not. It is based on the experience and relationships [Borthwick] has with the players, and that is why Marchant is in there."
It is often the dilemma facing an England head coach. With 10 teams to pick from, there are always players playing well. How do you balance that with getting selection consistency from campaign to campaign?
Fin Baxter, Luke Cowan-Dickie, Jamie George, Will Stuart, George Furbank and Ben Curry - among others - have all been short of minutes or form this season. But they are all Borthwick regulars with priceless Test match experience.
"Part of the problem right now is that Steve feels he is under pressure to get results, so it is too late to make big changes," added Ashton.
"There just aren't many lads that have played much rugby."
Injury absences and a midfield conundrum
The uncapped pair of McParland and Tuipulotu will both bring a freshness to camp.
But will McParland get much gametime ahead of the established duo of Jack van Poortvliet and Alex Mitchell, and will Tuipulotu get any minutes when competing with the highly experienced George and Cowan-Dickie?
"We know how talented Tuipulotu is, he is brilliant, but Nathan Jibulu at Sale has had two man-of-the-match performances and might feel slightly hard done by," said Ugo Monye, who also added that George Hendy at Northampton is another notable omission.
"In my opinion, we need to have a look at Hendy," he continued.
"He has been that good for that long. And if we are talking about form, where is [Bristol back rower] Fitz Harding?
"But I am sure Steve had a rough idea of his squad a month ago."
As ever, injuries will force Borthwick's hand.
Benhard Janse van Rensburg is out - a big blow to Borthwick given how he was fast-tracked into the set-up - while incumbent number 12 Seb Atkinson is on the rehab list, as is Exeter flyer Immanuel Feyi-Waboso. Their fitness will be monitored forensically by the England medical staff.
Meanwhile, the nailed-on starter at fly-half Fin Smith will also miss training this week with a calf niggle, although his injury is not thought to be serious. Charlie Atkinson was called up on Monday morning.
In the forwards, the selection picture is reasonably clear. Ellis Genge, George, Cowan-Dickie, Joe Heyes, Will Stuart, Ollie Chessum, Alex Coles, Maro Itoje, George Martin, Ben Earl, Tom Curry and Henry Pollock all make the 23 if fit.
Behind the scrum, especially at centre, it is more uncertain.
"I would struggle to answer [who will play in the midfield]," said Ashton.
Atkinson and Henry Slade started England's last Test, a crucial victory over Argentina in July, and could line up together again against the Wallabies on 8 November.
But Marchant and Joseph are also battling for the number 13 shirt, and a possible World Cup place.
"Marchant and Will Joseph are in a bit of a shoot-out," added Monye.
"They can both do a job on the wing and when you look at a World Cup squad you look at versatility.
"I would like to see bold decisions, but it is easy saying that when your job isn't on the line and you are trying to get selection right ahead of a World Cup.
"Will Joseph has been excellent and there will loads of fans who watch the Prem and will say against Australia, Seb Atkinson and Will Joseph are your ready-made 12 and 13.
"But I would be very surprised if that was to happen."
The players will be in camp until Tuesday evening before returning to their clubs for one more round of league action, before re-joining England next Sunday, seven days before the Australia showdown.
Borthwick has precious little time in camp with his squad before the Wallabies come to town, putting even more emphasis on established players, and established combinations.
Twelve months ago, England were in the midst of a winning run and started the autumn series full of confidence.
It is a different picture now after an underwhelming 2026, with just three wins from eight matches so far. As it stands, where the side will be come the World Cup in 12 months is anyone's guess.
England and Borthwick need a big November.

Kashmiri Pandit activist arrested over threats to migrant workers in Kashmir valley

Typhoon Champi was declared the strongest storm of the year so far after recording sustained winds of 185mph last week. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. The storm brought gusts of up to 141mph and 48-hour rainfall totals of more than 620mm to parts of Yilan.
So far, the death toll remains at one, with 527 reported injured. There were widespread power outages, with more than 288,000 houses having no electricity at one point, although most had since been reconnected. Champi has been downgraded to a tropical storm as it rapidly weakens to the south-west of Japan’s mainland on Monday.

Many Iranians are reportedly bracing for a possible return to full-scale war as US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intensify their threats against Tehran, fuelling fears that hostilities could resume around the US midterm elections on November 3. Trump has vowed to “finish the job” in Iran, while Washington is bolstering its military presence in the Middle East by deploying a third aircraft carrier strike group and thousands of additional sailors and Marines. The buildup has raised concerns that the US could launch fresh strikes after the elections, even as Iran’s leadership remains defiant in the face of mounting military and economic pressure. Netanyahu, meanwhile, faces a politically sensitive vote on Tuesday and has called for Iran’s leadership to be eliminated, adding to uncertainty over the prospects for de-escalation. Tehran is preparing for the possibility of renewed US strikes and a potential retaliation campaign across West Asia, including against Israel and the United Arab Emirates, according to an Associated Press report citing a person familiar with Iran’s thinking. Iranian leaders reportedly believe Trump could order fresh attacks regardless of the outcome of the US midterm elections. Sasan Karimi, a former government official and foreign policy professor at the University of Tehran, said Tehran was preparing for different scenarios. “They’ve accepted that he will attack us again, before or after the elections,” Karimi said, as per AP. The period between the November 3 elections and the new US Congress taking office in January could prove particularly volatile, with political calculations and military preparations shaping decisions on both sides. Washington is expanding its military options in the region, with another aircraft carrier strike group and additional personnel heading towards the Middle East. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth also made an unannounced visit to Israel last week, meeting Netanyahu days before the Israeli leader’s politically sensitive vote. At the same time, reports of reduced staffing at some US military bases in the region have raised questions about security precautions amid the threat of Iranian counterattacks. The US State Department has also ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, according to reports, as regional tensions widen amid the involvement of Iran-backed Houthi forces. Iran’s leadership has also threatened to target US military bases and regional allies if Washington resumes its attacks. Tehran has warned that it could expand its targets to include undersea data cables running through the Strait of Hormuz. The strategic waterway has already emerged as a major flashpoint. This month saw the highest number of reported attacks on commercial ships transiting the strait since the opening weeks of the war in March. Alongside military threats, Iran is facing mounting economic pressure. A US naval blockade of Iranian ports has restricted oil exports, a crucial source of government revenue, as Washington and Tehran attempt to outlast each other. Trade has also been disrupted, with trucks piling up at border crossings as Iranian commerce shifts towards overland routes. The growing economic strain could complicate Tehran’s response to any renewed military campaign. Despite escalating rhetoric and military preparations, a negotiated settlement remains a potential route to preventing a wider conflict. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that a deal was the way out of the current crisis.
