Colombia's president says two key leaders of National Liberation Army killed
Colombia's president says at least 10 members of the country's National Liberation Army, including two key leaders, were killed in a recent military attack
BOGOTA -- At least 10 members of Colombia’s National Liberation Army, including two key leaders, were killed in a recent military attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella announced Sunday.
He described the attack as “the hardest blow” to hit the guerrilla group in the last eight years.
The operation took place Thursday in a rural area of El Tambo, in the Cauca department of Colombia’s Pacific region.
Individuals known as “Marcos Pacífico” and “Ochenta” (or “Murillo”) — both senior leaders within the “José María Becerra” bloc of the group’s southwestern front — were killed during the operation. De la Espriella said their deaths have disrupted their “chain of command … and their ability to direct criminal activities.”
The president accused “Marcos Pacífico” of killing 62 people, recruiting minors and displacing some 500 people in his 24-year history with the guerrilla group. His influence extended across units in the departments of Cauca, Valle del Cauca and Nariño, de la Espriella added.
The president also accused him of masterminding “the illegal unrest that fueled urban terrorism in 2019 and 2021.”
While describing the operation as a “decisive” blow against the group, the Colombian president acknowledged that this single operation “does not end the threat” posed by the National Liberation Army, which could potentially regroup.
Recently, the top leaders of the National Liberation Army — a guerrilla group that has been armed since 1964 — were sentenced in absentia to prison terms ranging from 11 to 20 years for the forced recruitment of at least 60 minors. The Colombian justice system has ordered the arrest of suspects including Nicolás Rodríguez Bautista, alias “Gabino” — who served as the guerrilla group’s top commander from 1998 to 2021 — as well as Eliécer Herlindo Chamorro Acosta, alias “Antonio García,” the current top commander of the insurgency; Israel Ramírez Pineda, alias “Pablo Beltrán,” second-in-command; and Gustavo Aníbal Giraldo Quinchía, alias “Pablito,” third in the chain of command.
The conservative de la Espriella, who took office on Aug. 7, has ended peace negotiation talks started by his predecessor, Gustavo Petro and has pledged to take a “hard-line” approach.

Scientists at the ICAR-Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) have developed a new potato variety called ‘kufri jamunia’ that has higher levels of anthocyanins, vitamin C, and certain micronutrients than regular potatoes. The Central government has been promoting it of late as a means to address hidden hunger, i.e. when people consume enough calories but still do not receive the necessary nutrients.
Usually, experts who fortify foods, focus on items like rice and iodised salt, which a large number of people in India consume, often throughout the year, thus ensuring the added nutrients are delivered to a significant chunk of the population. Kufri jamunia is however a potato, which people in India generally consume much less consistently than rice or salt, and the micronutrient intake depends on preparation methods and how the body absorbs them.
What makes it different
Kufri jamunia offers nutritional advantages, but they are substantial in some aspects more than others. Questions also linger about its ability to resist disease and retain nutrients through different Indian cooking methods.
The variety reportedly has a mealy texture. In one CPRI assessment involving 64 people, 95% rated its overall acceptability ‘good to excellent’ and 56% said its taste was very good. This study cohort, though, is too small to generalise the results. CPRI researchers themselves have proposed that kufri jamunia can be used in curries, parathas, soups, baked goods, and dehydrated flours.
Importantly, kufri jamunia potatoes also have purple skin and flesh, which could affect consumer interest. Research on other biofortified foods has already shown that while people are generally willing to pay modest premiums — the national average cost of ordinary potatoes purchased wholesale is around ₹17/kg — whether they accept a new variety depends on its appearance, their awareness, taste, and of course local preferences.
How was is developed
The CPRI team developed the kufri jamunia variety by crossing two potato lines, MS/8-1148 and CP4242, in 2015. MS/8-1148 is high in vitamin C whereas CP4242 had purple skin and flesh. The result, formally called MSP/16-307, could naturally accumulate higher concentrations of specific nutrients as it grew. The team then conducted trials, including multi-location testing, in 2021-2023.
Based on the trial data, the Central Sub-Committee on Crop Standards, Notification and Release of Varieties for Horticultural Crops approved the variety in mid-2024 and the government notified it in November that year. The variety’s plants produce 10-12 medium to large tubers each and mature in around 90 days. The purple colour comes from anthocyanins — organic compounds also found in jamun and blueberries.
According to the Press Information Bureau, 100 g of kufri jamunia flesh contains around 42.75 mg of vitamin C (versus 23.15 mg in regular potatoes), 42.05 mg of anthocyanins, 2.28 mg of zinc (versus 0.28 mg), 3.22 mg of iron (versus 0.57 mg), and 161 micrograms of carotenoids. And per the CPRI team’s findings themselves, published in Potato Journal in 2025, 100 g of kufri jamunia was found to have a range of carotenoid levels, from 15.6 micrograms in Kanpur to 298.4 micrograms in Raipur, during the multi-location trials. Kufri jamunia also contains slightly less zinc than kufri neelkanth and slightly less iron than kufri manik; the latter are other coloured potato varieties developed at the Institute.
Anthocyanins are known to have antioxidant properties, although whether the same benefits will accrue when delivered by kufri jamunia potatoes is not known. And in the absence of similar studies, the same caveat goes for iron and zinc.
A 2016 study in Food Chemistry examined purple-fleshed potatoes and reported that steaming and microwaving generally preserved more of the nutritional substances than stir-frying did. However, again, research specific to kufri jamunia is not available.
Cultivation factors
Nutrient availability and delivery constitutes one half of a biofortification programme; the other half is determined by cultivation.
At the Modipuram research station, according to the Potato Journal paper, the team recorded an average yield of 49.01 tonnes per hectare after three months, across three seasons, whereas subsequent multi-location trials, including at Modipuram, recorded an overall mean of 31.96 tonnes per hectare across north (36.77 tonnes), central (33.79 tonnes), and eastern (25.91 tonnes) India.
On the other hand, at these locations, kufri manik yielded 31.52 tonnes per hectare and kufri neelkanth 36.61 tonnes per hectare. Further, kufri jamunia could moderately resist late blight, a disease caused by the water mould Phytophthera infestans, in laboratory conditions but has been reported as ‘susceptible’ in the field. Late blight is a devastator of potato crops and the CPRI team has already recommended that farmers apply fungicide.
Next, the multi-location trials also produced 29.19 tonnes of marketable potatoes per hectare, versus 33.48 tonnes for kufri neelkanth. So if the costs of cultivation were equal, kufri jamunia farmers could need a 15% premium on the selling price to attain the same gross revenue. (A study published by a CPRI in Indian Horticulture in 2020 estimated that, for regular potatoes, the seed material accounted for 40-50% of the production costs vis-a-vis regular potatoes, with a per-hectare seed cost of around ₹60,000-75,000 per hectare.)
Many unknowns
Taken together, there are many unknowns about kufri jamunia at this point to assess its overall cost-benefit ratio, including the cost of seeds and disease management, pricing, its uptake in the market, and how efficaciously it will deliver iron and zinc to the population. It would be premature as a result to deem kufri jamunia to be a proven solution to address India’s hidden hunger.

There is now proof for what we have suspected all along: What you eat will determine your quality of life. A new study that was conducted by Chennai-based Madras Diabetes Specialties Centre and the University of Reading, U.K., has found a link between quality of diet and the Asian Indian predisposition to high cholesterol. High and uncontrolled cholesterol levels are associated with a high cardiovascular disease profile.
The study, Low diet quality increases the genetic risk of high blood cholesterol levels in Asian Indian adults [CURES–165], was published last week in the international peer-reviewed journal PLOS ONE, and are considered to advance the understanding of how diet and genetic factors interact to influence cholesterol levels.
The researchers analysed data from 1,020 adults (25–80 years), comprising 452 men and 568 women, who participated in the Chennai Urban Rural Epidemiology Study (CURES). The study examined three genetic variants of two genes :TCF7L2 and FTO, with a known association with diabetes and other metabolic disorders.
Researchers found that a poor quality diet amplified the genetic susceptibility to high cholesterol. Study participants who already had a higher genetic risk and who consumed a poor-quality diet had significantly higher total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol levels. Conversely, researchers proved that among participants consuming medium- or high-quality diets, there were no significant differences in cholesterol levels between the high- and low-genetic-risk groups were not observed. Individuals with higher genetic risk had significantly higher fasting blood glucose and HbA1c levels.
Among the key messages is that genetic susceptibility alone does not necessarily translate into adverse cholesterol levels under all dietary conditions. Naturally, these findings support the role of sticking to healthy diets to counter cardiometabolic risk. This is particularly significant in India, witnessing a literal explosion of cases of diabetes, rising cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease. Researchers said there could be a role for precision nutrition, The findings also open up new possibilities for precision nutrition, where dietary advice is tailored to an individual’s genetic and metabolic characteristics.
Commenting on the results of the study, V. Mohan, Chairman, Madras Diabetes Research Foundation, who was also a co-author of the study, said the key message is that our genes alone “need not determine an individual’s metabolic destiny.” With adjusting of the diet, it is possible to lower the risk, even when the genetic load is present.

As it prepares to go public, Anthropic’s S-1 filing makes generative AI’s methane dependency glaringly obvious.
Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom
Anthropic is clear that data centers will run on gas, to the company’s own detriment.
“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense.”
In documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission Monday, Anthropic acknowledges that data centers are becoming increasingly reliant on “natural gas” — the fossil fuel industry’s marketing term for what is primarily methane — leaving the company’s AI data center buildout vulnerable to rising fuel costs and existing supply chain constraints. And in a possible catch-22, Anthropic admits that rising global temperatures — a symptom of burning fossil fuels — will increase the company’s operating costs.
“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense,” Anthropic says, adding that some of its planned data centers rely on electricity generated by natural gas turbines on-site. Anthropic leases capacity from hyperscalers, but it announced a $50 billion dollar plan last year to expand data centers in Texas and New York.
The US, the epicenter for data centers globally, is planning to build more fossil fuel generation capacity than it has in a decade as data centers demand more electricity. Donald Trump’s administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects while tilting the regulatory landscape in favor of fossil fuels, which Trump claims is a more important energy source for powering data centers around the clock than solar and wind farms that generate power intermittently.
Now, a shortage of gas turbines is slowing data center construction. Some developers are installing gas engines on-site as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to power grids. Developers are also turning to more simple turbine technology at these sites as they face backlogs from turbine manufacturers, making on-site power generation less efficient and more polluting as a result.
Data center electricity demand could wipe out decades of gains in air quality over the next five years, one recent Texas-based study found — raising levels of soot, smog-forming pollutants, and planet-heating carbon dioxide. Even as data centers create more greenhouse gas pollution, Anthropic’s S-1 points to climate change as a risk to its bottom line. It will have to pay more for electricity and water to cool servers at data centers as temperatures climb.
Nevertheless, Anthropic expects increased competition for natural gas and pipeline capacity from hyperscalers and cloud service providers rushing to build their own data centers. “This competition could drive up the price of natural gas,” the company notes.
Gas makes up the biggest chunk of the US electricity mix, 40 percent of the nation’s power generation. And Americans are already feeling the pain of rising costs as utilities scramble to upgrade energy infrastructure and meet rising power demand.
Pissed-off residents have successfully blocked dozens of proposed data centers across the US. Anthropic acknowledges that the specter of ballooning utility bills is enough to interfere with a data center project. “If our efforts to secure electrical power are perceived to affect other utility customers and the broader grid, regulators may impose conditions, standby charges, or other requirements intended to address such impacts,” it says.
If regulators push data center developers to shoulder more of the costs for new energy infrastructure, Anthropic says that could also raise its operating costs. And without a secure gas supply and the pipelines to transport the fuel, the company says, it might need to delay or abandon planned data center projects altogether.
Ultimately, these challenges could stunt Anthropic’s growth:
Any failure to secure access to adequate electrical power, any legal, regulatory, or other administrative action or change limiting the availability of electricity, or any significant increase in energy or compliance costs, could adversely affect our cost structure and limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers.

In July, as supporters of the Cockroach movement took to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, incensed over exam-paper leaks and demanding the resignation of India’s education minister, the rest of the nation realised that for the first time since the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) came to power in 2014, the curse of inertia and the grip of fear had been smashed irrevocably. Prime minister Narendra Modi’s image of invincibility has been punctured.
People in India have been conditioned to believe in an idea of intense slow-burn protests that eventually bring change – but the Cockroaches have shown us that the revolution can be fast-tracked.
This time the Cockroaches are demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, following reports in the Indian Express in late September that he had pushed through a purge of voter rolls. Round one of the Cockroach protests came to an end because the BJP was willing to sacrifice the education minister. Round two does not allow for such scapegoating. If Kumar goes, Modi must go too – it would be an open admission that the electoral system has been compromised.
The response of the BJP so far has been hysterical. The repressive apparatus of the state was out in full force: detentions and arrests of journalists, protesters being roughed up and beaten, an internet blackout in the capital. The Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke’s bravado in announcing his protest plans paid unexpected dividends the first time around. The second time, the continual broadcasting on social media by the three Cockroach leaders seemed like a lack of experience in organising and strategic thinking. Police forces detained them on touchdown at Delhi airport on the morning of the protest. They alleged that thousands of their members faced preventive detention or were not allowed to reach the capital city.
So at protests on 10 October, the CJP leaders were conspicuous by their absence. Only leftwing and Congress-allied student organisations, prominent gutsy young activists (Neha Bora, Aishe Ghosh, Gurmehar Kaur) and their elected political representatives held the ground and faced the worst of the police brutality.
The absence of the Cockroach leadership on the ground notwithstanding, the protests continued in pockets, eventually reaching a crescendo on 12 October. Heeding a call by Rahul Gandhi on behalf of the Congress-led opposition bloc, the streets of Delhi were filled in an act of defiance the like of which I have not witnessed in my lifetime. The state, however, seemed to have got the memo beforehand. The Delhi police and security forces numbered 90,000, 45 metro stations were closed in the inner city and trains to Delhi were cancelled. Student activists travelling to the capital were picked up en route from their railway carriages.
The following day, a small group of Cockroaches were arrested entering Jantar Mantar, which the Delhi police had banned from being used as a protest site. Two of the group’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained and subsequently sent to jail for five days.
Despite the high-handed approach of the police, the people are still clamouring for battle on the streets. Every screengrab, every video, every reel reinforces the feeling that we are witnessing a carnivalisation of the protests. The songs, the slogans, the sudden bursts of dancing, the satirical placards, the sheer joy of the crowds: this is Mikhail Bakhtin’s carnivalesque. What is the cause for such celebration? This: the state is evidently in retreat. People have begun to treat power as something to be ridiculed.
One of the most popular slogans has been Jab jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai (“Whenever Modi is afraid, he pushes the police forward”). The regime’s undiluted dread was most visible at Connaught Place in central Delhi on 16 October, when the CJP had called on people to gather at Central Park for a flag-waving celebration. The New Delhi Municipal Council shut down the park for two days and an elaborate fortification followed. The park was cordoned off, security personnel formed a human chain along the metal railings and 220 companies of the Central Armed Police Forces were deployed alongside the Rapid Action Force and the Delhi police.
Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke and communist student leader Neha Bora were both detained as they made their way towards Connaught Place. Neither was allowed to contact lawyers until late into the night, and lack of knowledge about their whereabouts caused panic online. Neha was released from detention the following morning, and Abhijeet could walk free on conditional bail.
For over a decade, the regime crushed students and dissenters by branding them anti-national and punishing them under the draconian Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The genius of the Cockroach protest lay in something very simple – how could the state frame the waving of the Indian national flag as an anti-national activity? We now have a government that is not confident of its own legitimacy; it views the tricolour as a weapon when it is in the hands of its citizens.
The powerlessness of the state could also be seen in its desperation to police the online space: it summoned Meta officials over the summer and imposed an internet shutdown earlier this month. For a party that coasted to power with post-truth propaganda on WhatsApp, its undisputed dominance on X and heavy investment in keeping social media influencers on its payroll, the algorithms (or their oligarch owners) may well have turned. It is impossible to capture the entire social media ecosystem with threats and purchasing power alone.
For the regime, it is a losing battle against the newfound visual grammar that has defined a wave of protests around the world: nothing is as seductive as young women defiantly clashing with uniformed police, or an opposition leader who climbs the barricades and waves the national flag. The German philosopher Walter Benjamin wrote about the tendency for fascism to lean into the aestheticisation of politics – today, looking at Delhi, he would be pleased to report back that the aesthetic can also be snatched back by the masses.
On 12 October, after the mass mobilisation, Gandhi addressed the media by saying: “This is tandav, Lord Shiva’s dance. There is no planning here”, and “This is the wedding procession of Shiva, anyone can join in”. These references to Shiva are a calculated manoeuvre. It is a nod to India’s majority Hindus who, time and time again, have been sold the lie that their sole protector is Modi.
Modi recently went Bhajan clubbing – a kind of rave setup with remixed Hindu devotional music – in a desperate attempt to establish his gen Z connections. But he may find the rug pulled from beneath his feet. Modi’s base rewarding the BJP election after election for weaponising their faith did not secure jobs for the next generation. And now it is their own children who are at the receiving end of the state’s violence.
Saving India cannot happen without pulling Hindus out from the vicious grip of extremist Hindutva. This is one unforeseen outcome of this protest and the wider movement. Whether it topples the government or not, it has shown it can unite people against the divisive force that is the BJP.
- Meena Kandasamy is a poet and writer based in Chennai

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs, criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.
So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective. However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.
So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?
Researchers at security company Calif were the first to identify the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and create exploits in early August—partially using frontier AI tools as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program, but also using expert human knowledge of PHP, its dynamics, and its weaknesses. Some of the underlying issues were identified in 2024 but were deemed too complex to exploit at the time. Following Calif’s discovery, researchers at OpenAI and the Google-owned security firm Wiz independently discovered PHP2Shell flaws using AI tools.
“The vulnerability had been known to the PHP team for years, but because it could not be leveraged by an attacker—at least, not a human one—it was not addressed,” says Sagi Tzadik, a security researcher at Wiz.
No software is perfect. There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially exploit vulnerabilities. This puts even more pressure on under-resourced IT teams, developers, and admins to keep up. Microsoft’s security updates included a record 1,453 security vulnerabilities this month alone. Meanwhile, Bank of America recently hired 1,000 consultants to fix flaws discovered by Anthropic’s Mythos. Security researchers emphasize, though, that AI is ultimately not doing anything new, but rather magnifying existing dynamics of vulnerability discovery and coordinated disclosure.
“We'll definitely see more of these long-life bugs that are in every version of the software for the last decade or whatever,” says Jake Williams, vice president of research and development at Hunter Strategy and a former NSA hacker. “But I think there’s only so much of this low-hanging fruit. There isn’t much else that has the specific reach of PHP. It’s a pretty wild attack surface—most other tools aren’t exposed to the internet by design.”
Researchers note, too, that even with frontier models, most examples of sophisticated AI-aided hacking also involve human expertise. As Ryan Austin, the Calif researcher who first discovered the PHP flaws, wrote this week, “No model is simply capable of unearthing ‘all bugs’ with simple prompts. At least for now.”
In short, security engineer and researcher Niels Provos says, everyone can dial back their freak-outs, at least a bit. “To be honest, I am not really worried,” he says, about AI finding an overwhelming number of historic bugs that are newly exploitable—or new vulnerabilities that couldn’t have been practically exploited without AI. “People have now been looking with AI for over a year, and it required a highly skilled team to find this one. I guess we will see whether I am completely wrong, but I doubt it.”

The condition of Helen Haines, the Australian MP hit by a car five days ago in north-east Victoria, has improved from critical to serious but stable.
The independent MP, 65, had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on Monday.
In the latest update on Saturday morning, the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said Haines was in a serious but stable condition, the first improvement since she was airlifted there.
Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, was arrested shortly after the incident and has since appeared in court on three charges.
The politician's husband, Phil Haines, said on Wednesday that the "horrendous incident" had caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind" were "in good shape".
Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.
Police said more charges might be laid, including attempted murder.
His lawyer said his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Investigators are looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident.
Nugent's family has said they were long-time friends with Haines.
Shortly after the alleged attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC television that there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.
Haines, known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action, entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife.

The story so far: Hundreds of women gathered outside Polish Parliament (Sejm) in Warsaw on Thursday (October 22, 2026), braving heavy rain to demand access to free and legal abortion, as demonstrations spread across more than 20 cities in Poland. Signalling rejection of the government’s record, protesters raised pro-choice slogans in a show of anger at Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s failure to deliver on his promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws.
The demonstrations came just two days after the lower house, the Sejm, passed two bills seeking to ease the country’s restrictive abortion laws. The proposed changes seek to roll back some of the restrictions on the rights of abortion imposed under the previous government, but their passage into law remains uncertain, with President Karol Nawrocki expected to veto the measures.
What does Poland’s abortion law say?
Poland has some of the most restrictive abortion laws in Europe. Since 1993, abortions has been allowed in Catholic Poland only on specific grounds. The restrictions tightened in October 2020, when the country’s Constitutional Tribunal ruled that abortion on the grounds of severe foetal abnormalities was unconstitutional. The ruling came into force in January 2021, effectively establishing a near-total ban on abortion. Since then, and under the current law, legal abortion is when a pregnancy threatens the woman’s life or health, or when a pregnancy results from a criminal act, like rape or incest. In cases involving rape or incest, termination is permitted up to the 12th week of pregnancy.
Abortion on request is not permitted in Poland, and women seeking such terminations outside the legal grounds face major barriers to accessing healthcare. The law also criminalises assistance in pursuing an unlawful abortion, with penalties of up to three years’ imprisonment. However, the woman undergoing the abortion is not criminally liable. The restrictions have prompted repeated nationwide protests, including demonstrations in 2016 and after the 2020 ruling, with activists accusing the authorities of curtailing reproductive rights and restricting access to abortion care.
When Mr. Tusk’s coalition, comprising parties ranging from the left to the centre-right, came to power in December 2023, replacing the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to liberalise abortion laws. However, disagreements between the coalition’s more conservative and liberal factions stalled reform efforts, fuelling criticism that the government had failed to honour its electoral commitments.
What do the two bills propose?
The issue has now returned to the parliamentary agenda, a year ahead of the next parliamentary election. On October 20, the Sejm passed two bills seeking to ease abortion restrictions.
The first bill seeks to partially decriminalise abortion by removing criminal penlties for terminating a pregnancy with a woman’s consent outside the grounds currently permitted by law, as well as for helping or encouraging such an abortion. It also proposes protections from criminal liability for doctors, nurses and midwives who terminate a pregnancy to avert a threat to the woman’s life or health, or in circumstances involving a high probability of severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities or an incurable condition threatening the foetus’s life.
The second bill seeks to restore abortion as a legal option when doctors identify a severe and irreversible foetal abnormality or an incurable condition threatening foetal viability. This would reverse the effect of the 2020 Constitutional Tribunal ruling, which removed foetal abnormalities as a legal ground for termination.
Both bills would need to clear further legislative and presidential hurdles before becoming law. Even if enacted, they would not legalise abortion on request and would leave Catholic Poland’s near-total ban unchanged. Protesters have dismissed the new measures, calling it token gestures rather than a genuine effort to reform the law, arguing that the government is seeking to demonstrate progress on an issue that could influence its prospects in 2027 parliamentary elections.
How do Europe’s abortion laws compare?
Abortion laws vary widely across European Union, with countries setting different gestational limits and conditions for access. While several countries permit abortion on request during the first trimester, others maintain restrictive legal frameworks.
France became the first country in the world to explicitly enshrine the freedom to have an abortion in its Constitution in 2024. Abortion is permitted on request up to 14 weeks of pregnancy and is covered by the public healthcare system. In Sweden, abortion is permitted on request up to 18 weeks, with medical abortions available at home under approved arrangements and costs covered by the state healthcare system. The Netherlands permits abortion until the foetus is considered capable of surviving outside the womb, generally around 24 weeks in practice, subject to legal and medical requirements.
Spain permits abortion on request up to 14 weeks of pregnancy, while Ireland allows it up to 12 weeks. Finland also permits abortion on request during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, following a reform that took effect in 2023. Portugal permits abortion on request up to 10 weeks.
Ireland legalised abortion following a referendum in 2018, while Spain’s 2023 reforms removed the requirement for parental consent for 17-year-olds seeking an abortion.
Malta has historically maintained one of the world’s most restrictive abortion laws, criminalising the procedure in almost all circumstances. Before 2023, doctors who performed an abortion to save a woman’s life could face up to four years in prison, while women could face up to three years. In 2023, the country introduced a narrow exception to the near-total ban, allowing doctors to terminate a pregnancy when a woman faces an immediate risk to her life or when her health is in grave jeopardy that could lead to death. In non-immediate cases, the decision must be confirmed by a panel of medical specialists. The reform did not legalise abortion on request

What have Man Utd changed to turn around WSL form?

Derby day underlined the changing picture at Manchester United, with Eva Olid's team proving they are made of stern stuff by fighting back for a point against rivals Manchester City.
This was the strongest performance yet under new head coach Olid, who after a slow start is seeing signs of real progress, exemplified in a hard-earned 1-1 draw on Sunday.
United not only ended City's 100% start to the Women's Super League season, but they have also extended their own unbeaten streak to eight matches in all competitions.
It is a remarkable turnaround considering United were without a win and low on confidence after their opening three WSL games.
Their disappointing start to the season was epitomised by a 5-0 drubbing at Chelsea's hands, but "everything" about the performance against City pleased Olid.
"I think it was one of our best performances in general, in terms of the fight and hard work and how we were pressing," Olid said.
"How this team has built in confidence from day one to now, in a short period of time, has been massive. It is still a process, but today was a huge performance."
United now sit fourth in the table after seven matches.
So what has led to their turnaround?
- Getting to know Man Utd boss Olid 
  - Published16 October
Returning to old ways
The most noticeable changes have happened on the pitch as Olid, who joined in the summer, conceded her side needed to revert to old ways.
They were struggling, initially, to adapt to her new style which demands lots of possession, an attacking mindset and high-risk football.
United toiled in defeats by London City Lionesses and Chelsea, having just two shots on target and less than 40% possession in both matches.
Olid felt her team were trying to do too much and had lost sight of some of their strengths, including their defensive organisation.
She urged her players to revert to what they knew before their 1-1 draw with Arsenal, which showed signs of improvement.
"The things they were good at before, they need to keep and at the same time, little by little, we need to implement our new style," Olid said before that game.
"It's trying to find this balance. Maybe they thought I would expect them to do everything in the first match but that is impossible. You need time."
That draw at Emirates Stadium was the catalyst for change at United, offering a foundation to build upon.
They had a tough start but then had a run of games against lower-ranked opposition, and two successive WSL matches at home.
They won the maximum nine points, scored six goals, conceded just two and almost doubled their possession percentage.
By returning to a more familiar defensive structure and adding in elements of Olid's new style, they began to cause more problems up front too.
Having had just 197 passes ending in the final third in their first three games, they recorded a combined 529 against West Ham, Liverpool and Charlton Athletic.
They quadrupled the number of shots they took too, going from 10 to 42 and won more duels in the air.
That helped to build confidence going into Sunday's derby at Leigh Sports Village, and when Elisabeth Terland fired in a late United equaliser it did not feel like a shock.
Overcoming 'transitional period'
Perhaps the biggest changes at United have been off the pitch.
Olid explained that her side had navigated a "transitional period" and had taken part in big discussions following their five-goal home humbling by Chelsea.
Players needed to find confidence and Olid said talks had to bring a solution.
"It has been a lot of hard work to change that, and a lot of honest conversations about what we could do and how we could connect," said Olid on Sunday.
"Sometimes you need a difficult moment to react and see where the problems were [that] we had to solve as a team. It had to happen, to be the team we are now."
The team's form at the start of the season had an impact on individuals.
United vice-captain Ella Toone missed out on England selection for the first time under Sarina Wiegman - albeit she was later summoned as a squad reinforcement.
Toone responded at club level by scoring in United's 3-1 win at Charlton in mid October.
Summer signing Andrea Medina has grown to become a crucial member of the United squad, and the international break proved to be a valuable time for Olid to adjust to her new role, reflect on what needed to change and to spend time on the training pitch.
England defender and United captain Maya le Tissier was among those to return with renewed energy having impressed for her country during the break.
The backroom staff positions were also confirmed and Olid has been able to build a group she hopes can lead United to success going forward.
Fellow Spaniard Jose Herrera joined as assistant coach, alongside Gavin Beith, who worked with Olid at former club Hearts.
Speaking about the international break, Olid said: "I had time to re-organise everything, the roles for the new staff and how we are going to work together.
"This break, for me, was amazing. It was like a new start. It was about keeping the good energy from the last matches but then having a new start."
Now they have proven they can compete with the WSL's best, Olid hopes United can push on and build on their draw with City.
"We need to have our feet on the floor. This season is long and with really good teams. We need to keep improving and learning," Olid said on Sunday.
"If we have the desire and fight we had today, not a lot of things can stop us. We still need to keep improving, but today I could see moments."

Bengaluru-based AI-powered trading platform Tradl has raised $4.1 Mn (about ₹40 Cr) in a seed funding round from Nexus Venture Partners and Stellaris Venture Partners, sources told Inc42. The funding round also saw participation from a few angel investors, the sources added. The startup's MCA filing further confirmed the fundraise. Questions sent to Tradl, Stellaris Venture Partners, and Nexus Venture Partners didn’t elicit any response till the time of publishing this story. Founded in 2025 by Shubham Bansal and Nilesh Raj, Tradl combines AI with quantitative analysis to help retail traders identify opportunities, analyse stocks, and test trading strategies. The cofounders are IIT Guwahati graduates. Bansal previously spent around five years at Goldman Sachs, while Raj worked at fintech startup Stable Money. Bringing AI To Trading Tradl’s toolkit includes an AI-powered stock screener, technical charts, and backtesting tools that allow users to test trading strategies against historical market data. It also helps traders track sector rotation and monitor corporate events that could influence stock prices. The startup lists chart pattern alerts, broader market insights, and personalised option chains among its other tools, although these are marked as available through private access on its website. According to Tradl, its AI interprets natural-language queries and translates them into instructions for its quantitative engine. The engine then processes market data using fixed rules to generate consistent results for the same query and dataset. The startup’s stated aim is to give retail traders access to the depth of analysis typically available to institutional trading desks. It lists the NSE, the BSE, and the MCX as exchange partners, and CMOTS as a data partner on its website. Tradl’s fundraise comes amid growing investment in Indian AI startups. The segment attracted $438 Mn across 35 deals in Q3 2026, up 265% YoY, making it the most-funded sector during the quarter. AI is also becoming a feature of platforms serving retail investors and traders. Investment and stock broking platform Trackk raised $3.7 Mn in a seed round led by Lightspeed, with participation from Info Edge Ventures, earlier this year. The startup offers AI-led stock discovery alongside broking, derivatives trading, and portfolio tracking tools. More recently, IPO-bound investment advisory platform StockGro raised ₹110 Cr from existing backers as part of its ongoing Series B round. StockGro combines investment research and trading insights with AI-powered research tools.

Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India’s election chief on Sunday, as a court ordered the release of the “cockroach” movement founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and two other senior leaders.
Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday, as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi.
Indian authorities on Saturday deployed a sweeping crackdown across Delhi and detained thousands of protesters as the youth “cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fuelled anger at the prime minister, Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Reuters reported police detained more than 2,000 people to thwart Saturday’s protest. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.
Most detained on the first day of protests were released on Saturday night, police said.
Opposition parties and critics of Modi’s government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters.
The UN human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said: “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled.” He urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
India’s foreign ministry said the UN’s approach was “selective” and its statement constituted “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
The protests are calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years.
Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party.
Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
The BJP and the commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The “cockroach” movement, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi’s education minister.
The CJP has called its protests against Kumar “Season 2” on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India’s election system was reformed.

A woman wearing blue overalls and a pink tank top sits on a bench in a workshop lined with tools. Holding a broken copper wire in one hand and a small mechanical tool in the other, she looks at the camera and smiles. “Let’s make money stripping …” she says, pausing for effect. “Wire!”
This play on words is common in a specific corner of TikTok where users document the process of stripping copper wire in order to sell it for extra cash. Most of these creators don't appear to collaborate or use a common hashtag, and they haven’t coined a new term ending in -maxxing. But many of their videos have a similar, visually striking setup: A complex appliance is broken down into bits, or an industrial wire is split like ropes of licorice, and in the end, what’s left is a bundle of glistening amber.
The participants are diverse: Some are hobbyists or electricians looking for extra income. There are also people who claim to be saving for a big purchase, and others who appear to be cash-strapped teenagers. They speak a wide range of languages, including English, French, Spanish, German, and Romanian. At least one has an Etsy shop for selling hand-cast copper bricks, also known as ingots, which are made by pouring molten metal into molds.
Selling scrap copper is nothing new. The metal is relatively scarce, a strong electrical conductor, and fully recyclable—qualities that have made it a particularly valuable scrap metal for centuries. But copper prices reached an all-time high this year, making it an opportune moment for scrappers. In September, according to International Monetary Fund data, copper was worth about $14,473 per metric ton, or about $7.23 per pound, more than double what it was worth in September 2020.
While there’s no reliable data on how often people sell scrap copper, rates of copper theft—often involving metal taken from vehicles, plumbing, building roofs—may offer some clues. Craig Depken II, chair and professor of economics at the University of North Carolina, Charlotte, who has studied the phenomenon, says it tends to increase under two conditions.
The first is when the price of copper is increasing, much like it is now. The second is when people’s level of “economic distress” is high enough to make them believe the potential monetary benefits of stealing copper outweigh the risks of getting caught. (It’s legal to sell lawfully obtained copper everywhere in the US except Minnesota, which requires a state-issued license.)
On TikTok, it’s easy to find copper-themed accounts with hundreds of thousands of followers. On TikTok Shop, beginners can even buy their own wire stripper—the small tool that eats a cord and separates copper from its exoskeleton. The most popular option has sold more than 20,000 units globally at the time of writing.
Wire Transfers
The final price of recycled copper depends on a few factors, including its quality, grade, and whether it’s still “insulated” in plastic or rubber. Insulated copper can go for a fraction of the price of stripped copper, so many resellers remove it themselves to earn more. But even with a wire stripper, the process can be tedious. For some, sharing content about it appears to be a way to make the repetitive task more bearable.
People have posted about hosting a wire-stripping “girls night,” “movie night” and even “date night.” In one video from August, the creator @Payciencu.u strips wire on a bed near a man in a red sweatshirt. “How down bad are you?” reads the text overlay. “Well I’m stripping wire just to hang out with him sooo.”
Other creators treat copper scrapping as a full-on side hustle or hobby, posting time-lapses, tutorials, and lists of the “worst cables to strip for copper.”
Benjamin Stickle, a criminal justice professor at Middle Tennessee State University and author of the 2017 book Metal Scrappers and Thieves, identified three main types of legal scrappers: those trying to make ends meet, workers selling scrap metal they obtained on the job, and people raising money for a charitable cause.
Electricians, who are plentiful among wire-stripping TikTokkers, neatly fall into the worker category. Other creators are harder to classify, especially if they’re also earning money from TikTok itself.
The creator @Courtney2291, who did not respond to WIRED's inquiries, began documenting her efforts to strip enough copper to save $20,000 for a three-bedroom home earlier this year. She sourced wire and old machinery from family, her scrap yard, and Facebook Marketplace, stripping it almost daily. On October 10, a little over six months after she started, she announced she had reached her fundraising goal.
However, most of the money didn’t come from selling the copper itself. According to a scrap yard receipt Courtney shared, she earned just $99 selling 30 pounds of copper stripped over six months. One TikTok video, meanwhile, generated $1,446 after racking up 6.8 million views, according to an earnings screenshot she displayed in another video.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, Courtney says she plans to keep posting. “Once the house is mine, and it’s all set up and ready to be lived in, then I’ll continue pretty much the same kind of content,” she said. Her new goal will be to pay off the loan on the two acres of land where her home will sit.
Strip Tease
Other popular copper creators, including King of Copper and Queen of Copper take a different approach, emphasizing scale and spectacle over personal storytelling. Their videos show them buying crates and trunks with hundreds of pounds of old wire, and then, little by little, stripping every piece
Neither claims to be affiliated with the other, despite their similar names and videos, but they occasionally repost each other's content. Both have amassed hundreds of thousands of followers, though how much they earn from TikTok and YouTube is unclear.
King of Copper is currently more than 70 days into a self-described quest to obtain, strip, and sell 1 ton of copper. In early September, 44 days into his journey, he claimed to have collected 271 pounds.
In one recent video, King of Copper spent five hours stripping wire, melting the copper in a black furnace, and then pouring it into six-ingot molds, producing what he claimed was about $90 worth of metal. In another clip, he spent two hours meticulously dismantling a 110-pound air conditioner and extracted roughly 7 pounds of copper, which he valued at $47.
His videos are mesmerizing to watch, but it’s unknown how much he might earn from them, and King of Copper did not respond to inquiries from WIRED.
Strip Mall
Another way copper accounts can earn revenue is by marketing wire strippers and other goods for sale on TikTok Shop. When viewers purchase products through links in their videos, creators can earn a commission on each sale. Courtney, for instance, has advertised her own wire stripper. But many of these salespeople, like the creator @Dragonslayer_Industries, don’t speak much about copper outside of their ads.
“If you’ve got any scrap wire laying around, you need this wire stripper right here,” Dragonslayer Industries says in a January video before feeding a bright green wire through a machine linked for purchase. “This thing is basically just gonna print money for you. Probably pay for itself in the first hour you use it.”
“It's crazy, I only got this because my neighbor was stripping wire by hand,” he said in a June comment on one of his videos. “I got the free sample and thought l'd do 2 videos and give it to him. I thought it was such a niche thing that they probably wouldn't sell. It's been my biggest seller since l started doing affiliate videos. I can count on 5-10 of these a day selling.”
In May, he claimed to have helped sell thousands of wire strippers. It’s unclear how much he’s earned, since TikTok Shop merchants set their own affiliate commission rates. Dragonslayer Industries did not respond to WIRED's inquiries, but in a recent video he noted that it's not in his “best interest” to devote much time to wire stripping since he makes “more money” from doing other things.
But human salespeople like him face plenty of competition from AI-generated ads on TikTok Shop. Even in the specialized market for wire strippers, there’s a huge number of videos featuring AI-generated imagery and voice-overs, some using remarkably similar scripts about making “eight grand a week” from selling scrap copper.
Online, copper scrapping can seem like a solitary pursuit. Offline, however, scrappers sometimes form the kinds of communities that are less apparent on TikTok. Stickle tells WIRED that scrappers he spoke to often worked in small teams, split their profits, and looked out for one another. People struggling to get by, especially those who were experiencing homelessness, sometimes received donated metal from their fellow scrappers.
Stickle adds that they also would lean on friends who had trucks for help transporting large hauls. “If they came across a large amount [of metal] that they couldn't just dolly back to a place,” Stickle says, “they had somebody they'd call.”
