I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year. Not all are winners, and many should be avoided, no matter how slick the marketing or how cheap the discount. Good news: It’s my job to recommend laptops that fit your budget and won’t make you regret your purchase six months later. These are my favorite laptops that I’ve tested myself and would highly recommend you buy.
For more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops. My guide on How to Choose a Laptop may also help if you’re undecided.
Updated October 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations after testing all the new Nvidia RTX Spark laptops, as well as the new Googlebooks. The Surface Laptop Ultra has replaced the Dell XPS 14, and I've added back the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 at its discounted price.
Featured Products
The Laptops I Recommend Most
When friends or family ask what laptop to buy, I always start with the MacBook Air. It is far more powerful than its compact size suggests. It’s a shame about the recent $200 price increase from $1,099 to $1,299, but even at that new price, it remains my top pick because it nails the big picture. Everything from the trackpad to the speakers is of the highest quality, and it delivers all the performance and battery life the average person needs.
With the latest M5 chip, its GPU matches the M3 Pro MacBook Pro, easily handling everything from gaming to video editing. That’s not at all what the MacBook Air is designed for, but the performance is there when you want to dabble. It’s what makes it feel like a do-it-all machine, all contained in a fanless chassis that’s still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. Oh, and did I mention it’ll last well over a full workday away from the wall socket and perform just as well on battery as when plugged in? In almost every aspect, it’s the gold standard.
While the lower price of the new MacBook Neo might be tempting, the MacBook Air is the better choice for anyone working at a computer all day. With its superior performance, extra memory, faster storage, and Thunderbolt ports, you will never have to question if you have the right tool for the job. (And unless you already know you need a MacBook Pro, you probably don’t.)
Speaking of price, I have to mention the new Dell XPS 13 next. I like just about everything about this laptop, whether it’s the compact size, the excellent build quality, or the gorgeous screen. It’s not OLED, but it’s sharp, bright, and color-accurate. It also includes a 120-Hz refresh rate, which makes animation and motion on the device look super smooth. The XPS 13 is filled with features like that, which don’t normally end up in a laptop at this price. While it doesn’t have what I’d call powerhouse performance, the Intel Wildcat Lake chip inside gets the job done for basic, day-to-day computing tasks. That translates to great, all-day battery life, competitive with the MacBook Air. Just don’t try to play games, edit high-resolution video, or take it to engineering school.
The XPS 13 is especially good for those who want a compact device to travel with. With its tiny bezels, it’s still one of the best laptops to use on a plane. But even beyond that, it’s just one of the best laptops you can buy under $1,000 right now. The Dell XPS 13 is primarily being talked about as a budget laptop, thanks to its $700 starting configuration. But that model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which limited performance in my testing. You’ll probably just want to avoid that 8 GB model. Most people will want the upgraded 16 GB model, which you can get for $900. It’s the best hardware you can buy for under $1,000.
If you want a Windows laptop that still feels high-end but has a bit more performance, I would point you to the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. It might be the prettiest Windows laptop you can buy right now. The device is beautifully built and incredibly sturdy, with a thin chassis, an oversized haptic trackpad, and polished metal edges. I also appreciate the three Thunderbolt 4 ports split between both sides for convenient charging, as well as the surprisingly good speakers. I tested the high-end model, which features a fast Snapdragon X2 Elite, 32 GB of RAM, and a gorgeous 2880 x 1800 OLED display. The screen offers near-perfect colors, excellent brightness, and astounding HDR performance. It doesn’t get much better than this. It’s usually quite expensive, but we’re finally seeing discounts that bring it to a more reasonable price. There’s also an Intel model with a very efficient, powerful chip that would be a good choice. I’d go with whichever is cheaper right now.
And lastly, for something with a larger screen, I’d recommend the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x. It’s a particularly good alternative to the 15-inch MacBook Air, at a much lower cost. These days, you can buy the upgraded model with the 2560 x 1600 OLED display (and 165-Hz refresh rate) for $1,000, on sale at Amazon. While it’s slightly thicker than the MacBook Air, it leaves more room for extra ports including HDMI, USB-A, and an SD card slot. And while the Snapdragon X2 Plus isn’t quite an M5 killer, I was happy with the performance and battery life provided. Lenovo also sells a cheaper version directly, but it has a lower-resolution IPS screen that I haven’t tested. The $30 it costs to upgrade the display to a higher-resolution OLED is well-worth it.
Cheap Laptops That Are Actually Good
While “cheap” means something different to everyone, the best budget laptops generally fall under $750. This is where Windows truly shines, offering great specs for less money. Thanks to the latest processors from Qualcomm and Intel, these laptops now offer battery life that rivals Apple. The best affordable laptop I’ve checked out is the HP OmniBook 5. The model I tested has a Snapdragon X processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. Discounts fluctuate frequently, but HP always has some version of the OmniBook 5 with a Snapdragon CPU at under $700. The specific discounted configuration seems to change every few days, though, so shop carefully. I'll be testing the latest model soon, which switches to Intel processors and starts at $699.
I also recently tested the new HP OmniBook 3, which uses the same chip as the OmniBook 5. It frequently sells for less than the OmniBook 5 by at least $100 or so. HP is selling this configuration of the 14-inch model for under $550. While the OmniBook 3 is a good alternative, the OmniBook 5 is much thinner and looks more modern. Neither laptop has a particularly great touchpad, though, which is easily the biggest flaw in both laptops. Between the two, the OmniBook 5 is the better buy if you can afford it.
The MacBook Neo is Apple’s new entry-level laptop. It initially started at an aggressive $599, but that price has recently been raised to $699. Even at that price, the laptop shines when it comes to the display. It offers the best screen you can find at this price, bringing the macOS experience to an unprecedented value, even at $699 (or $799 for the 512 GB model). Apple clearly prioritized the front-of-screen experience, delivering a premium feel across the display, build quality, and keyboard. While the 8 GB of RAM, outdated ports, and slower SSD are notable drawbacks—making the MacBook Air a far better choice for remote workers—the Neo is an extremely premium-feeling laptop available for students, travelers, and casual users. Thanks to the lower-powered A18 Pro chip, though, performance does take a hit. So, be careful about buying this laptop if you work at a computer all day.
Given how good some of these budget laptops are, it’s a bit harder to find a place for Chromebooks. Perhaps that's why Google introduced the next evolution of the platform, so to speak: the Googlebook. The first batch has been released into the world, and I've tested a number of them. Googlebooks are similar to Chromebooks in use case, but they run entirely on Android and include some exclusive Google Gemini features. I like the close integration with Android, but Googlebooks ended up being a bit of a letdown, mostly because they're so expensive. The Acer Googlebook 14 and Dell XPS Googlebook are the two standouts in my book, as both use a Snapdragon X-series chip to deliver really great battery life. The XPS Googlebook is particularly pretty, as the chassis is nearly identical to the XPS 13. But $999 is a tough price to swallow. It ultimately has some of the same limitations as Chromebooks, as you can't download applications from the web and are forced to rely on the Google Play Store. The Acer Googlebook 14 is probably my top pick, as it comes in the cheapest at $899. Even that isn't exactly what I'd call a “budget laptop,” though.
That's why I strongly recommend the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514, especially when it's on sale for under $700 (which is frequent). It uses an efficient (and responsive) MediaTek Kompanio Ultra that delivers excellent battery life. For most people, I wouldn't recommend spending over $500 on a Chromebook because if you're paying more, you should consider the MacBook Neo or the HP OmniBooks, which offer more than a Chromebook's limited scope. But the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 might be the best combination of display, touchpad, and battery life at this price, making it a good choice for the right person—so long as you know what you're paying for.
Truly cheap Chromebooks come with bigger compromises, especially in display quality, touchpad feel, and battery life. If you really need something dirt cheap as a starter laptop for a kid or as a secondary device, I'd recommend the Asus Chromebook CX14. It has a modern design, enough ports, a good keyboard, and decent storage.
Powerful Laptops for Those Who Need It
While the laptops above are great for most people, content creators and gamers need extra performance. For the former, the 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro is the ultimate choice. It combines immense power with surprising portability and fantastic battery life—a rare feat. The M5 generation is the most impressive yet, with a greatly expanded GPU and significantly boosted on-device AI processing thanks to a more efficient Neural Engine and faster memory bandwidth. While it is one of the most powerful AI laptops available, the MacBook Pro isn’t for everyone; it is built specifically for professional creatives and engineers running heavy, demanding applications. It’s become more expensive in 2026, though, and the competition from the Windows side is finally heating up.
I'm talking primarily about the launch of Nvidia's new RTX Spark “superchip” and the new laptops that use it. To be clear, despite Nvidia's involvement, these aren't gaming laptops. Like the MacBook Pro, they're designed first and foremost for running heavier creative applications and on-device AI. The Surface Laptop Ultra is a great example, which has a lot in common with the standard 15-inch Surface Laptop. But the differences internally are substantial. The Surface Laptop Ultra uses a single chip that integrates the CPU, GPU, and memory together, allowing up to 128 GB of memory to be shared across the system. That's not unlike how Apple Silicon works, dramatically increasing the on-device AI performance. So, if you've been curious about running LLMs right on your laptop without relying on the cloud, these RTX Spark laptops are a great place to start. The other two RTX Spark laptops I tested, the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 and Lenovo Pro 9n, share a lot with the Surface Laptop Ultra (including performance). The OmniBook Ultra is the thinnest of the three, but I prefer the Surface Laptop Ultra's Mini-LED display and 3:2 aspect ratio.
Perhaps the most common use for extra laptop performance, however, is gaming. If you plan to boot up graphically intensive games more than a couple of times a week, you will want a dedicated gaming laptop. After testing dozens over the past year, I’ve come back to the Lenovo LOQ 15 as my top pick. There are cheaper RTX 5050 models, such as the Alienware 15 or MSI Cyborg A15, but prices have been increasing on these laptops over the past few months. The Alienware 15 with the RTX 5050, in particular, has seen a $600 price jump, which makes it incredibly overpriced.
That’s led me back to the LOQ 15, which has stayed steady at $1,300 at Walmart and gives you an RTX 5060 for graphics and a bright, colorful screen. You won’t find a cheaper gaming laptop that doesn’t make some significant compromises in either performance or screen quality, both of which can sour the gaming experience. And while I wish the LOQ 15 were still selling for under $1,000 as it did at launch, it's still the best gaming laptop for the money right now. It’s really the only gaming laptop under $1,500 I’d currently buy, given where prices are.
There’s also a whole world of gaming laptops outside the budget tier, though. I’ve tested an assortment of options, and I always come back to the Razer Blade 14 and Razer Blade 16. Portable, minimalist, and extremely well-made, their sleek design means they work just as well for school or work as they do for gaming, without the bulk of a traditional gaming laptop. While you can buy more powerful options, nothing quite matches the Razer Blade. They’re expensive, but if you can afford them, they’re as premium as gaming laptops get. I’ll soon be testing the latest version of the Blade 16, which includes Intel’s new Panther Lake chips and should have vastly improved battery life.
Other Good Laptops I’ve Tested
If you choose one of the laptops above, you will be very happy with your purchase. However, if you are looking for a specific feature or a different price point, I have included a few other options below that I’ve recently reviewed and enjoyed using. Each of these recently tested laptops has at least one minor drawback, but they could still be the perfect choice depending on your needs and current discounts.
Framework Laptop 13 Pro for $1,599: We’ve always loved Framework laptops at WIRED, mainly because their internal components are so repairable and upgradable. Users can easily swap out nearly every part, including the CPU. The Framework Laptop 13 Pro uses the same internal structure as the basic Framework Laptop 13, but upgraded with a haptic touchpad, an aluminum chassis, and a brighter (and sharper) display. The result is the Framework Laptop I’ve always wanted, especially with an all-black aesthetic that hints at ThinkPad inspiration. But most of all, if you’re going to try and make a laptop last for many years, it makes sense that it would be something more premium. This one actually feels like it’s worth the investment.
Microsoft Surface Laptop 13.8 for $930: The Surface Laptop 13.8 (also known as the 7th Edition) was one of my favorite laptops throughout 2024 and 2025, primarily because of its premium build quality, great battery life, and 3:2 aspect ratio screen. And while I still love this laptop, it’s risen dramatically in price and no longer feels like a great value, especially since it’s two years old now. The 2024 model now starts at $1,200, though I’ve occasionally seen it dip under $1,000. The next-generation model with the Snapdragon X2 chips costs $1,700. I have seen that price come down as low as $1,350 on discount.
Dell 14 Plus for $1,199: There was a time in 2025 when the Dell 14 Plus was as affordable as $600. It was easily the best deal in the world of Windows laptops, primarily because the Dell 14 Plus has a 2560 x 1600 display and a smooth touchpad—two things laptops at that price typically lack. These days, it’s up to over $1,000, though for a 1 TB configuration, that is still a reasonable price. The XPS 13 is the better overall laptop, but the Dell 14 Plus offers more ports and storage for the price.
Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 Ultra for $2,250: I like this laptop quite a bit. The OLED screen is sharp, bright, and quite colorful—very similar to the HP OmniBook Ultra. It also has many of the other great features on premium Windows laptops these days, including a haptic-feedback touchpad and a very slim profile. Unfortunately, it’s only available right now in a very expensive, maxed-out configuration with 32 GB of RAM and at least a terabyte of storage. I don’t think that’s a good pairing for this ultra-light laptop. Even with half the memory and storage, though, this would be too expensive compared to the competition.
Asus Zenbook A16 for $2,200: The Zenbook A14 and A16 are Asus’ ultralight laptops, weighing just 2.16 pounds, making them some of the lightest laptops you can buy right now. This second-generation Zenbook A16 is still incredibly light and now comes with second-generation Snapdragon X2 chips. It’s unique for its portability, and the Qualcomm chips deliver great battery life and performance. However, given the dramatic price increase, I’d suggest buying the 2025 model instead, which consistently comes in under $1,000.
Alienware 16X Aurora for $1,950: Another solid gaming laptop with the typical Alienware flair. Its standout features are its higher-resolution display and great build quality. The price fluctuates frequently, though, and in most cases, the LOQ 15 is the better option (unless you really want that higher-resolution screen).
Laptops to Avoid
Dell 14S: This is the 2026 successor to the Dell 14 Plus, which I recommended above. This is a solid laptop with a premium design and a highly reflective OLED display. It also performs well, thanks to the latest Intel Core Ultra Series 3 chip. But it’s far too expensive right now. Until the price comes down, I prefer just about every other Dell option, including the Dell 14 Plus, Dell XPS 13, or Dell XPS 14.
Lenovo LOQ 15 Essential: This is a “new” model that came out this year, even though it uses a CPU from 2023. But honestly, this is just too expensive. I’ve seen it on sale for under $1,400, but even then, the standard LOQ 15 costs about the same and has a far superior display.
MacBook Pro M5: It’s not a significant step up from the MacBook Air in performance, and it’s much thicker. You’re paying for the Mini-LED screen and extra ports. Unfortunately, it got the biggest price bump, up $300 to $1,999. It’s not a bad laptop, but you’re better off with the MacBook Air or a more powerful M5 Pro/Max configuration.
Acer Swift 16 AI: This is one of the few laptops you can buy with the powerful, efficient new Intel Core Ultra X9 chips. However, the Acer Swift 16 AI takes an experimental approach with its oversized trackpad, making it very difficult to use. Even at a discount, you’ll find it frustrating.
Asus TUF Gaming A14: There’s a lot I like about this gaming laptop. The design is portable yet modern, and the display is sharp. And while the TUF Gaming A14 is impressive technically (using the interesting AMD Strix Point chip), the lack of a discrete graphics card doesn’t provide enough gaming performance to justify its very high price. I haven’t tested the options with dedicated graphics cards, but they tend to be more expensive than counterparts from Lenovo, Acer, or Alienware.
Asus Vivobook 14: I recommended this laptop a lot throughout 2025, but it doesn’t hold up as well these days. While the Vivobook 14 has great battery life, the HP OmniBook 5 14 offers a much better display and similar specs, making it a better laptop.
How Much Should You Spend on a Laptop?
If you’re shopping for a laptop, you probably already have a budget. But some context might help put things in perspective. The cheapest laptops cost around $200, but laptop prices can range as high as $5,000. Meanwhile, the average amount people spend, according to the best data we have, is around $750. That lands decidedly in the midrange, splitting between the more expensive devices that are more than $1,000 and the budget-tier machines you find below $700.
When we talk about pricing, it’s often the “starting” price of the laptop, meaning the lowest-priced configuration. This is really important to consider, as you want to compare devices apples to apples as much as possible. For example, a cheaper laptop might start at $750 with 256 GB of storage, while a more premium laptop might start at this same price but come with 512 GB or even 1 TB of storage. Increasingly, you can find some really decent laptops around this price, some of which we’ve listed.
If your budget needs to be under $750, though, there are still good options. Laptops below this price tend to come with compromises. Most commonly, it’s the quality of the display and touchpad that suffers, as these are things you can’t gauge from a spec sheet or reference photo. Or it might be a performance-related issue, such as the 8 GB of memory in the MacBook Neo. If you’re shopping for something under $500, Chromebooks often give you the best bang for your buck.
So, why spend more? Well, there are two primary reasons. First, you might want a more premium design, perhaps one that has a more daring aesthetic or high-end components. Take the MacBook Pro, for example. It starts at $600 more than the MacBook Air but comes with a brighter mini-LED screen, significantly better speakers, and more ports. The second primary reason to spend more than $750 or so is to get more performance. Whether for gaming or content creation, laptops with discrete GPUs cost more, which is why it’s hard to find a worthwhile gaming laptop for less than $1,000. If you’re buying a gaming laptop, plan to spend a few hundred bucks more.
What Are the Best Laptop Brands?
Unlike the smartphone world, the biggest laptop brands have been around for more than 40 years. Besides Apple, four laptop brands stand out for adopting the latest technology and trends while providing reliable support and service.
Lenovo is the biggest PC brand in the world, at least in terms of global shipments. It’s perhaps most well-known for its familiar sub-brands like ThinkPad and Yoga, but it also isn’t afraid to take risks with more experimental designs and advanced technology. Lenovo has also made a name for itself in the gaming space with its Legion laptops, known for balancing performance and features at competitive prices.
Asus has quickly become a favorite, notable for the sheer number of laptops available in the consumer market. The company takes a similar approach to Lenovo, which has led Asus to innovate quickly on new technology and designs while also launching premium laptops at more affordable prices than its competitors. Gaming, in particular, is a space Asus has come to dominate, with the ROG Zephyrus, Strix, and TUF brands leading the way.
Dell and HP are generally more conservative, but both have recently undergone significant rebranding. In 2024, HP replaced its Spectre and Envy lines with the OmniBook name. Meanwhile, Dell briefly retired its well-known Inspiron and XPS sub-brands in 2025, though it has since reversed course and brought the XPS line back.
Other notable laptop brands include Microsoft Surface, Samsung, Acer, LG, and MSI, though none have the same global footprint as the top four.
How Do I Choose the Right Laptop?
If none of these laptops resonate with what you're looking for, that’s OK! There are far more laptops than we have time to test. To help you make smart choices, we put together a complete laptop buying guide. We also cover the CPUs and GPUs you need to know. We recommend sticking to these guidelines:
RAM: We recommend 16 GB of RAM. That’s become the new standard, even in more affordable laptops. Upgrading to 32 GB is even better, so you won't have to worry about running out of memory, especially if you’re a gamer or video editor. The recent memory shortage has led to some dramatic price increases, largely based around configurations of RAM. Apple’s launch of the 8 GB MacBook Neo this spring has led to the return of high-end 8-GB Windows laptops as well, such as the Dell XPS 13.
CPU: For Windows laptops, you have three CPU brands to choose from: Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm. Intel’s Core Ultra Series 2 launched in late 2024 and delivers a huge boost to battery life. It also has the best integrated graphics of the three. Core Ultra Series 3 is just now rolling out and, based on my testing, is extremely impressive in performance and efficiency. While AMD chips are primarily used in gaming laptops, they’ve struggled to gain ground on Intel elsewhere.
Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, however, have seriously challenged Intel over the past year with their ARM architecture, offering some of the best battery life we’ve ever seen on Windows machines. The second generation, Snapdragon X2, was announced last fall and rolled out slowly throughout 2026. They improve performance, but in many cases, they've led to more expensive laptops, while previous-gen laptops are still available that cost less.
Starting this year, there's also the choice of Nvidia’s new RTX Spark platform, which gives you the option of 18-core or 20-core CPUs. More on that in the GPU section below.
Apple Silicon is what powers all the modern MacBooks, the latest of which is the M5 chip. Read our in-depth guide on Which MacBook to Buy for more information
Graphics: Want to play AAA PC games, edit video on your laptop, or run local AI models? You’ll want some powerful graphics on hand. At this point, Nvidia is the primary option. The RTX 5090 launched in 2025 is still the most powerful new GPU available, but the 5040-series still remains a good option.
Integrated graphics have improved significantly over the years, though, especially on processors made by Apple, AMD, and Intel, such as the Apple M5 or the Intel Core Ultra X9 388H. Nvidia's RTX Spark platform uses a single “superchip” that provides unified memory to both the CPU and GPU to improve AI performance.
Screen: The display depends highly on the size of the laptop. A 1,200-pixel resolution (HD+) screen on a 13- or 14-inch laptop looks sharp enough to get by, but you’ll want more pixels on larger displays, such as a 2560 x 1600, 2880 x 1800, or 3840 x 2400. While IPS screens are good enough for most people, OLED and Mini-LED are becoming more common, offering better color accuracy, deeper contrast, and excellent HDR performance.
Connectivity: We generally recommend at least two USB-C ports, along with one HDMI and one USB-A port for legacy devices. (Remember that nearly all laptops today use one of those USB-C ports for the power adapter.) Thankfully, most laptops still have headphone jacks, but always check, because a few models have dropped them. Lastly, make sure it supports Wi-Fi 6E or newer. Even if you don’t have a Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 router yet, you'll likely have one in the future (see our Best Routers or Best Mesh Systems guides if you need a new one).
Battery life: Battery life is extremely competitive these days, with Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel all making highly ambitious battery-life claims. Most laptops with the latest chips (and without discrete graphics) will get you more than 10 hours of battery life, or many more if your workload is lighter.
Intel vs. AMD vs. Qualcomm
As mentioned, in Windows-based laptops, there are three primary options for CPUs: Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. All three companies offer good processors, but it really depends on the type of laptop. For premium laptops, you’ll want something like the Intel Core Ultra 258V or Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite. Meanwhile, for budget laptops, Snapdragon X is the best choice. And for gaming laptops, I’d recommend something from AMD, such as the Ryzen AI 9 365. All three companies have announced next-gen chips for 2026, and there’s some exciting stuff coming soon.
Intel’s latest chips, known as either Core Ultra Series 3 or codename Panther Lake, are slowly rolling out in new laptops, such as the Dell XPS 14. These chips represent a massive leap forward in both CPU and integrated graphics performance. While highly impressive, they will soon face fresh competition from upcoming AMD and Qualcomm releases.
Qualcomm made a major impact in 2024 with its Snapdragon X chips. Similar to Apple's M-series, these ARM-based processors prioritize efficiency to drastically improve battery life. This has been a game-changer for Windows laptops across different price points. The Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite is the highest-end option for performance, but the Snapdragon X Plus and base Snapdragon X still offer equally strong battery life, despite showing up in much cheaper laptops. The sequel was unveiled in late 2025, and now in 2026, we’re seeing those laptops roll out. Unfortunately, like Intel’s latest chips, laptops with this next-gen silicon tend to be significantly more expensive than their predecessors.
AMD has grown into a competitive player in the gaming laptop space. Its latest processors, including the Ryzen 9 9950X3D and 9900X3D, are the most powerful gaming chips you can find in a laptop. Unfortunately, it’s still hard to find many laptops supporting these killer chips. AMD also offers its Ryzen AI 300 H and HX chips, which are more commonly found in gaming laptops. While they also offer a mainstream Ryzen AI 300 series, these chips aren’t found in many laptops and currently fall short of the battery life offered by Intel and Qualcomm.
Nvidia's RTX Spark platform just hit the scene, promising to deliver power and efficiency especially when running AI-based operations. It's not as ubiquitous as Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm chips, but it's something to watch for.
How I Test Laptops
I have been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, and WIRED contributor Chris Null has been testing them for 25 years. We test each laptop we review in a variety of situations, including both synthetic benchmark tests and real-world use cases. We make comparisons against similar equipment. We don’t just look at the specs—our reviews evaluate performance, usability, portability, and price to help you find the right laptop for your needs.
We put every laptop through a gauntlet of tests before writing a review and assigning a rating.
Hands-on use: We evaluate the exterior of the device. We compare how thin and light it is against other laptops. We repeatedly open and close the lid to test the quality and ease of the hinge. We push on weak points like the keyboard and lid to test build quality. We also extensively test the keyboard and touchpad for comfort and precision. By using each laptop as our daily driver for days or even weeks, we can spot real-world quirks—like awkward port placement, excessive bloatware, or unexpected problems that may make the laptop difficult to use—that you won’t see on a spec sheet.
Sights and sounds: Once we boot up the device, it’s all about the sights and sounds. The screen is paramount, as it’s your window into everything the laptop has to offer. While you can tell a lot about brightness, color, and contrast just by looking, we go beyond subjective testing. We use a Spyder colorimeter to precisely measure brightness, contrast, color saturation, and accuracy. For HDR-capable screens, we also test peak brightness with HDR content. Finally, we evaluate the webcam and speakers to ensure they are ready for your video calls and streaming sessions.
Performance testing: Finally, we test performance. We always evaluate a laptop based on what it’s intended for—we don’t expect a $500 budget laptop to run like a gaming powerhouse, or a gaming rig to get 18 hours of battery life. Our testbed includes more than 20 synthetic benchmarks, which we constantly adapt based on the device's CPU and operating system. These include tests within Geekbench, PCMark, 3DMark, Procyon, GFXBench, Puget Bench, Superposition, Cinebench, and various gaming-related tests such as 3DMark and Cyberpunk 2077. While we don’t generally report raw scores, we pay close attention to what they tell us. We also monitor fan noise, surface temperature, and overall battery life during these tests.
It’s a lot, I know. But we’re thorough, because we want to stand by our recommendations and ensure that the laptops we rate highly are worth the money.

After the first round of the Brazilian presidential election three weeks ago, the leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva reportedly told allies he could not understand how he finished second after a government he considered the best of his three terms.
A mood of dismay swept Brazil’s left, and because 9 million voters for the other candidates, all of them on the right, were expected to mostly transfer to senator Flávio Bolsonaro, analysts widely saw the far-right senator’s victory as certain.
Then, on the night after the election, students from the Fluminense Federal University took to the streets of Niterói, a city of 480,000 across Guanabara Bay from Rio de Janeiro, to protest against the return to power of a member of the Bolsonaro family, whose patriarch, former president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father, is under house arrest for attempting a coup.
Two days later, another student protest took over downtown Rio and, in the days that followed, similar ones spread across the country in organic demonstrations that analysts and Lula himself agree gave new life to his campaign and played a decisive role in his historic comeback in the runoff.
“I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” Lula said in his victory speech on Sunday night after defeating Bolsonaro.
Political scientist Fábio Vasconcellos said Lula’s victory, in which for the first time in Brazil’s democratic history a second-placed candidate overturned a first-round defeat in the runoff, could be explained by a combination of the streets, social media and the machinery of government – in recent weeks, Lula approved a “package of benefits” at the limits of what electoral law allows, including increasing and bringing forward payments from the main cash-transfer programme for poor families.
“The streets and social media almost overlap,” said Vasconcellos, a researcher with the Representation and Democratic Legitimacy group at the Federal University of Paraná.
Two days after the first round, congressman André Janones, a Lula ally, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”, where Janones sent audio messages, videos – often beginning with shouts of “Guys, urgent!” – and dozens of daily instructions on how to make pro-Lula content perform well on social media.
The channel had 60,000 followers by the end of its first day and, by election Sunday, more than 10 million, and Lula’s digital reach overtook Bolsonaro’s.
In his victory speech, Lula called Janones “our general”, who had the role of “raising the morale of our troops every day”. The congressman’s relentless efforts, which included a 24-hour YouTube live stream on the eve of the vote, led to him being admitted to hospital last week – the only day the WhatsApp channel went silent.
Lula’s campaign also overhauled his online communications, and the incumbent, who turns 81 on Tuesday, began recording selfie videos despite not owning a mobile phone. On Sunday night, he said he had been given a phone and that “from now on I’m going to talk a lot to the Brazilian people, many times a day, directly”.
With the streets and social media, “the mood of defeat was gradually replaced by hopes of a comeback over those three weeks,” said Vasconcellos.
Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, said Lula’s comeback also represented “a broad rejection of the Bolsonarista project for Brazil”.
She has been interviewing undecided voters since May and said “the fear voters had, workers had, of losing rights and also of a possible concentration of power in Bolsonaro’s hands was very clear”, which meant that even people who did not like Lula voted for him this time.
Bolsonaro had won 56.1m votes in the first round and received 3.7 million more in the runoff. Lula, by contrast, went from 53.9m to 64.2m. The more than 10m-vote increase came both from persuading voters to turn out after historically high abstention in the first round and from convincing voters from other candidates, including Bolsonaro.
“Some undecided voters we interviewed said Bolsonaro was a playboy who sided with big business, while at the same time spontaneously saying that, if he won, there would be a dictatorship in which people would lose rights,” said Rocha.
Bolsonaro was also embroiled in several controversies recently, including saying he would use the new, even more conservative congress to change the constitution and “re-democratise” Brazil, as well as the two federal police inquiries in which he is under investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering.
Many analysts have also pointed to the weight of Lula himself. “If it were another candidate, Bolsonaro would already have won in the first round,” said political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles.
Marco Aurélio de Carvalho, Lula’s campaign manager, answered without hesitation when asked what explained the historic election fightback: “President Lula. We have a great statesman on our team. We have a star player. That’s what absolutely made the difference. I haven’t the slightest doubt about it.”
The question already occupying the minds of Brazil’s left is what happens next, given that Lula has said this was his last election.
“That is a very big challenge because, in the polling on this, Lula’s dominance is still very strong. There is no one in his party with the same leadership,” said Rocha.
Vasconcellos believes Lula’s re-election campaign, “from what we saw on the streets, offered the Brazilian left an opportunity for renewal”.
“Lula’s party can learn from what happened and find better ways to connect with young people and urban voters who feel their concerns are not being heard,” he added.

Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient in more than a decade became infected, amid fears the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.
The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.
The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.
The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases and that, if it did, it would make that information public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.
Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.
Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.
Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”
The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.
Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.
Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.
The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.
The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only globally to the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

A House lawmaker is investigating whether the three largest pharmacy benefit managers targeted independent pharmacies with audits in retaliation for supporting a bill that would require the companies to adjust payments to the retailers.
James Comer (R-Ky.), who heads the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, late last week sent letters to CVS Caremark, OptumRx, and Express Scripts, claiming that independent pharmacies “experienced an unusual surge in burdensome audits” after many openly backed the legislation he introduced last year.
Called the Pharmacists Fight Back Act, the bipartisan bill would require pharmacy benefit managers participating in the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program to fairly reimburse pharmacies for the actual cost of medicines and to pay a reasonable fee for dispensing the drugs.

All signs point to Thomas Markle Sr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” although a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”, the Philippine interior minister has told the Guardian.
Authorities in the south-east Asian country are analysing digital images allegedly belonging to the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex that were said to have been found at his former home in Cebu. Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, reported to authorities last week that he had apparently discovered a stash of child sexual abuse images.
Jonvic Remulla, the interior minister, said: “In these cases where family disputes are mixed up, we have to consider all the angles. Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings. The forensics data will be complete in a week.”
Remulla said a statement would be released once the data had been analysed, without giving a specific date. “Please give us a week to determine the contents and to come up with a definitive picture,” he said. “We will release a statement then.”
Markle Sr has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”. Philippine police are also investigating a laptop found at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr had been living until he returned to the US earlier this year.
In a statement given to Agence France-Presse, Remulla said the Philippine national police inspected Markle’s former home and found a “trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop”.
“The PNP will coordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him,” he said.
Markle Sr has told the Mail the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”. He said: “This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”
The duchess, already estranged from her father, broke off all contact with him last year, reportedly telling him she and the authorities were aware of allegations he had abused young girls, it is understood.
In a final letter to her father first reported by the Sun on Sunday, sent while he was in a hospital in the Philippines having had a leg amputated, Meghan made clear he would never see his grandchildren Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, and that she would never contact him again, it is understood.
The Sun reported on Friday that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu. Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the newspaper said.
Meghan has revealed she learned of allegations against her father in 2019, having been told by the Metropolitan police, and said she was given assurances these claims were being investigated. Sources said she had been advised that speaking publicly about the claims could have jeopardised any potential legal case and also put her at risk of legal action.
On Saturday the Met confirmed it had passed a letter “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom” to Meghan and the Duke of Sussex in 2019 but did not share details with other law enforcement agencies. Scotland Yard is considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct to review its actions.
The duchess was “upset and really frustrated” that the Met had not acted on allegations made in that letter, sources said.
In a new interview with the Mail on Sunday, Markle Sr said he had “never had sex with anyone under the age of 18”, telling the paper that when he was single he travelled to the Philippines at least twice and paid for sex.
He is reportedly in a Florida rehabilitation centre after his leg amputation.
In a statement on Friday, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed”.
She said: “In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
Sources later clarified she had misremembered the year in which the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.
The FBI said in a statement on Friday that it was “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law.”

A day before the counting of votes, Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) Rajya Sabha member Sanjay Yadav on Monday (October 26, 2026) wrote to the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) of the Election Commission of India (ECI) to ensure free, fair and transparent counting of votes for eight seats in the Bihar Legislative Council polls comprising four Graduates’ and four Teachers’ constituencies.
In the four-page letter, Mr. Yadav urged that all ballot papers whose validity or invalidity is disputed should be examined and decided, in accordance with the applicable election rules, before first-preference counting begins. He added that no doubtful ballot paper should be left undecided until a subsequent round or the final result.
He further wrote that reasons for decisions should be recorded, and authorised election agents should be given an opportunity to raise objections as permitted by the rules.
He also said that no counting officer, staff member or election agent should make any additional mark, signature, line, tick, cross or other notation on a ballot paper, except where expressly permitted by the applicable election rules, adding that the original condition and integrity of every ballot paper must be preserved.
Ban on violet pens used for voting
In the letter, Mr. Yadav wrote that pens of the same type as the violet pens used for marking preferences on ballot papers during polling must not, under any circumstances, be available to or possessed by any counting officer, counting staff member or election agent at the counting centre.
“This safeguard is necessary to prevent unauthorised marking or tampering with ballot papers. In the Chandigarh Mayoral Election case of 2024, the Supreme Court examined the issue of unauthorised markings on ballot papers and the process by which votes were declared invalid. Appropriate safeguards must therefore be implemented to preserve the original condition of ballot papers and prevent unauthorised interference during counting,”Mr. Yadav wrote.
The RJD leader pointed out that all counting officials should follow the applicable election rules and prescribed standards uniformly when determining whether ballot papers are valid or invalid, adding that no ballot paper should be rejected arbitrarily or merely on the basis of personal opinion or vague suspicion.
In the letter. Mr Yadav highlighted that voter eligibility and ballot-paper validity are separate matters; where a legally recognised objection or order of a competent authority exists concerning a voter’s eligibility, the relevant records and prescribed legal procedure should be followed. He added that no ballot paper should be rejected solely on the basis of an unverified allegation.
Videography and preservation of records
He also demanded that videography and monitoring be ensured, as permitted by the applicable rules, particularly during scrutiny of doubtful ballot papers, decisions on valid and invalid ballots, and preparation of counting sheets. Mr. Yadav said that all relevant records should be securely preserved for subsequent examination, if required.
Every authorised election agent should be given a reasonable opportunity, in accordance with the applicable rules, to observe the counting process and raise objections regarding doubtful ballot papers or counting irregularities. Objections and decisions should be duly recorded, Mr. Yadav demanded
The number of valid and invalid ballot papers, the relevant stages of counting, including first-preference counting, and the counting sheets should be reconciled and verified in accordance with the applicable rules. Any discrepancy should be resolved through the prescribed procedure before the result is declared.
He also mentioned that all officials and counting staff should be directed to maintain impartiality, transparency and strict compliance with election rules. Mr. Yadav further wrote that any complaint regarding unauthorised interference or counting irregularities should be investigated fairly, and appropriate action should be taken in accordance with the law.
A copy of the letter is also sent to Vinod Singh Gunjiyal, Bihar Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), as the counting of the votes will begin at 8 a.m. on October 27 at eight counting centres.
Later in the day, a six-member RJD delegation also submitted a memorandum to the Bihar CEO with similar demands. The results of Kosi, Tirhut, Patna, Darbhanga (graduate constituencies) and Saran, Tirhut, Patna, Darbhanga (Teachers’ constituencies) will be declared. The M-Vave FM-1 is exactly the kind of device I have a weakness for. I may not have an intended use for the frequency-modulation synthesizer, but when a low price meets a high coolness factor, I’m powerless to keep it out of my cart.
Initially billed as a pocket cousin of the famous Yamaha DX7 synthesizer, the FM-1 is a bargain at only $59.72 after fees. At release, it was a cool device that did what it said on the box, but not much else.
But in July, some intrepid tinkerers on Reddit’s r/synthdiy board began reverse-engineering the FM-1’s stock firmware to expand the device’s abilities. By September, custom firmware began appearing. We’re not even through October, and there are already more community firmware projects available to install on the FM-1 than I could ever hope to cover.
I decided to check a few of them out. And just in case you were wondering: Yes, it plays Doom.
Stock firmware and FM1 Open
On October 17, M-Vave announced FM1 Open, a software package that encourages FM-1 owners to develop custom firmware for the synth-turned-whatever-else-you-can-imagine. Alongside the FM1 Open package came an SDK, a browser-based workbench, and version 15 of the stock firmware, now an open platform you can flash and build on. The unit’s 27 physical piano keys and modest 1.54-inch TFT display lend themselves well to a host of projects, musical or otherwise.
Normally, when an enthusiast community reverse-engineers a closed device, an official patch quickly follows. M-Vave has taken the opposite approach, though. The application source is published under GPLv3, and the company even includes an in-browser emulator to test custom firmware prior to flashing actual hardware. There’s a caveat, however: The underlying synth engine that powers the stock FM-1 package is still distributed as a closed binary, so it’s the application layer of the stack that’s actually open. I don’t think that diminishes M-Vave’s gesture toward the community, but it’s worth noting.
Proceed at your own risk
Before you rush to AliExpress, be aware that flashing custom firmware comes with risks. The JieLi chip powering the FM-1 keeps firmware in a single flash bank, so an interrupted update can leave the device in a difficult-to-recover state. As long as the flashing process completes without interruption, you should be fine. But nothing is foolproof, and there’s always a risk of bricking a device if something goes wrong.
You will need to grant permission for your browser to write to the FM-1.
You will need to grant permission for your browser to write to the FM-1.
Flashing will also wipe all information on the device. Before you try to load a new firmware package on the synth, back up your saved projects and settings because they will disappear. I was starting from a blank stock canvas, so there was no real risk.
The unit I received was running stock v14 firmware, and community guides repeatedly warn users to update to the stock v15 firmware before attempting to install custom firmware. Guess who didn’t listen? I blindly assumed that since I’d just received my FM-1, it would be running the latest firmware package (v16 now). I was wrong.
I attempted to run before I could walk. Don’t be me.
I attempted to run before I could walk. Don’t be me.
Caught in the excitement, I tried to flash Doom directly onto the v14 firmware package, and the installation failed about 80 percent through. Still, it wrote something. The synth worked, but the device stopped speaking the same language as the installers. Thankfully, M-Vave anticipated careless users like me and thoughtfully included a “force-flash” tool in the FM1 Workbench. It restored my unit to stock v15 in about 10 seconds, saving me a huge headache.
The lesson is simple: Always check your current firmware version.
Custom firmware packages
The development scene around the FM-1 is exploding, and new options are appearing all the time. You can browse the listings to see what you might like to try, and a community tip from the fm1-custom-fw GitHub offers some good advice:
While not an absolute hard rule, there is a prominent community recommendation to avoid flashing one custom firmware directly over another. To minimize bricking risks, some users suggest rolling back to the official stock firmware (v15) via M-VAVE’s official updater first, and only then flashing the next custom firmware build. Alternatively, you can use TransitFM1—a dedicated lightweight bridge firmware by Quixotic7 designed with crash-guarded boot stubs and stock V15 identity emulation to safely transition between custom builds.
Some other tips I picked up along the way from community discussions and my own mistakes:
Ensure that the FM-1 is fully charged and connected to your PC via USB.
Use a Chromium-based browser for the package installation process. The installers depend on WebUSB and Web MIDI support in the browser, so options like Firefox are out.
Select the FM-1 from a list of available models where applicable.
Use the package’s web-writer to flash the firmware to your FM-1. Do not unplug or power off the unit at any point during this process. Make sure the PC you’re writing the package from isn’t at risk of going to sleep during the write.
Here are some projects to try.
Doom
What better way to measure the value of any electronic device than asking, “will it run Doom”?
Pen for scale. It’s so cute!
Credit:
Nick Indge
Pen for scale. It’s so cute!
Credit:
Nick Indge
The FM-1 already has several Doom-related projects up and running. Playing on a 240 x 240 display with mini piano keys will never be my preferred way to take down demons with a shotgun, but that doesn’t make it any less cool to see the game running on a $60 synthesizer clone. It’s a novelty, but the clone version played surprisingly well. The short draw distance means enemies occasionally pop out of nowhere, but who doesn’t love a jump scare while demon hunting?
While the stock firmware aims to re-create the Yamaha DX7 experience, Melodee takes its cues from the mid-’80s Casio CZ-1, a full-featured synthesizer that uses phase distortion to create a sound modern artists are still chasing. Melodee comes with four engines: a CZ-1 emulator, a DX7-style engine, a percussion engine for the 808s, and my personal favorite, a Commodore 64 SID sound chip emulator.
The FM-1 loaded with the Melodee firmware package.
Credit:
Nick Indge
The FM-1 loaded with the Melodee firmware package.
Credit:
Nick Indge
As a child of the 8-bit era, I’ve always had a soft spot for the amazing soundtracks built around the technological limits of the day. Composing chiptunes always seemed like an interesting hobby, but I never had the right tools. Now, thanks to Melodee, I have a pocketable chiptune keytar I can take anywhere.
Ready to make some beats?
Credit:
Nick Indge
Ready to make some beats?
Credit:
Nick Indge
Want to re-create that classic Cash Money sound on a $60 budget? The FM-1 now has you covered—this could be your chance to become the next Mannie Fresh.
Felucca
This is where a capable device becomes the deal of the year. Felucca is the foundation for many other community firmware projects, transforming the FM-1 into a true multi-engine synth. The stock firmware lets you select different instruments, but you can play only one at a time. Felucca runs independent instruments simultaneously, letting you create a full-band sound all by yourself.
Trying my hand at beatmaking inside Felucca.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Trying my hand at beatmaking inside Felucca.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Felucca includes more than a dozen sound engines, from phase distortion to virtual analog, plus a built-in sampler. Other highlights include a RAW in-browser web editor that makes arranging tracks less painful than working on the FM-1’s tiny screen, and a full multi-track pattern sequencer built into the device. If you want to make music, this is a great place to start.
SLOOP
Boot logo for SLOOP.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Boot logo for SLOOP.
Credit:
Nick Indge
SLOOP is the FM-1’s groovebox solution. Cards on the table: Before writing this article, I wasn’t familiar with what a groovebox was. In a nutshell, it’s a self-contained music studio that can be operated without a PC. SLOOP turns the FM-1 from an instrument you play into one you compose with. You program drums and bass on a grid, chain loops together, and let the machine keep the beat going while you layer other sounds on top.
8-track recording environment in SLOOP.
Credit:
Nick Indge
8-track recording environment in SLOOP.
Credit:
Nick Indge
SLOOP adds drum machines and synth layers to the FM-1, running on Felucca’s sound engines. The result is a legitimate eight-track, battery-powered beat maker that fits in your pocket. Unlike Felucca, SLOOP is designed more for live performance, letting you build and stack layers of sound as you go. I didn’t always fully understand how I arrived at the results I produced in SLOOP, but I was having too much fun to care.
In the studio
After exploring some of the available custom firmware packages, I decided to take my own advice and try Felucca as a starting point for actual recording. I connected the FM-1 to my PC using the same USB connection I’d previously used for flashing. Audacity recognized Felucca immediately, and I was able to select it as a recording device. From there, I could select any instrument or effect on the device and record it live over USB to Audacity tracks.
That’s all well and good if you’re sitting at a desk with a PC, but what if inspiration strikes while you’re out and about? That’s where Felucca’s self-contained recording process shines.
The FM-1 appears as a recording device in Audacity.
Credit:
Nick Indge
The FM-1 appears as a recording device in Audacity.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Creating music entirely on the FM-1 was more intuitive than I expected. Once I pulled up the Felucca controls cheat sheet, the process was smooth: use the Algorithm knob to switch between recording tracks and Presets to switch instruments. From there, I could build and layer my creation track by track.
I put together a four-track beat loop after about 15 minutes of fiddling with the firmware. I just felt my way around in the dark, auditioning sounds and slipping them in wherever I thought they fit. It was about as simplistic as it gets, but with some time and practice, I think I could churn out something worthwhile. If it was this straightforward for me, just imagine what someone with actual musical talent could achieve.
I’ll admit that my fingers were occasionally too big for the task. The FM1’s soft-touch keys feel great, but my index finger sometimes slipped off the intended note and onto an adjacent key. It’s not a dealbreaker, but there were a few times I had to retry a part due to hitting a wrong note.
My finger would occasionally slip off the intended key.
Credit:
Nick Indge
My finger would occasionally slip off the intended key.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Since there doesn’t appear to be an on-device export function, transferring the track to my PC was as simple as opening Audacity and hitting record while playing a beat on the FM-1. I retained live control throughout recording, too. Toward the end of the sample below, you can hear me fading out the audio by turning down the master volume knob. The same approach would let you weave any number of live modulations into a recording. You can hear my modest attempt at a quick beat below.
Final thoughts
The FM-1 is the type of technology I love. I’m the furthest thing from a professional musician, but the price is low enough and the device is versatile enough that I can play around without feeling guilty about a $1,500 synth setup gathering dust in the corner.
My 10-year-old has been taking piano lessons for a few years now and has clearly inherited my urge to tinker with tech. The FM-1 could be the perfect holiday gift he never knew he needed. I’ll probably order another one for him since I still want to play with mine. At this price, I don’t have to sweat it.
M-Vave didn’t send this unit for review; checkout curiosity just got the better of me. I’ve since ordered the company’s SMC-PAD sampler, too, but that’s another article for another day.
Nick Indge is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica covering hardware, embedded systems, and self-hosted infrastructure. A former security investigator turned tech writer, he writes to help readers escape subscription traps and regain ownership of their digital lives. He lives in Chicagoland with his family and a goofball husky.

I am very lost in Los Angeles. I’m also sweating because I'm running as fast as I can, slapping my hands against the wet glasses frame on my face to boost the volume of the pulsing techno beats blasting into my ears—and anyone else’s if they happen to be nearby. It’s only the second time I’ve gone on a run in the city, and I decide to let myself get completely off course.
“Hey Meta,” I pant. “I need to get back; tell me where to go.”
The music dims, and the AI agent barks turn-by-turn directions in my ears. After getting turned around a couple of times, I eventually make it back. The navigation wasn’t perfect, but it got me where I needed to be.
This feature has long been available in Meta’s smart glasses. But now I’m wearing the new Ray-Ban Meta Audio, camera-free glasses the company announced in September. The only big change between these and Meta’s other glasses is the lack of a camera, but losing that one feature makes a world of difference.
It makes sense that Meta started with cameras on its glasses. After all, its primary breadwinner is Facebook, a visual platform driven by all the photographs and memes your uncle can use AI to generate. The platform is designed to capture content and beam it to the world—sometimes whether people like it or not.
It took waves of privacy controversies for Meta to finally ditch the cameras. People have found the camera-enabled glasses creepy, calling Meta’s products “pervert glasses” because they have been used by weirdo pickup artists to record people without consent. Some users also shared techniques for removing the indicator light on the glasses designed to let people around the wearer know they’re recording. (Meta released a software fix for this that disables the cameras entirely if the indicator light has been tampered with.)
It didn’t help that the company tried to put facial recognition technology on the glasses, which it denied at first, then later admitted to, and removed. In September, the company was sued for its facial recognition systems. (Meta insists that all the very public pushback did nothing to encourage it to release audio-only glasses.)

What is the Video about?
On October 13, AISA president Neha Bora sent a video message to the Socialist Students’ Front (SSF) of Bangladesh on the occasion of the organisation’s sixth central conference. The video was uploaded to SSF’s Facebook profile.

The Socialist Students’ Front is a Left-wing student organisation associated with the Socialist Party of Bangladesh (Marxist). SSF was established in 1984.

She added, “Neha used the term ‘religious fundamentalism’. She is speaking against such violence. Right-wing voices are trying to distort her message and misleadingly associate her speech with the violence.”
Neha Clarifies: ‘Message Directed at SSF’
Following the circulation of the clip, Neha herself posted a clarification on Instagram.
In the video, she says, “Right-wing accounts removed the logo of the SSF’s central conference and other identifying graphics from the original footage to use it for propaganda against me”. She explains, “These visual elements established that the video had been recorded for the Socialist Students’ Front’s sixth national conference, addressed to its activists to express solidarity with their struggles for democracy, students’ rights, education and communal harmony.” “And the student activists in India draw inspiration from these struggles,” she added.
Neha asserts that her message was “directed at the organisation’s struggles for democratic rights, student rights, accessible education and communal harmony”. She said that her reference to “drawing inspiration from Bangladesh concerned the progressive and secular elements of its student movement, rather than the entirety of the uprising or the political forces that subsequently gained influence.”

Ollie Davies, Sam Konstas and Campbell Kellaway were options. Nathan McSweeney, too.
The problem Australia have is that unlike in previous eras when they had players averaging north of 40 and banging out domestic runs - often in English county cricket as well as at home - waiting in the wings, they don't now.
All of the prospects mentioned above average mid-30s or lower in first-class cricket.
Will Bavuma extend excellent record as captain?
South Africa, by contrast, have a pretty much guaranteed source of runs in captain Temba Bavuma, whose brilliant 179 from 334 balls in Gqeberha means he is averaging 49.95 across his last 28 Tests.
His nuggety ton last time out was scored after he came in at 12-2.
He was at the other end as the Proteas slumped to 110-6 before pushing them to 425-9 and was ultimately left to celebrate a 12th win in 14 Tests as skipper.
This feels like a great chance to make that 13 from 15 unless Australia are able to pull something out of the bag in Cape Town.
Unlike in 2018, something within the rules this time.

A recent review of international clinical practice guidelines published in The Lancet Rheumatology highlights a shift in the management of non-specific low back pain towards clinical assessment, patient education, physical activity, and exercise, while discouraging routine imaging when there is no suspicion of serious disease.
Examining guidelines issued between 1994 and 2026, the review underscores the importance of assessing symptoms and identifying warning signs before deciding on investigations or treatment. Bengaluru-based specialists said the approach reflected a growing emphasis on restoring function and avoiding unnecessary investigations and interventions.
Ravikumar Mukartihal, senior consultant orthopaedic and robotic joint replacement surgeon at SPARSH Hospitals, Bengaluru, said the approach had moved from investigation-driven care to one focused on clinical assessment and restoring function.
“Most cases of non-specific low back pain do not indicate a serious structural problem and can be managed without extensive investigations or invasive procedures,” he said.
Treatment should focus on understanding symptoms, reassuring patients, maintaining normal activities, prescribing appropriate exercises and physiotherapy, and using medication judiciously, he said.
Treat the patient, not the scan
Karuna Kabadi, neurosurgeon at Apollo Speciality Hospital, Jayanagar, said a disc bulge or prolapse described in an MRI report was an observation about the disc, not necessarily a diagnosis explaining the pain. “Many of us may be having disc bulges but do not have symptoms and feel perfectly fit,” she said.
Back pain can arise from muscles, ligaments, and joints, and may also be associated with systemic diseases. A disc bulge may cause symptoms when it irritates or compresses a nerve, resulting in shooting pain in the buttock or leg, commonly known as sciatica. A detailed history and clinical examination help doctors assess the likely cause, with imaging supporting the diagnosis where necessary, she said.
Ravikumar T., Head and Consultant of the Department of Orthopaedics at Ramaiah Memorial Hospital, said incidental findings on scans could cause unnecessary anxiety if patients interpreted them as proof that their spine was damaged.
“Treat the patient and not the scan,” he said, noting that disc bulges and mild degenerative changes were also seen in people without back pain.
Non-specific back pain can involve several factors, including muscle strain, weak core muscles, poor movement patterns, sedentary habits, stress and inadequate sleep. Clinical examination helps assess pain, movement limitations and neurological signs before treatment is decided, he said.
Movement over prolonged rest
The review found that most guidelines recommended taking a patient’s history, conducting a physical examination and assessing psychological factors, including risk-stratification tools where appropriate. Routine imaging was generally discouraged without indications of serious pathology.
For acute low back pain, recommendations commonly included self-management, heat therapy, spinal manipulation and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). For chronic pain, they included exercise therapy, psychological interventions and multidisciplinary care, with acupuncture and spinal manipulation recommended in some guidelines as part of broader treatment programmes.
Dr. Ravikumar T. said treatment had moved away from prolonged bed rest and early reliance on strong painkillers towards reassurance, education, continued activity and structured physical therapy.
“Movement is medicine,” he said, warning that avoiding activity out of fear of scan findings could cause muscle deconditioning and prolonged disability.
Dr. Kabadi said sitting for long hours and reduced daily movement contributed to mechanical back pain. Staying active, avoiding prolonged sitting and following guided physiotherapy and muscle-strengthening exercises could help, although consistency was essential.
When is a scan necessary?
Doctors stressed that discouraging routine imaging did not mean scans were unnecessary. Imaging remains important when there are warning signs of serious disease, progressive neurological deficits or persistent symptoms for which the findings could change treatment.
Surgery also has a role in selected patients, but decisions should be based on clear clinical indications rather than an MRI finding alone, Dr. Mukartihal said.
The specialists said the focus should be on appropriate clinical assessment and treatment tailored to each patient, with the aim of restoring movement and function while avoiding unnecessary investigations and procedures without overlooking serious underlying conditions.

Amgen's Imdelltra used in combination with AstraZeneca's immunotherapy Imfinzi reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to the Astra drug alone in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, according to data from a study presented at a major medical meeting on Saturday.
Imfinzi is currently the standard of care following chemotherapy for patients with this very aggressive and hard-to-treat disease whose cancer does not worsen after initial chemotherapy.
The study found that those given both drugs lived for a median of 21.1 months, compared with 12.7 months for those treated only with Imfinzi.
"If you give Imdelltra earlier and earlier, you get bigger clinical benefit," said Paul Burton, chief medical officer at California-based Amgen. He called the results "unprecedented in advancing the treatment of extensive-stage small cell lung cancer."
Imdelltra's U.S. list price is about $30,000 per cycle, or over $390,000 a year. Wall Street analysts have estimated annual sales reaching more than $2.5 billion by 2030, according to LSEG data.
The Amgen drug is currently approved for adults in the advanced stages of small cell lung cancer that has worsened despite chemotherapy, based on data showing that Imdelltra reduced the risk of death by 40%.
Full results of the 563-patient trial were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid and published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Amgen had previously announced that the Phase 3 study was successful.
Imdelltra belongs to a dual-target class of drugs called bispecific antibodies designed to pull immune system T cells into contact with cancer cells to destroy them. Imfinzi is an older type of immunotherapy that essentially blocks the mechanism tumors use to hide from immune-system assault.
Most lung cancer cases are non-small cell, while up to 15% are the small cell variety targeted by Imdelltra. About 250,000 new cases are diagnosed worldwide each year, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health.
Very few people diagnosed with small cell lung cancer are candidates for surgery, and most are initially given radiotherapy and chemotherapy, Burton said.
Survival rates depend on when the cancer is diagnosed, but the overall 5-year rate is only around 9%, according to the American Cancer Society.
Amgen said that nearly 80% of trial patients treated with the combination were alive after one year, compared with 53% of those on Imfinzi alone, as patient follow-up continues.
Serious side effects, including low white blood cell counts, occurred in 20.9% of patients on the dual therapy and 10.8% with the single therapy. A potentially dangerous condition known as cytokine release syndrome, an aggressive inflammatory response, was reported in 49.6% of patients who received Imdelltra. But only one case was serious and there were no CRS-related deaths.
Adverse events led to discontinuation of the combination therapy in 5.7% of trial patients and 5.8% of patients given only Imfinzi.
