Venezuelan opposition leader María Machado returns after months in exile
- Published
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile.
"I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated prior efforts to re-enter the country came to no avail.
In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro.
The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal which granted very favourable terms to the US.
Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands.
She then began travelling to the capital Caracas in a caravan of cheering supporters. More supporters have lined the route of her journey to the capital.
She was photographed smiling as she leaned out of the sunroof of a car as she entered Caracas late on Sunday night.
"Night of reunion in our Caracas. For the reunion of each family, for the Freedom of each political prisoner, for the Freedom of Venezuela," she wrote on X.
Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González, confirmed her arrival, writing in a statement: "I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil."
"Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" González said.
He added that he will soon join Machado in Venezuela to advance the country "toward freedom".
An advisor to Machado said in September that over the previous few weeks Machado had attempted seven times to return to Venezuela, but was denied each time. There have been reports that the US was involved in delaying her return, which it has denied.
It's unclear what Machado plans to do next now that she's back, but she has previously said she would run for president again if an election were held. Her ability to return to her country was always contingent on approval from the Trump administration, which it appears has now been granted.
A staunch supporter of democracy, Machado won an independent presidential primary election - held outside the Maduro government's official election authority - in 2023, earning more than 90% of the vote.
Despite winning the primary, Maduro's government barred Machado from running for office, accusing her of fraud and tax violations. Machado denied the allegations, calling them politically motivated. She spent her final days in the country hiding in safehouses before her fleeing to Norway to accept the Nobel Prize.
In the 2024 election, Machado's ally González ran in her place against Maduro.
The electoral authority, which is closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.
The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.
Maduro was removed from the country by US forces in January, and is currently jailed in New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges. He has pleaded not guilty.
A spokesman for Machado called her return "a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future".
"We thank President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the US Government, Congress, and allied governments for their continued leadership and support," her spokesperson, David Smolansky, added.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said, "I don't know anything about" her return, and added that he hoped she was "safe".
"I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe," he said.
In January, Machado visited the White House and gifted her Nobel prize award to Trump. The committee that issues the prize had said "it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised his country's role in securing her return through political reconciliation talks.
"The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms Machado to Venezuela is the direct result of the US supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile," he posted on X.
He added: "We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy."

The candid meeting that 'changed' Spurs - are they finally on way back?
- Published
Whisper it quietly, but could Spurs finally be on their way back?
Tottenham's 2-0 win at Chelsea on Saturday moved them up to the heady heights of 12th in the Premier League - their highest league position since 2 January.
And, after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes, there are growing signs Roberto de Zerbi's side are showing there is real light at the end of a pretty dark tunnel.
Saturday's impressive win at Stamford Bridge was just the second time they have won two league games in a row in 42 attempts - inspired by starring roles from James Maddison and Mathys Tel.
It was also the first time they have enjoyed as much as 68% possession in a match since April 2025.
The win was deserved too, although Chelsea certainly gave them a helping hand with goalkeeper Mike Penders punching the opener into his own net and Cole Palmer sent off for two yellow cards.
Spurs had taken seven attempts to get their first league win of the season against Coventry on Monday and on Saturday they looked transformed from the side that did not even score a goal until September 1.
It left De Zerbi glowing with positivity, despite another injury setback for Maddison, as he highlighted a team meeting earlier this month that sparked their revival in fortunes.
"Seven points after Manchester. Before Manchester we spoke a lot, we had a big meeting," he said. "We removed the masks and spoke honestly and clearly in front of ourselves. From that moment, I think something started to change within us.
"I think we have put something different into Tottenham in the last period. Not a different attitude, but different relationships with the players, different relationships within the group.
"We have changed the spirit of the group and improved the performances of the players, especially some of the more fragile players, maybe the younger players. We have suffered enough."
Former Chelsea goalkeeper Rob Green added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "A dream afternoon for Tottenham. They looked controlled, looked at ease, they looked like they were comfortable on the ball.
"Results like this galvanise a side. When you look at the players coming back, yes Maddison got injured and he'll be a question mark over the next few weeks, but players coming back, momentum coming back - you feel, and say it quietly, Tottenham might just be coming back."
'A big statement' as Maddison and Tel star
Italian De Zerbi was appointed Spurs boss at the end of March 2026 with the club in crisis.
He arrived as the club's third manager of the campaign and, with seven games remaining, Tottenham were just one point clear of the drop zone.
After securing safety, albeit after a few scares, the club spent more than £300m on summer signings for the first time in their history as they backed De Zerbi to restore them to former glories.
And, after a slow start to the campaign and still lacking firepower in attack, the long-suffering Tottenham fans will be left feeling more positive than they have done for a long time.
"Tottenham have made a big statement in a really convincing performance," former Arsenal defender Martin Keown told BBC Sport.
"I thought Maddison was magnificent in midfield. He's like the Artful Dodger, isn't he? That midfield is full of mischief, but he's brave against the ball.
"I thought Tel was magnificent out on the left-hand side, [Mohammed] Kudus on the right was also really effective, and everybody really managed to handle the ball really well on the night.
"Spurs had almost 70% possession, which is remarkable for a team which was just a few places from the bottom of the table. I think what's changed for Spurs is the key personnel."
De Zerbi ran on to the pitch to celebrate with the travelling supporters at the final whistle, while his coaches and substitutes raced towards the players in the corner of the ground.
He has previously spoken of how he inherited players that cried after matches and lost all confidence - and believed his unprecedented control over the summer transfers was vindication for Spurs from last season.
It was fitting that Tel, who has attracted criticism from his own supporters since arriving from Bayern Munich for £30m in June 2025, provided the decisive moment to seal just a second league success in 36 years at Chelsea - a stunning low finish after a driving run.
The French forward, 21, told Sky Sports: "It is very special because we have come to Chelsea so many times and not got a win. We showed great mentality today and we need to enjoy this win.
"We created a lot of chances today. We walk out together, the goal is something special for me, I'm happy about it and let's keep pushing now."
Summer signing Matheus Fernandes added: "We are here to change the club's mentality, we want to beat the top teams, and make this victory for the fans."
Summer signings starting to settle as rebuild under way
In the summer, Spurs twice broke their transfer record with three of their first signings, as they added centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton, Fernandes from West Ham and Sandro Tonali from Newcastle.
And all three impressed De Zerbi against Chelsea as he added: "Jan Paul van Hecke played very well, Matheus Fernandes played very well, Sandro Tonali played very well.
"I think it was Tonali's best game since joining Tottenham. Omar Marmoush played a good game. It was a tough game for him, but he fought in the right way.
"Mathys Tel played very well too. I think we won the game with our two wingers, Mohammed Kudus and Mathys Tel. They made the difference."
It was notable Fernandes, 22, was criticised by his manager last month.
The return of Maddison, who missed almost all of last season with a serious knee injury, was key in Monday's 3-1 home victory over Coventry City - and he again looked impressive before being withdrawn in the second half with a suspected groin injury.
"I don't think it is a very important problem," said De Zerbi. "I hope it is not a big problem. He is a special player for us. We need him."
Maddison is part of a returning group of players, including Kudus and Dejan Kulusevski, who are making comebacks from lengthy absences.
Spurs are now unbeaten in three games, with back-to-back victories following the 1-1 draw at Manchester United in which they were arguably the better side.
As well as the team meeting before the Old Trafford encounter, Spurs enjoyed a warm-weather training camp in Marbella, where heavyweight boxer Anthony Joshua paid them a visit.
It feels as though some semblance of the old Spurs is returning, although they remain unconvincing in attack with just eight goals in as many games.
Manchester City loanee Marmoush misfired again and his replacement Dominic Solanke was underwhelming in previous matches, while Richarlison has been frozen out in the reserves after being left out of their Premier League squad.
But after this notable derby victory at Chelsea - earning a clean sheet there too for the first time since 1986 - it felt like the first part of De Zerbi's rebuild is well under way.

Britain's posh schools are heading to India for students and profits
- Published
On the outskirts of Chandigarh city in India's north-western Punjab state, a 473-year-old legacy British public school opened its first all-girls international campus earlier this year.
In contrast to the prominent Gothic-style central building on the school grounds in Bedfordshire, England, the Indian premises are more modern, with purpose-built academic blocks. But a conspicuous red-brick clock tower bears the imprint of the school's British heritage.
The Bedford School, Mohali, is the newest in at least half a dozen British public schools (elite, fee-paying private schools with a long history), including three of the country's oldest, that have set up shop across the length and breadth of India. Their expansion comes amid tighter market conditions in China and the introduction of VAT on private school fees in Britain from 1 January 2025.
Since 2023, Bengaluru - India's Silicon Valley and a hub of software and start-up companies - has been home to the prestigious Harrow School, alma mater of India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Shrewsbury School has a campus in Bhopal in central India, while Wellington College has chosen to set up base in Pune, a western city that calls itself the "Oxford of the East" for its well-regarded universities and colleges.
Millfield, Queen Elizabeth's School and a few others are reportedly on their way with satellite campuses in the coming years.
For decades, India has been home to well-established local boarding schools modelled on the colonial British public-school system, serving elite, aristocratic families. But this market has rapidly expanded with newly wealthy Indian families increasingly aspiring to give their children more global exposure.
"Our international curriculum is quite a driver for many of them," Caroline Pascoe, head of school at Harrow in Bengaluru, told the BBC.
Harrow and Bedford are among the few schools in India that follow an all-through Cambridge curriculum - a global education framework recognised at 10,000 schools worldwide - from primary through to A-levels.
Harsimran Singh Kocchar, whose own extended family runs a chain of schools across India, says he decided to send his five-year old daughter Parineet to Bedford Mohali because of the "holistic focus of the school on character development, confidence and not merely academics".
He said he was also drawn to the fact the school did not have a "VIP culture" unlike many Indian equivalents.
"All kids are treated the same. Children of ministers and bureaucrats don't get greater privileges," said Singh.
Beyond the growing ranks of well-heeled local families, non-resident Indians who have either returned home after long stints abroad, or those still in the UK or Middle East wanting their children to connect to their roots, are also a significant market for these schools, says Pascoe.
Sixty per cent of Harrow's staff in Bengaluru are international and, like the others, it has imported its unique traditions to its Bengaluru campus: teachers are called Beaks, and students wear the traditional Harrow hats and uniform and take part in The Long Ducker - a cross-country race that happens across its schools globally. There is also a house system - a hallmark of traditional British education.
These quintessentially parochial quirks are blended with local customs such as singing the Indian national anthem every morning or celebrating Ganesh Chaturthi, a major Hindu festival.
While India's growing economic credentials and burgeoning population of newly minted millionaires are a natural tailwind for expansion, this growth is partly being driven by a slowdown in China.
Much of the expansion of British public schools abroad in the past decade was driven by China and Hong Kong - half of the 151 satellite campuses operated by 50 UK schools are situated in these countries.
But that growth has slowed following changes in regulation, and "increased scrutiny, and even resistance, from national governments", according to a 2025 study by the UK-based Private Education Policy Forum (PEPF, external) think tank.
A new 2024 Chinese law that required schools to integrate patriotic education into all subjects further challenged expansion and even led to planned campuses being cancelled, prompting these schools to consider other locations like India and Vietnam, according to PEPF.
Moreover, in the 2024 Autumn Budget, Britain introduced a 20% VAT on private school fees. Naomi Atkins, founding principal at Bedford School Mohali, says this has forced many private schools to look overseas.
"They are in a desperate situation. Even those that hadn't previously looked for international expansion are now suddenly active in India," she told the BBC.
But India has not been an easy market, she admits.
Most of these schools are set up in partnership with local investors or operators.
While in the past schools in other countries might have been able to do deals at 10% of revenue - the fee that they would charge the local partner-investor - margins in India may have shrunk to as low as 1% in some cases, says Atikins.
There has also been some over-estimation of the size of the market, she says.
Even though India has nearly 250 million children enrolled in schools, English education is deeply entrenched in the country and competition from local players is much more intense compared with other non-English speaking countries like China, Korea or Vietnam.
India's per capita income is also far lower and the high price-points of the British schools - which can charge up to £15,000 or more for full boarding - can limit growth.
"I've worked in Indonesia, Malaysia and China but Indians are much more price-sensitive - they like a bargain," says Atkins.
That is why Bedford Mohali has set its fees at roughly half those charged by other British schools.
Between 2011-12 and 2022-23, the satellite campuses of British schools generated £152.4m in profit, according to PEPF, and this profit has grown substantially over the years.
But in India, it appears growth is likely to be slow and steady rather than explosive.
The country's old colonial roots and new money afford the legacy institutions a significant business opportunity, but it is unlikely to be big enough to offset the loss of the Chinese market, at least immediately.

Swiss Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland
A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria has been medically evacuated to Switzerland with her husband
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria was medically evacuated to Switzerland with her husband Monday, officials said, as Nigerian authorities continued monitoring 52 people who had been in contact with her.
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Pate said the woman, the country’s first case in the current outbreak, left the capital, Abuja, early Monday with his approval. Her condition had improved significantly, and she was stable, conscious and able to communicate, he said.
“This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place,” Pate wrote on X. Her husband, a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria, has shown no symptoms.
The World Health Organization’s regional director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, said the evacuation was arranged because the couple are Swiss citizens and that Nigerian medical teams had stabilized the woman after treating her through the acute phase of the illness.
Switzerland will take over her care and monitor her husband, while Nigeria will continue following 52 other contacts, Janabi said.
“With the evacuation of the patient and her husband, Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases,” he said, stressing that vigilance remained critical.
Pate said containment measures remained in place and urged Nigerians to remain vigilant.
The woman tested positive after returning to Abuja from Uganda. Nigerian authorities said Friday they had yet to establish how she contracted the virus.
Switzerland’s foreign ministry told The Associated Press that she had not visited Congo and was believed to have been infected while traveling to Uganda with her husband.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had both traveled through Uganda’s Entebbe International Airport on Oct. 3. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but later declared itself free of the virus.
Kenya has recorded nine cases, including two deaths, since confirming its first case earlier this month.
The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened longstanding fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus.
The latest figures from Congo’s health ministry show more than 9,900 cases, including more than 4,800 deaths, since the outbreak began in May.
The WHO has said the outbreak is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is on track to surpass the death toll of the deadliest: West Africa’s 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed 11,000 people. Nigeria was among the countries affected, recording 20 cases before its outbreak was declared over after three months.

Unveiled at CES 2026, the TDM Neo is a pair of on-ear headphones that transform into a Bluetooth speaker. It caught the imagination of the attending media, won a handful of awards, and inspired countless column inches.
Given the current state of the portable audio industry, it's easy to understand why. Most designs seem to revolve around incremental updates and new colorways rather than genuine technical innovation. Neo is an exciting alternative, and it’s little wonder the startup brand went on to smash its Kickstarter targets.
I’ve spent the past couple of weeks listening to the headphones and Bluetooth speaker, and have lost count of the number of times I’ve showed off the clever twist-and-fold mechanism to friends. But has TDM managed to produce a genuine tech twofer, or designed a novelty product that gives you the worst of both worlds?
Twist and Shout
The twist-and-fold mechanism on the Neo is clever and addictive. Rotate the ear cups around the cushioned but flexible headband, bring them together, and strong magnets snap everything firmly in place. Once connected, the headphone drivers disable, and the outward-facing Bluetooth speakers kick in. Twist them apart and you've got your headphones back.
It’s innovative, and the engineering is impressive. Once in speaker mode, the two rubber TDM logos sit closely together and form a protective base, while the asymmetrical twisted headband cocoons the ear cups together. It works well—it never once popped open accidentally. The action is smooth, the connection reassuringly solid, and switching between modes works exactly as intended.
The Neo has four 40-mm drivers—two for the headphones and two for the speakers. The outward-facing speakers are each rated at 5 watts (for a total of 10). Ten watts is not a lot for a modern Bluetooth speaker, but wattage doesn't automatically tell you how loud or good a speaker will sound, especially in the current age of digital signal processing. The highly regarded $55 JBL Go 5 has just 4.5 watts of output, for instance.

Trump told reporters on Oct. 16 that neither he nor Musk were responsible for the decision to slow down SpaceX services in Ukraine. Writing on X, Musk said (archived) the "US military and ultimately POTUS" were responsible for the secure Starshield system and that the commercial Starlink product could not be used for "offensive military action."
Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 14, 2026
Snopes could not independently verify Reuters', The Telegraph's or The Wall Street Journal's stories because they relied on anonymous sources.
When asked about the reports, the White House referred us to Trump's Oct. 16 comments. A Pentagon spokesperson said via email, "There has been no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
Considering the fact that Trump and members of his cabinet publicly and repeatedly denied having given the order to slow down Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine, in direct opposition to Reuters', The Telegraph's and The Wall Street Journal's reports, we cannot give this claim a rating.
On Oct. 24, Zelenskyy said (archived) on X that Starlink and Starshield speeds were "where they need to be."
SpaceX did not return a request for comment on who ordered the slowdown of Starlink and/or Starshield services in Ukraine on or around Oct. 14 or on why this occurred.
Starlink is a satellite internet service. Using SpaceX's rockets, the company has sent more than 11,000 of its own satellites into low-earth orbit. The satellites communicate with each other and Starlink terminals on Earth to connect customers to the internet. Starshield is similar, but is designed for government use.
Ukraine has used Starlink terminals since February 2022. The New York Times reported in July 2023 that artillery teams, drone commanders and pilots could watch drone footage simultaneously using a Starlink connection, which allowed them to find and hit targets faster.
What happened to SpaceX services in Ukraine?
On Oct. 16, Beskrestnov said that SpaceX had "implemented a speed limit for Starlink terminals while in motion" of 100 mph when those terminals were using the military-grade Starshield network that the company supplies to governments. The restrictions meant that if a terminal moved faster than 100 mph, its internet connection would cut out.
The Associated Press, which interviewed Beskrestnov after the speed limitation came into force, said such a restriction posed a problem for Ukrainian drones, which frequently travel at speeds faster than 100 mph.
For example, the Assocated Press reported that Russian Shahed-class drones could fly at more than 250 mph. Being restricted to 100 mph meant Ukrainian drones could not chase down or intercept Shahed-class drones and were in turn more vulnerable to Russian offenses. (Shahed is the name of an Iranian-designed drone that Russia frequently uses for attacks inside Ukraine.)
On Oct. 16, Zelenskyy told reporters (archived) in Brussels that the Ukrainian military uses Starlink to "intercept jet-powered 'shaheds'" as well as for "mid-range strikes against enemy military targets in our temporarily occupied territories." He added that troops also "receive food and water delivered by drones using Starlink."
That same day, Zelenskyy said speed restrictions had not been fully lifted. It is not clear exactly how long the restrictions have been in place.
On Oct. 17, Zelenskyy reportedly told journalists that Ukraine had driven Starlink terminals at speeds higher than 100 mph outside Ukraine and those terminals had continued to receive a connection, suggesting the speed restrictions affecting the country's troops were deliberate and only applied in Ukraine.
Trump, US officials said they had 'nothing to do' with SpaceX service slowdown
Speaking during NBC's "Meet the Press" on Oct. 18, Zelenskyy blamed the Starlink and Starshield speed restriction on the U.S. government and SpaceX. He said (time code 21:25), "It was the message from American government to limit this bit, and, technically, SpaceX did it."
Zelenskyy made this claim despite Trump saying of the decision two days earlier (time code 11:21), "I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," referring to Musk.
Trump did not elaborate on how SpaceX might have suddenly placed limits on Starlink or Starshield speeds in Ukraine without the knowledge of himself, Musk or another decision maker.
Also on Oct. 18, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any United States involvement in slowing down Starlink in Ukraine. He said (time code 00:42), "We had nothing to do with it. I don't, I don't — The United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down."
Rubio also repeated Trump's Oct. 16 suggestion that the slowdown somehow occurred without a major decision maker, saying, "It sort of happened."
The Secretary of State also claimed Ukraine does not have access to Starshield, SpaceX's secure network for government entities. This is at odds with Beskrestnov's Oct. 14 statement that said restrictions applied to Starlink terminals on the Starshield network. On Oct. 19, Rubio told journalists in Uzbekistan that Ukraine had "benefited" from Starshield, though did not elaborate on how.
Snopes asked Beskrestnov to clarify whether Ukraine had access to Starshield. We await replies to our queries. The State Department referred us to Rubio's Oct. 19 remarks.
In response to a request from Ukraine's former Minister of Defence Mykhailo Fedorov to have speed restrictions on Starshield lifted, Musk wrote on X:
Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.
If Beskrestnov is correct that the October speed restrictions applied to the Starshield network, Musk's statement would likely place the responsibility for any changes with Trump or the U.S. government as the owner of the system. Trump and the Pentagon both denied having made changes to capabilities they provided to Ukraine.
On Oct. 24, Musk wrote on X (archived) that Ukraine had "violated" Starlink's terms of service by using it for "offensive drone strikes to kill people." Musk appeared to suggest that SpaceX had restricted service in Ukraine in order to close a "loophole" that had allowed it to use the civilian satellite internet for offensive strikes.
Musk claimed Zelenskyy had admitted in an Oct. 16 X post to using Starlink for offensive strikes. Zelenskyy wrote at the time that Ukraine used Starlink for "for mid-range strikes against enemy military targets in our temporarily occupied territories."
Musk's Oct. 24 post appeared to suggest SpaceX made the decision to restrict Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine. He did not clarify whether he, as the company's CEO, had given the green light for that decision.
In response to Musk's post, Beskrestnov wrote on Facebook (archived) that Ukraine could not use Starlink for strikes within Russia because the service does not work in that country, appearing to suggest that Ukraine had not broken any terms of service.
Starlink troubles come at unsettled time for US-Ukraine relations
The sudden restrictions on SpaceX services came amid tensions between Ukraine and the United States. During an Oct. 15 Newsmax interview, Trump said he found Zelenskyy "more difficult to deal with than Putin" and appeared to repeat an earlier call for elections in Ukraine to replace its president.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy told British broadcast journalist Piers Morgan on Oct. 14 that he felt "betrayed" by Trump after the Starlink speed restrictions. He said he believed this was deliberate act by SpaceX and the U.S. that, he added, resulted in Ukrainian lives being lost.
Additionally, on Oct. 18, Zelenskyy told NBC's "Meet the Press" that intelligence sharing from the United States to Ukraine had been "blocked for some period of time" but that U.S. officials had "de-blocked" it.
The next day, Zelensky posted on X that he had "no early warning from our partners" before Russian strikes on Kyiv and other regions overnight. He added in a separate post that units using Starlink or Starshield services still did not work at speeds above 100 mph "in various sectors of the front."
Rubio said on Oct. 19 that the U.S. has never stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, a claim repeated in the Pentagon spokesperson's statement to Snopes.

Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
- Published
A magnitude seven earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens of others, according to Chinese state media reports.
The centre of the quake hit Baqên County in the Nagqu region as on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau.
The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa.
Authorities have declared an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 32 others have also been injured.
Power has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, local reports said.
Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas.
Strong tremors were also felt in the cities of Qamdo and Nyingchi in Tibet.
Videos on social media show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark, although these have not been independently verified.
The region is prone to devastating seismic activity.
In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China.
Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing.
Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China.
With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): About 30 medical college professors in five government medical colleges are about to retire. It will create a vacuum in teaching and treatment in the hospitals attached to their respective government medical colleges.
There are 5,444 sanctioned posts of doctors in government hospitals and 3,571 posts are still vacant.
As per Gandhi Medical College, Bhopal, Dr RK Singh (cardiology) and Dr Rajiv Gupta (cardiologist) are retiring in December this year. Similarly, Dr Anna Alex, Dr Aruna Kumar, Dr Rekha Wadwani, Dr Arvind Rai of GMC and Dr Navneet Saxena, dean of Jabalpur Medical College, are retiring in 2027. Dr Kavita Singh, GMC dean, is retiring in January 2028.
Dr Ajay Sharma, professor of cardiology at GMC, said, “In the cardiology department, Dr RK Singh and Dr Rajiv Gupta are retiring in December this year. On the retirement of Dr RK Singh and Dr Rajiv Gupta, we will only be left in the department, leading to the risk of losing recognition of DM level course, as it takes time in recruitment. ”
Dr Rakesh Malviya, Medical Teachers Association president, said, “ For the 2026-27 academic year, medical teachers (including Professors, Associate Professors, and Assistant Professors) born between April 1961 and March 1962 are reaching the age of 65 and are scheduled for superannuation.
Anyone born between January 1, 1962, and December 31, 1962, is scheduled to retire in the corresponding month of 2027.”
No DPC done for promotion, clearing the way for recruitment
Despite letters from the General Administration Department and Directorate of Medical Education sent to government medical colleges to hold departmental promotion committee meetings, no headway has been made.

Sultanpur (UP), Oct 26: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi was acquitted by a special MP-MLA court here on Monday in a defamation case related to his remarks against then BJP president Amit Shah in 2018.
Gandhi, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha and Raebareli MP, appeared before the court for the pronouncement of the verdict.
Plaintiff Vijay Mishra's lawyer Santosh Pandey said Gandhi has been acquitted by the court.
Congress workers celebrated the verdict outside the court complex with beating of drums and distributing sweets among themselves and chanting "Satyamev Jayate" (truth alone triumphs) as Gandhi emerged from the premises after his acquittal.
The matter was being heard in the court of Special Judge for MP-MLA cases Shubham Verma.
After the verdict, Mishra's counsel Pandey said the court had accepted the CD he had submitted as evidence. He added that he intended to challenge the matter.
"The court held that the statement was not defamatory and that my client, Vijay Mishra ji, is not the aggrieved person. So, I respect the court's order. I will take copy of it and study it and file it in appellate court after consulting my client," Pandey told PTI Vidoes.
Mishra said, "Gandhi has been acquitted in light of insufficient evidence. We will take the order copy, study it and then proceed for appeal in court according to the counsel we get".
A lawyer from Congress's legal team, who was present in Sultanpur, told PTI: "We were convinced that the case was filed less on merit and more due to extraneous considerations. That is why we were convinced the case would be decided in our favour."
Gandhi arrived at Lucknow's Chaudhary Charan Singh International Airport this morning. Hundreds of Congress workers and local party leaders had gathered at the airport to welcome the Raebareli MP.
Some vehicles trailing Gandhi's convoy had piled up on the Purvanchal Expressway while the motorcade was on its way to the court in Sultanpur from Lucknow.
Around six vehicles linked to Congress workers from Amethi were involved in the collision but none suffered serious injuries, a police official said.
Security arrangements were strengthened in Sultanpur, particularly around the court complex, in view of the proceedings, police officials said.
The case relates to the remarks made by Gandhi against Shah at a rally in Bengaluru ahead of the 2018 Karnataka Assembly elections.
Mishra, a local BJP politician and former chairman of the District Cooperative Bank in Sultanpur, filed the defamation complaint against Gandhi on August 4, 2018.
Gandhi appeared before the court in 2023 and secured bail. The court had earlier fixed October 13 for pronouncing its verdict, which was subsequently scheduled for October 26.

France has released its Global Health Strategy for 2023-2027, in Lyon today, in the presence of three French Ministers, the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, the Minister of Health and Prevention, the Minister of Higher Education and Research, and WHO’s Director-General.
As a lead player for shaping global health policies, France has called on national and international stakeholders to support building a new global health architecture towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and in particular SDG3, focused on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all, at all ages.
The new Health Strategy aims to help reduce health inequalities and strengthen the One Health approach to better prevent and prepare for future global health emergencies. It urges the global community to address the health consequences of climate change and the environmental impact on health systems.
To underscore WHO’s and France strong collaboration and in recognition of France’s pivotal global health role, Dr Tedros travelled to France to join the launch event.
“France was a founding member of WHO in 1948 and has been a strong friend to WHO throughout the 75 years since then,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health, and the new Global Health Strategy will enhance that role. It aligns well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, empower and perform for health.”
France shares key health priorities with WHO, adopting a crosscutting approach and prioritizing universal health coverage (UHC) as part of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. France also provides support for transformative initiatives at WHO such as the WHO Academy and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) which the Ministers visited today.
Dr Tedros addressed the audiences at the Academy and IARC together with Ms Catherine Colonna, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention, and Ms Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research.
"The World Health Organization, whose 74th anniversary we are celebrating today, must continue to play a central and driving role,” said Ms Catherine Colonna, the French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “France will continue to support the WHO and its ambitious governance and financing reforms."
"France is also committed alongside the WHO Academy through several partnership with universities, research institutes, and public health institutions," remarked Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research. "Our goal is to enrich the learners' experience through a diversified training portfolio within the Academy."
"The launch of this Global Health Strategy is the perfect opportunity to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the WHO. The Organization plays a central role in global health, and we must continue to support it," said Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention. "This is why, I am announcing today, France is keen to host, in the first quarter of 2024, in partnership with the WHO, the first international financing conference for the fight against meningitis."
The 2023-2027 French Strategy for Global Health is the fruit of collaboration involving a wide range of French actors: public agencies, civil society organizations, higher education and research organizations, scientific institutions, foundations, organizations of human, animal and environmental health specialists, local government bodies and the private sector. They will all be represented within a monitoring committee to track the Strategy’s implementation and progress.
From left to right: Minister of Health and Prevention H.E. Aurélien Rousseau, WHO’s Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs H.E. Catherine Colonna, and Minister of Higher Education and Research, H.E. Sylvie Retailleau.

Ray-Ban heir Leonardo Del Vecchio seeks to buy Italian newspaper critical of him, owners reject offer
The publication’s seven founding shareholders, including editor-in-chief Marco Travaglio, said that they had no intention of selling.
The majority shareholders of Italian newspaper Il Fatto Quotidiano on Monday rejected a takeover proposal from Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio, heir to the founder of Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica, amid a long-running public dispute between the billionaire and the publication.
Del Vecchio, 31, had sought permission to conduct due diligence before proceeding with a voluntary offer to take Societa Editoriale Il Fatto (SEIF), the Milan-listed parent company of the newspaper, private, Reuters reported.
The publication’s seven founding shareholders, including editor-in-chief Marco Travaglio, said in a statement on Sunday night that they had no intention of selling. Together, they hold a majority stake in the company.
Del Vecchio says he wants to protect editorial independence
The proposed acquisition comes amid repeated clashes between Del Vecchio and Il Fatto Quotidiano over its reporting. On X on October 22, Del Vecchio accused the newspaper of running a smear campaign against him and used derogatory language to describe its journalists.
On Monday, he said his interest was in improving the publication’s financial position while preserving its reputation for independent journalism and investigative reporting.
He argued that the newspaper’s willingness to publish critical coverage was something he wanted to retain, adding that his proposal was intended to help secure its future rather than influence its editorial stance.
SEIF had a market value of approximately 5.5 million euros ($6.16 million) at Friday’s close. Its shares rose 17.3% by 1216 GMT on Monday.
Ray-Ban heir has existing Italian media interests
Del Vecchio has already established a presence in Italy’s media industry through his holding company, LMDV, which is facing debt pressures.
His interests include a 30% stake in Il Giornale, a newspaper previously owned by the Berlusconi family, and ownership of the QN network of regional newspapers.
The proposed purchase of Il Fatto Quotidiano would have expanded his media portfolio, but the founding shareholders’ refusal to sell has stalled the initiative.
Inheritance battle adds to billionaire’s public profile
Del Vecchio remains embroiled in a dispute over control of Delfin, the family holding company, following an inheritance battle. He has also clashed with EssilorLuxottica chief executive Francesco Milleri.
The businessman has attracted attention beyond corporate affairs. Earlier this month, he appeared on the Pulp podcast, hosted by a rapper and a YouTuber, where he discussed past problems with drug addiction and made claims about his sexual history.

The Indian Institute of Technology Bombay on Friday said its researchers have developed a low-cost device that can screen for anaemia and sickle cell disease using a drop of blood.
A research team from the Department of Chemical Engineering, led by Mahesh Tirumkudulu, has developed a simple, low-cost point-of-care approach that uses the length of a blood smear (the distance that a drop of blood spreads across a glass slide) to detect anaemia, and detect and monitor treatment for sickle cell disease. IIT Bombay said.
Prof Tirumkudulu's team built their own automated device to have a uniform method of creating a smear. Under these controlled conditions, the researchers observed that blood from different people gives different smear lengths, and this difference holds useful information.
Prof. Tirumkudulu explained that more viscous blood spreads less easily and, therefore, produces a shorter and thicker smear under the same conditions.
Once the team confirmed that the method could sense small differences in blood viscosity, they decided to investigate whether those differences could help identify disease. It was found that anaemia lowers red blood cell concentration and haemoglobin, while sickle cell disease makes red blood cells rigid.
The researchers said their patented automated smearing device can be manufactured cost-effectively. Also, the test itself requires only a pipette, glass slides, an inexpensive chemical, vials for the sickling treatment, and a ruler or imaging device to measure smear length, they added.
"This makes our technique particularly useful in places where conventional diagnostic laboratories are difficult to access, and it doesn't require any special expertise to use," said Dr. Mahrukh Mir, a former PhD scholar in Prof Tirumkudulu's lab, and the first author of the study.
The researchers pointed out that blood viscosity cutoffs vary for various groups of people because certain genetic differences affect how blood reacts when oxygen levels drop.
Also, the anaemia test could miss identifying some patients when the usual link between viscosity and anaemia does not hold, such as in a rare condition called hyperviscosity syndrome, where blood plasma is unusually thick.
Currently, the technology is licensed to Rheoheme Private Limited, an IIT Bombay startup, and the team is now working with the National Institute for Research in Tribal Health, Jabalpur, in Madhya Pradesh and All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Nagpur, toward regulatory approval, while exploring extending the device to measure clotting time and glucose levels.
"Our initial aim was to understand the physics of spreading blood drop, and that led to the medical applications," added Prof Tirumkudulu.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Leaders in the US Space Force would like to have a new spaceport up and running in four years, adding a third heavy-lift launch site to relieve pressure from bases in Florida and California that have shot rockets into orbit for nearly 70 years.
The obvious problem with that ambition is 2030 is four years away, and Pentagon officials have not determined where the new spaceport should go or how to acquire land for it.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink first mentioned the service’s search for a third launch base in May. A congressionally mandated study of the Space Force’s launch infrastructure identified the need for “another site that’s capable of heavy and super heavy launch capability,” Meink said in a House Armed Services Committee hearing.
The Trump administration released a space transportation policy in August that endorsed the construction of more launch and reentry sites for commercial and military missions. This week, the Space Force general responsible for procuring launch services for the military laid out an “aspirational” timeline for a new launch site.
“We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist,” said Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, head of Space Systems Command. “That is not an inconsequential demand to build a spaceport when you factor in orbital regimes, safety, access to commodities, the Americans that live near it. In many ways, it’s much like an airport, but even louder. So there’s a lot of consideration.”

Adinath Kothare has shared a behind-the-scenes look at the physical and prosthetic transformation he underwent to portray two contrasting characters in Nayyi Navelli. The actor revealed that transitioning from Raja Awasthi, a wholesome family man, to Ravan, a character defined by pride, greed and tyranny, was one of the most challenging experiences of his career.
Adinath Kothare on his physical and prosthetic transformation for Nayyi Navelli: “Going from Raja Awasthi to Ravan has been the most challenging, painful, yet deeply rewarding experience”
Directed by M. Balaji and produced by Aanand L. Blending fantasy and comedy, the film continues its theatrical run into its third week.

This insane transformation truly took a village. A huge shoutout to the incredible teams who made it happen. A tight hug and endless gratitude to my amazing co-actors for their constant support and motivation: @yamigautam @anurag.thakurrr @sunita_rajwar @suneelshine @susmita_mukherjeeofficial @mitavasisht @kullubaaazi @pratiekpachori and the entire Awasthi family! I am in absolute awe of our captain, @directormbalaji for making this wild circus of fantasy and comedy come alive so beautifully! Endless gratitude to my visionary producers @aanandlrai & #himanshusharma, and the magician casting director, @castingchhabra for believing I could pull this off. Thank you for the overwhelming love, everyone! Nayyi Navelli is now successfully running in its 3rd week at the Box Office!”

The transformation required Adinath to portray two characters with contrasting appearances and personalities. While Raja Awasthi represents a caring family man, Ravan embodies pride, greed and tyranny. The shift called for physical preparation, prosthetic work and coordination between the makeup, costume and other production teams.
In his post, the actor acknowledged the contribution of the crew, his co-stars, director M. Balaji, producers Aanand L. Rai and Himanshu Sharma, and casting director Mukesh Chhabra. His note highlighted the collaborative effort behind the transformation and the support he received throughout the process.
As Nayyi Navelli continues its theatrical run, Adinath's behind-the-scenes video offers a closer look at the preparation involved in bringing his two contrasting characters to the screen.

Thousands of observers expected at polling places to monitor the vote on US election day
A sprawling election protection effort involves training observers to look out for any interference or ICE presence during the midterms
Democrats and outside watchdogs are planning a massive presence at the polls on US election day driven by concerns that US President Donald Trump will further leverage the vast resources of the federal government to interfere with a midterm that could hobble his final two years in office.
They will not be the only ones there. A sprawling election protection effort on the left that is expected to deploy tens of thousands of monitors will be met by the largest-ever monitoring programme by the Justice Department and still more observers from Republican-aligned groups. The result could be unlike anything seen at the polls in modern times.
The effort among Democratic and charity groups includes training volunteers to stand watch outside polling places and report activities they consider concerning. The network includes traditional government watchdogs such as Common Cause and the American Civil Liberties Union as well as a flood of volunteers assembled by state Democratic parties, congressional leaders, national activist groups and organisations focused on protecting democracy.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”

“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.

Actress Vidya Malavade has opened up about how she deals with scam calls and the precautions she takes to protect her personal information. The actor, who plays the lead role in Story TV’s Scam 2024 – The Digital Arrest Story, said she disconnects calls as soon as she suspects something is amiss. She also recalled a recent incident at a hotel that prompted her to reconsider handing over her Aadhaar card as identification.
Scam 2024 actress Vidya Malavade reveals how she identifies fraud calls; shares why she chose passport over Aadhaar card
Recalling her experiences with fraudulent calls, Vidya said, “I have received a lot of scam calls, but I have always managed to identify them. Fortunately, I haven't had too many such incidents because the moment I sense that something isn't right, I disconnect the call. I also feel that speaking to someone over the phone for too long could put your personal details at risk. I had even heard that if you speak to someone on the phone for a long time, your voice can be cloned. So, the moment I feel that someone is asking for a password, PIN or any such information, that's it. I disconnect the call."
The actress also shared an experience from a recent hotel stay, when a co-star pointed out the personal information that could be exposed through her identification document. She explained, “Just last week, I was staying at a hotel as we were there for a performance. When they asked for ID proof, I was about to hand over my Aadhaar card, but my co-star immediately asked me, ‘Why are you giving your Aadhaar card?’ I hadn't even realised that it contained all my personal details. That's when I handed over my passport instead.”
Vidya’s experiences connect with the subject of her latest series, which explores digital fraud and the methods scammers use to manipulate their victims. Reflecting on playing Priya Sharma, a working professional whose life changes after she falls victim to a digital arrest scam, the actress spoke about how the story affected her.
“I have played women who fight on a field, as the last line of defence. What frightened me most while playing Priya was realising she could be any of us. Our parents. Our neighbours. Priya is educated, she is careful, she does everything right, and she still loses everything in a single afternoon. Now think about people who aren't as familiar with the digital world. That is what makes this story matter. If it makes even one family pause before that one scam phone call, it has done more than most stories ever get to.”
Marking Vidya’s debut in the microdrama format, Scam 2024 – The Digital Arrest Story follows Priya as she becomes entangled in a larger network of deception involving fake identities, fear and intimidation. As she discovers that others have also been targeted, her journey takes an unexpected turn.
The series also features Pratik Sehajpal, Vineet Raina, Sandeep Aurora, Priyanshi Tripathi, Puja Jha, Ayushi Tyagi, Shital Tejwani, Ashok K Jha and Yogesh Pawar. Scam 2024 – The Digital Arrest Story is currently streaming exclusively on the Story TV app.

How AI is transforming hurricane forecasts
Hurricane forecasters are increasingly using artificial intelligence to make predictions — and they say the technology is rapidly transforming the field.
When the first hurricane of the Atlantic season formed this month, an AI model beat out traditional models at predicting where it would go.
In early October, Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm. Conventional forecasting models initially predicted it would head further west, toward southeastern Louisiana.
But Google DeepMind's artificial intelligence model called it right out of the gate: the hurricane was going to hit the western Florida Panhandle.
"Google DeepMind, in particular, has really proven itself the last few years as the gold standard model," says Michael Lowry, a longtime meteorologist and hurricane expert in Miami, who has previously advised both the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the National Hurricane Center (NHC).
"That model has been, by far and away, the best performing computer model that we've ever seen. Period."
A different kind of model
The National Hurricane Center first started incorporating the Google DeepMind model into its official forecasts last year.
By the end of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, it was already one of the best at predicting a storm's path and strength, says Brian McNoldy, a hurricane researcher for the University of Miami.
Usually, new models take years to refine after first being introduced.
"It's something we're not used to – to have a model, the new kid on the block, very quickly becoming the best model out there," McNoldy says. "This pretty much came out of the gate in first place, and that's a pretty impressive feat."
Traditional physics-based hurricane models use real-time atmospheric data, like temperature, humidity, pressure and wind shear, as measured by satellites and aircraft. Then they use complicated equations to predict what path a storm might travel and how strong it could get.
An AI model operates very differently: it relies more on history. It identifies patterns by analyzing thousands of past storms along with atmospheric data.
"The AI models don't really know anything about the atmosphere other than the current picture," Lowry says. "Beyond that, it's not leaning on the governing equations of the atmosphere, the physics, to make predictions."
Most of the people designing and developing these models aren't even meteorologists, Lowry notes: "They're software engineers, and they're developing neural networks."
A "neural network" is a set of computer algorithms modeled on the human brain and trained to find patterns in massive amounts of data.
As a result, the models can seem like a "black box," Lowry says: "We don't know why they might get a forecast right. We also don't know why they might get a forecast wrong."
It can be unsettling for meteorologists to depend on a system they don't totally understand – especially during storms when millions of people might be relying on their forecasts.
"It makes us a little uncomfortable, because we like to know why you're getting the right answer," McNoldy says. "And I feel like we don't – or at least I don't know why."
Not all AI models have performed well, though. There are lots of unproven weather forecasting AI models out there, Lowry says.
The two that have so far proven to be the most accurate, despite some pitfalls, are the models developed by Google DeepMind and by the U.K.-based European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).
Relying on a "blend" of models
Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center use several proven models – both AI and traditional – when putting together their official forecasts.
"Every storm has different forecast challenges," says NHC Director Michael Brennan. "That's why we take that consensus approach and use that blend of the best models."
And it's still humans who have to interpret the results of those models before deciding what to tell the public.
The NHC provides updates every six hours during active hurricanes. The models by themselves can sometimes show drastic changes from one update to the next. Forecasters have to translate those shifting predictions into clear guidance that people can act on.
"That's one thing that the human forecaster provides a lot of, is continuity," Brennan says. "We're using our expertise and our understanding to translate that hurricane forecast into the hazard space, and that's what people really need to pay attention to."
Scientists expect rapid advances
The Google DeepMind model still needs some work, Brennan says. While it topped other models in tracking the path of Isaias, it didn't do as well as the NHC's blended forecast in determining the intensity, or strength, of the storm.
Brennan's team gives regular feedback to Google DeepMind to help improve the model. Google didn't respond to questions from NPR for this story.
The "future of forecasting has always been changing," Brennan says. "It's never just one thing that's driving those improvements."
It wasn't that long ago when forecasters couldn't predict how strong a storm would be even within a couple of days, he notes. That changed, because of advances in prediction models and better data collected by satellites and planes.
"Errors are about half of what they were, say, at the time of [Hurricane] Katrina, in terms of intensity forecasting," Brennan says.
The exciting thing about AI, says meteorologist Michael Lowry, is how quickly it's improving. AI updates take only months or even weeks, unlike traditional models, which are updated annually at best.
"They are making advancements in skill and hurricane predictions over the course of a year that would have taken us 10 years, a decade or more, to make," Lowry says.
But even with AI coming in fast and strong, Lowry says he's not worried about artificial intelligence replacing people.
"For me, I don't feel some sort of existential crisis with AI," Lowry says. "If anything, I think it is a boon for our business."
