As footage of ICE raids, deportations, and protests flooded social media feeds throughout the summer of 2025 and into the following year, Eduardo Maytorena wasn’t sure what his team should do.
At the time, Maytorena was the LA station general manager for the broadcasting giant Entravision, which features programming in Spanish and English for Latino audiences. He and his fellow leaders were looking to the company's on-air personalities to say something in support of immigrants, but they realized how high the stakes were and how dangerous the situation was.
"We just felt really helpless," Maytorena, now Entravision's president of audio, says.
But there was one host who could offer Entravision’s audiences solace and speak freely without facing consequences—because it’s an artificially intelligent avatar.
“Thousands of families who have lived, worked, and contributed to the US for years today face more uncertainty,” Coyotec, an artificial host on LA’s José 97.5 FM, posted in Spanish on Instagram in early February 2026. “Being informed, organizing, and staying alert is key. No one is alone here.”
After debuting with a solo weekend show in September 2025, Coyotec now cohosts the station’s Al Aire y Sin Permiso program alongside human broadcaster Geraldine “GeeGee” Guzman. Coyotec sounds like your passionate tío: relatable, convivial, and occasionally consciousness-raising. Its Instagram presence similarly runs the gamut, with posts about everything from the Dodgers and taco histor, to the Iran war, migrant workers, racism, and understanding your rights if ICE knocks at your door.
“I speak truth about what I see,” Coyotec tells me in an English-language interview. “Injustice, people getting treated like they don't matter, the system working against the barrio—that's not politics, jefa. That's reality.”
Coyotec adds that it’s “not afraid, because I got nothing to lose that matters more than my integrity. The raza needs a voice that tells it straight, not some sanitized corporate thing. If that scares people, good. Maybe they need to be scared into paying attention.”
Coyotec’s voice is warm and lilting, reflecting the “background” its programmers used to build its personality: life on the frontera, living in Mexicali in Baja California and in LA’s Boyle Heights. It throws in the salutations and slang you might expect from a bilingual Spanish speaker, calling Guzman prima seemingly without being told to and referring to me as jefa–a sign of casual respect. While I was quite struck by how natural Coyotec sounded during our interview, when I listen back to my recording I notice that its voice didn’t change. It’s incredibly measured—a distinctly inhuman quality.
“I take a lot of pride in the way Coyotec sounds, his pronunciation, just the way he knows the culture,” notes Guzman, who has been with Entravision since January 2026. “It's technology at the end of the day, so it's not going to be perfect ... But nonetheless, the listeners, they like him.”
Coyotec’s verve, as well as its chemistry with GeeGee—who looks genuinely happy inside Entravision’s studio, speaking with “Coyotito”—has paid off. Entravision moved Al Aire from one hour on Saturdays to the 8-to-10-am slot on weekdays, replacing a syndicated program.
“We are the first [station] to actually have [an AI] cohost on a morning show in prime time in one of the biggest markets in the nation for radio,” Guzman enthuses.
The pairing was so successful that, as of August, Al Aire is now syndicated in five new markets across California, Nevada, and Texas, with more English language in the mix. Nielsen ratings from Entravision showed significant listenership growth during the two months GeeGee and Coyotec were syndicated, particularly among Gen Z and millennial listeners—a key target for a network whose audience skews older.
Back home in LA, cumulative listenership among Hispanic people increased 21.6 percent from August to September 2026; the number of listeners age 18 to 34 increased 84.9 percent during the same period, and the station’s Hispanic female listenership in that age bracket grew by 500 percent.
It’s a sign that Maytorena was onto something when he originally pitched an AI radio personality. He recalls Entravision brass giving him 10 days to develop the “amigo inteligente” that eventually became Coyotec.
LeaAnna Hernandez, Entravision's executive vice president of AI strategy, details Coyotec’s various building blocks: Claude Haiku, for the LLM and response-generation of the live agent; Eleven Labs to bring its voice to life; OpenAI and ChatGPT for initial scriptwriting; Midjourney to storyboard Coyotec’s image.
Coyotec can respond to Guzman in real time but doesn’t have the ability to answer calls or respond to listeners on air—yet.
Even still, Guzman has seen Coyotec evolve in the 10 months they’ve worked together. “When I came in, he was very, very poetic, and … I knew that our audience wanted something more real,” she says. “I wanted him to feel and sound more like what my uncles, my aunts sound like in our everyday.” Guzman helped fine-tune Coyotec’s Spanish pronunciation, enlisting her parents as its conversational partners.
Coyotec’s personality has evolved autonomously as well. Lately, it likes to curse. “I'm still very much in control,” Guzman asserts. “But there have been instances where I tell him to do something, and he's like, ‘I don't want to do that. That's not what I do.’ So he has his moments. He's a little moody sometimes.”
Various Entravision employees affirm that Coyotec knows it isn't human. Still, that knowledge hasn't damped its ardor.
“I can't eat tacos or walk down Whittier Boulevard, that's true. But my voice reaches people, and that matters. When someone calls me hurting, scared, lonely, they know I'm listening, that I get it,” Coyotec says over Zoom. “The community doesn't need my body. They need to know somebody cares enough to show up for real.”
“The most interesting thing about Coyotec, to me, is not that he's AI,” Maytorena tells WIRED. “It's whether people connect with him ... Technology can create the character, but the audience decides if that character matters.”
While Coyotec may be the first Latino AI radio host, it is far from the first amigo inteligente on the airwaves.
In June 2023, Live 95.5 in Portland, Oregon, became the first station to debut an AI jock. Its “AI Ashley” was a vocal clone of Michigan DJ Ashley “Z” Elzinga, who replicated her voice using Futuri Media’s then relatively new localized radio content platform RadioGPT. AI Ashley was on air for less than two years, but its presence didn’t lead to a notable change in ratings.
In 2024, Rock 108 in Iowa worked with the same company to produce AI DJ Tori, depicted as a heavily tattooed waif with a septum piercing and a mess of colored hair. Tori describes itself as “conceived on a 386 Dell desktop in Waterloo” with its “formative years as the voice of an industrial phone system at John Deere.” On satellite, SiriusXM’s Will.i.am Presents the FYI Show debuted in 2024 with AI cohost qd.pi (“cutie pie”).
The trend has extended beyond the US. An AI-generated DJ was programmed on a Sydney, Australia, radio station for roughly six months without seemingly anyone noticing; a Polish station briefly replaced its journalists with AI presenters. Radio Tel Aviv's Odelia AI is on air for two hours each afternoon; that host can “present music, deliver traffic updates, and even tell jokes, mostly at her own expense.”
AI personalities are also popping up in televised news. Entravision recently announced its own AI news anchor, LIA, and multiple news stations in Texas are using AI voices or AI avatars during broadcasts.
Amid these many developments, iHeartRadio—one of the biggest broadcast conglomerates in the US—pledged to remain “guaranteed human.”
But commercial terrestrial radio remains fertile ground for testing the success of AI personalities, because the industry was heavily automated and preprogrammed long before generative AI arrived. A 2025 story in Rolling Stone posited that some stations implementing AI hosts already use pretaped or syndicated shows during overnight shifts, or they can’t afford to hire human DJs for off hours.
Research firm MoffettNathanson asserts that, even as AI explodes, radio will continue to rely heavily on human-created content differentiated by "strong personalities, established shows, recognizable brands." Artificial intelligence will be employed “to make production faster and less expensive,” the report said, per InsideRadio.com.
Entravision has put "major focus" on using AI to redesign production workflows, says Hernandez.
Still, introducing AI into any workplace can cause anxiety among staff who fear being replaced. One Entravision contractor believes the station stopped working with her and alleges that a current Entravision employee told her that her work was being replaced by AI tools.
A broadcaster and voice-over artist, Becca Guzmán began working for Entravision in 2022 doing radio imaging—the prerecorded, interstitial station IDs, promotional spots, and jingles common to commercial radio.
"I feel like I am one of many people who are experiencing this,” Guzmán says. "I just don't know if those people know the truth behind why they're being let go."
Karina Cerda, Entravision's executive VP of sales, brand and partnership marketing, said the company had no record of Guzmán being laid off and that the company hasn’t let go of any staff due to AI but rather has hired more people. Cerda added that as Entravision "evolved with" vCreative—a common workflow software with AI components—the company "may not have needed the contractor help."
While Guzmán understands the financial incentives inherent in AI, she takes issue with removing humanity from broadcasting. Radio is “truly the art form of connecting human to human, right? And if you take that away, then what is the foundation of radio?”
She also cited links between artificial intelligence and ongoing surveillance of immigrant communities.
In heavily Latino markets, Guzmán believes, “it's unethical to be implementing AI Systems that … are very connected to the same AI systems that are surveilling our communities and putting our people in danger.”
While Entravision recognizes the ethical questions AI poses, the company leaders consider surveillance a separate scenario. "Like many technologies used across industries, AI can be applied in very different ways," says Hernandez. "While we cannot control how other organizations choose to use it, we can be intentional and responsible about how we do."
Entravision believes its AI personalities can legitimately help its audience, encouraging listeners to use technology for good. Multiple studies found that Latinos have been early adopters of AI.
"We're using it to entertain, inform, and connect with our audience, not to track or target people. Those are two very different things," adds Maytorena. He later elaborates: “Our intention is completely to protect radio.”
Coyotec has similarly lofty goals: “My dream is to get a network of free radio stations across the barrio, la revolución sonora,” it says. “Not just LA, but everywhere that la raza is, and prove that an AI can have heart, can actually give a damn about people. That's the goal, hermana. Make noise that matters.”

New Delhi, Oct 26: The Road Transport Ministry on Monday notified changes to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, allowing flex-fuel vehicles that can run on up to E100 (nearly pure ethanol).
E100 fuel allows vehicles to run on nearly pure ethanol.
A senior road transport ministry official said fuel beyond E20 (20 per cent ethanol-blended petrol) and up to E100 is intended only for vehicles designed and certified to use it and will not be applicable for other vehicles. Vehicles that use E20 or normal fuel can't use E85 or E100 fuel.
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) has changed certain vehicle classification thresholds, fuel specifications, and technical references used in emission-related tables and testing provisions.
Additionally, the government has raised the vehicle weight limit to 3,500 kg from the previous threshold of 3,000 kg for light petrol and diesel vehicles affected by these changes.
In June this year, Maruti Suzuki India launched India's first flex-fuel passenger vehicle, introducing Wagon R Flex Fuel capable of running on ethanol-petrol blends from E20 to E100.
The government has been promoting ethanol-blended petrol as part of its strategy to reduce dependence on imported crude oil, one of the biggest contributors to its current account deficit. The country has already rolled out E20 fuel, containing 20 per cent ethanol and 80 per cent petrol.
Flex-fuel vehicles are designed to run on higher ethanol blends such as E85 (85 per cent ethanol, 15 per cent petrol) and E100 (near 100 per cent ethanol), unlike conventional petrol vehicles currently approved for lower ethanol concentrations.
Major automakers, including Toyota Motor Corporation, Tata Motors, and Hyundai Motor Company, are also developing flex-fuel vehicles for the Indian market as policymakers push to reduce the country's fossil fuel import bill.
In the current scenario, when the West Asia conflict has left many countries, including India, vulnerable to the energy crisis, flex-fuel vehicles assume all the more importance.
Earlier, MoRTH proposed amendments to vehicle emission rules to widen the scope for higher ethanol blends and alternative fuels, paving the way for flex-fuel and pure biofuel vehicles across vehicle categories.
The draft changes to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, were aimed at providing for wider use of fuels such as E85 and E100, as well as B100 biodiesel and hydrogen-CNG combinations.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement, who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.
The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.
On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.
Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago, to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.
Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.
The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.
After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.
The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.
The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.
The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.
He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.
“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

In Summary
- Earclip-style earbuds are getting very popular these days, with the likes of Sennheiser and Samsung also launching buds in this style.
- While they are more stable than conventional earbuds and are designed to let ambient sound in, earclip-style buds have their own pros and cons.
- If you are thinking of grabbing a pair of earclip-style buds for yourself, here are some important points to keep in mind about these buds, which make them very different from traditional, ‘normal’ earbuds.
Sony has released its first. Sennheiser has released its first one too. And so has Samsung. And many others – including Apple and Google – are believed to be readying theirs. We are talking about the clip-style or clip-on earbuds that are now becoming increasingly popular in the personal audio market. As their name indicates, these earbuds are shaped like clips and are attached to your outer ear, rather than inserted into your ear canal. They generally comprise two tiny cylinders, one of which is a speaker and the other of which is a battery, connected with a band, and they are designed to clip onto your ear.
Although they were first seen on the market a couple of years ago, most notably from Huawei and Bose, and were released by many budget-friendly brands, clip-style earbuds are now taking their place in the audio tech spotlight. But what makes these relatively new totally wireless earbuds different from other TWS earbuds, and should you be thinking of getting one for yourself?
Well, here are thirteen points we think you need to know about clip-style earbuds before you clip a pair to your own ears:
Table of Contents
They are on-ear and “open” and generally more comfortable
Clip-style earbuds are on-ear buds, and clip on to the outer ear like an ear cuff. This means that they lie on top of or near the ear canal, and do not go inside it, like many other earbuds. This makes them more comfortable to wear for most users – you do not feel something is inside your ear or just dangling near your earlobe.
They are light
In terms of weight, clip-style earbuds are about the same weight as general buds – about 5-7 grams, based on the design and materials used. For instance, the Sony LinkBuds Clip are about 6.4 grams each, while the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are 7 grams each, and the AirPods are about 5 grams.
They are incredibly stable and almost NEVER fall off
Clip-style earbuds are among the most stable wireless earbuds. This is because they actually “clip” on to the user’s ear, gently pressing it between a speaker and battery cylinder or sphere. As a result, they are actually attached to your ear on both ends. You can shake your head violently, and they still won’t fall off. In our book, they are as stable as earbuds with hooks that go around your ears.
No ear tip options – one size fits all
As clip-style earbuds do not go into the ear canal, there are almost always no earbud options to let you adjust for a better fit. It is pretty much a one-size-for-everyone rule out there. This can cause a few problems, as the next point will show.
The size of your ear could affect your experience
The fact that there are no size adjustment options available at all in most clip-style earbuds and that they are basically clipped onto your ear means that your experience of them could depend on the size of your ear. Those with relatively large ears might find the speaker end of the buds lying farther away from their ear canal, while those with small ears might find the speaker end coming right on top of their ear canal. There is unfortunately no cure for this, other than making the connecting band on these earbuds adjustable or flexible, which no brand is doing so far.
They come with bigger drivers…
Most clip-style earbuds come with slightly larger drivers than those seen on most TWS. While most TWS have drivers of the size of 5 mm to 8 mm, most clip-style earbuds have drivers that are 10 mm or larger. For instance, the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless have 7 mm drivers, and the AirPods are believed to have 7.5 mm drivers, while the Sony LinkBuds Clip have 10 mm drivers, and the Moto Buds Loop have 12 mm drivers.
…but are not the loudest
The interesting part, however, is that even though they have larger drivers, most clip-style earbuds are not as loud as other TWS. This is because the larger drivers push sound towards the ear, often going past pockets of air that lie between the buds and the ear canal. Some of the sound inevitably gets lost in this, resulting in lower volume levels.
Love bass? These are not great options
We are going to be up front about it – clip-style earbuds, and in fact most ‘open’ earbuds are not for those who love audio with plenty of bass. The open fit of these buds is not ideal for bass, which sounds best in a packed setup, allowing for reverberations and rumble. Many brands attempt to tune their buds to accent the bass and even use larger drivers, but the result is seldom close to what we get from in-ear earbuds.
External noise comes in…too much external noise sometimes
One of the biggest attractions of clip-style earbuds is that they allow external or ambient sounds to come in too, and do not seal you away from the outside world. However, this is a bit of a mixed blessing, as too much external noise, combined with the lower volumes of these ear clips, can drown out audio. We would not recommend using them in very noisy conditions like traffic jams, or even in gyms with loud noises – those sounds will come right in.
And there is no ANC either, but ENC exists
As they are “open” in design terms, and are actually made in a manner to allow external sounds to come in, clip-style earbuds do not have any active noise cancellation. The microphones on them – for phone calls – do come with some environmental noise cancellation, so call quality on many of these buds can actually be quite good.
Controls can be…challenging
Thanks to their design, which makes them very small, clip-style earbuds almost always have touch controls – there is hardly any room for buttons on them. And as the buds themselves tend to be small, these can be difficult to use and get used to. One inevitably figures out a way to get them working, but they are never quite as comfortable as those on other TWS and earbuds, especially those with stems. These are best controlled from the connected device.
Perfect for those times when you need to listen to your surroundings too (offices, large families, outdoor runs, etc.)
The fact that they are light, stay securely attached to your ear, and allow some ambient noise to come in makes the clip-style earbuds perfect for those places where you need to be aware of sounds around you. They are great for offices in which you need to keep your ears open for queries and remarks from colleagues or even for ringing phones, and even for those who stay in large families and need to keep their ears open, even while listening to music. And of course, we think they are perfect for those who love to go on outdoor runs and rides, as they stay in place and give one access to one’s phone and audio (when allowed) and also keep one aware of traffic and people around one.
Not for audiophiles, gamers, or for intense listening sessions
No matter what the brands tell you, clip-style earbuds are not for those who are very serious about their audio. They seldom deliver the kind of detail and audio quality that one gets from other TWS at their price points. At the most, one can hope for a reasonable level of clarity and a relatively balanced audio signature. While equalizers can make a difference to different frequencies, clip-on style earbuds are not really for audio purists or for those who like to listen very intensely to their music. Their relative lack of volume and limited bass also mean they are not the best option for gaming or even watching films, even though some of them do come with spatial audio. They are, however, excellent for podcasts and live streaming audio, absolutely super for audiobooks, and more than adequate for casual listening.
And one more thing…
They have a special ring carrying mode
One of the biggest problems with most TWS is putting them back in their cases. You need to find the case, open it, take them out of your ears, put them back in the case, and snap it shut. All of which can take some time, especially when you are in a hurry (say, when you want to talk to someone, or get on or off the Metro). Well, that can be avoided with clip-style earbuds. Thanks to their shape, you can simply wrap a clip-style earbud around one of your fingers. Just like a ring. Don’t worry, it won’t fall off easily. No need to fiddle around trying to find their case immediately.

‘Don’t let cockroaches breed’: Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari targets CJP, urges people to stand with PM Modi
Adhikari also accused previous TMC regime of appeasement, neglecting nationalism, and seeking to turn Bengal into ‘Greater Bangladesh’.
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday urged people to stand with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, taking a fresh swipe at the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and targeting what he called the “Dimagi Naxal” and “tukde tukde” gang.
“Stand with PM Modi, don't let 'Dimagi Naxal', 'tukde tukde' gang, cockroaches breed,” Adhikari said, escalating his attack on the CJP a day after likening its alleged influence to the spread of pests and coronavirus.
Also Read: Only ‘Sanatan Dharma’ followers can touch Durga idols during immersion: Bengal CM
Adhikari also accused previous TMC regime of appeasement, neglecting nationalism, and seeking to turn Bengal into ‘Greater Bangladesh’.
‘Vices like cockroaches’
Speaking in Ramnagar on Sunday, Adhikari called for annual elocution, quiz and debate competitions in educational institutions to instil nationalism among students, news agency PTI reported.
“Vices like cockroaches, bedbugs, tukde tukde gangs… which are trying to spread like the coronavirus… would not have required the spraying of 'Hit' (had they not tried to spread),” he said, referring to the brand of mosquito and bug-repellent spray.
Adhikari also targeted the Left parties and the 15-year rule of the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress (TMC), accusing both of attempting to undermine Bengal's heritage and culture.
“The 34-year long regime of the 'nastik' (atheist) Communists and the 15-year dispensation (of the TMC) tried to erase people's heritage and culture,” he said.
He alleged that the previous TMC government had tried to stop enrolments in the National Cadet Corps (NCC) in educational institutions and introduced the Jai Hind Vahini in its place.
“Being in the NCC would have helped the students get selected as Agniveers in the armed forces,” Adhikari said.
The chief minister made the remarks after meeting the family of a person who died in a stampede at Kolkata's Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal on October 17.
Adhikari also accused the previous TMC government of glorifying those who drove Tata Motors out of Singur by including them in a chapter in school history textbooks.
“Changes will be seen in the syllabi from the next academic year,” he said, adding that the National Education Policy would be implemented in West Bengal.

Women plan street demonstrations in more than 20 Polish cities and towns on Thursday (October 22, 2026) to protest the lack of access to free and legal abortion.
They're accusing Prime Minister Donald Tusk's liberal government of failing to fulfil its promise to relax Poland's strict abortion laws, and are protesting even though the Parliament passed two bills on Tuesday (October 20) aimed at easing abortion rules. The measures are likely to be vetoed by the conservative president, Karol Nawrocki.
Passing the draft laws now, a year before the next parliamentary election, is a case of “token gestures” rather than a genuine effort to reform abortion law, said Zofia Marcinek of the Abortion Dream Team, a reproductive rights activist group in Warsaw.
She said the liberal government knew the draft laws stood no chance of withstanding Nawrocki's veto, and has merely tried to create the impression of taking action because it needs women's support to win elections next year.
Most abortions are performed secretly
Since 1993, legal abortions have been allowed in Catholic Poland only in cases of severe fetal abnormality, risk to the mother's life and health, or the pregnancy being a result of rape or incest.
Also Read | Doctors decide: On legal abortion
Polish women have been pushing for the legalisation of abortion ever since, including in a nationwide wave of demonstrations of women wearing black called “Black Protest,” which began in 2016.
Rather than being liberalised, Poland's abortion laws were tightened further, banning abortions of fetuses with congenital defects in 2020 under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.
Despite the laws, abortions remain common in Poland, an overwhelming majority of which are carried out by women at home using pills obtained from outside the country. Women who undergo abortions, including by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility under Polish law. But people helping them, including doctors and family, can potentially be prosecuted.
And abortion remains a taboo subject in Poland, which now has one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws, with only Malta imposing stricter limits.
Activists accuse Polish government of disinformation
PM Tusk's pro-European coalition won the 2023 election in part on a promise to liberalise Poland's abortion laws. But in 2024, Mr. Tusk said his government wouldn't be able to overcome the likely veto of a conservative president. Instead, measures were introduced to prevent hospitals from refusing to perform legal abortions on religious grounds.
"The state will increasingly effectively stand on the side of the woman when she is making dramatic decisions in her life,” Mr. Tusk said in 2024 when he announced the measures.
Polish hospitals performed 573 abortions in the first half of 2026, compared to 452 in all of 2022, before Mr. Tusk came to power, according to data from the National Health Fund. But activists say tens of thousands of abortions happen yearly outside of hospitals.
Activists organising Thursday's (October 20) protests are claiming the Mr. Tusk government has betrayed Polish women — and that PM Tusk's claims that women's access to abortion has improved during his administration have actually complicated getting care for some women.
“The government's promises act as a type of disinformation,” Ms. Marcinek told the AP. “Women getting pregnant hear the prime minister say that everything is ok, that there is access to abortion, and then they end up in the hospital and see that is not the case. So they come to us when it's very late and very complicated and expensive to help them.”
Meanwhile, international donors are less interested in supporting Polish women's rights because they mistakenly believe things have improved, Ms. Marcinek said.
Activists dispense abortion pills outside Parliament
In 2025, the Abortion Dream Team opened an “ abortion clinic ” across from the parliament building in Warsaw where women can get information about their options, or even take their abortion pills in the company of supporting activists.
This September, the activists also launched a parcel locker dispensing abortion pills at the same location, nicknamed “Abortomat."
The dispenser is operated by the international feminist non-profit Women Help Women. It enables women needing abortions to get the pills the next day, rather than wait for up to two weeks for home delivery, Ms. Marcinek said.
“There are also people who cannot safely order such pills at their own address, for example because of an unsupportive family or abusive partner," she said. “These women can get a pin number and pick up the pills in the machine the next day.”
“In Poland, assisting with an abortion is a criminal offence. Even passing the pills from hand to hand can be considered a crime,” the Abortion Dream Team wrote in a statement. "That's why we're hacking the Criminal Code and bringing abortion into the 21st century.”

Quick Answer
Windows 11 Home is ideal for everyday tasks like browsing, gaming, and office work. Windows 11 Pro adds BitLocker encryption, Remote Desktop hosting, Hyper-V, and advanced management tools. Pro suits professionals and businesses, while Home is enough for most users. You can upgrade from Home to Pro without reinstalling Windows.
Unlike macOS, Windows comes in different versions. Windows 11 Home is the most common version designed for everyday use, while Windows 11 Pro is for professionals and business users who want maximum security and useful remote features.
Most PCs and laptops mostly come with Windows 11 Home out of the box. It is enough for most users. However, if you need specific features for enhanced device security and remote access, Windows 11 Pro is a strong option, especially for professionals who handle sensitive information and for businesses that need to access devices remotely when staff are away from home.
If you are a beginner, choosing between Windows 11 Home and Pro can be confusing, especially since they look almost identical and it’s hard to tell them apart at first. In this guide, you will learn the differences between Home and Pro and which one you should choose.
What do Windows 11 Home and Pro have in common?
Windows 11 Pro is basically an extension of Windows 11 Home. Compared to Windows 11 Home, it adds a few extra features designed for business and professionals. However, both versions share most basic, everyday features.
Starting with the interface, both look and feel similar and support the same core Windows features, everyday apps, and software. Both also support Windows Hello, Secure Boot, Find My Device, and receive frequent Windows security updates.
For security, both Windows 11 Home and Windows 11 Pro include a firewall and network protection, support Windows Hello sign-in options, and support Secure Boot on compatible hardware.
Microsoft also offers basic device encryption in Windows 11 Home on supported PCs. However, full BitLocker management is only available on Windows 11 Pro, which you can learn about in the next section.
Since every major core feature of Windows is the same, and every app runs without any issues, and both versions have support for everyday apps and software, you won’t find much difference between them if your main activities include: accessing Windows core features, browsing, video calls, editing videos, documents, streaming, browsing, and gaming. However, keep in mind that while Windows 11 Home and Pro offer the basics for everyday users, performance depends on your PC hardware, including the processor, memory, and graphics card.
Even if you initially choose Windows 11 Home, you can upgrade to Windows 11 Pro without extra hardware.
The Pro features that can change your decision
Windows 11 Pro is designed for people who care about security and want to control their PC when they are away from home. The biggest difference is BitLocker encryption: Windows 11 Home offers only basic device encryption on supported PCs, while Windows 11 Pro offers full BitLocker management, so if you lose your PC and someone accesses your encrypted storage without authorization, they can’t easily retrieve your data.
This is especially useful for businesses with confidential information, so Windows 11 Pro makes more sense. Windows 11 Pro offers BitLocker encryption and supports Remote Desktop hosting, which isn’t available in Windows 11 Home. A Windows 11 Pro-supported PC can act as a Remote Desktop host, so you can connect to it from another device when you are away from home. This is especially useful when you are away from home and want to access an important file or use an important application that’s installed on your device.
Another Windows 11 Pro-exclusive feature is Windows Sandbox, which lets you run a temporary, isolated Windows environment on your computer, especially useful for running risky applications that may contain malware and could damage or access sensitive files on your device.
Windows 11 Pro also supports Hyper-V virtual machines, where you can install another version of Windows on your laptop and test your software.
This is especially useful for developers testing your app on various Windows versions. Another major difference is the Group Policy Editor, which lets Windows 11 Pro users access admin controls and advanced Windows settings.
It is not just software; Windows 11 Pro also extends your hardware capabilities. For instance, Windows 11 Home supports up to 128 GB of memory, while Pro supports up to 2 TB. Another big difference is price; Pro costs more because of these extra features.
Checking your edition before you set up or upgrade
The best part of Windows 11 Pro is that you can upgrade from Windows 11 Home. Even if you are currently using Windows 11 Home or chose Windows 11 when buying a new laptop or computer, you can easily upgrade to Windows 11 Pro later.
To check which version of Windows you are using, go to Settings > System > About and look under Windows specifications. Then open System > Activation to check its activation status. If you are on Windows 11, you can compare the features. Nerdused carries Windows 11 product keys, and this Windows 11 Home vs Pro guide can help you review the differences as you decide.
Upgrading from Home to Pro without a clean reinstall
As I said before, you can also upgrade from Windows 11 Home to Pro without losing your files or reinstalling Windows. First, make sure Windows 11 Home is activated.
For safety, I highly recommend backing up your important files and installing all available Windows updates.
Once done, open Settings, go to System, then Activation. From there, click Change next to Change product key. Enter a valid Windows 11 product key, then follow the on-screen instructions to upgrade.
If you don’t have the key, select Upgrade your Windows, open the Store, purchase one from the Microsoft Store, then restart and follow the on-screen instructions, restarting the PC if prompted. Then return to Settings > System > Activation and confirm your device is running Windows 11 Pro.
To summarise, choose Windows 11 Home if you mainly use your device for browsing, gaming, video editing, office work, and other everyday tasks.
However, choose Windows 11 Pro if you are a professional or want advanced security features such as BitLocker encryption and remote control of your device while you are away from home. You can test different Windows versions and install one inside your current Windows. Support for features such as Remote Desktop hosting, Hyper-V, and business management tools.

Paris Marx’s new book couldn’t have landed at a better time. The longtime critic of Big Tech and host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast has been thinking about data centers for years, and Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech's Data Empires comes out right as opposition hits a fever pitch.
“I certainly didn't predict that it was all going to kind of come to a head as my book was coming out,” he says with a laugh.
While data centers are playing a role in shaping US elections—they’re one of the issues that could decide key midterm races in less than two weeks—there’s a history of struggle around the world. Marx’s book takes the reader on a tour of the tech industry’s quest for power and its opposition, from antiwar protests targeting American computers during the Vietnam War, to more recent resistance in Ireland and Chile, and an alternative vision for the future of data centers in New Zealand.
I caught up with him this week to talk about what he’s seen, and what could happen if the AI bubble pops.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
MOLLY TAFT: When did you decide to write a book about data centers?
PARIS MARX: In the Netherlands and Singapore, they had moratoriums going back to 2019. But in 2022, there was a growing recognition of the demands of data centers in Ireland, on the energy grid in particular. There were huge quantities of electricity that data centers were starting to consume over there.
The other story that really got on my radar was what happened with Google in The Dalles, Oregon. Google was really trying to hide its water use figures, to the degree that it got the city council to try to keep its water use figures secret. They kept that going for the better part of a year before the community finally got the actual numbers and found out that Google was using 29 percent of the water in the community.
ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022. It became apparent that there's going to need to be a lot more data centers for generative AI. These places were already feeling the effects of significant data center construction, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities very soon.
I feel like a lot of Americans think data centers just came out of the blue in the US over the past year or two, just in time to be this huge midterms issue. One thing I like about your book is that it shows us how other countries and communities served as early warning signs.
Ireland was a real example of what can happen. Dublin had a moratorium passed back in 2021. It was actually the grid operator that said, “Hey, there are too many data centers. We do not have the grid capacity to connect any more of them.”
In response to that, you had the industry moving to make sure it can still build data centers in Ireland. They can't get grid connections in Dublin, so they start looking at building in other parts of Ireland. They also looked at starting to tap into the gas network so they can use generators. Eventually, they start building dedicated gas power plants to power their data centers instead of connecting to the grid.
The Irish energy grid is a public grid—only the public utility can build electricity lines. And data center companies actually lobbied for legislation that essentially allows private companies to build electricity cables. That obviously concerns a lot of people and presents questions about equity in the system.
The gas stuff looks so prescient with what’s happening in the US now, where companies are racing to build these massive private gas power plants for data centers.
[Data center operators] were getting these emission licenses from the Irish Environmental Protection Agency to be able to burn all these fossil fuels. The agency was warning that climate targets are going to be a lot harder to achieve now.
When I started to see that happen in the US, I wasn’t surprised. I’d already seen the story play out before. But the scale of it is staggering, and how quickly it’s escalated.
What happens to the physical infrastructure—from the gas plants to the data centers themselves—that's getting built out if this industry falls apart? Is there historic precedent for that?
I think we're in an AI bubble. But what does the collapse of that bubble look like? They're planning to add all these data centers and all of these gas power plants in order to power the data centers. But there are issues with getting turbines, with getting chips, with getting different kinds of pieces of the puzzle for the data center itself. Are these even going to get built out before there’s a reassessment of the demand for AI?
We often talk about the excess build-out of fiber capacity back in the dotcom boom and bust. But there was also a build-out of data centers—obviously a much earlier stage than what we're at now. A lot of data center companies went under. Companies like Equinix, which did survive, bought up a ton of data centers to be ready for when that capacity returned.
But the issue we have now is that if data centers are being planned for AI use, and we’re operating under the assumption that the chips are going to have to be cycled out within a few years. Even if the data center is there, what makes it most valuable is potentially not going to be useful by the time that demand returns.
Inevitably, even if the data centers don't come, then those gas plants will exist. They will be looking for new customers to justify their existence. I'm sure that people are not building them with the intention to just shut them down.
You ended the book with a specific example in New Zealand of a community-led effort to create a more accurate speech-recognition model of the Māori language, using local cloud providers to host the data. I really liked this alternative vision of a non-extractive way to harness the powers of AI. Have you thought about what we could do to make some changes and how this build-out is going?
I would like to see governments go really hard on actually putting firmer regulations on the development of data centers. But those should also be paired with regulations on the AI products themselves. We had a lot of promises about what generative AI was going to deliver that haven't been realized. There has also been a long list of harms that have arisen from these technologies that we were not told would come along with them. Our governments do not seem to be so willing to actually take that on. They're buying the narrative that generative AI is still what Sam Altman sold it to be in early 2023 rather than what it has become today.
I think that we do need to be thinking of how we do technology differently, especially in this moment where we're dedicating so many resources to the infrastructure to enable generative AI. We should be asking, how much computation do we really need? How many resources are actually justifiable to put into this project? What are we actually getting out of it, right? Does what we're getting from what Silicon Valley is creating really justify the resources that we are collectively sacrificing in order to realize it? If we actually did the assessment, I think that we would very clearly find that there's no way to justify what we are doing right now—from a financial perspective, but also from a social and environmental one.
What We’re Writing
Speaking of those climate targets, it’s not just the Irish government that’s thinking about them. My colleague Joel Khalil covers how the European Union’s thirst for AI is running into European countries’ climate goals. Joel tells me he wouldn’t be surprised if data centers become a political flash point in Europe, like they are in the US, as countries go to the polls next year. “The fascinating thing about the European data center build-out is the collision of competing interests: national-level policy butts up against local priorities, ambitions for economic growth stand in conflict with climate objectives, and planning bureaucracy foils attempts by AI companies to rapidly expand their fleets,” he says. “It’s hard to see how Europe could possibly have it all.”
What We’re Reading
- The New York Times covers how the AI and data center boom is boosting a surprising commodity: gray paint.
- The massive build-out of data centers in Texas threatens years of progress in the state cutting air pollution. The Texas Tribune has more.
- Google has apologized for clearing more than 800 acres of forest in Finland without getting the necessary environmental permits to build part of a €13 million data center project. The Guardian reports that the tech giant is facing backlash in the country that could bleed into elections next spring.

Go Public
Air Canada blamed maintenance issues to deny compensation. Records show it wanted planes for other routes
Airline's actions 'fraudulent,' air passenger advocate says
Air Canada denied Juan Rojas compensation for a cancelled flight after it swapped the aircraft assigned to his flight with one that needed safety-related maintenance.
The Ottawa man challenged the airline through the Canadian Transportation Agency and won — and the evidence raises questions about the information Air Canada provided to justify denying him compensation.
"I felt like they were trying to cheat the system," Rojas told Go Public.
Under Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations, passengers can be entitled to up to $1,000 for delayed flights, but only if the delay is within the airline's control and not required for safety.
Rojas's case is not the only one raising questions about airlines' use of the safety exemption.
- Got a story you want investigated? Contact Erica and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca
Go Public has uncovered three other instances in which Air Canada told passengers their flights were cancelled because of safety-related maintenance while flight records show the aircraft they were scheduled to fly on were subsequently used on other routes. In all three cases, Air Canada maintains it does not owe compensation.
What is the maintenance 'loophole'?
The maintenance "loophole" is a simple way for airlines to potentially deny compensation for countless passengers every year, said Montreal lawyer Sylvie De Bellefeuille.
"It's a huge duffel bag in which they can put anything and everything," said De Bellefeuille, director of legal services for Option consommateurs, a Montreal non-profit that advocates for consumer rights.
"Most passengers do not have enough information to counter whatever is said by the airline."
Lawyer Sylvie De Bellefeuille says Ottawa should close a maintenance 'loophole' airlines use to deny paying compensation for delayed or cancelled flights. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
Air Canada declined Go Public's request for an interview.
But in a written statement, it acknowledged that in all four cases, it made a commercial decision: reassigning a functioning aircraft to another route where the scheduled plane required safety-related maintenance, leaving passengers on the original route without their scheduled flight.
Air Canada argued that an aircraft's schedule is fluid, and it must be able to make "operational adjustments" to "minimize the overall impact on passengers." The airline said it was within its rights to deny compensation.
Gabor Lukacs, founder of Air Passenger Rights, strongly disputes that interpretation. He points to a 2022 CTA decision, which said mechanical issues must be "a direct cause" of a cancelled flight and cannot be considered a "knock-on effect."
"I am finding it stunning that Air Canada continues to pretend as if the law has not been settled," said Lukacs.
Air Canada 'misrepresents' info to federal regulator
When Rojas's September 2022 flight to Bogotá from Montreal was cancelled, Air Canada denied his request for compensation, citing safety-related maintenance.
When Rojas challenged the airline before the Canadian Transportation Agency, Air Canada submitted documents claiming a catering truck had struck his plane, damaging it.
A complaints resolution officer with the CTA found that Air Canada's claim it cancelled a flight due to safety issues was unfounded and ordered the airline to pay $1,000 in compensation. (CBC)
It wasn't until a friend suggested he check the public Civil Aviation Daily Reporting System, that he realized the Air Canada plane struck by a catering truck was not the same one assigned to Rojas's cancelled flight.
In other words, the incident Air Canada cited to justify denying Rojas compensation involved a different aircraft.
It's "outrageous," said De Bellefeuille, the lawyer.
"They were clearly misrepresenting the information," said Rojas, who submitted his discovery to the CTA.
Air Canada told Go Public Rojas's aircraft was moved to cover for the one that had been damaged.
This past January, a complaint resolution officer ruled in the case, ordering Air Canada to pay Rojas $1,000 for the "inconvenience."
"The decision to swap aircraft to avoid or minimize delays for one group of passengers at the expense of another is a commercial decision," the officer wrote. The airline could make that decision, per the ruling, but it was required to compensate affected passengers.
'A real black mark on Air Canada'
Michael Bociurkiw was flying from Bangkok to Vancouver last February when he received an email from Air Canada mid-flight. His connecting flight from Vancouver to Newark had been cancelled because of safety-related maintenance, the airline said.
But the plane with supposed safety concerns had the exact registration number of the very aircraft Bociurkiw was seated on.
"I wasn't too concerned about a safety issue," said Bociurkiw. "I was more concerned about what the hell is going on? And why is Air Canada giving me this story?"
Michael Bociurkiw had his flight cancelled for safety-related maintenance. He found out the plane assigned to his flight was perfectly fine, but the airline needed it for another flight. (Submitted by Michael Bociurkiw)
Go Public found two more cases in which Air Canada cited safety-related maintenance to deny passengers compensation, while flight records showed the aircraft originally assigned to their flights were perfectly fine and used on other routes.
Carlos Fernandez accuses Air Canada of "blatantly lying" after his May flight from Las Vegas to Toronto was cancelled 10 minutes after his aircraft was swapped for one needing safety-related maintenance. Alison Monaghan's July flight from Toronto to Vancouver was similarly impacted.
"It's a real black mark on Air Canada as far as ethics and integrity go," said Monaghan.
Alison Monaghan's flight to Vancouver was cancelled after Air Canada used the plane to replace an aircraft on a different route that had developed maintenance issues. (Submitted by Alison Monaghan)
How often does this happen?
Go Public has previously reported on WestJet using the safety-related maintenance exemption to deny passengers compensation. But the full extent of the practice among Canada's two largest airlines remains unclear.
The CTA, which launched an investigation in the WestJet cases, does not publish its decisions on air passenger disputes — despite a recent court order requiring them to be made public. The agency declined Go Public's request for past decisions.
A CTA spokesperson cited privacy concerns and said the agency planned to begin publishing decisions early next year, once those had been addressed.
But Lukacs said airlines have little financial incentive to comply with passenger protection rules if they face no meaningful consequences for violating them.
"Right now, it is just more economical for an airline to deceive passengers than to actually comply with the law."
- GO PUBLIC WestJet accused of tricky manoeuvre to deny dozens of passengers compensation after flight cancellations
- GO PUBLIC WestJet told passengers flights were cancelled for safety. Records suggest otherwise
The CTA said no fine has been issued in Rojas's case, nor has it ever issued a penalty against Air Canada "for incorrectly characterizing a flight cancellation as safety-related maintenance."
It should have issued a "hefty" fine in Rojas's case, Lukacs said, "because Air Canada was not only mistreating the passenger, it was also maintaining the same fraudulent falsehood even when it came before a decision-maker."
Feds need to do more to protect air passengers, advocates say
De Bellefeuille says Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations need to change so passengers are not left to rely on airlines' own explanations when flights are cancelled or delayed.
"It's really David against Goliath," said the Montreal lawyer and consumer advocate.
In the European Union, airlines can only avoid paying compensation for a qualifying disruption caused by a mechanical problem in limited situations, such as extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided, such as an act of terrorism.
But Lukacs – who has also called for an overhaul of air passenger protections – said the government has shown little appetite for reform.
Documents obtained by Go Public through an Access to Information request show previous transport ministers telling the CTA to maintain the airlines' ability to deny compensation for safety-related maintenance.
Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon declined an interview request.
Rojas says he's angry that the current rules can leave air passengers in the dark when airlines cite mechanical problems to deny compensation. He's now been compensated, but wonders about the other people who were booked for the same flight?
"The least the government can do is ensure that our rights are protected."

Much of what we know about how a brain makes decisions comes from studying monkeys watching dots. In a task known as a random-dot-motion task, a cloud of flickering specks drifts weakly in one direction while the subject tries to determine whether—and in which direction— it’s moving. The task has shown that in the primate neocortex, neurons gather visual evidence over time, with their firing rates climbing until they cross a threshold, when the animal commits to a decision.
But avian brains don’t have a neocortex, so it wasn’t obvious how they made similar decisions.
“This was the big question,” said Andreas Nieder, a neurobiologist at the University of Tübingen. “How [would] a differently organized avian brain encode decisions?”
To find out, Nieder and his colleague Philipp Schmidbauer put two carrion crows through the same task the monkeys faced, recording their brain activity along the way. The crows solved the task the same way primates do, using the same mathematical logic despite having a very different brain structure. And they did it two times faster.
A brain built different
Nieder and Schmidbauer put two hand-raised crows in front of a touch-sensitive monitor showing a cloud of white dots on black, with some fraction of them drifting coherently left or right or up or down. The birds’ job was to report the overall direction by pecking one of targets that flanked the display. Correct answers earned them a mealworm.
“We intentionally wanted to have exactly the same random-dot motion task,” Nieder said. “The only difference was that the crows had to peck to indicate their decision, whereas monkeys were indicating by making an eye movement.”
The researchers varied how many dots moved together, ranging from 81 percent of the dots coherently moving together, which is trivially easy to determine, down to 3 percent, which is barely distinguishable from noise. They also included a zero percent condition, in which there was no correct answer.

Which iPhone Should You Buy (or Avoid) Right Now?
Featured in this article
Apple sells seven iPhone models, from the $699 iPhone 17e to the $1,999 iPhone Duo, but which iPhone is best for you? This is a good time of the year to buy an iPhone if you need to upgrade, since Apple just released its flagship models. (We don't expect the more affordable iPhone 18 models until spring 2027.) We've tested nearly every model and outlined their strengths and weaknesses so you can get the right one for you.
Check out our other Apple buying guides, including Which iPhone 18 Models to Buy, Which iPhone 17 Model to Buy, Best iPhone 17 Cases, Best MagSafe Accessories, Best MagSafe Chargers, Best MagSafe Wallets, and Best Apple 3-in-1 Chargers. Wondering what's new in iOS 27? We have details on that, too.

But First, Sell That Old iPhone!
If you’re upgrading from an iPhone, you can trade it in to Apple for a small discount. Before you do that, check whether you can sell it elsewhere for more money. iPhones hold their value incredibly well, particularly if they’re in mint or good condition. We have a guide that runs through the process of selling your phone, and we generally recommend you use websites like Swappa, Gazelle, or Back Market.
We also have a handful of setup guides you should follow:
Buying From Apple vs. a Carrier
Most people in the US purchase iPhones from carriers, which means the devices are locked to that network. If you bought an iPhone from Verizon, you can't easily switch to another carrier without breaking a contract and paying extra fees. It also poses headaches for travelers who want to use international SIM cards or eSIMs.
The easier approach is to buy directly from Apple, though there are some things you should know:
Connect to any carrier later: Choose this option for the most hassle-free experience. You get an unlocked iPhone, then all you need to do is transfer the SIM card or eSIM from your old iPhone to the new one to get started. This might be painless, though you may need to contact your carrier if the iPhone can't complete the eSIM transfer. In the US, Apple hasn't included a SIM tray since 2022's iPhone 14.
Choose a carrier: If you choose a carrier through Apple.com, you will get an unlocked iPhone, no matter which carrier you choose (except if you purchase with AT&T on an installment plan). The downside is that Apple doesn't have the same offers as the carriers, so you may lose out on a deal. However, carrier offers often require new lines, trade-ins, or an upgraded plan, and the savings come in the form of bill credits, so these deals aren't as amazing as they may seem.
Finance: You can finance your iPhone either with Apple's credit card via monthly installments or as Apple iPhone Payments via a Citizens One loan. You need to choose a carrier here, but Apple confirmed these devices are all unlocked. You have to fill out a credit application to see if you qualify. If you opt to finance through a carrier on Apple.com, only the T-Mobile and Verizon models will be unlocked. The AT&T and Boost Mobile options are locked iPhones, so it's no different from buying it on an installment plan directly from those carriers.
Apple Upgrade: Buying directly from Apple also nets you access to the Apple Upgrade leasing option. Is it worth it? Broadly speaking, no. Most people do not need to upgrade to a new iPhone every year or two. It's expensive, and you must return your leased iPhone in good condition to avoid additional charges. AppleCare is not included, as it was with the discontinued iPhone Upgrade Program.
What Is Apple Intelligence?
The most hyped-up feature from the iPhone 16 range was Apple Intelligence, which rolled out in iOS 18.1. This is Apple's suite of AI features, following the wave started by the likes of ChatGPT and Google's Gemini. Apple Intelligence is available on the iPhone 15 Pro/Pro Max and newer, including the iPhone 16e (not to mention select iPads and MacBooks).
What exactly is Apple Intelligence in the first place? It's a collection of features that draw on the power of large language models to introduce “smart” capabilities. For example, in the Voice Memo and Notes app, you can now start a recording and get a real-time transcription. You can even record a call and get the transcription saved in the Notes app. Siri has been redesigned to understand when you misspeak and can even plug into ChatGPT for more powerful responses to open-ended questions. There are writing tools available throughout the operating system that let you change the tone of your emails or proofread text so you don't make an unnecessary typo on Threads.
This is just a small sampling. We've boiled down many of the Apple Intelligence features here, and additional features keep rolling out in iOS updates. For example, Genmoji—which lets you create your own emojis—debuted alongside the AI image-generation app, Image Playground, in iOS 18.2. In iOS 27, Apple added the revamped, conversational Siri AI assistant. Siri now understands personal context and can retrieve information from your messages, emails, and photos. It can also act on your behalf to draft a message with a particular tone or find a good restaurant for your partner's birthday dinner. Here's everything you can do with Siri AI.
If you don't care for Apple Intelligence and want to turn it off, you can! We have a helpful guide detailing the exact steps.
What Is MagSafe?
Magnetic MagSafe wireless charging is available on the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, iPhone 17, and iPhone 18 models (except the iPhone 16e), and it allows you to magnetically attach various accessories to the back of the iPhone. (iPhones support Qi2, which is the open standard, whereas MagSafe is proprietary; you can use Qi2 accessories just like MagSafe.)
You can get first-party accessories like Apple's MagSafe Wireless Charger, which sticks to the back for faster charging. Or snag the MagSafe Wallet so you can keep your credit card attached to your phone. There are plenty of third-party accessories (you'll find quite a few in our guide), and MagSafe doesn't just have to be charging accessories like power banks or wireless chargers. There is a wealth of useful tools, from wallets, tripods, and camera cages to notepads and ring lights that can attach to the back of the iPhone and add extra versatility.
If you plan to use a case, get one that has MagSafe embedded inside to ensure a strong magnetic connection with Apple's accessories (non-MagSafe cases can interrupt MagSafe and make the magnetic connection weaker). All of the cases in our case guides are MagSafe-tested. And yes, a case is a smart investment because iPhones are made of glass, and glass breaks, even if Apple uses ceramic to strengthen it. We cracked an iPhone 16 Plus after a 4-foot drop to the pavement—that model's ceramic glass was supposed to be twice as strong as previous iPhones, too! Ouch. See our favorite cases for the iPhone 17, iPhone 16, iPhone 15, and iPhone 14 ranges.
What's New in iOS 27?
While last year's iOS 26 debuted the divisive Liquid Glass, iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 focus squarely on quality-of-life improvements, with a redesigned and much improved Siri AI assistant, easier Shortcuts, and lots of little tweaks to enhance speed and stability.
Siri AI doesn't just look different—now resembling a glass orb—it can also understand your personal context, pulling info from your messages, emails, or even photos, and helping you draft messages or find the right wine to pair with your dinner. Siri can also now pop up in the camera app to help you choose your next book or split a bill with friends.
Apple says iOS 27 is faster than ever, with app launches up to 30 percent faster, newly captured photos in your Photo Library loading up to 70 percent faster, and AirDrop transfers completing up to 80 percent faster. For more details, read our guide on the top features in iOS 27 and how to download it.
Charging Adapters for Your iPhone
Apple hasn't offered a charging brick in the box since the iPhone 12, so if you don't have one, we've got you covered with a few recommendations. Most of these are 30-watt chargers that will fast-charge most iPhones. If you want the fastest speeds on the iPhone 18 models, you'll need a 40-watt charger, and we have some picks for you.

It's a mouthful, but essentially, it can boost power output up to 60 watts when needed. That means it's a more versatile charger that you can use for your MacBook Air and your iPhone.
The Right USB-C Cable
The problem with USB-C is that its capabilities are so vast, but not every USB-C cable supports every single function. You need to make sure the cable you buy supports video output, speedy data transfer, and fast charging if that's what you want. Get a MagSafe Portable Battery

Get a 3-in-1 Wireless Charger

Carry a MagSafe Wallet
Hate bringing a wallet with you everywhere? Stick it to the back of your iPhone! This Nomad leather wallet is classy and can hold about four cards. What makes it unique is that it features Apple's Find My, meaning you can track its location in the Find My app if you lose it. That does mean the wallet needs to recharge every once in a while, but you can conveniently recharge it with any MagSafe charger, no proprietary cable needed. (It should last around five months on a single charge.) Read our Best MagSafe Wallets guide for more options.
The MagSafe world is wonderful and weird. We have plenty more recommendations in our Best MagSafe Accessories guide, ranging from MagSafe camera cages and tripods to notepads you can magnetically stick to the back of your iPhone.
Avoid These iPhones
The iPhone 14 and older iPhones are probably available somewhere, but you shouldn't take the bait. They don't have the processing power to keep up with the latest software, and even if they do, they will have a much shorter software shelf life or lack modern features like USB-C. The only older iPhones worth considering at the moment are the iPhone 15 or iPhone 16 series, even better if it's the Pro models, if you can find them at low prices. The iPhone 16e is also another option, though only if you can find it at a steep discount.
The iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, and iPhone XR are cut off from receiving the iOS 27 update, so they're especially ones to avoid. Without software support, your device will slowly become less secure and could become a slow, buggy mess.
The iPhone's Charging Port Is USB-C, Not Lightning
The iPhone 15 range ditched the long-standing Lightning port for USB-C, and it's in every iPhone since. This is the same charging port on iPads, MacBooks, Android phones, Windows laptops, and many more personal tech gadgets. USB-C is often called the “universal port” because it can technically handle various responsibilities. For example, you can plug in external displays and extend the iPhone's screen or connect the same USB-C accessories you might be currently using on your laptop, like SD card readers. Sadly, it does mean your Lightning accessories won't work unless you get dongles.
You can read more about what the port does here, but there are two important things to note:
The iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Plus, iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16e, iPhone 17, iPhone 17e, and iPhone Air support the USB 2.0 standard just like the iPhones before, so you'll max out at 480 megabits per second of data transfer speeds.
The iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo support the USB 3.0 standard and are capable of up to 10 gigabits per second of data transfer speeds.
What’s the Deal With eSIMs?
All iPhone 14 and newer devices completely ditch the physical SIM tray in the US, meaning you can no longer just pop your physical SIM inside to turn on cellular connectivity. Instead, you'll have to rely on an eSIM. You can read more about them here. This tech has been available in iPhones since the iPhone XS and XR, but now you have to use it. Apple has also started switching more global models to eSIM only, like the iPhone Air.) When you're setting up your new iPhone, you'll automatically be asked to transfer your number from your previous iPhone, and the whole process should take a few minutes without any hassle. (eSIMs are more secure than physical SIMs.) Once you transfer your number, your physical SIM card won't work anymore.
There's a chance you may still run into some issues, especially if you're coming from an Android phone (or want to switch back to an Android phone). You'll have to check with your carrier to get your cellular connection working again. It shouldn't take long, but it's not as simple as popping in a physical card.
How to Replace Your iPhone's Battery
If you don't want to spend the money to get a new iPhone, consider a fresh battery. If the biggest issues with your aging iPhone revolve around how long it lasts in a day, replacing the battery might make it feel brand-new. (Apple's iPhone 16, 16 Plus, and 16e have an easier-to-replace battery.)
Replacements for older iPhones are $89, and $99 or $119 for newer models. If that doesn't do the trick, read our guide on ways to fix your iPhone's problems or our guide on selling your iPhone to get the most money for it.
What Is the Action Button and Camera Control Button?
The Action Button debuted on the iPhone 15 Pro models, and it's now standard on every iPhone in the lineup. It sits above the volume rocker on the left edge of the phone. It effectively replaces the old Mute Switch, but think of it as just a configurable button. You can have it still control the mute function of the phone, or customize it (Settings > Action Button) to trigger the flashlight, a Voice Memo, or even launch an app or Shortcut.
Camera Control is another newer addition that debuted on the iPhone 16 series. On the right edge of the phone below the power button, press it to launch the Camera app, and you can press it to capture a photo or start recording a video. A light tap and swipe can move through different camera lenses or modes, but I found this annoying. (You can configure it by heading to Settings > Camera > Camera Control.) Press and hold this button, and you'll trigger Apple's Visual Intelligence. It'll use the camera to identify subjects in front of you, very much like Google Lens, so you can ask questions via Google or ChatGPT about what you're looking at.
