The affidavit was approved unanimously by the CEC and both Election Commissioners
NEW DELHI: Election Commission on Monday filed a counter-affidavit in the Supreme Court defending its functioning and the conduct of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The poll body rejected allegations of irregularities and questioned the basis of a petition challenging its decision-making process.According to Bar and Bench, the poll body said the petition was built entirely on a single news report. The affidavit, approved unanimously by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, addresses concerns over the Commission's internal decision-making, alleged changes to voter enrolment forms, deletion of names and the functioning of its electoral databases.
The response came after a plea filed by Rakesh Kumar Singh in the apex court. The petition sought the suspension of the CEC and challenged his alleged unilateral decision-making powers. It also sought to declare the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and all related actions invalid.
What EC said in its 15-point rebuttal
In its counter-affidavit, the EC made the following submissions, as reported by Bar and Bench:
Affidavit approved unanimously by all three members: the CEC and both Election Commissioners
All three SIR orders (June 2025, October 2025, May 2026) were unanimous decisions of the Commission
Notes, queries or suggestions by the CEC or ECs while a file moves are not decisions of the Commission
Files go to one EC, then the other EC, then the CEC. In urgent cases, approval is taken electronically and recorded on file later
Any officer issuing orders beyond delegated powers will face action
July 28 work allocation order was issued by an Additional Secretary on deputation. Both ECs wrote to the Cabinet Secretary the next day. The order was never implemented after the ECs' joint direction of July 30

Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann are emerging as early contenders to become the next Manchester United head coach if Michael Carrick loses his job.

Should Carrick be dismissed, the 20-time English top-flight champions will be looking to appoint their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Sir Alex Ferguson departed the club in 2013 on the back of winning their most recent title.

A group of 21 news publishers has reportedly challenged India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act in the Supreme Court (SC), arguing that the law could undermine investigative journalism and expose journalists’ sources. The lawsuit, filed on October 6, argues that the law’s provisions on consent, data erasure and government access to information could restrict news reporting and force publishers to remove factual stories. The case is scheduled to be heard on October 27, according to a Reuters report. The challenge comes nearly a year after the Centre notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 in November last year. The broader DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules establish a framework governing how organisations collect, process and protect individuals’ digital personal data. The Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), which represents the publishers, has argued that the law does not provide a specific exemption for journalistic activities. According to the confidential filing, the association reportedly said that the absence of such safeguards could compromise press freedom and investigative reporting. The DNPA’s members include Mukesh Ambani-owned Network18, Gautam Adani-owned NDTV, the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group. Publishers Vs The DPDP Act A key concern raised by the publishers is the requirement to obtain consent before processing personal data. The DNPA has argued that requiring journalists to notify the subjects of investigations and seek their consent could allow them to destroy evidence or intimidate witnesses. The association has also flagged provisions allowing individuals to withdraw consent and request the erasure of their personal data. According to the filing, the absence of a public-interest safeguard could force publishers to remove or substantially redact factual news reports. The publishers have further raised concerns about provisions empowering the government to seek information from organisations handling personal data. They argue that these powers could expose confidential journalistic sources and discourage whistleblowers from sharing information about corruption, corporate wrongdoing and electoral malpractice. The filing also challenges the government's power to restrict access to information in the public interest, arguing that the provisions could curtail press freedom. The DNPA has sought the quashing of several contentious provisions of the law, most of which are scheduled to come into effect from May 2027, Reuters reported. The association has also argued that the government has granted broad exemptions to the state without extending corresponding protections to the press. What The DPDP Framework Provides The DPDP Act, enacted in August 2023, establishes obligations for processing digital personal data. The later DPDP Rules, notified in November 2025, provide a phased implementation framework, giving organisations up to 18 months to comply with specified requirements. The framework requires platforms to obtain consent for processing personal data, provide clear information about its use and implement security safeguards. It also gives individuals rights to access, correct, update and seek the erasure of their personal data, subject to the applicable provisions. The latest case marks one of the most prominent challenges to the DPDP framework so far, raising questions about how India’s data protection requirements will interact with press freedom and investigative reporting. The Act provides for financial penalties of up to ₹250 Cr for failing to implement reasonable security safeguards. Other violations, including certain breaches of obligations relating to children’s personal data, can attract penalties of up to ₹200 Cr. However, the publishers argue that the framework does not adequately account for the requirements of investigative journalism, particularly when reporting involves personal information collected in the public interest. The government has maintained that the framework protects citizens’ privacy while supporting responsible data processing.

Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan
- Published
Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast.
Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday.
One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate.
Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El Niño heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far.
On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) .
After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island.
Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan,
However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches.
Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said.
Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains.
Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island.
Taiwan's $5tn (£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather.
Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual.
In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company.
More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines.
Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan.
Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties.
Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane.
While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea.
This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms.
The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El Niño - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons.

Antonelli delivers 'the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet'
- Published
The race that took Kimi Antonelli to the brink of a record-breaking world championship was, in the words of his Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff, "the best he has delivered so far" and "the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet".
Not yet. Not quite. But so very near.
The 20-year-old Italian's victory in the United States Grand Prix puts him in an impregnable position.
Antonelli is so far ahead in the points that the only way he could not win the title in Mexico City next weekend is if either his team-mate George Russell or Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton win the race. Even then, Antonelli will guarantee the title if he finishes ninth, or 10th if it's Hamilton.
He arrived here thanks to one of the most dominant victories of the season, in a car in which Russell could finish only eighth, albeit hampered by a five-second penalty.
While Russell was toiling and failing to pass McLaren's Oscar Piastri, Antonelli was operating on another level entirely, as he has so often this season.
"Exceptional," Wolff said, "and I think he's outperformed the car."
- Antonelli wins in US but has to wait to secure title 
  - Published6 hours ago
- Antonelli superb and Leclerc close to perfect - driver ratings 
  - Published2 hours ago
Antonelli came to Austin already in a strong position in the championship, knowing he would clinch the title if he won with Russell finishing lower than eighth and Hamilton lower than fourth.
He achieved his part of the bargain but Russell and Hamilton did just enough to keep things alive until this coming weekend. Russell was eighth and Hamilton fourth.
Some drivers tighten up when they get this close to achieving their lifetime's ambition. Not Antonelli. He said he was going to treat this like any other weekend, but it wasn't just talk. It's exactly what he did.
"He comes in," Wolff told BBC Sport after the race, in a conversation after finishing his official news conference, "sits on my chair, feet up, and keeps chatting away and saying: 'This is so funny. I'm not thinking about the championship at all.' And in a kind of youngish excitement, almost like it's surreal. And that's why it's not so important."
Did Wolff think that was because Antonelli's lead was so large that he had no need to feel any pressure, or was it innate?
"The advantage helps," he said. "But it's also innate in him and I don't think that it's something to be trained for. He's not over-thinking it."
Wolff's claim about this being Antonelli's best performance so far might surprise anyone who watched him win his home grand prix at Monza from 19th on the grid.
When this was pointed out, Wolff replied: "My problem is that I don't remember past races. So now you're saying Monza was actually also pretty good, obviously with the advantage of the home crowd and seeing all these tifosi that were a little bit confused, wearing red, and an Italian with the Mercedes outfit up on the podium. And I think we're going to see more Kimi caps, Mercedes caps next year.
"So both of them were pretty good. But the headline that this is the best we can keep."
Antonelli agreed. "Monza, we clearly had the fastest car," he said. "We were just super quick, so of course it was incredibly special coming from the back. But it was also a track where it was relatively easy to overtake, and we were so quick.
"Definitely, Monza was a super-special one, and one that I will remember forever. But this one probably, in terms of execution, was better, because the way we built up and the way we built the performance throughout the weekend was very good."
Mercedes went to Austin with both cars in the new upgraded specification that had proved unconvincing, to say the least, when it made its debut in Malaysia two races ago.
There, Wolff said he thought it had made the car 0.3secs per lap slower. The team split the cars in Singapore to try to understand the package better, and then used it on both cars in Austin. Antonelli stuck it on pole and dominated the race. Russell's performance looked more like the one the car produced in Malaysia.
"The update we put on the car is difficult to operate," Wolff said. "And Kimi landed it.
"Maybe it's a bit harsh to say but I think his driving style just glues with the car. We saw that in qualifying yesterday where on his last lap he could have been another 0.15-0.2 secs up. And on the other side George just struggled so much. And I believe this is because the operational window of the car is so difficult."
When Antonelli clinches the title, he will become the first Italian to do so since Alberto Ascari in 1953. It's a remarkable statistic for a country which is so engrained in the sport, and it certainly resonates with his compatriots.
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "As an Italian, wow, we need to go back to Ascari, the names that they created the inspiration for all of us. To see an Italian achieving this level of performance and results in Formula 1, that's particularly thrilling, as an Italian person in motorsport."
Stella's answer continued into an area that begins to explain the way in which he has proved so superior to Russell this year.
"Going more into the technical, and specifically this season, Kimi is a very interesting one to look at, because he pretty much attacks all the times," Stella said.
"You see how often he's just going off track, and you see his onboard (camera), he's pretty aggressive. But at the same time, this seems to be not only kind of an aggressive driving, or an attacking driving, but effective.
"And if we think how much we talk in these media sessions about the cars being difficult to drive consistently fast, it should be recognised how much he's been able to harness his driving style with what is required of the cars.
"But at the same time, almost contradicting what I'm saying, when is the time to bring home the result, he's been able to do it.
"So he's the deserving leader of this championship. He's writing an important piece of history for motorsport, because once he achieves the championship, he will be the youngest."
Antonelli will beat by more than three years the previous record for youngest winner of the championship, Sebastian Vettel in 2010.
As with the title itself, he is aware of the forthcoming achievement, but not letting it affect him.
"I'm going to approach it with the same mindset," he said. "Just trying to have as much fun as possible, trying to hopefully fight for another win.
"It would be best to finish on a high, and that's the goal. But I'm just going to try to enjoy the rest of the season from now on."

My father, John Staley, who has died aged 88, was field director for Oxfam in south India and Sri Lanka during the late 1960s and early 70s, when he was responsible for Oxfam’s funding of several hundred local, national and international voluntary agencies.
His role included aid administration, policy formulation, project appraisal, recommendations for funding, disaster relief and liaison with government and non-government organisations. He led Oxfam’s response in India to a drought in Maharashtra in 1973, which fed more than 20,000 people as part of a work-for-food programme, and was made MBE in 1974 for services to the Indian people.
 
John was born in Epsom, Surrey, the only child of Robert, a doctor, and Sylvia, a housewife. He went to Marlborough college in Wiltshire, and then, after national service, to Cambridge University, where he studied natural sciences and economics (1957-61).
At Cambridge he met Elizabeth Pott, and they discovered a shared love of travelling on an overland expedition to Pakistan with friends. They married in 1962 and did PhDs together at the University of the Punjab in Lahore, studying the economics and geography of mountain communities in northern Pakistan.
In 1966 they returned to the UK, where they finished their PhDs and where John did some freelance lecturing at the Commonwealth Institute, the Pakistan Society and the Royal Central Asian Society before taking up his field director post at Oxfam in 1967.
John eventually became research director for Oxfam in India (1975-76), and during that time discovered the concept of experience-based training, by which small groups of people learn about the behaviour of groups and organisations from their own analysis of their experience of the group.
In 1976 he and some Indian colleagues founded Search, an organisation that developed and used these experience-based training methods to train people in development work in India. He was seconded by Oxfam to Search from 1976 to 1980, and then, in 1982, returned to the UK to become a lecturer and later senior lecturer in development studies at Selly Oak Colleges in Birmingham – remaining there until his retirement in 1999.
 
Thereafter he wrote, travelled, took part in his local U3A in Great Malvern, Worcestershire, and cared for his garden and a small local wood that he and Elizabeth bought as a retirement project. Over the years John wrote three books, Words for My Brother (1982), People in Development (also 1982), and Enticing the Learning (2008).
 
Elizabeth died in 2019. John is survived by their children, Eleanor, Joanna and me, and grandchildren Isabelle and Freddie.

Unacademy cofounders Gaurav Munjal and Roman Saini are raising a ₹700 Cr venture capital fund to back AI and deeptech startups, less than two months after upGrad completed the acquisition of the edtech startup. Named Longshot Capital, the Category II AIF has secured commitments of around ₹250-300 Cr and is targeting its first close in January 2027, ET reported, citing sources. Munjal and Saini declined to comment on the development. The Bengaluru-based fund plans to invest in 25-28 startups at the seed and pre-Series A stages, with initial cheques of $500,000 to $1.5 Mn and a targeted ownership stake of 8-12%. Saini will run Longshot Capital full-time, while Munjal will be involved part-time alongside his role heading Unacademy. Both founders will serve as general partners of the investment firm. The fund plans to deploy its capital over three years and will invest in India-based startups as well as companies founded by entrepreneurs of Indian origin. Its investment mandate will span AI-led businesses and deeptech segments such as manufacturing, space, defence and robotics, rather than consumer brands and retail businesses, the report said. The fund will have a lifespan of 10-11 years, allowing it to back businesses with longer gestation periods, particularly in AI and deeptech, according to the report. Its prospective investors include startup founders, family offices and overseas institutions. The fund formalises more than a decade of angel investing by Munjal and Saini. The two have collectively invested over ₹25 Cr through more than 200 angel cheques in companies including Pine Labs, Dhan, Seekho, Ultrahuman, Snabbit, Swish, STAGE, and Third Wave Coffee. In August, the duo also invested in Superleap, an AI-native customer relationship management platform. The proposed fund comes amid growing investor interest in frontier technologies, with Indian AI startups raising $438 Mn across 28 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 265% YoY. Meanwhile, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals during the same period, up 176% YoY. Unacademy Founders’ Second Act The move adds Munjal and Saini to a growing group of startup founders transitioning from personal angel investments to institutional fund management. Snapdeal cofounders Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal raised ₹333 Cr in external capital for Titan Capital in 2024. Freshworks founder Girish Mathrubootham cofounded the AI-focused Together Fund, while CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti joined Singularity Growth as a general partner after his exit. Myntra founder Mukesh Bansal operates venture studio Meraki Labs. The latest development comes over a month after upGrad acquired Unacademy in an all-stock transaction valuing it at ₹1,955 Cr, more than 90% below its peak valuation of $3.4 Bn in August 2021. Founded in 2015 by Munjal, Saini and Hemesh Singh, Unacademy started as a YouTube channel before evolving into an online learning platform focused on competitive exam preparation. It raised around $880 Mn from investors including SoftBank, Peak XV Partners, Elevation Capital, General Atlantic, Temasek, and Tiger Global. The startup became a unicorn in September 2020 and reached its peak valuation of $3.5 Bn in 2021, amid a pandemic-led boom in edtech investments. However, the reopening of educational institutions and a slowdown in demand for online learning forced Unacademy to rethink its business strategy. Unacademy undertook multiple rounds of layoffs, cut cash burn and scaled down several verticals as it sought to move towards profitability. It also expanded into offline coaching centres to tap demand for in-person test preparation. Unacademy subsequently explored acquisition opportunities with multiple players, including Allen Career Institute, K-12 Techno Services and upGrad. Its earlier merger discussions with upGrad fell through over valuation differences before the two companies revived negotiations and signed a term sheet in March. The acquisition was completed in September. Meanwhile, Munjal, on X yesterday, pushed back on criticism against the risk appetite of Indian deeptech investors, highlighting that startups like Astrobase, Airbound and Sarvam AI have been able to raise large rounds in short time periods. He also noted that consumer tech companies like Groww, Eternal and Meesho, all of whom went public in recent years, have provided “spectacular outcomes”.

On 22 October 2026, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur admitted that “face-offs” with Chinese forces had taken place at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border. Following the ITBP chief’s remarks, India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated on 23 October 2026 that the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) becomes “disturbed” when Chinese troops diverge from established patrolling patterns.
In this context, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming to show Chinese soldiers confronting and inspecting Indian soldiers in Arunachal Pradesh. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing a confrontation in Arunachal Pradesh, where Chinese soldiers are intercepting and restricting the movement of Indian troops.
Fact: While the reports have confirmed face-offs between Indian and Chinese forces along the Arunachal Pradesh border, this video actually depicts a counter-terrorism mock drill conducted in Karnataka in April 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led to the original footage (archived) uploaded on the ‘Jagdamba Motors’ Instagram page on 30 April 2026.
The full-length video clearly shows shop signboards, such as “Jagdamba Tools” and “Balaji Tiffin, Tea Centre & Chat”, written in Kannada, indicating that the video was shot in Karnataka, not Arunachal Pradesh.
Furthermore, we contacted the phone number displayed on the “Jagdamba Tools” signboard and spoke with the owner, Sohan Singh Rajput. He confirmed that he recorded the video outside his shop near Devanahalli, Karnataka, in late April 2026, and that it actually depicts a mock drill conducted by Indian forces. We also found some other videos (here and here) of Indian forces participating in exercises at this exact location.
Moreover, the official Indian Army Fact-Check handle clarified that the footage shows an old counter-terrorism mock drill conducted near Bengaluru, Karnataka, and is not a confrontation between Indian and Chinese soldiers in Arunachal Pradesh.
To sum it up, an old video of an Indian counter-terrorism mock drill in Karnataka is being falsely shared as a recent confrontation between Indian and Chinese soldiers in Arunachal Pradesh.

That is not to denigrate the achievements of Sri Lanka for chasing down a colossal 430 and Pakistan for their successful pursuit of 242 after having been 154-9. Those should be lauded.
But they did expose a few cracks in England that were not really visible during the home ODI summer as Harry Brook's team recorded bilateral series wins over India and Sri Lanka.
England are not in the disarray Manchester United are. The coach won't be sacked and the captain is unlikely to be dropped for slamming the coach's tactics. But there are things to fix. Some easy, others a little more difficult.
England missing senior players, including Archer
It is worth noting that an England side sat on three defeats from three in the tri-series - they lost their first game against Pakistan after botching a chase of 303 - is missing some key personnel.
Jos Buttler (injured), Jacob Bethell (recovering from injury) and Jofra Archer (rested) are not here. Adil Rashid has not been picked for the last two matches. Josh Tongue missed Sunday's loss.
Having Rashid - whose recent omission has been somewhat of a mystery - and Archer would clearly have bolstered the bowling, while Bethell and Buttler could have acted as strong sounding boards for Brook when things started to unravel in the field.
Bethell and Buttler's absences were also keenly felt with the bat as, let's be honest, that is where this weekend's game was lost.
The Lahore strip was not the Rawalpindi road on which England and Sri Lanka struck a combined 859 runs but neither was it a minefield.
The fact Pakistan's No 8 (Shadab Khan) scored 113 not out and England's No 10 (Gus Atkinson) hit an unbeaten 36 shows you that.
England's 241 all out was under par. They should probably never have defended it. It's just the way they failed to defend it that rankled.
The lack of middle-overs wickets that blighted England against Sri Lanka - and has done in ODIs for some time - was not an issue versus Pakistan as Jamie Overton and Liam Dawson excelled.
This time the problems came when their opponents were nine down.
England's Curran conundrum
During the dismal 2025 Champions Trophy campaign in Pakistan - losing all three of their games - England were crying out for the variety Sam Curran's left-arm box of tricks provides.
Since his white-ball reinstatement, Curran has made a difference, notably with a clutch final over as England staved off a humbling defeat to Nepal in the T20 World Cup in India earlier this year.
But he has had a tough time in Pakistan over the last few days, perhaps owing to the rustiness caused by missing the last two months with a groin injury.
None of Curran's variations have really worked.
His moon balls, bouncers and yorkers have been more predictable than Manchester United getting to the autumn and changing manager. A stage we may be at again.
Curran's 42 with the bat helped rally England from 52-4 against Pakistan and, in isolation, his bowling figures of 0-32 from eight overs are solid. That doesn't tell the entire story, though.
In his fifth, sixth and seventh overs, Curran offered up boundary balls to Shadab and then a single, while also failing to sufficiently test No 11 Haris Rauf when he had the opportunity.
Three days prior, the all-rounder was flogged for England's most-expensive ODI bowling figures as Brook persevered with him for too long. Curran's 2-103 from nine overs against Sri Lanka trumped his own 0-98 from 9.5 overs versus West Indies back in 2023.
Stuart Broad is one of many who think you get the best out of Curran when he has a defined and prominent role - and England need to work out what that is as he feels rather bit-part at the moment. If his toils with the ball continue that could be no part.
Should Overton continue to excel in the middle overs, banging out a hard length and nabbing crucial wickets Liam Plunkett-style, and offer a bit more with the bat than he is currently doing, Curran could be at risk, especially if England want to get another out-and-out seamer into the XI as they prepare for the 2027 World Cup in Africa.
Why is Rashid not playing?
They also need to find a way for Rashid to return to the side at some stage - unless the leg-spinner's recent absence is because they have moved on from a man who has been a linchpin for well over a decade.
The fact Rashid, 38, is in the squad to tour Australia next month would suggest not. His spell on the bench is perhaps due to still working back to full fitness following a hand injury that ended his home summer prematurely.
But his ODI figures in 2026 have not been amazing - nine wickets in seven games at an average of 36.22 and a strike-rate of 37.50 after a quality 2025 when he averaged two wickets a game (30 in 15 fixtures at an average of 23.63 and strike-rate of 24.10).
Sky Sports' Nasser Hussain said last week that Rashid's performances had "dropped off".
Rashid being omitted for Liam Dawson - who has done excellently in the tri-series, it must be said - for tactical reasons in Rawalpindi and again in Lahore has raised questions that were not there before.
Questions across the board are inevitable when you fluff your lines twice in a week. At least coach Brendon McCullum, perhaps unlike Michael Carrick at Manchester United after Como and Bournemouth drubbings, will be around to try and provide the answers.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has withdrawn the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 (MSMER-2023), with effect from October 17. The move has raised questions about how violations by medical colleges will be penalised, and how compliance with prescribed standards will be verified under the remaining regulatory framework.
The MSMER-2023 was withdrawn with immediate effect through a notification dated October 14, published in the Gazette on October 17. There is no single new regulation replacing MSMER 2023. Instead, the requirement for medical colleges to submit Annual Disclosure Reports (ADRs) will continue under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and other applicable regulations, the NMC said.
Rules on penalties, enforcement removed
The withdrawal comes close on the heels of a nationwide agitation for greater accountability in the undergraduate medical entrance examination.
Healthcare activists and medical education experts have raised concerns about three key areas that may fall through the gaps with the withdrawal of these regulations: the alleged removal of specific penalties under MSMER-2023, including fines of up to ₹1 crore for specified violations and personal fines of up to ₹5 lakh for faculty and administrators submitting false records; the verification of colleges’ annual disclosures on faculty, infrastructure, clinical facilities, and patient load; and the removal of the specific procedures and timelines for enforcement and appeals laid out in the MSMER-2023.
‘Patients at risk’
Bejon Kumar Misra, consumer rights activist and founder-director of the Patient Safety and Access Initiative of India Foundation (PSAIIF), said the withdrawal raised concerns about transparency, accountability, and the quality of medical education.
While the NMC Act, 2019, provides statutory powers for inspections and enforcement, Prof. Misra said that withdrawing a detailed regulatory framework without clarifying equivalent safeguards creates uncertainty over how institutional deficiencies and false disclosures will be addressed.
“Medical colleges cannot be judged merely by their buildings, equipment, or number of approved seats. The real measure of medical education is the competence of graduating doctors, the availability of qualified faculty, adequate supervised clinical exposure, and their ability to deliver safe and ethical patient care,” he said.
Prof. Misra has also written to the Union government, warning that misleading faculty declarations, inflated patient records, or inadequate clinical training going undetected could ultimately put patients at risk. He urged the Union Health Ministry and the NMC to clarify the enforcement mechanisms that will remain in place and to ensure that medical education standards are independently verifiable.
‘Dilution of regulatory oversight’
Babu K.V., an ophthalmologist and medical activist, said the withdrawal could dilute the penalty framework. He explained that by denotifying the stronger MSMER 2023 September regulation and retaining the June regulation, some clauses have been deleted.
“Like the clause 8(2)c, which states that monetary penalty not exceeding ₹5 lakh [will be imposed] for the faculty/Head of the Department (HoD)/Dean/Director/doctor submitting false declaration/documents/records (including patients’ records). Further, they can also be charged or penalised for misconduct under the Registered Medical Practitioner (Professional Conduct) Regulations in vogue,” he said.
“This is the key regulation ,where the individual doctors are made accountable and hence deleting it is dilution of regulatory oversight,” Dr. Babu explained, refuting the NMC’s argument that there is no dilution of regulatory oversight.
‘Eliminates duplication’
However, a senior NMC official told The Hindu that the decision had been “misinterpreted”. The withdrawal followed a review by the Commission’s legal team, which recommended streamlining regulatory powers and removing overlapping responsibilities, the official said.
The Commission functions through four autonomous boards, of which two set standards for undergraduate and postgraduate medical education. Another assesses and rates medical colleges and undertakes institutional inspections and regulatory action, while the fourth oversees medical registration, professional conduct, and ethics.
The NMC maintains that the move eliminates duplication without diluting standards, and that its inspection and verification powers remain intact.
Not retrospective
The Gazette notification provides that the withdrawal will not affect actions already taken, approvals granted, or rights, obligations and liabilities accrued under MSMER-2023. Applications, proceedings, appeals and inquiries pending before the withdrawal will continue to be dealt with under the regulations, insofar as applicable. Matters arising after the withdrawal will be governed by the NMC Act and the statutory and regulatory provisions then in force.
India had 846 medical colleges, 1,39,864 MBBS seats and 86,360 postgraduate medical seats, according to government data cited in August 2026. “With medical education expanding, the key question is whether the regulatory framework that remains can ensure that colleges meet prescribed standards and face effective action when they fail to do so,’’ Dr. Babu said.

Director General of Police Mahesh Kumar Aggarwal transferred the investigation into the alleged death by suicide of Class XI student A. Akilan (16) in Coimbatore to the Crime Branch Criminal Investigation Department (CB-CID) on Monday (October 26, 2026).
The DGP’s order stated that the case, which was registered by the Peelamedu police in Coimbatore under Sections 115(2), 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita read with 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act in connection with the death on October 22, has been transferred to the CB-CID for further investigation.
The order directed the Coimbatore City Police Commissioner to hand over the original case file and all connected records of the case to the DGP, CB-CID, immediately. The DGP, CB-CID, will nominate an investigating officer, who will take up the investigation.
Personnel from the city police handed over a copy of the order to family members of the deceased, who along with relatives and members of various political parties and organisations have been staging a protest near South Taluk office for the past few days, demanding arrest of all persons who abetted the suicide.
Akilan, who belongs to a Scheduled Caste community, was found dead in his house on October 21. The police arrested two of his classmates, who belong to different dominant castes, two days later for allegedly having subjected him to caste-based harassment. The police were also investigating allegations levelled by Akilan’s mother against a teacher and the headmaster.
The post-mortem of the deceased was held at the Government Medical College and ESI Hospital on Monday. However, the family did not accept the body. Akilan’s parents had earlier said they would accept the body only after the arrest of all those who they accused of having harassed their son on caste grounds.
Solatium and govt. job
Backward Classes Welfare Minister V. Sampath Kumar on Monday handed over an order sanctioning ₹6 lakh in interim compensation to Akilan’s family.
He also handed over a government job appointment order to Akilan’s sister, Nethra, as a junior assistant at the Anaikatti Tribal Residential School. The Minister met the family at the South Taluk Office in Coimbatore and offered his condolences.
(Assistance for overcoming suicidal thoughts is available on the State’s health helpline 104, Tele-MANAS 14416, and Sneha’s suicide prevention helpline 044-24640050.)

Watch: Why is the UK reviewing its Chagos Islands deal?
The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said, after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it".
The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.
The BBC's diplomatic correspondent Caroline Hawley looks at why the government's agreement with Mauritius has stalled.

Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner.
After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court.
The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down.
Kumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year.
Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back.
However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates.
In a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “vote chori” (cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”.
Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions.
“Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served for India, the youth won’t stop,” he said.
The SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi.
Mahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls.
“There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.”
Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.”
Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar.
The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.

Tata Communications plans to invest $400-450 Mn (around ₹4,350 Cr) to build 10,000 km of AI-ready connectivity infrastructure across India in a bid to capitalise on rising demand for data centre connectivity and compute infrastructure. The investment will be used to build a new high-speed fibre network connecting major data centres and AI hubs, allowing transfer of large amounts of data faster with minimal delays. The network will also connect to Tata Communications’ existing global network. The company plans to add around 6 petabits per second (pbps) of network capacity under the programme, taking its total capacity to approximately 7.25 pbps once the expansion is completed. The proposed capacity addition is scheduled between FY30-36 and will be financed via operating cash flows. Its existing network capacity utilisation stands at around 70%-80%. Tata Communications said the investment will help it cater to demand from hyperscalers, AI platforms, cloud providers, global capability centres (GCCs), enterprises and digital-native businesses. The network is designed to support the high capacity, reliability and low latency required to move data between computing infrastructure and data centres. The first phase will focus on the Mumbai-Pune-Hyderabad-Chennai corridor, one of India’s key AI and hyperscale growth routes. Subsequent phases will extend connectivity to emerging data centre clusters in other parts of the country as well. The expansion is expected to connect India’s key AI and data centre hubs with international cable landing stations, strengthening connectivity between domestic infrastructure and global AI hubs and allowing for large volumes of data to be shared quickly and reliably between computing facilities. “The AI economy needs more than compute. It needs a network built for speed, scale and resilience,” said Tata Communications’ CPTO Rupesh Chokshi. E2E Networks To Add Compute Capacity The announcement comes as Indian infrastructure providers step up investments to support growing demand for AI training and inference workloads. Earlier today, cloud and AI infrastructure provider E2E Networks announced plans to expand its AI factory capacity by nearly 59%, adding around 5.4 megawatts (MW) of capacity through NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and other Blackwell GPUs. The proposed expansion will take E2E Networks’ AI factory capacity to approximately 14.6 MW. The company said the additional capacity will support large-scale model training, post-training, production inference, agentic AI and multimodal applications. The company is seeing demand from foundation model builders, AI-native startups, enterprises, higher education and research institutions, and public-sector programmes. It also highlighted growing demand for AI infrastructure hosted in India, particularly among organisations operating in regulated and data-sensitive environments. “India’s AI builders are moving beyond the pilot stage. They now are actively consuming AI tokens in production at previously unheard of scales,” said Tarun Dua, founder and managing director of E2E Networks. This capacity expansion comes on the back of heightened demand for E2E Networks’ GPU services. Its operating revenue jumped 411% to ₹223.8 Cr in the second quarter of FY27 from ₹43.8 Cr in the year-ago quarter. It posted a consolidated net profit of ₹72.7 Cr during the quarter under review, reversing a net loss of ₹13.5 Cr a year earlier. It also signed a multi-year cloud GPU contract worth approximately ₹1,000 Cr during the quarter.

What to know about China's plenum as Xi seeks stronger party discipline
HONG KONG — China's political leaders and elites began a four-day meeting Monday to discuss strengthening the ruling Communist Party's discipline, as Chinese President Xi Jinping pushes for greater loyalty and reliability from officials while deepening his yearslong campaign against corruption.
This week's closed-door gathering, known as the fifth plenum of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, comes roughly a year before Xi is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader and personnel changes to key leadership bodies.
Xi began the meeting by delivering a work report and speaking about a draft policy decision on advancing "full and rigorous party self-governance," according to China's official Xinhua News Agency. The policy aims to make cadres more disciplined, effective and less corrupt.
While Xi has consolidated his grip on power, analysts say the plenum will offer him an opportunity to further align what Chinese officials do with what Beijing wants.
"The plenum is a chance to ensure the new generations rising the ranks share Xi's assessment of the opportunities and risks China faces," said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London's Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.
Here's what to know about one of Beijing's most significant political meetings this year.
Xi targets underperforming cadres and corruption
Xi's anti-graft drive has been a defining feature of his rule since he came to power in 2012. Purges of officials — including some viewed as his political rivals — have been carried out on a scale that led critics to argue the campaign was also used to consolidate his power.
But his focus has expanded to cracking down on underperforming cadres too. In recent years, the number of officials punished for "formalism" and "bureaucratism" — misconduct such as dereliction of duty, inaction and reckless acts that seriously hinder development — has surged.
Xi's policy proposals reflect his emphasis on the party's "self-revolution," a concept centered on the party reforming itself through efforts such as rooting out corruption and building ideological commitment, analysts say.
Osman said the disciplinary crackdowns are now aimed more at institutional longevity.
"It's less about purging elite rivals and more about building a disciplined system that can sustain Xi's political priorities across leadership cycles," she said.
Record-high disciplinary campaigns also do not necessarily mean a rebound in corruption, but rather that Xi has been steadily raising the bar for the party's expectations of officials, she added.
Mingda Qiu, senior analyst of Eurasia Group's China practice, said Beijing has been building its agenda for months.
"The message is clear: the anti-corruption campaign is not winding down. Officials are not only tested for loyalty, but also for compliance and action," he said.
Xi said in a January meeting that while decisions by the party's top leadership were smoothly implemented in general, inspections and audits found problems such as failures to comply and improper execution, according to an October article in the Qiushi Journal, a publication of the central committee.
Xi warned against "two-faced people" who might profess political loyalty while privately defying orders and doing as they please.
"During leadership transitions, we must keep our eyes sharp, elevate good cadres who are truly loyal and reliable, consistent in word and deed, and willing to take responsibility, and never allow 'two-faced people' or those driven by self-interest to slip through," Xi was quoted as saying.
Xi's purges of top army officials will be put on display
The number of empty seats in the conference hall this week will help observers gauge how widespread Xi's purges have been.
Neil Thomas, senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, and his colleagues Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang noted that while Xi's civilian purges are record-breaking, 42 out of 44 officials affiliated with the military elected as full central committee members in 2022 have also been purged or disappeared.
The central committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 full and alternate members. Thomas and his colleagues estimated turnout this week could be less than 80%, potentially setting a record low at any plenum since the end of former leader Mao Zedong's rule in 1976.
Attention will also be on new demands on the officials who remain.
Thomas expects tighter scrutiny of public spending and major projects, more use of technology to uncover corruption, and tougher consequences for officials who fail to deliver on Xi's priorities.
New personnel appointments are possible, though Xi may wait until a once-in-five-years Communist Party Congress next year to anoint his picks, said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London. If he does fill any openings, it will be with loyalists, he added.
Hints at a Xi successor are unlikely
The underlying theme of the fifth plenum is that it will be another opportunity for Xi to position himself for an unprecedented fourth term in office.
Xi, who removed presidential term limits in 2018, is viewed by some as the most powerful Chinese leader since Mao. He is widely expected to be confirmed as party leader for the next term in the fall of 2027.
Ahead of that, Thomas said new ideological language reinforcing Xi's authority might emerge at this week's meeting.
He said the plenum should prepare the ground for Xi's fourth term and reinforce expectations of political and policy continuity.
"After Xi has purged so many of the people that he promoted at the last congress, watch for tougher scrutiny of the officials competing to join his next leadership team," he said.

Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
- Published
For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.
But that may end soon.
Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.
New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.
The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.
Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally.
"Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.
Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.
A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.
BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.
Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.
But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business.
A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level.
"A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.
Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.
Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.
While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".
While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.
Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.
Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.
Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible.
While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".
Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.
The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.
But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.
Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.
Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."
While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.
Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).
Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.
Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.
Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies.
"This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.
Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work.
"Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.
Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.

Srinagar, Oct 26: The Consulate General of India has assured all possible assistance to Indian Umrah pilgrims affected by ongoing flight disruptions, stating that efforts are underway to facilitate the early return of stranded passengers.
In a communication to JKNC MP Chowdhary Mohammad Ramzan, Fahad Suri, representing the Consulate General, said the Consulate was fully aware of the difficulties being faced by Indian pilgrims and was extending all possible assistance to affected nationals.
He informed that 24×7 control rooms have been established in Jeddah and Makkah to address the concerns of pilgrims. The Consulate is also maintaining regular contact with affected pilgrims, tour operators and the concerned Saudi authorities.
According to the communication, teams from the Consulate, with the support of Indian community associations and volunteers, are facilitating essential medicines, food and other immediate requirements, particularly for vulnerable pilgrims.
The Consulate is also coordinating closely with the Saudi Ministry of Hajj and Umrah regarding pilgrims’ welfare and with local authorities on visa-related matters.
Regarding the return of affected passengers, Suri said the issue of alternative flight arrangements and additional flight capacity had been taken up with the concerned authorities in India and the airlines.
He added that some affected pilgrims had already returned through available scheduled flights, while efforts were continuing to facilitate the early return of the remaining passengers.
Assuring continued support, the Consulate stated that it remained available to extend necessary assistance in specific cases brought to its attention.

India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

MADRID — With the first pivotal trial showing a customized mRNA treatment improved outcomes for cancer patients presented here this weekend, the conversation has already turned to how melanoma specialists should adopt the medicine — and how widely these novel vaccines can be deployed.
“In principle, this type of approach may be applicable to other types of tumors,” James Larkin of London’s Royal Marsden Hospital, the scientific co-chair for this year’s European Society for Medical Oncology meeting, said at an opening press conference.
The trial, from Merck and Moderna, demonstrated that the bespoke mRNA-based vaccine intismeran reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42% when combined with Merck’s checkpoint inhibitor Keytruda versus Keytruda alone. The results are a clear victory for the field after what Vinod Balachandran of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center called in a lecture a “long and sordid” history of trying to develop cancer vaccines that, until now, has essentially added up to 100 years of failure.

Air conditioners must be switched off after 5 PM in Hyderabad water board offices. The instruction forms part of a drive to reduce water and electricity use. Every office must cut consumption by at least 20% compared with its previous usage. Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board Managing Director K. Ashok Reddy issued the directions. According to him, conservation must start within the organisation before officials ask citizens to save water. The aim is to make office practices reflect the advice given to residents. “Change must begin with us, and we must set an example for everyone. Before telling people to use water sparingly, we must practise it ourselves,” the Hyderabad Mail quoted Ashok Reddy as saying. “We cannot change society without changing ourselves, and we cannot tell others what we do not practise ourselves. Therefore, the change in conserving water and electricity must begin in our own offices,” Reddy added. Expected El Niño conditions in the coming period are behind the emphasis on saving water. Reddy stressed the need to protect water resources and build a public conservation movement. He wants the board’s offices to lead by example. Under the instructions, all office ACs must be set at 25°C. Their use must stop after 5 PM. Exceptions are allowed only for essential maintenance work, with special approval from senior officials. The restriction therefore forms part of the board’s effort to prevent unnecessary power use. Offices must also collect water discharged by ACs instead of letting it go to waste. This water should be reused for gardening, cleaning, and other activities that do not require drinking water. The measure brings water reuse into the same conservation effort as electricity savings. Officials must check buildings, toilets, pipelines, taps and storage tanks for leaks. Any leaks found must be repaired immediately. Officers responsible for these areas must monitor them closely to prevent wastage, the Hyderabad Mail reported. The electricity instructions extend beyond air conditioners. Lights, fans, computers and other equipment must be switched off whenever unnecessary. Particular attention must be paid to power wastage after office hours. Reddy said every employee should treat electricity conservation as a personal responsibility. Each office must regularly review its water and electricity consumption. Officials must compare current figures with earlier usage and work towards the minimum 20% reduction. Heads of offices will be responsible for implementing these instructions. Reddy warned that negligence in preventing wastage would be viewed seriously. He said there would be no tolerance for lax implementation. Conservation, he stressed, should show in everyday functioning rather than remain a publicity exercise. He urged employees across departments to work together and turn small savings into daily habits. Such habits could bring significant reductions in consumption, he said. The board will also recognise offices that implement the measures and meet the savings target. Officers and employees performing well will receive appreciation certificates every month. Alice Augusta Ball lived a very short life. In 24 years, she had remarkable achievements, and was predictably forgotten for a while, until the world was shaken up to her brilliance. Her work on distilling chaulmoogra oil for use as effective treatment for leprosy brought hope to a number of patients globally.
An African American woman born into middle class in the late 1800s, Alice Ball benefitted from an early exposure to chemical processes as her family was involved in photography. She went on to shine in science at school, and could hope to move on to university, a rare opportunity for a woman and a person of her race at that time. She lived up to her potential and at the University of Washington, racked up her skills in chemistry and pharmacy. She finished two degrees – a bachelor’s in pharmaceutical chemistry and a bachelor’s in pharmacy – thus arming herself for a career –short lived, but so sparkling, people are still talking about her, though subsequent innovations have transformed care for leprosy.
With a full scholarship, another rarity for the times, Alice moved to the College of Hawai‘i, and became the first woman and the first African American to earn a master’s degree in chemistry. We mention it because it is an achievement, but also because it was an achievement that attracted the kind of attention a career flourishes on. It is said that Harry T. Hollmann, a public health officer, thought her thesis research on extracting active compounds from the kava (awa) root might have implications for his passion – finding cures for leprosy.
Leprosy or Hansen’s disease is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, and was discovered by Norwegian physician Gerhard Armauer Hansen in the 1870s. While it is prevalent in people living in tropical regions, leprosy which affects the nervous system, also has the moniker of being the world’s oldest disease. Evidence of leprosy has been found in skeletons from back in 2000 BCE. Those affected develop visible skin lesions and extremities including fingers and toes malformed and misshapen fingers. Sometimes amputations were also performed on limbs that could not be salvaged. As a result of the disfiguration, the stigma surrounding the disease was so high, those with leprosy had to be sequestered in camps and asylums outside the community.
Alice did accept Hollman’s invitation and what she managed to achieve was to revolutionise the field of leprosy care in the very near future. Described as the Ball Method, Alice devised a method that would “convert the oil’s fatty acids into water-soluble ethyl esters that could be injected into patients. Until then Chaulmoogra oil was promising as treatment for leprosy, but it was thick, not soluble in water, besides difficult to inject and swallow. Soon the world adopted the Ball Method and the landmark contribution changed life for the better for people who were battling leprosy across the world, without hope until then. Alice was in her early 20s at the time of this achievement.
Records of the time say, since the new formulation dispersed in the bloodstream instead of pooling under the skin, patients for the first time celebrated as earlier, there was none of the severe local reactions and oozing oil that the injections caused. Used on patients at Kalihi Hospital in Hawai‘i, researchers managed to show that patients administered the new formulation, became ‘bacteriologically negative, their lesions resolved, and many were discharged from isolation to rejoin their families, without fear of infecting them.’ This injectable preparation remained the best available treatment worldwide until sulfone antibiotics, Dapsone, in combination with other drugs, replaced it in the 1940s, facilitating a future unimaginable until then, for those who were diagnosed with leprosy and condemned to social isolation.
However, Alice’s contribution never made it to the headlines thanks to a set of factors – her gender, age and race were primary. She died young, it is speculated that it could be a result of a laboratory accident, a senior male colleague, her department head Arthur L. Dean appropriated and published her work without sharing any credit, in fact, promoting it as the ‘Dean method’, accounts of that period list.
It went unchallenged until decades later, when researcher Harry Hollmann revisited the archives and credited Ball. Finally, the historical records were righted, and Alice Ball’s name was affixed to the method she had painstakingly developed. By 24, despite the disdvantaged circumstances she worked in, Alice Ball had changed the world, it is a matter of speculation how much she would have achieved had she lived longer, but a safe bet to say she would have left a deeper impact. For the punch she packed in her short life, and the revolution she managed in that life, it’s time we say her name, say “Alice Augusta Ball.”
