Racecourse fined after jockey taken to A&E in horsebox
- Published
A racecourse has been fined £6,500 after a jockey was taken to hospital in a horsebox instead of an ambulance.
The incident took place in March at Sedgefield Racecourse in County Durham.
A disciplinary panel of the British Horseracing Authority (BHA) found that the racecourse had failed to comply with five "general instructions" within its Rules of Racing.
The injured jockey's identity was kept private but it was reported that he suffered a left clavicle and shoulder injury after a fall, and was examined by a doctor at the course.
He was cleared to race again but said he was still in pain, which resulted in a doctor advising him to go to A&E.
By then all the ambulance crews had left the venue, and he was taken in a horsebox with the medical staff following behind.
"The 'general instructions' require proper transfer to hospital with accompaniment from qualified medical staff not, as here, being followed in a car," the BHA panel said.
It also added that the jockey was in too much pain to get into the following car.
The other failings at the venue included a telephone line not working and "tired worn rooms not conveying a clean clinical area".
The racecourse has acknowledged the "errors and shortcomings" and an inspection took place in April which revealed "significant progress".

Anthropic filed its hotly anticipated IPO prospectus on Monday, spelling out parts of the company’s business, strategy, and risk profile ahead of its public debut. Though the filing, known as an S-1, is several hundred pages long, it has some notable omissions—namely, certain financial figures.
“Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $_____ for the three months ended September 30, 2026,” reads the first of dozens of such examples.
It’s relatively common for companies to redact certain information in their S-1 filings, and Securities and Exchange Commission rules allow for a certain degree of leniency around the practice, particularly when it comes to information considered “confidential.”
Still, it’s helpful to know what, exactly, these companies decide to leave out. In Anthropic’s case, the missing details largely revolve around financials for its most recent quarter, which concluded at the end of September, and lease agreements tied to its compute investments. While experts expect many details to be disclosed before Anthropic goes public, their current absence may hint at the uncertainties of investing in artificial intelligence, as companies work to secure sufficient compute.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.
Michael Dambra, accounting and law professor at University at Buffalo School of Management, tells WIRED that there are “practical reasons” for its third quarter numbers to be absent: September 30 was only a few weeks ago, and “closing the books for a company of this size takes time.”
Companies can also be liable for misstatements in their registration statements, “so there is a strong incentive not to publish numbers before they have been fully vetted,” Dambra says. SEC rules require that “Anthropic would need to update the filing with third-quarter financials” if the company goes public any later than about mid-November, he says.
As for data center lease agreements, Erica Neuman, an accounting professor at Youngstown State University, says it’s “not unusual” for companies to redact confidential details from “contract exhibits,” which could include lease terms.
However, Neuman adds that it’s worth scrutinizing whether Anthropic’s redactions would prevent, or make it more difficult, for investors to analyze Anthropic’s financial obligations and whether they may impact the company’s cash flow.
Many of Anthropic’s financial obligations relate to compute, which is the “most significant operating cost in our business,” according to the S-1. It’s also a business risk for the company, and it’s laid out both in terms of undersupply and overinvestment. (Parts of the AI industry have been warning that chip constraints could slow the progress of AI.)
Anthropic’s prospectus puts more emphasis on the risks of overinvestment, stating that the company needs to make forward investments in compute resources that will seem “irresponsibly large” at first glance.
Chips, Anthropic explains, are approached as a “single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners,” including Amazon, Google, Nvidia, and AMD. The company notes that it has entered into contracts “with an aggregate committed spend of more than $____, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.” Some of these contracts are set to be completed before December of 2030, while others may extend through 2045.
Though the prospectus touches on Anthropic’s compute uncertainties due to factors like limited land and power resources, Patrick Moorhead, CEO and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy believes investors are owed more detail.
“It’s about characterizing the odds and impact individually across each of the areas. Anthropic owes investors more information, such as a probability of these individual issues, characterizing the percentage chance and the degree of the impact,” he tells WIRED. “Not ‘could materially impact.’”
Anthropic does provide some eye-catching estimates in footnotes. Since December 31, 2025, it has started or amended “compute and infrastructure” leases with “future minimum payment obligations” worth approximately $417 billion in aggregate. Since June 30, it’s added another $245 billion to its future payment obligations, all related to infrastructure agreements. It also expanded “certain existing commercial agreements” that it caveats “have not yet been finalized,” for an additional $125 billion to $150 billion.
Include “short term” agreements with “minimum non-cancelable payments,” Anthropic says, and that’s another $21 billion. In total, it will owe, at minimum, an estimated $808 billion if it follows through on all of this.
Ben Bajarin, chief executive and a principal analyst at Creative Strategies who tracks the chip industry, says that this is likely just the first draft of Anthropic’s prospectus, and that he expects a lot of gaps to be filled in an updated version.
Despite how common S-1 redactions are, Dambra describes them as “controversial.” While companies may argue that they’re “protecting proprietary information,” Dambra says that skeptics accuse them of using redactions “opportunistically” in order to “avoid disclosing politically or socially sensitive information.”
However, Dambra argues that redacting information may come at a cost. He notes that companies with redactions in their S-1s were also more likely to “underprice” their shares at the initial public offering.
When companies redact information in their S-1, Dambra says they typically understand that they’ve created an “information gap” between them and outside investors. Understanding that investors will treat this gap with “suspicion,” companies may feel inclined to “entice” them to participate in the IPO by setting a lower starting price.
It’s unclear what Anthropic’s opening price may end up being, or how investors may be interpreting the redactions in the company’s S-1. But according to Bajarin, the whole AI industry is one form of “blank” or another when it comes to crunching the numbers based on access to chips and infrastructure right now. So, yes, it’s all a risk.
“All of this,” he says, “just shows how absurdly early we are in enterprise adoption of an AI market that will be more than $3 trillion yearly and likely growing.”

New-age tech stocks lost over $11 Bn in combined market capitalisation this week, with Swiggy leading a broad sell-off amid weakness in the wider Indian equity market. The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

14 workers trapped in pulley lift in Bengal coal mine after glitch, rescue ops on
At least 14 workers of Eastern Coalfields Limited (ECL) were trapped inside a pulley lift that malfunctioned around 200 feet underground at ECL's Kumardihi 'A' Colliery in West Bengal. Rescue teams are working to free the entangled rope, while food and water are being supplied to the trapped workers.
At least 14 workers of Eastern Coalfields Limited (ECL) were trapped inside a pulley lift that developed a technical glitch around 200 feet underground at a coal mine in West Bengal's Paschim Bardhaman district on Monday evening. Trade unions said the workers were safe and the rescue operation could take around three hours.
The incident took place at Kumardihi ‘A’ Colliery in Asansol. The lift, locally known as a ‘doli’, was being used to transport workers between the surface and the underground mine when its operating rope got entangled in the pulley drum inside the engine room, stopping the lift movement.
There were varying accounts of the number of workers stranded underground. While initial information suggested that 14 workers were trapped, an ECL official put the figure at around 10 to 12. Trade union representatives said 12-14 workers were inside the affected lift system.
Rescue and repair efforts were launched soon after the incident. Teams are attempting to free the entangled rope by rotating the drum in the opposite direction so that the lift can be operated again, and the workers brought to the surface.
Trade union leader Mintu Banerjee said the operation could take another two to three hours, depending on how quickly the technical fault was fixed. He said drinking water, dry fruits and other food items were being supplied to the stranded workers through the rope system.
An ECL official said there was no shortage of fresh air underground and that the workers were responding from below, indicating that they were in contact with those at the site.
Local MLA Jitendra Tiwari said the immediate priority was to bring all the workers out safely. He confirmed that the stranded workers were responding and that food had been sent to them.
Tiwari said questions about the cause of the malfunction and possible lapses in safety arrangements should be taken up after the rescue operation. He added that the role of trade unions, safety committees and other concerned authorities would be examined once the workers were brought out. If any negligence was established, strict action should follow, he said.
CONCERNS OVER LIFT MAINTENANCE
The incident raised fresh concerns over the maintenance of lifting equipment used to transport workers in underground mines.
Some workers claimed that the equipment had undergone repairs a few months ago and alleged that the doli had developed technical problems on earlier occasions as well. They also flagged previous instances of the lift getting stuck and concerns over the condition of its rope.
The claims have brought the focus back on the maintenance of underground transportation systems and the safety checks carried out on such equipment.
For now, rescue teams are working to resolve the technical fault and restore the lift's operation. Further details on the exact number of workers trapped and the progress of the rescue operation are awaited.

Scarborough's Eric Bauza, modern voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and others, dead at 46
Emmy-award winning voice actor's family said he passed away 'suddenly' in an Instagram post
Eric Bauza of Scarborough, Ont., the Emmy-award winning voice actor best known for the iconic Bugs Bunny, has died. He was 46.
Bauza's family announced he had passed away "suddenly" in a post to his Instagram profile Sunday night. The family did not say the cause of death, but indicated they would share more at a later time.
Bauza grew up watching Bugs Bunny's exploits on the Looney Tunes cartoons at his home in the city. In 2020, he was charged with bringing the character to life in all his carrot-munching, prank-pulling glory.
"It is a dream come true," Bauza told host Ismaila Alfa on CBC Radio's Metro Morning at the time.
In addition to Bugs Bunny, Bauza voiced multiple other characters including Daffy Duck, Tweety Bird and Marvin the Martian. It took two auditions and plenty of practice to land the parts, he told Alfa.
In 2020, he gave his advice to young voice actors, telling them to remember that, at its base, it's "about the acting, first."
"You have to instill a performance that's grounded in reality," he said.

Rubio turns to small Indian town as US faces high oil prices
- Published
The western Indian port town of Jamnagar is not a usual stop for foreign leaders, yet it featured prominently in US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recent visit.
So, why did Rubio visit the town? And, more importantly, why did he skip the Indian capital, Delhi?
The answer to both questions may have less to do with India and more to do with Donald Trump administration's domestic compulsions – or, more precisely, its domestic oil needs.
Rubio arrived in the financial capital Mumbai on Tuesday, where he met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and some of the country's top business leaders. He officially ended his trip in Jamnagar - in the western state of Gujarat - home to the giant oil refinery owned by one of Asia's richest men, Mukesh Ambani.
It was his second trip to the country this year and experts say what is significant this time is the timing of the visit as well as his choice of destinations.
The Trump administration is under pressure to keep fuel prices in check ahead of November's US midterm elections, while rising tensions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies.
With little new refining capacity expected in the immediate future in the US, India's ability to process large volumes of crude oil offers Washington a potential way to ease pressure on the fuel markets.
And that puts Reliance's Jamnagar refinery at the centre of the equation.
The visit, however, comes at a tricky moment in India-US relations. Trump has imposed tariffs on Indian goods, there are sanctions against Delhi for buying Russian energy (though currently paused) and there is a trade deal between the two countries that has remained elusive for around 20 months now.
Announcing the visit, the US State Department had earlier said that it would focus on energy cooperation, commercial investment and economic ties.
The official itinerary also did not include Delhi, which raised some questions, especially from Indian opposition politicians. But analysts say the choice was strategic.
"Delhi is where the trust gap is largest. Officials there are unhappy with a number of decisions and policies from Trump's administration," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC.
But former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautions against reading too much into him skipping the capital.
"This was primarily an energy-focused visit," she says. "And after all, Rubio did meet the foreign minister in Mumbai."
The meeting between the two foreign ministers at the Taj Hotel covered trade, investment, energy security and defence cooperation, according to official statements. India's foreign ministry also said both sides welcomed progress in trade negotiations and reaffirmed their commitment to concluding a deal, which has long been in the works.
But once the diplomatic meetings were over, Rubio headed to Jamnagar, where the crown jewel of the Ambani business empire is located. This came to define the trip.
Shankar says the refinery visit "showed how much importance the US is attaching to getting more refined fuel into the market before the November midterms".
Reliance's Jamnagar complex can process about 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, roughly 1.5% of global refining capacity, according to the company website.
It is also a major exporter of diesel and other petroleum products, giving it a crucial role in global fuel markets.
During a tightly controlled visit on Wednesday, with limited media access, Rubio toured the facility and met members of the Ambani family, including Mukesh Ambani.
The company later released a statement, saying, "the visit included wide-ranging discussions on the global energy landscape and opportunities for commercial partnerships across conventional and new energy". It, however, did not specifically address any commitments to buy crude oil or supply refined products.
Just a day earlier, while speaking to the press, Rubio had called India a "refining superpower" and said the US wanted Reliance to process more Venezuelan oil.
"They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They've done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, that's something they could do," he told reporters.
Rubio added that oil from Venezuela "can certainly provide relief" in the short term and can possibly help ease supply pressures amid tensions in the Middle East.
Reliance was once among the largest buyers of Venezuelan crude before US sanctions disrupted trade. After Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was captured in a US intervention earlier this year and Washington eased sanctions on the country's energy sector, Reliance re-emerged as a major importer.
Experts also say the visit might ease some tensions in the Delhi-Washington relationship over India's purchase of Russian oil.
India became one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Between December 2022 and July 2026, it accounted for 37% of Russia's crude oil exports, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
And Reliance was among the Indian companies that processed Russian crude.
In August 2025, US President Donald Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods over its Russian oil purchases, taking total tariffs on many Indian goods to 50%. The US, however, withdrew the additional penalty in February 2026 but India's import of Russian oil has continued to be an irritant in Washington-Delhi ties.
India has always said that securing affordable and reliable energy for its 1.4 billion people was its priority.
Then earlier this month, the US itself temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.
In that context, experts say Rubio's Jamnagar visit is aligned to three goals that the US appears to be pursuing: reducing India's dependence on Russian crude, encouraging greater imports of Venezuelan and American oil, and advancing a trade deal in which energy cooperation could become a key area of agreement.
There is also another possible business angle behind this push.
Kugelman says Rubio had two reasons to meet the Ambani family. First, to secure greater refining of Venezuelan oil and second to seek assurances that Reliance remained interested in backing a proposed Texas refinery.
In March, Trump announced a proposed refinery at the Port of Brownsville in Texas on his Truth Social platform. He said that it would be the first major new refinery in the US in 50 years.
Reliance has not publicly commented on it and there are no details on the project or when the work is expected to begin.
"The Texas facility may not be as immediately important to US interests as the arrangement tied to Venezuelan oil, but I still think it's part of the story," he says.
However, analysts point out that closer cooperation with Reliance and progress on energy security do not necessarily mean a trade deal is imminent.
"I don't think anyone really expected a trade deal to be announced at this point, but this trip seems to have helped get the relationship back on track, to the extent that it can, given the significant points of tension that remain," Kugelman said.
Rajani Sinha, the chief economist at credit rating agency CareEdge, told the BBC that greater cooperation could allay energy security concerns in both countries, help push the stalled trade negotiations forward and "boost trade and sentiment" in India.
Meera Shankar says that India is possibly "waiting for the US to formalise its tariff positions so that we know whether Delhi has a preferential trade deal".
She adds that, although ties between the two countries have been strained in recent times, their bilateral trade continues to grow.
India's merchandise exports to the US was $50.81bn between April and September, up 11.1% from the previous year, according to India's ministry of commerce. Its imports rose to $32.33bn from $25.66bn in the same period. India's merchandise trade surplus with the US narrowed to $18.48bn from $20.07bn a year earlier.
"The economic relationship remains strong, but a long period of uncertainty could eventually affect it," Shankar said.
So, for now, the visit may have possibly helped get the relationship back on track, but whether that translates into a trade agreement or a lasting shift in energy ties remains to be seen.

Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasrin, who is currently living in Kolkata, on October 20, Tuesday, wrote on Facebook that although Leftists in West Bengal organise bookstalls during Durga Puja, such stalls are absent during other ‘religious’ festivals such as Christmas and Eid. She questioned why Leftists choose not to sell books promoting ‘atheism’ during other religious festivals, but instead promote them only during a Hindu festival.
In her post, she wrote (translated from Bengali), “Someone asked, “Have you ever seen Leftists selling books on atheism to Muslims near an Eidgah on Eid? Have you ever seen them selling books by Richard Dawkins or Christopher Hitchens to people attending Christmas prayers on Christmas Day? Then, quite naturally, the question arises: why do they want to sell books on atheism specifically at Hindu Durga Puja pandals?” What answer do the Leftists of Kolkata have to this question?”
This post has garnered over 7,000 likes and 1,300 reshares, and garnered significant traction, although she had disabled the comment section of the Facebook post.
Nasrin, who has been in exile since leaving Bangladesh in 1994 amid death threats and protests over her writings critical of the ‘dogmas’ of Islam, was forced to leave Kolkata in 2007 following violent protests against her autobiography ‘Dwikhandito’ and pressure on the then CPI(M)-led Left Front government.
She remained unable to return to West Bengal for nearly 19 years, with successive CPI(M) and Trinamool Congress (TMC) governments in power. However, in July 2026, following the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) coming to power in the state, Nasrin returned to Kolkata and was publicly welcomed and celebrated by sections of the Right-wing BJP-RSS ecosystem.
Against this backdrop, her recent Facebook post questioned what she portrayed as the Left’s selective promotion of atheism. Moreover, her statement comes on the heels of state authorities demolishing and damaging certain bookstalls set up by Left parties near Jadavpur’s 8b bus stand on October 17.
Fact Check
Alt News found several social media posts and news reports that refute Nasrin’s claim that the bookstalls are exclusively set up during Durga Puja.
The Students’ Federation of India (SFI) and the Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI) have been organising a bookstall near Park Street, where Christmas is celebrated in Kolkata, for at least 10 years. Prominent Left leader Biman Bose has also visited the stall. The bookstall has been featured on the social media handles of SFI, DYFI, CPI(M) and other affliated organisations, and has also been covered by the media. The Telegraph reported the setting up of the bookstall at Park Street for the first time in 2016, Alt News also founds images of stalls from 2017, 2022, 2024.
Below are images of a bookstall set up by SFI-DYFI during Christmas in 2017:
Below are images of a bookstall set up during Christmas in 2022:
Below are images of a bookstall set up during Christmas in 2024:
Similarly, the SFI-DYFI local committee in the Khidderpore area of Kolkata organised a bookstall during Eid this year. Khidderpore has historically been home to a significant Muslim population. The bookstall was organised for two days and was featured on the Facebook page of the CPI(M) Kolkata Port Assembly Committee.
Below are glimpses of the stall set up on Eid at Khidderpore:
Further, Nasrin claimed that the Leftist bookstalls only sell books promoting atheism. However, the images on social media, posted by people who bought books from hundreds of these stalls, clearly show a vast array of books from across genres being sold in these stalls.
An Alt News correspondent visited the CPI(M) bookstall set up near Jadavpur 8B bus stand and encountered a diverse section of books, ranging from Bengali classics, poetry, history among others. Books on Ramkrishna and Vivekananda were also available at the stall.
CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh made a video, interviewing a woman who visited the stall and described herself as a devotee of spiritual leader Lalon Fakir. In the video, she shared her book haul which comprised books on Lalon Fakir, and other Hindu spiritual leaders like Nityananda Mahaprabhu, and even a cook book.
CPI(M) leader Sudip Sengupta, who is in charge of the 8B bookstall regularly posted pictures of the stall on his Facebook page. In one such image, physician Dr. Arjun Dasgupta was seen holding a book on Swami Vivekananda, along with a book on the Second World War.
According to Dasgupta, apart from Leftist books, the stall also contains books such as Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s Anandamath. “I was looking at some old pictures my family took at the Jadavpur 8B stall, and I could see Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s books behind me. His books include ‘Anandamath’, which has the song ‘Vande Mataram’. So it is simply not true that these stalls only sell books promoting atheism. These stalls are part of Bengal’s culture, and anyone who loves books should stand against efforts to shut them down,” said Dasgupta.
“We Bengalis feel that a book is a book, whether it is sold at an ISKCON stall or a CPI(M) stall. We love books and naturally gather around any stall that sells them. When we were children, these stalls introduced many of us to great books from around the world. I vividly remember my father buying me a copy of ‘Ispat’, the Bengali translation of Nikolai Ostrovsky’s ‘How the Steel Was Tempered’. I think thousands of people like me have similar memories,” he added.
Similarly, the Rashbehari-1 area committee of the CPI(M) set up a book stall near the Kalighat temple during Durga Puja. Images of the stall show stacks of books ranging from Bengali children’s classics such as Thakurmar Jhuli to literary works including ‘Ichhamati’ by Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay, ‘Kapalkundala’ by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, ‘Grihadaha’ and ‘Devdas’ by Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay, among others. Books on Maa Sarada, and books written by Rabindranath Tagore were also visible at the stall.
Thus, the findings above show that Nasrin’s claim that Leftists organise bookstalls only during Hindu festivals such as Durga Puja is false, as there is documented evidence of Left organisations organising bookstalls during both Eid and Christmas. Her claim that books exclusively on atheism are sold at the stalls is also false, as there is documented evidence of books of various genres being sold across Left bookstalls.

After Vice City, Ambrosia is one of the most interesting locations in GTA 6. While Vice City dazzles with high-rises, neon-lit streets, and beaches, Ambrosia paints a contrasting picture in the State of Leonida.
GTA 6 Ambrosia Overview
Ambrosia is one of the six major locations in GTA 6, featuring extensive industries, agricultural fields, biker groups, and local politics.
Its identity revolves around the American industry, traditional local values, and the influence of a motorcycle club.
Rockstar’s official promotional postcard for major GTA 6 map locations includes Ambrosia, titled “Keeping Leonida Sweet.” This indicates how the Allied Crystal sugar refinery is basically the biggest factory in this region.
Although the industry is a recognizable landmark in GTA 6, the official images depict storage areas, vehicles, and extensive infrastructure. The broader setting also includes roads, residential areas, agricultural lands, and other buildings.
Another major part of Ambrosia’s identity is the biker culture, as the promotional material features members of the Final Chapter MC. The postcard description mentions the biker gang provides almost everything beyond the refinery’s jobs, hinting at a powerful relationship between the club and the surrounding community.
Where to Find Ambrosia in GTA 6
Ambrosia is a confirmed region that is located right at the center of the state of Leonida, the GTA 6 map that is twice in size compared to RDR 2.
The official postcard identifies the area by name and mentions that Ambrosia is in the heart of Leonida; however, the studio has not released a complete, fully labelled map.
So, the exact position and size should not be described using unofficial map reconstructions as if they’re established facts.
The official images provide several visual clues about the area, though. The refinery dominates the industrial landscape while other images show bikers, open fields, vehicles, and structures beyond the main facility. A large body of water also appears in the broader regional imagery.
Key Areas and Locations in Ambrosia
Among the several key landmarks located in the GTA 6 Ambrosia region, the industrial facility is the defining factor. You can also find some local business shops, agricultural fields, motorsports, and a home base for the off-road culture.
While exploring the key areas in Ambrosia, you might come across several side activities in GTA 6 that can be worth completing once you’re done with the main story. So, here’s a brief about all the key locations in Ambrosia:
- Allied Crystal Sugar Refinery
- Lake Leonida
- Agricultural land
- Off-road tracks
Allied Crystal Sugar Refinery
The Allied Crystal Sugar Refinery is the one industry that has kept Leonida running. It provides jobs for the local population and acts as the central pillar of the area’s economy.
This is an industrial complex with tall processing structures, storage facilities, access roads, and some GTA 6 vehicles associated with the site. Until the official game release in November, it remains unconfirmed whether players will be able to have complete access to these buildings.
Lake Leonida and Surrounding Wetlands
Lake Leonida is an important geographical feature in the wider world of GTA 6 and adds a contrast to the landscape of Ambrosia. Near the lake, you can find waterways, vegetation, and open terrain, which means Ambrosia is not defined exclusively by factories and roads.
Rockstar has shown several airboats and watercraft in the official GTA 6 trailers that can be used as a mode of transport for crossing the massive lake in this region. You can also expect fishing activity in GTA 6 in these regions of Ambrosia.
Industrial District and Agricultural Fields
Beyond the Allied Crystal refinery, Rockstar’s official screenshots showcase an environment shaped by open agricultural land surrounded by buildings, roads, and fields. This setting creates a distinct feel different from the Vice City Skyline in GTA 6.
This way, we know that Ambrosia’s economy is not limited to a single industry. There’s one particularly striking image where a field is shown engulfed in flames. This instantly raises a ton of questions: whether it’s an agricultural operation, an accident, or a side mission for Jason and Lucia in GTA 6.
Motorsports and Off-Road
Motorsports and off-road vehicles naturally fit into rugged settings. Unlike the dense traffic and polished roads of Vice City, Ambrosia’s open spaces appear to be suited to a different style of driving.
The monster truck image from Rockstar is especially notable because it supports the identity of Ambrosia roads in GTA 6. Away from the city center and narrow streets, you might need such vehicles to traverse the muddy and rocky terrain.
Key Characters and Factions in GTA 6 Ambrosia
Among the characters linked to the Ambrosia region, the biker gang and the industrial political characters play a key role. So, here’s all we know about them:
Final Chapter MC
The Final Chapter MC is the most important faction associated with Ambrosia in GTA 6. The initials MC stand for Motorcycle Club, and this local biker gang acts as a major force in this region.
The members of the Final Chapter MC are seen wearing club jackets and riding choppers and cruiser motorcycles. One visible detail is the year 1982, stating when their club was first established and its history in this fictional world of Leonida.
It appears that the Final Chapter MC plays a role in the local economy since it provides everything else except for the jobs at the main sugar industry. Once the game is out, you may dig deeper into this area and find out whether there are any smuggling networks that could help raise your criminal profile in GTA 6.
Allied Crystal and Local Politics
The Allied Crystal is not just an industrial name. Through the official promotions, you must have noticed the name associated with political campaign signs in the area where the biker gang pass through.
These details suggest how the industry and local politics can interact and influence the stability of Ambrosia in GTA 6. The fictional advertising shows ‘Erin Henshaw’ running for office, directly facing off against ‘Keever’.

Saudi Arabia’s King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud has ordered a package of financial support measures, including an additional monthly allowance of 500 Saudi riyals (around $133) for eligible citizens, as the kingdom prepares to introduce changes to electricity and water consumption tariffs from January 1, 2027.
The measures, proposed by Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, will benefit eligible civilian and military employees, retirees, certain family members of deceased contributors or retirees covered by the Social Insurance Law, and households receiving social security support, according to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).
Multiple news outlets have reported the measures, citing the royal decree and official announcements by Saudi Press Agency.
The support package is intended to help citizens manage the financial impact of the revised electricity and water tariffs. The directives also include changes to minimum wage thresholds for Saudi employees under the kingdom’s Nitaqat Saudization programme, which regulates the employment of Saudi nationals in private-sector companies.
Under the royal directives, eligible civilian and military employees covered by civil service pay scales and employment programmes will receive an additional SR500 per month.
The increase will also extend to eligible retirees and family members of deceased contributors or retirees covered by the Social Insurance Law, subject to the applicable rules.
Families receiving benefits under the social security system will also receive an additional monthly payment of SR500, in accordance with the relevant regulations and procedures.
The measures are designed to provide financial relief to eligible households ahead of the electricity and water tariff adjustments scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027.
The announcement comes as Saudi authorities seek to cushion the impact of changes to essential utility costs while continuing efforts to strengthen employment and income opportunities for Saudi citizens.
The royal directives also provide for a phased increase in the minimum monthly wage required for a Saudi employee to count fully towards a private-sector company's Saudization quota under the Nitaqat programme.
Under the first phase, the threshold will rise to SR5,000 per month, effective six months after implementation of the measure begins.
It will subsequently increase to SR6,000 per month, effective 12 months after the first increase is implemented.
The Nitaqat programme is designed to encourage private-sector employers to hire Saudi nationals by linking companies' compliance with Saudization requirements to the proportion of their workforce made up of Saudi citizens.
The revised wage thresholds aim to improve salary levels for Saudi employees and support more sustainable employment opportunities in the private sector.
The changes are part of the wider package announced by King Salman following a proposal from Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
The financial support measures coincide with adjustments to electricity and water consumption tariffs announced by the Saudi Electricity Company and the National Water Company, effective January 1, 2027.
The additional monthly payments for eligible beneficiaries are intended to help offset the financial impact of these changes.
The royal directives cover both direct financial assistance to eligible households and measures intended to improve wages and employment conditions for Saudi nationals.
While the SR500 monthly allowance is intended to provide immediate support to eligible beneficiaries, the phased Nitaqat wage changes focus on the longer-term objective of strengthening Saudi participation in private-sector employment.

Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees across India, the US, the UK and Canada, its second voluntary exit programme this year and a much wider one than the first. Announced on Monday in a memo from Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, the Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) covers more than a quarter of the company's roughly 223,000 employees. It reaches up to level 70 on Microsoft's internal scale, which takes in general managers and some staff with vice president titles, though not corporate vice presidents.
Unlike the retirement buyout Microsoft ran earlier this year, this one has no age or tenure cut-off, and performance plays no part in who qualifies. Eligible employees will get an email with their individual terms within hours. They have until the first week of December to decide, and those who accept will leave at the end of the year.
"This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,"
 Coleman wrote. It also gives participating organisations 
"another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs,"
 she added.
Microsoft's voluntary exit offer pays out like its standard severance
The package matches Microsoft's standard severance. That means base pay linked to tenure and level, continued stock vesting, healthcare for a fixed period and career transition support. What it leaves out is the extended healthcare that made the retirement programme an easy yes for many long-serving staff.
Severance in Microsoft's US layoffs earlier this year started at 60 days of base pay and went up to 39 weeks for most employees. Staff at level 64 and below got a week of base pay for every six months of service, while levels 65 to 67 got two weeks.
Not every team is in. Business leaders decide whether their groups participate, and sales is sitting this one out. Marketing, commercial business, security, and discovery and quantum teams are excluded too, according to people familiar with the matter. Copilot, CoreAI, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance and HR are among those taking part, while Cloud + AI and Microsoft AI are partially in.
Buyouts now sit alongside layoffs in Microsoft's AI-era job cuts
The VEO builds on the Voluntary Retirement Program from this spring, the first in Microsoft's history. That offer went to roughly 8,750 US employees at senior director level and below whose age and years at the company added up to at least 70. About 30% took it, and Microsoft booked a $900 million charge for it in April.
The turnout helped shrink the layoffs that followed, Coleman said later. Microsoft still cut 4,800 jobs in July, about 2% of its workforce, and several hundred more in September, after cutting over 15,000 in 2025. Headcount stood at 223,000 on June 30, down from 228,000 a year earlier.
The company is under pressure to hold down operating costs while it spends tens of billions on data centres and AI infrastructure. Still, Microsoft says the buyout is not a sign it needs fewer people, nor a replacement for layoffs, which remain on the table. It expects a much smaller share of employees to accept this time.
Quarterly earnings on Wednesday could offer a first look at what the offer will cost. Coleman called the programme "new for us" in her memo, and said in July that Microsoft was studying whether voluntary exits could become a regular, even annual, fixture. How many of these 60,000 employees take the deal will likely settle that.

In his last Ranji Trophy innings, Ayush Badoni amassed a career-best score of 217. In his previous innings against Jharkhand, in the 2024-25 season, he had racked up 205. There was an air of inevitability, then, to the 26-year-old sparkling on day one of Delhi’s Ranji Elite Group-C duel against Jharkhand at the JSCA International Stadium.
On a balmy Monday in Jharkhand’s capital, Badoni brought up his sixth First-Class hundred and remained unbeaten on 105 to steer the visitor to 309 for five at stumps. As chanceless as Badoni’s ton was, he couldn’t have helped Delhi stage a commendable recovery without the company of Sumit Mathur, who contributed 50 in an unbroken partnership of 128 runs for the sixth wicket. A moment of fortune fell Mathur’s way as he was called back on 36 despite holing out at long-on because Anukul Roy had overstepped.
Other than this lapse, the partnership between Badoni and Mathur struck no false note. On a pitch where all five wickets fell to the tweakers, the Delhi skipper put on a masterclass in facing spin, cutting, driving and sweeping with regal ease. He consumed just 111 deliveries to reach the three-figure milestone.
READ | Getting bench strength tested is good, says Jharkhand coach Ratan Kumar
Such authority seemed a distant possibility when Delhi was reduced to 181 for five. In the first session, Priyansh Arya and Sanat Sangwan were undone by off-spinners armed with a newish ball. Priyansh was castled by Kounain Quraishi while Sangwan was bowled in identical fashion by Utkarsh Singh.
Between lunch and tea, Delhi found itself in further strife. Yash Dhull’s full-blooded drive was brilliantly snaffled by Anukul on his follow-through. Ayush Doseja’s attempted drive off Quraishi was sliced as pacer Jatin Pandey ran back from cover point and put in a last-ditch dive to complete a stunning catch.
By the close, though, Badoni had not just taken firm control, but also shown signs that another big hundred could be in store.

EXCLUSIVE: Parallax Films has boarded international sales for Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting, directed by Chinese artist-filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong, which is receiving its world premiere in the main competition section of Tokyo International Film Festival.
Qiu is known internationally for his debut narrative feature A New Old Play, which won the Special Jury Prize at the 2021 Locarno Film Festival.
Rooted in the folklore of China’s Sichuan province, Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting unfolds through four separate feasts spanning four millennia, that “bring the living and the dead, gods and ghosts, to the same table”. The word “fuxi” in its title is a Sichuan expression meaning “the joy of the belly”.
Parallax describes the film as a “handcrafted mythic fantasy” referencing Qiu’s unique style of filmmaking that combines painting, theatre and cinema. “Rather than reproducing reality, Qiu uses hand-painted scenic flats, handmade props and theatrical staging to give physical form to his imagination, creating a cinematic universe entirely his own,” Parallax explains.
Watch on Deadline
The cast includes Lee Kang-sheng, Taiwanese filmmaker Tsai Ming-liang’s longtime leading actor, playing two grandmothers in different chapters of the film, marking his first female roles on screen. He is joined by actor-filmmaker Lee Hong-chi, whose directorial debut Love Is A Gun won the Lion of the Future award at Venice, and Annie Chen, known for her role in Netflix series Born For The Spotlight.
Produced by David Tang, Ningyuan Ding and Zhao Jin, Fuxi is a co-production between Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. The project received support from international film funds and project markets including Hong Kong-Asia Film Financing Forum (HAF), MPA APSA Academy Film Fund, Red Sea Fund, Doha Film Institute and Network of Asian Fantastic Films (NAFF) at Korea’s Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival.
The film’s visual world also extends beyond the screen in Fuxi: A Feast For The Universe, Qiu’s large-scale solo exhibition at A4 Art Museum in Chengdu. Bringing together paintings, sets, props and installations, the exhibition translates the film’s imagined universe into a new spatial narrative.
The deal for world sales on Fuxi extends Parallax’s relationship with Qiu, with the company also representing his seven previous films, which include A New Old Play, experimental documentary shorts and documentary features.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Australian judge rejects prisoner's human rights challenge to Vegemite ban
MELBOURNE, Australia — A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state's ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian."
Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of the state of Victoria last year.
He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to "enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background," court documents showed.
Justice Claire Harris accepted prison authorities' refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite "limited his cultural rights" under the charter.
But she found the ban was justified in meeting authorities' goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system.
"The limitation on Mr. McKechnie's ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner," Harris wrote in her 47-page judgment.
Prison officials testify Vegemite could impair drug sniffer dogs and be used to make alcohol
Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state's 12 prisons for the past 20 years because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs' ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content.
McKechnie, who represented himself in court by video link from maximum security Barwon Prison west of Melbourne, argued that the fact that neighboring New South Wales state did not ban Vegemite from its prisons was evidence that there were "less restrictive means reasonably available" to achieve such drug and alcohol outcomes.
Most Australians revere Vegemite as an unfairly maligned culinary icon, and more than 80% of Australian households are estimated to have a jar in their pantries. Vegemite is typically considered an acquired taste at best by those who weren't raised on it.
The last U.S. president to visit Australia, Barack Obama, once said: "It's horrible."
Prisoner argues Vegemite ban contributed to vitamin deficiency
McKechnie had initially testified that the lack of Vegemite had contributed to his thiamine deficiency.
He said both Vegemite and pork were sources of thiamine, also known as vitamin B1. As a Jew who observed kosher law, he told the court he couldn't eat pork either and took daily doses of the vitamin.
Vegemite has long been marketed as a source of B vitamins thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3) and folate (B9) which are promoted as healthy additions to the diets of growing children.
But McKechnie dropped the thiamine issue as "not important," after lawyers for the prison authorities objected to his evidence.
Prisoner said Vegemite ban left him feeling 'deprived, sad and disconnected'
McKechnie said not eating Vegemite made him feel "deprived of being able to practice my Australian culture, sad and disconnected from my family and community."
The judge responded that "it is difficult to accept that the inability to consume Vegemite, rather than the fact of his imprisonment, is a material cause of his sadness and disconnection from his family and community."
McKechnie cited an article published in the food studies journal "Gastronomica" in 2003 that said, "Vegemite may be the best predictor of national identity of any food in the world."
The article, based on research by Australia's Queensland University in 1995, found that a "taste for the spread strongly correlates with early exposure and to Australian birth and ancestry."
McKechnie also referred to the Australian Olympic Committee overturning an Chinese import ban on Vegemite ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing.
He cited Australian band Men at Work's 1980s international hit "Down Under" that mentions a "Vegemite sandwich."
On the effectiveness of smearing contraband with Vegemite, McKechnie cited a Melbourne newspaper article from 2017 that reported a man's unsuccessful attempt to use the odor of the spread to conceal illicit drugs that he attempted to smuggle into a music festival in Victoria. The attempt was thwarted by police sniffer dogs.
Judge rejects evidence that Vegemite doesn't interfere with drug sniffer dogs
The judge upheld prison authorities' argument that McKechnie had failed to provide any proper foundations for his opinion that Vegemite does not interfere with drug sniffer dogs.
McKechnie also argued that Vegemite contained "no live yeast" and that any piece of fruit would be more useful in making alcohol than the spread.
A state prison department manager, Kevin White, cited publicly available research that said Vegemite helped home-brewed beer ferment more quickly.
Vegemite's owner, Bega Group, did not respond to a request for comment on Monday.

When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.
As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials prepare for an important meeting this week discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.
The “fifth plenum” starts on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption.
As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.
Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.
Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.
Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.
“Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.
The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.
The upcoming meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.
Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.
In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.
The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.
In January, Zhang Youxia, China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)
A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.
Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.
Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.
Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.

A debate on the Special Intensive Revision process examines opposing perspectives on voter roll revisions, deletions, and electoral integrity across multiple states. One side raises concerns over arbitrary voter deletions prior to elections, questioning procedural changes regarding voter forms and demanding transparency from electoral authorities while highlighting widespread public demonstrations. In contrast, the counter-perspective maintains that voter list revisions have historical precedent across decades and address duplicate, shifted, deceased, and absentee entries rather than causing disenfranchisement. The discussion centres on appellate mechanisms for voter restoration, consensus in official filings before the apex court, and differing views regarding whether electoral disputes reflect legitimate democratic concerns or political reactions following electoral losses. The exchange underscores the ongoing dispute over institutional credibility, electoral processes, and upcoming state polls.
The Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in Karnataka has come under scrutiny following the submission of thousands of Form 7 applications for voter deletion. Election officials have submitted over 61,000 deletion forms without specifying mandatory reasons, following the removal of 1.07 crore names during the enumeration phase. Earlier records show that over 1.28 lakh deletion applications were filed prior to the exercise, including bulk submissions by third parties in northern constituencies. The Congress has demanded an investigation into third-party applications, while the BJP dismissed the criticism, arguing that the revision process is constitutional.
Israel is heading into a crucial parliamentary election for the 26th Knesset, marking the first polls since the October 7, 2023 terror attacks. Longest-serving Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a formidable challenge from former Israel Defense Forces chief Gadi Eisenkot. Voters are weighing key issues, including the Gaza war, the conflict with Iran, national security challenges, legal troubles, and the rising cost of living. Opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu's Likud-led coalition nor Eisenkot's alliance is projected to hit the magic 61-seat majority mark in the 120-seat Knesset. With both major blocs ruling out alliances with Arab parties, the political landscape faces complex coalition arithmetic, opening up possibilities that include a potential national unity government or re-election.
The Election Commission of India has submitted an affidavit to the Supreme Court refuting allegations of unilateral decision-making by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. India Today accessed the affidavit, which maintains that all key decisions were passed unanimously alongside the two Election Commissioners. Addressing controversies regarding voter registration, the poll body stated that Form 6 was never amended, affirming that statutory changes can only be instituted by the Central Government. Instead, the commission clarified that an additional declaration regarding voter mapping was introduced to streamline verification and prevent repetitive document submissions. The poll body further indicated that unmapped voters do not need to attend formal hearings, with Booth Level Officers assigned to collect necessary documents directly. Officials also stated that experts from IIT and IISc will review the software, and denied that names were added or deleted without state election officer approvals. The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear multiple petitions regarding these issues.
A major political faceoff has erupted ahead of Diwali over the INDIA bloc's planned November 1 rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan. Despite strong appeals from local traders highlighting prospective festive business losses, the Opposition alliance confirmed it will proceed with the demonstration against alleged vote theft and the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. The Opposition maintained protests will halt if Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns. In response, the BJP has mounted a nationwide padayatra counteroffensive under its campaign against anarchy, featuring senior leaders across multiple states. Meanwhile, political rhetoric intensified sharply following controversial remarks directed at Prime Minister Narendra Modi, drawing severe condemnation from the BJP.

You know who doesn’t care about AI, recession indicators, or You Can See Everything FOMO? Birds.
Birds don’t even know you exist, nor would they care about you if they did. In this era of everything all the time, it’s almost life-affirming to interact with a being who has a brain the size of a garbanzo bean, that isn't able to drive or vote.
There are probably entertaining dramas playing out in your yard right now that you don’t even know about. Mine include a crow with one eye and a greedy Steller’s jay that fills his crop with peanuts until it’s translucent.
Now that smart bird feeders have been around since 2020, even moderately priced models come with high-resolution cameras, 4K video recording, and AI ID that rarely misses. Many of them require minimal maintenance other than filling the seeds. (As long as you're following the 5-7-9 rule of pole-mount placement, to keep squirrels away.)
Below are some early Black Friday sales on models I have been using and enjoying for years and would not hesitate to buy for a gift (or myself).
Top Picks
Birdfy Original (Blue) With Solar for $127 (29% Off)
For some reason, this deal is only on the blue version of this feeder; the yellow costs an extra ($13). Anyhow, if you've only got $130 to spend, Birdfy's enduring original is your best bet. Sure, there are sturdier, better-designed feeders (like Kiwibit, below), and feeders with better camera quality (like Camojojo's 32MP Hibird), but you will either pay extra or run into janky apps and paywalled features.
If you're just looking for a reliable feeder that will last through the seasons and sports a high-quality, easy-to-use app without major features being paywalled, you won't do better than this model. It comes with an auxiliary solar panel that mounts separately, but if you don't want solar, you can pay even less—just $110. I would recommend it, though—Birdfy's panels have been very reliable in my experience, and I think it's worth the extra $17 to not have to worry about bringing it in to charge. (Note: This model only supports 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi.)
Kiwibit Feeder 2 With Solar Roof for $170 (29% Off)
This isn't the latest and greatest Kiwibit model (that would be the Feeder 2 Pro, $220), but the regular Feeder 2 is still exceedingly well designed, and this is the lowest price I have ever seen it. The generously sized, 1.5-liter seed hopper is bifurcated for two different types of feed and pulls right out of the body via a handle on the top—no need to take the whole feeder down to refill.
The 8-megapixel photos and 4K video quality are top-tier at this price point, and the solar roof kept everything charged through all kinds of weather during my test. The app is easy to navigate and functional without a Kiwibit Plus subscription, but more and more features are starting to be paywalled, as I found when I recently reviewed the Feeder 2 Pro, which I don't love. Note that this feeder only works on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi and the warranty is only one year, compared with the above Birdfy's two-year warranty.
Kiwibit 4K Feeder With Auxiliary Solar for $140 (26% Off)
Despite the different name, this Kiwibit model has the same camera and hardware as the Feeder 2, just without the built-in solar roof. Still, I had no issues installing the included 3-watt solar panel on the back of the wall mount (I always pole-mount my feeders to keep squirrels away), so if you're interested in Kiwibit's sturdy build quality and high-resolution imagery and want to save $30, this is a totally viable option.

A stroke is an urgent situation where either the flow of blood to the brain is cut off, or there is a rupture of the blood vessels in the brain. Oxygen and glucose are the two elements essential for brain activity. Interruption of their supply results in impairment of brain activity and eventual damage of brain tissues -- and this damage occurs in minutes. The first few hours of a stroke, therefore, determine how damaged the brain can become.
Types of strokes
Strokes can be categorised into ischemic strokes and haemorrhagic strokes. In ischemic strokes, the stroke occurs due to the blocking of an artery by a blood clot. In haemorrhagic strokes, there is a rupture of the blood vessel, which leads to blood in the brain tissue. Regardless of the type of stroke, the result is damage to the brain tissue, which can result in vital body functions including speaking, movement, vision, memory and coordination becoming impaired.
An ischemic stroke is accompanied by oxygen starvation of the affected brain tissue. Due to insufficient energy resources, brain cells cannot function normally. The chemical composition of the brain cells, therefore, changes, which results in the accumulation of toxic substances that harm brain cells and other structures. With continued oxygen starvation, cells continue to deteriorate. The damage, however, does not occur uniformly. In the central area of the brain (core) where oxygen starvation is critical, damage can occur rapidly and irreversibly. Around this area, there is a zone called the ischemic penumbra. Here, even if blood flow is low, brain cells can survive for a certain period of time. They can be saved if blood flow is restored promptly.
The effect of bleeding in a haemorrhagic stroke is brought about by the leaking of blood into the brain when there is a rupture of a blood vessel. This may lead to injury of brain cells, and also interfere with proper blood and cerebral spinal fluid flow in the brain.
The first few hours
There are only so many minutes that the brain can withstand interrupted blood flow. Brain cells (neurons) begins to undergo irreversible damage within 3 to 5 minutes of interrupted blood flow. With each minute that goes by, 1.9 million neurons, i.e. 32 neurons per second, die due to lack of oxygenation, which is why we emphasise that ‘time is brain’. The first few hours are critical since at this point, one needs to assess what kind of stroke it is and start appropriate treatment.
In some cases of ischemic stroke, intravenous thrombolysis, the administration of drugs that dissolve the clot within the blood vessels, might be given in the first 4.5 hours after symptoms develop. In some patients with large vessel blockage, there might be indications for mechanical thrombectomy. In simple terms, a mechanical thrombectomy involves the removal of the clot using special equipment, and it might be done up to 24 hours after the patient was last seen without symptoms. In cases of haemorrhagic strokes, others strategies must be employed: this includes blood pressure control, correction of the consequences of taking blood thinners, management of intracranial pressure, and surgical procedures, where necessary.
Not all patients automatically qualify for all interventions. There are other issues that have to be taken into account, including the patient’s medical status, imaging studies, timing of stroke symptoms, and dangers involved in the therapy. Even some of those who come after these time windows, can still be eligible for certain treatment procedures after imaging is done.
How brain function is affected
The effects of a stroke vary, depending on the site and degree of damage within the brain. Movement centres can be damaged leading to weakness or paralysis that usually affects one side of the body. Speech centres could be damaged causing speech problems and comprehension difficulties or trouble reading and writing. A stroke involving the visual pathways leads to a sudden loss of vision or partial visual fields. If the cerebellum or the brainstem is involved, there could be a problem with dizziness, poor coordination, problems swallowing, double vision or loss of balance. There could also be memory, attention and decision-making problems and problems with emotional regulation.
It is important to know and understand these symptoms since sometimes a stroke occurs without the characteristic facial drooping or arm weakness of the disease.
Recognising warning signs
The BE FAST method is an effective means of identifying the symptoms of a stroke:
- B – Balance: Sudden loss of balance, dizziness or difficulty walking
- E – Eyes: Sudden blurred vision, double vision or loss of vision
- F – Face: One side of the face is drooping or numb
- A – Arms: One arm is weak or dropping down
- S – Speech: Slurred speech
- T – Time: Call for help immediately
Sudden changes in vision, lack of balance, confusion or even a severe headache without apparent reason might be symptoms of a stroke as well. Disappearing symptoms within a minute or two shouldn’t be considered harmless and require immediate medical examination.
After the golden hour
The ‘golden hour’ is significant to preserve as much of brain function as possible and to ensure best possible outcomes, but this does not mean medical professionals cease working after this window is over. Medical teams will continue monitoring the condition of the patient, controlling blood pressure and preventing additional harm to him or her. In case the condition of the patient becomes satisfactory, it is likely that he or she will be offered physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy and cognitive therapy.
It is worth noting that every stroke patient has his or her own path to recovery, which depends greatly on the level of injuries, the affected area of the brain, timely assistance and the patient’s health in general. For all individuals, however, it is important to understand how the brain functions, remember the signs of a stroke and seek timely help for oneself or a loved one.
(Dr. B. K. Madhusudhan is lead consultant – neurology, Aster RV Hospital, Bengaluru. madhusudhan.bk@asterhospital.in)
